General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

How real estate leaders can coach authenticity, not personas

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1040 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As our industry pours resources into scripts, systems and personal branding, it is worth asking whether all that polish is quietly working against us.
  • In a world of increasingly manufactured everything, authenticity has become the rarest and most valuable competitive advantage an agent has, and most of our training accidentally trains it out of people.
  • Recent findings suggest that the agent, Brian, was describing why door knocking works so well for him, and as he talked, it was obvious the real driver was not the tactic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As our industry pours resources into scripts, systems and personal branding, it is worth asking whether all that polish is quietly working against us. On a recent POWER AGENT® coaching call, an agent’s success with door knocking led me to a conclusion I think the whole business needs to sit with.

In a world of increasingly manufactured everything, authenticity has become the rarest and most valuable competitive advantage an agent has, and most of our training accidentally trains it out of people.

Recent findings suggest that the agent, Brian, was describing why door knocking works so well for him, and as he talked, it was obvious the real driver was not the tactic. It was him. His warmth, his playfulness, his complete comfort being himself. Homeowners respond to that because they can feel it is real. That points to a truth our profession keeps rediscovering and forgetting. People do not ultimately choose a technique or a brand. They choose a person. We are in the business of human beings, not human doings, and much of our industry has that inverted.

Recent findings suggest that consider what so much of real estate training actually produces. It teaches agents to perform a role, the polished professional, the confident closer, the branded persona. Agents show up to appointments doing that role so diligently that the actual human disappears behind it. And clients feel the absence. They cannot connect with a performance, so trust never forms, and the agent concludes they need a better script, when in fact they need less of one. The very tools meant to make agents more effective often make them less human, and therefore less trusted.

This has sharpened in the current era, and leaders should take note. Consumers are saturated with polish and increasingly skeptical of it. Automated messages, staged content and slick presentations have trained the public to discount them. Against that backdrop, a genuine human being who is simply and comfortably themselves stands out dramatically. Authenticity is no longer just a nice quality. It is a differentiator, precisely because it is scarce and cannot be faked at scale. The agent who is real has an edge that no amount of production spend can replicate.

In a recent development, there is also a consistency dividend that matters for production. When agents do the prospecting that fits who they actually are, in the style that feels natural to them, they do it consistently, because they do not dread it. The agent forced into a persona that is not theirs, they burn out and quit the activity.

The agent who found their own voice keeps going. Authenticity is not only about connection with clients. It is about sustainability of effort, which is the real engine of long-term production. Helping an agent find their genuine style is one of the highest leverage things a leader can do.

I watched this land on the call through an agent named Kim, who is 63 years old. She noted that at her age, being herself is a lot easier. She is right, and it points to a developmental truth leaders can shortcut for their people. Younger agents often imitate the top producers they admire, borrowing voices and styles that are not theirs. With experience comes the freedom to stop, to accept that not everyone will connect with you and be at peace with it. The best leaders help agents reach that freedom years earlier than they would on their own, because a self-assuredand authentic agent outperforms an imitative, anxious one every time.

In a recent development, step back and the strategic picture is clear. Every technology and every trend in our industry keeps commoditizing the transactional parts of the job. What cannot be commoditized is a trusted human relationship, and that is built only by a real person being real. So, the authenticity of your agents is not a soft cultural nicety sitting off to the side of the business. It is the thing the business will increasingly compete on, as everything else gets automated and easier to copy. Investing in it is investing in the last durable moat your people have.

For leaders looking to build this into a culture, here is where to focus:.

In a recent development, 1. Coach the person, not just the script. Help each agent find the version of the fundamentals that fits their real personality, rather than forcing one style on everyone.

Industry observers note that 2. Reward authentic voice. Celebrate agents who show up as themselves, so the culture signals that genuineness is an asset, not a liability.

Industry observers note that 3. Match activity to temperament. Let agents lean into the prospecting that suits them, which drives the consistency that drives results.

4. Give permission early. Teach younger agents that they do not have to imitate the top producer to succeed. Their own style is their advantage.

Recent findings suggest that 5. Model it from the top. Leaders who are visibly, comfortably themselves give the whole team permission to do the same.

In a recent development, powerfact: In a market saturated with polish, the agent who is simply, authentically themselves stands out. Authenticity is not a soft quality. It is a scarce competitive advantage that cannot be manufactured.

It has been revealed that none of this diminishes skill or professionalism. It relocates them. Skill matters, but it has to be delivered through a real person, not a performed one, or it never reaches the client. The agents and teams that will thrive as the market gets harder and the noise gets louder are the ones who understand that the human being is the product. Build a culture that frees people to be themselves, and you will have built something the competition, with all its polish, cannot copy. That is an advantage worth far more than another script.

Recent findings suggest that serve don’t sell. Coach don’t close.

UPDATED 19:00 EST / NOVEMBER 13 2026.

A glitch in Microsoft Corp.’s network has disrupted the work of businesses and government agencies in more than 70 countries.

It has been revealed that the bug, which reared its head on Thursday about 12:35 p.m. EST, knocked the organization’s popular Exchange Online platform offline. Organizations use the cloud service to store employees’ inboxes and calendars. Microsoft has still not fully restored its infrastructure.

Sources indicate that deployments of Exchange Server, a version of the platform that users run on-premises, are not affected. However, the outage did disrupt a number of Microsoft Teams and Microsoft Copilot 365 features that rely on data from users’ Exchange inboxes. Intune, a tool that administrators use to manage employee devices, is also experiencing technical issues.

In a recent development, the outage has hit numerous companies worldwide. Workhorse Group Inc., an electric vehicle maker, pushed back its earnings call from today to Monday. Shipping giant Maersk and stock exchange operator Euronext notified customers that they’re experiencing communications problems.

The public sector is also impacted. Several U.S. municipalities reported technical problems, while a number of court cases had to be delayed. In the U.K., the National Pharmacy Association warned that the Exchange Online outage may slow prescription processing. Hospitals, public transportation agencies and schools are affected as well.

The operator of Downdetector, an outage tracking service, received downtime reports from hundreds of thousands of people.

Sources indicate that parts of Microsoft’s infrastructure started recovering early this morning. In an update published at 2:30 a.m., the company stated that it was seeing “positive results” after patching an “upstream authentication/routing configuration” module. About three hours later, Microsoft’s systems in the Asia Pacific region began regaining service access. North America and Europe followed suit shortly there.

Microsoft shared its first explanation of what went wrong around noon today. “The incident was introduced by an concern during an earlier network capacity upgrade that surfaced following a recent network change,” the tech giant explained. “We have addressed the underlying issue and continue to restore service to remaining customers and regions.”.

Microsoft added that the outage wasn’t caused by a cyberattack or artificial intelligence agents.

Recent findings suggest that the company’s status page indicates that infrastructure restoration work is still ongoing. As a result, some consumers may have trouble accessing Exchange Online and certain Microsoft products that interact with it. The company is monitoring the backlog of emails that piled up while the service was offline to ensure no data loss occurs.

Microsoft aims to release a detailed technical report about the outage once all its services are fully restored.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 12, 2026 at 12:15 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 12:16 pm.

Docugami, the Seattle-area startup led by XML co-creator Jean Paoli, has been acquired by Inveniam, a Detroit-area manufacturer that uses blockchain to help investors verify the data behind assets such as commercial real estate and private loans.

The deal follows a partnership this summer in which the companies released DGML, Docugami’s open-source format for turning business documents into data that AI agents can use and check.

According to recent reports, financial terms of the acquisition weren’t disclosed. All of Docugami’s employees are joining Inveniam, a Docugami spokesperson said. The team numbers about 50 including contractors. Paoli becomes Inveniam’s chief product and technology officer, and Docugami will keep operating from Kirkland, according to the announcement.

Paoli co-founded Docugami in 2018 after more than 20 years at Microsoft, where he helped create XML and the Office file formats.

The startup, based in Kirkland, Wash., raised a $10 million seed round in 2020 led by SignalFire, with backing from Bob Muglia, the former Microsoft executive and Snowflake CEO. Grammarly, the writing-assistant tech giant now known as Superhuman, later disclosed that it had taken part in the round, its first investment in another company.

Prior to the acquisition, Docugami ranked No. 155 on the GeekWire 200, our list of the Pacific Northwest’s top independent, privately held startups.

Recent findings suggest that DGML labels each piece of a document by what it is — a base rent, a loan payment, a liability cap — so a single figure can be traced back to the page it came from. Inveniam records a digital fingerprint of each of those data points on its blockchain, called NVNM Chain, so any later change shows up.

Inveniam executives remarked Thursday morning on a livestream with Paoli that DGML solves a problem they’ve had in bringing on new clients: every client’s documents are different, which required templates and standard formats before the data could be used.

“One promise I want to make personally: DGML stays open and its openness is strategic to Inveniam,” Paoli wrote in a LinkedIn post.

In a recent development, inveniam, led by CEO Patrick O’Meara, also acquired Mantra, a crypto manufacturer that provided the original technology for NVNM Chain, earlier this year. Mantra co-founder John Patrick Mullin remarked on the livestream that NVNM Chain will move to its own independent blockchain, with the main network expected to launch in the next few weeks.

Recent findings suggest that fees on that network will help fund buybacks of an NVNM cryptocurrency token, Mullin noted. O’Meara proposed a separate session on when that token will launch.

#6187. Why database touch looks fail real estate agents

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (955 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Why database touch looks fail real estate agents

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (955 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that agents are consistently trained to do their touches.
  • If I walked up to your front door 32 times a year, rang the bell, and remarked, “Just a reminder that I’m in real estate,” how long would it take you to look into a restraining order?
  • It has been revealed that agents are constantly told they need to remind people that they are in real estate.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that agents are consistently trained to do their touches. “Have you done all your touches?” “Have you done your outreach?” “Are you touching people?” “Are you sending things of value?” That antiquated philosophy needs to stop and almost nobody in this industry cares to address it or examine why it fails. It is wildly ineffective, and I would argue that most of the time it hurts the agent’s brand rather than helping it.

If I walked up to your front door 32 times a year, rang the bell, and remarked, “Just a reminder that I’m in real estate,” how long would it take you to look into a restraining order? Nobody would call that a relationship. Yet the same schedule applies when it arrives as an email one week and a postcard the next.

It has been revealed that agents are constantly told they need to remind people that they are in real estate. That is an interaction about what the agent cares about, not what the other person cares about. Trust isn’t built by constantly telling someone how amazing I am, why they need me, or why I’m relevant or crucial. That is blatant narcissism, and yet somehow we call it great top-of-mind marketing.

The National Association of Realtors’ 2025 Profile of Home Buyers and Sellers shows the problem. Ninety-one percent of buyers mentioned they would use their agent again or recommend them. But among repeat buyers, only 18% went back to an agent they had worked with before, and among sellers the figure was 29%. The touches are supposed to close that gap.

Sources indicate that the industry explains that clients forget, so its answer has always been more reminders—the rest of the survey points somewhere else. 80% of sellers contacted only one agent before hiring, and 66% hired someone referred to them or someone they had used before. Sellers are not comparing the agents who emailed or mailed them the most. They call the one person they trust. Seeing your name in their inbox every month does not make you that person.

One of the agents I coach has phenomenal email automation, with reminders and alerts set up for everyone they have ever worked with. By their own count, 90% of their business comes from less than 5% of the people in their database. If 90% of your business comes from less than 5% of those people, why are you digitally harassing the other 95%?

In 2003, researchers Russell Hill and Robin Dunbar measured how many people we keep up with by using the most ordinary list there is, the one for Christmas cards. Participants logged every card they sent and everyone in the household it went to. Networks averaged about 150 people, and participants stayed in touch weekly with the people they felt closest to.

Sources indicate that A later study by Sam Roberts and Dunbar followed people for 18 months. Friendships lost closeness when contact dropped off, while family relationships were far less affected. Contact matters, and the touch prepares are right about that much. They go wrong by treating a Christmas card to the whole database as the same act as staying close to 150. A mailing treats everyone alike, so the people who matter most get the same thing as the strangers, and the relationships that produce business fade.

Sources indicate that pick your 150. Write down the people you would be glad to call and stop when you reach that number. They will be past clients and friends whose lives you know something about. Dunbar’s later research found an inner circle of about 15 inside the 150. Give those 15 their own rhythm, a conversation with each of them every month, because in my experience that inner circle is where most referrals come from. A database you can’t keep up with starts to feel like a weight. A list of 150 is small enough that you notice when one of them is about to move.

Industry observers note that reconnect at four months. A conversation creates what I call mind share: the trust that comes from talking with someone. Name recognition never builds it, and without the next conversation it fades. In my coaching, I see it run low about three to four months after the last conversation. Once a week, scroll back about four months in your text messages, pick three people, and send something like “Hey, was just thinking about you. Hope all is well; would love to catch up.” Leave real estate out of it. Anyone in your text messages already has a relationship with you that a mailing list never will, so the message reaches someone who trusts you at the point where that trust is lowest. Keep it to three. Send 30, have 10 people answer and your afternoon is gone, which is the fastest way to make sure you never do it again.

If you lead agents, ask how many conversations they had with their 150 this month, not how many touches they made. That number tells you whose relationships are fading before the referrals stop. We keep overcomplicating this business by pushing agents to do more and more, which only creates overwhelm and makes them more likely to do less. We owe them better.

Lance Pendleton is the founder of PreTSD Consulting and the creator of Reframe Lab. He was previously National Head of Agent Development at Compass and Chief Innovation Officer for the largest Sotheby’s International Realty affiliate in the US. He is affiliated with the Real brokerage.

Amazon is the best organization in America, according to Forbes.

The Seattle tech giant took the No. 1 spot on the publication’s 2027 “America’s Best Companies” list, moving up from No. 2 last year and edging out Apple.

Three other Washington state companies landed in the top 50: Microsoft at No. 6, Costco at No. 13 and Alaska Air Group at No. 39.

Sources indicate that last year’s No. 1, Berkshire Hathaway, slipped to No. 4. Nvidia ranked No. 3 on the same day CEO Jensen Huang resigned, following his admission of an extramarital affair. JPMorganChase, Alphabet, Royal Caribbean Group, Walmart and Marriott International round out the top 10.

According to recent reports, now in its third year, the ranking scores thousands of the largest public and private U.S. companies on factors including customer and employee sentiment, financial performance, creditworthiness, cybersecurity and innovation. Forbes said it worked with 12 data organizations to build the index.

Sources indicate that forbes noted Amazon’s financial strength and size, its standing in news and social media, and the range of voices across the company and its leadership lifted it to No. 1. Apple scored especially well on employee satisfaction, customer loyalty, financial strength and innovation.

In a recent development, forbes also pointed to Amazon’s speed, citing a feature that lets customers shop by text message. An employee suggested it in October and it launched Nov. 6.

“Innovating for customers, doing it fast, working backwards from their needs, that’s really at our core,” Beth Galetti, Amazon’s senior vice president of people, experience and technology, told Forbes.

In its own blog post Thursday, Amazon highlighted everything from faster delivery and custom AI chips to warehouse robotics and higher pay for frontline workers.

Sources indicate that the ranking comes after a year of workforce cuts at Amazon. The company eliminated about 30,000 corporate jobs in rounds confirmed in October 2025 and January 2026, including more than 4,500 in Washington state. Smaller cuts followed throughout the year, including layoffs of fewer than 1,000 corporate employees in October, mainly in its Stores unit.

FHA’s MMI Fund stays 5x above floor, fueling calls to cut insurance premiums

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Federal Housing Administration (FHA)’s Mutual Mortgage Insurance (MMI) Fund posted a strong financial performance in fiscal year 2026, even as its capital ratio declined from 2025 levels, renewing industry pressure to cut annual mortgage insurance premiums amid affordability concerns.
  • The MMI Fund had a capital reserve ratio of 10.29% as of Sept.
  • According to recent reports, “Over the past year, the MMI Fund remained strong despite a year-over-year decline,” the report states.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Federal Housing Administration (FHA)’s Mutual Mortgage Insurance (MMI) Fund posted a strong financial performance in fiscal year 2026, even as its capital ratio declined from 2025 levels, renewing industry pressure to cut annual mortgage insurance premiums amid affordability concerns.

The MMI Fund had a capital reserve ratio of 10.29% as of Sept. 30, down from 11.47% a year earlier, according to FHA’s Annual Report to Congress released Monday. It’s the 12th straight year the fund has remained above its 2% statutory minimum.

According to recent reports, “Over the past year, the MMI Fund remained strong despite a year-over-year decline,” the report states. “Both the Single Family forward and Home Equity Conversation Mortgage (HECM) programs have separately maintained capital levels above the 2% ratio for the last six years.”.

It has been revealed that the fund’s economic net worth ended FY 2026 at $182.6 billion, a $6.3 billion decrease from 2025. Total capital resources, however, increased by $9.3 billion to $148.9 billion, signaling continued strength in FHA’s insurance capacity even as modeled future performance softened.

Scott Turner, secretary of the Department of Housing and Urban Development, wrote in the report that under the Trump administration, HUD has continued “our work to streamline and deregulate FHA Single Family programs, while remaining vigilant stewards of taxpayer resources by eradicating fraud, waste, and abuse within our programs.”.

Joseph Gormley, assistant secretary for housing and president of Ginnie Mae, wrote that the administration has eliminated roughly 150 “burdensome and unnecessary” policies, implemented alternative credit scoring models and updated FHA’s appraisal technology submission processes.

Gormley added that HUD has proposed a reform to the partial claim process through a Reinstatement Advance Payment, “which we intend to implement in Fiscal Year 2027.”.

According to recent reports, in a recent interview with HousingWire, Gormley mentioned the administration is “comfortable” with the fund’s capital levels, signaling no immediate changes to FHA premiums or broader pricing. But the fund’s continued strength is fueling fresh calls from the mortgage industry to reduce FHA’s annual mortgage insurance premiums and ease monthly payments.

Bob Broeksmit, president and CEO of the Mortgage Bankers Association (MBA), stated in a statement after the report’s release that the 2026 results create room for “targeted changes that improve affordability for borrowers.”.

“FHA should modestly reduce annual mortgage insurance premiums, lowering monthly payments for moderate- and lower-income homebuyers,” Broeksmit noted. “Given the slowdown in the housing market, any MIP reduction should be carefully calibrated and paired with additional safeguards to limit multiple layered risk factors on individual loans and protect the fund’s long-term health.”’.

The Community Home Lenders of America (CHLA) also weighed in on the report, urging the FHA to end its life-of-loan policies on mortgage insurance.

“FHA Life of Loan premiums were intended as a stop-gap fee hike in 2013 to respond to financial concerns resulting from the 2008 Housing Crisis.” the group said in a statement. “With today’s MMIF report showing a long-term 12 year run of solid financial performance and bulging FHA reserve levels, it is long past time to stop overcharging homeowners for FHA loans, in order to help them in asset building.”.

Within the overall fund, the single-family forward loan program reported a standalone capital ratio of 10.47% in FY 2026, compared with 10.95% in 2025. HUD attributed part of the decline to the growing share of loans with reduced annual MIPs following a premium cut in 2023, as well as slower home price appreciation and updated macroeconomic forecasts that increased projected losses.

Sources indicate that the reverse mortgage book saw a much sharper move. The standalone capital ratio for the HECM program fell to 5.43% in 2026, down from 24.06% in 2025. HUD noted that HECMs, which account for less than 4% of the MMI Fund, are more sensitive to home price movements. Meanwhile, loan payoffs — viewed as the most favorable recovery outcome for HECMs — have become less common.

It has been revealed that “Lower actual and forecast loan payoffs increased losses,” the report stated. “Finally, the HECM program spent substantial capital resources on assignment claims in FY 2026, reducing available cash.”.

Overall, in FY 2026, FHA insured more than 935,000 single-family home mortgages, 83% of which were used by first-time homebuyers. FHA also endorsed more than 24,000 reverse mortgages through the HECM program.

It has been revealed that as of Sept. 30, the agency managed active insurance on more than 8.4 million forward mortgages with $1.7 trillion in unpaid principal balance and $63.5 billion in outstanding HECM obligations.

#6183. Breaking: Using AI for listings, where marketing ends and misrepresentation begins

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1339 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Housingwire ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Using AI for listings, where marketing ends and misrepresentation begins

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1339 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the years, I have seen too many six-figure lawsuits over the words ‘fully-renovated.’.
  • According to recent reports, in real estate, a single, seemingly innocuous word or phrase can carry significant legal ramifications and consequences.
  • By modifying agent and seller property descriptions, AI has inadvertently and undeniably introduced this latest layer of exposure and risk to the way agents and their clients do business.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the years, I have seen too many six-figure lawsuits over the words ‘fully-renovated.’.

According to recent reports, in real estate, a single, seemingly innocuous word or phrase can carry significant legal ramifications and consequences. Descriptions with words including “fully renovated,” “brand fresh,” “resolved” and “permitted” can and too often do cause years of unexpected, costly litigation for buyers, sellers and even their respective agents more often than people may think. Each word can change a buyer’s understanding of a property and potentially expose a seller, agent, and/or brokerage to liability if the property description no longer matches the reality of the property’s true condition.

By modifying agent and seller property descriptions, AI has inadvertently and undeniably introduced this latest layer of exposure and risk to the way agents and their clients do business.

It has been revealed that according to the National Association of Realtors 2026 Technology Report, nearly half of Realtors surveyed use AI daily or weekly. Among those agents surveyed who use AI, 75% use it to write listing descriptions and more than half use it for social media posts, emails, or follow-up communications. Other industry research highlights that AI adoption may be moving even faster. A 2026 Delta Media survey found that 82% of real estate agents asked use AI to write listing descriptions, which is up from 58% in 2024.

Creating consumer-facing content is the most common use of AI in our industry, helping to craft the words consumers see when considering one of the most important decisions of their lives. At the same time, the biggest challenges brought by AI appear to be growing far more rapidly than the policies and oversight needed to control them.

Surely, most sellers or agents are not deliberately leveraging AI-generated property descriptions to misrepresent properties. The more likely outcome is that an agent will provide accurate information into an AI tool to create a more compelling description, and in turn, the AI tool changes the description to one that is less accurate, thereby exposing an agent and seller to unexpected pitfalls.

For instance, rulings in lawsuits can depend on specific legal complications concerning whether a property is represented, whether by an agent or AI, as partially or fully renovated  or whether a defect was described as repaired or permanently resolved. Lawsuits pertaining to undisclosed permitting issues often concern whether work awaiting approval is described as being in the “final stages of permitting.” The aforementioned are only a few of examples of obstacles an agent or seller may encounter and such compliance issues are challenging companies across industries more often than ever before.

Sources indicate that the pitfalls of AI are not limited to the sale of real estate. AI has rapidly morphed from an experimental marketing tool to common resource for many areas of business, but especially marketing. Teams use it for everything from drafting copy to generating or cleaning up images to analyzing customer behavior. Work that used to take hours can be done in minutes, if not faster.

Marketing across industries relies on speed that the AI gods are now supercharging. Through their use of artificial intelligence, marketing teams can create dozens of variations of print or digital ads, internal or external emails, social media posts and listing descriptions. The speed at which content is being created naturally removes some of the checkpoints that were in place when it took longer to create or more people were involved in the process.

However, increased efficiency and speed often translate to increased exposure to risk and liability.

Sources indicate that A listing description does not have to be completely fabricated to cause a problem. It can come down to the embellishment of one or two words.

Outside of real estate, AI-generated marketing can introduce unsupported claims, make definitive statements from what was originally nuanced, or alter the meaning of disclosures. Without the necessary checkpoints, it can lead to tremendous legal complications.

Accordingly, companies and their employees must take seriously the need for more extensive oversight to stay compliant.

The reason real estate is a great example of how AI can impact compliance is the industry’s significant regulatory requirements, including fair housing laws.

For example, if an agent uses AI to make a listing description more appealing to a certain buyer profile, the language used could potentially implicate protected characteristics or discourage certain groups from being interested in the property without the agent even realizing it.

Even if the agent did not intend to be discriminatory, it is still a compliance problem.

Recent findings suggest that fortunately, most real estate professionals recognize and consider the risks associated with AI use. A 2026 Realtors Property Resource survey found that 92% of agents surveyed were using or planning to use AI, while 63% identified accuracy of AI-generated content as their top concern.

Industries like financial services, insurance, healthcare, employment, and other highly regulated fields face their own requirements governing advertising, disclosures, accessibility, privacy, and discrimination.

Sources indicate that A common answer to how to lower AI risk is to keep a “human in the loop.” If your strategy includes having someone simply click “approve” before AI-generated content goes out, that’s not enough. Reviewers need to know what they are looking for and the potential risks this content creates, such as unsupported claims, industry-specific advertising rules, and whether it misleads consumers. In addition, has confidential or proprietary information been entered into an AI platform to create the content?

It has been revealed that the same principle applies when employees or consumers turn to AI for legal, financial, or other professional advice. I find myself repeating one simple phrase constantly: “AI is not an attorney.”.

AI can certainly be useful to organize information, generate ideas, and streamline work processes. But it can never replace professional judgment.

A glaring problematic approach taken by many businesses these days appears to be that they are thinking of AI oversight backwards: providing employees free rein to use it and then creating a policy only after something goes wrong.

Instead, real estate professionals must be armed with tools, policies, and guidelines, and practical guardrails now, before AI continues to be utilized further.

At minimum, businesses should identify which AI tools employees are approved to use, what information can and cannot be entered into them, when AI-generated content requires additional review, and an approval and compliance review for any public-facing content.

The level of oversight must reflect the level of risk. Generating ideas for an article headline is a lot different than using AI to determine which consumers should receive a certain ad. Summarizing notes from an internal brainstorming meeting is not the same as synthesizing confidential client information to create a strategy.

Training is just as notable as policy, and it is not enough to send out a document once via email announcing how employees are expected to use AI in the workplace.

The companies that manage AI most effectively will be those where legal and marketing work collaboratively.

Recent findings suggest that legal and compliance teams need to understand marketing workflows and how AI is being used so they can create guardrails. Marketing needs to involve the legal teams early enough in the process so it’s not an afterthought right before launch.

With the way AI is accelerating work, things are happening too promptly for either to operate in a silo.

It has been revealed that we are not trying to slow innovation. We are working to create an environment where teams can move quickly because there are established boundaries and protections to keep risk as low as possible.

AI is going to continue to transform marketing, and businesses should be able to leverage this tool while remaining compliant. At the end of the day, the technology may be fresh, but accountability is not.

Hila Pooli is general counsel at First Team and a 2026 HousingWire Insider.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 12, 2026 at 2:41 pmNovember 12, 2026 at 2:41 pm.

Nick Huzar co-founded Juicer Energy in 2023 to make electric vehicle charging more widespread and reliable. Now the Seattle-area startup is pursuing a broader goal: helping buildings manage rising electricity demand and costs.

Industry observers note that juicer installs and operates EV charging systems at apartment buildings, hotels and other properties. It is also developing battery systems to store electricity on-site and help manage the power needed for charging and other building uses.

The push comes as data centers and the growing use of electricity for transportation, heating and other needs put more pressure on the grid. Batteries can help balance supply and demand by storing energy when electricity is plentiful and releasing it when demand peaks. In some cases, they can reduce the need for costly grid upgrades or upcoming power plants built to meet peak demand.

Industry observers note that “We think there’s a big opportunity there,” Huzar said. He spoke at an event this week hosted by GeekWire and Bank of America at the Bellevue showroom of Ferrari of Seattle.

Other companies are similarly pairing EV charging with battery storage. Fellow Seattle startup Electric Era has deployed battery-backed fast chargers at retailers including Costco and convenience stores. ADS-TEC Energy and XCharge also sell fast-charging systems with integrated batteries.

Huzar, OfferUp’s co-founder and former CEO, sees an opportunity to make buildings more self-sufficient by combining hardware and energy-management software. He said Juicer has a project scheduled to come online in 2027 with 70 chargers in one building.

His longer-term vision also includes tapping the energy stored in vehicles connected to those buildings.

Sources indicate that “Imagine you’re an apartment owner and you have 20 EVs, 40 EVs plugged in,” Huzar said. “That is a huge amount of power. Like you’re a mini power plant at that point.”.

Industry observers note that he described feeding excess electricity back to the grid as a possibility that remains years away. He also predicted that most businesses, apartments and homes would have on-site batteries within the next decade, in part because battery costs continue to fall.

Juicer started with EV charging, Huzar noted, “but the more we’ve gotten into this, the more we realize that we actually can build an asset for buildings versus relying on the grid.”.

#6181. NiCE’s next-generation Cognigy bets the hard part of AI agents is running them, not building them

NiCE’s next-generation Cognigy bets the hard part of AI agents is running them, not building them

📅 14 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1634 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.
  • The contact center has been the low-hanging fruit for the artificial intelligence industry.
  • However, to date, the industry has spent the past two years arguing over which AI agent is the smartest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 19:49 EST / NOVEMBER 13 2026.

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.

The contact center has been the low-hanging fruit for the artificial intelligence industry. Ask any information technology or business leader what they want to use agentic AI for, and they will say it’s to improve the customer experience, which starts with the contact center.

However, to date, the industry has spent the past two years arguing over which AI agent is the smartest. That’s the wrong debate. Model capabilities are improving so swiftly and are getting so much cheaper that raw intelligence and reasoning are becoming the least differentiated part of the stack.

The real challenge for enterprises is operating a fleet of AI agents reliably across complete customer journeys, with the visibility and control a large business requires. Without that, the human, or worse, the customer, is left connecting the dots among the outputs of the growing number of agents they are communicating with.

According to recent reports, that’s the thesis behind the next generation of NiCE Cognigy, which NiCE Ltd. launched this week. The release includes a redesigned Agentic Experience Studio, an AI Assist companion spanning the building, testing and improvement of agents, reusable “skills” that package instructions and tools, turn-by-turn tracing and native voice-to-voice model support.

Default speech-to-text, text-to-speech and large language models are now included in the per-conversation price, with premium models from Deepgram, ElevenLabs and Anthropic available with a few clicks and billed by usage.

Ahead of the launch, I attended an analyst briefing with Nhu Ho, senior product marketing manager at NiCE Cognigy, and with Clement Boutier, director of product management, who leads the team that built the release and owns the platform roadmap.

Here are the notable points from this release:.

Sources indicate that ho opened with a chart showing how long AI can work on its own before a human has to step in. In 2020, it was seconds; in 2024, it was minutes; and this year it’s roughly 16 hours. The footnote was interesting, as it calculated that figure at a 50% success rate. “Capable and dependable do not always mean the same thing,” Ho said. “That is exactly where the platform matters.”.

According to recent reports, for CX leaders, that’s a solid benchmark to consider. A 50% success rate is a research milestone. In a contact center, it’s a churn event or a compliance violation. As models commoditize, value shifts to the system around them: testing, tracing, guardrails and deterministic fallbacks. NiCE doesn’t build frontier models, and frontier model builders don’t run contact centers. Positioning Cognigy as the layer that makes AI dependable is a smart place to plant a flag.

Industry observers note that cognigy earned its pre-acquisition leadership position by handling complex production deployments for large brands such as Lufthansa, Mercedes and DHL. But that flexibility and customizability added complexity. Boutier put it this way: “The large number of options when configuring an agent creates friction to get started, which slows things down.” The upcoming studio lets a builder stand up an agent in a few clicks, with models already provisioned, while power-user tools, including full access to the agent’s system prompt, are available in advanced sections.

Sources indicate that this is notable because NiCE aims to create a “1+1=3” value proposition for its current customers. NiCE needs Cognigy to expand broadly across the CXone installed base, not just among expert teams at the largest enterprises. Boutier described three builder personas: smaller businesses building simple agents, contact center administrators and team leads, and engineers at technically sophisticated companies. AI Assist is aimed squarely at the first two.

In the demo, it built an agent, tested it, fixed the problems it found, and deployed it to WhatsApp. The flip side is that lowering the barrier means more agents built by less experienced people, which makes the governance features the real story of this release.

In a recent development, despite all the agentic hype, most enterprises aren’t ready to hand over entire journeys to an autonomous agent. Boutier outlined three modes: traditional natural language understanding, hybrid and fully agentic. Hybrid “is actually where most of our customers are,” he remarked, while fully agentic deployments are at the “beginning of the adoption curve.” This approach lets customers ease into agentic, build confidence and move to fully autonomous at their own pace.

According to recent reports, niCE designed the product for that approach. An agent can serve as the orchestration layer, calling existing flows as tools. Flows can also be placed in front of agents, for example, to scrub credit card numbers or other personal data before any data reaches a model. Ho described the release as “an evolution, not a replacement,” with production deployments, application programming interfaces and integrations continuing to run unchanged.

That’s a meaningful advantage over AI-native challengers whose pitch effectively requires a rebuild. Contact centers are the fastest-moving environments, and deterministic workflows aren’t legacy baggage. They’re how a business enforces what a large language model shouldn’t be deciding.

Industry observers note that “You can have the best builder experience, but if you don’t have any feedback loop on what you’re building, you’re never going to build a great agent,” Boutier mentioned. The latest tracing shows each turn: which skill loaded, which tool was called and with what arguments, and when the agent handed off to a flow.

The Simulator now supports multivariate testing of up to 10 variants, using an LLM-as-judge to run synthetic customers against an agent. Boutier ran the same agent on two models and found that one was faster and consumed fewer tokens. This shifts model selection from a preference to a data-backed economic decision.

Voice-to-voice support may be the first feature customers deploy. Boutier noted that buyers are open to using a speech-to-text and text-to-speech cascade, “but what they realize is that voice-to-voice models sound just better.” In the demo, the agent delegated tool calls to a separate model while continuing to talk, making the conversation sound far more natural.

According to recent reports, cognigy now serves as both a Model Context Protocol client and server and supports agent-to-agent connections, including one customer linking Cognigy to agents built with Microsoft’s tooling. NiCE is also co-developing the Personal Agent Protocol with Meta and Sierra, which isn’t live yet. Boutier described Cognigy as “the front door” of the contact center, where a consumer’s personal agent must authenticate before it can proceed. It’s great to see NiCE collaborating with Sierra, a direct competitor, on this, as it makes things easier for a customer.

According to recent reports, the industry views agent identity as a shared responsibility. But as Sierra outlines, companies can also let personal agents work through their websites and APIs, so the front-door position depends on enterprises routing that traffic through Cognigy. This lets brands interact with personal agents safely.

There has been a wave of companies banning personal agents, which I think is a mistake. If something is good for a consumer, it will happen, so it’s better to be on the leading edge of enabling it rather than fighting it.

This release is less about latest capabilities and more about NiCE betting on where value will accrue as AI agents mature. Intelligence is getting cheaper. Dependability, governance and the ability to blend autonomous reasoning with deterministic control are not.

It has been revealed that niCE is the market leader in contact center as a service, as Cognigy was in conversational AI. Now the challenge is to get an easier-to-work-with Cognigy into the hands of thousands of CXone customers without creating a sprawl of individually governed agents. This will allow NiCE to maintain its industry leadership as personal agents arrive. As it does that, the Cognigy acquisition will move from an add-on to a core component of the NiCE platform.

According to recent reports, zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

Crypto exchange Gemini has unveiled the biggest losers in the altcoin space for 2026 so far, as many of the crypto world's biggest digital currencies have been seeing massive double-digit price plunges.

Crypto exchange Gemini recently shared a list of 10 cryptocurrencies that have seen particularly brutal losses since the start of 2026 in a post on the X social media platform.

Topping Gemini's list of the biggest losers for this year is Bitcoin Cash (BCH), which has crashed a shocking 61.76% year-to-date.

Coming in second is Polkadot (DOT), with a 53.03% price decline, while Cardano (ADA) holds third place after shedding 48.04% of its value.

Ripple-related XRP and the top meme cryptocurrency Dogecoin (DOGE) are next in line, with losses of 43.43% and 42.38%, respectively.

Several other major cryptocurrencies are also seeing considerable losses, such as Sui (SUI), which has fallen 42.08%, Hedera (HBAR), which has dropped 38.13%, Solana (SOL), down 34.02%, Avalanche (AVAX), which has lost 33.40%, and Kaspa (KAS), which has gone down 30.75%.

Declining liquidity in the market, weakening speculative interest, lackluster institutional interest and general macroeconomic conditions are all major factors causing most major altcoins to underperform so far.

But for some, other complications within their ecosystems are also proving troublesome.

It has been revealed that for instance, in the case of Cardano, the platform is seeing limited decentralized finance activity. As of Nov. 9, the total value locked in its DeFi ecosystem reportedly dropped below $50 million.

For XRP, things are a bit different.

While Ripple continues its expansion in the institutional payments sector, stablecoin and tokenization areas, this hasn't necessarily led to sustained buying interest in XRP.

In fact, spot trading volume for XRP fell 53.5%, while perpetual futures trading volume dropped 44%.

Dogecoin, on the other hand, has been contending with waning speculative interest in meme cryptocurrencies.

Its institutional investment narrative also hasn't really caught on yet, with Bitwise announcing in September the shutdown of its Dogecoin ETF as the product failed to draw investor interest.

Bitcoin Cash has been seeing particularly sharp declines as it is now experiencing a reversal of its stellar 2025 performance, when the cryptocurrency soared around 38%.

Selling pressure picked up in May and June 2026 as BCH saw back-to-back monthly drops of over 30%.

A rebound could be seen in September after CME Group announced Bitcoin Cash futures, but this proved insufficient to stop the ongoing downtrend.

Tech Report: Lenders increasingly pull with new credit score model, but few use it for pricing

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (674 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mortgage lenders are frequently pulling credit scores with VantageScore 4.0, but most of them still price with Classic FICO, according to a new Bank of America Global Research report based on Recursion data.
  • Since October, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have required that agency MBS pools disclose both Classic FICO and VantageScore 4.0 whenever both are pulled, and to identify which score was used for pricing.
  • It has been revealed that according to Bank of America, 148 sellers in October delivered agency MBS loans for which a VS4 score had been pulled.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mortgage lenders are frequently pulling credit scores with VantageScore 4.0, but most of them still price with Classic FICO, according to a new Bank of America Global Research report based on Recursion data. The report, released on Friday, shows that Rocket Mortgage and United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) are driving nearly all of the production actually priced with the new scoring model in the agency mortgage-backed securities (MBS) market.

Since October, Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac have required that agency MBS pools disclose both Classic FICO and VantageScore 4.0 whenever both are pulled, and to identify which score was used for pricing.

It has been revealed that according to Bank of America, 148 sellers in October delivered agency MBS loans for which a VS4 score had been pulled. That figure rose to 173 sellers during the first 10 days of November. But the number of lenders actually pricing loans with VS4 remains much smaller. Only eight lenders sold loans priced with VS4 in September, which rose to 22 in October and 37 to date in November.

Recent findings suggest that in October, 20% of conventional issuance reported a VS4 score, BofA noted. Of that subset, 39% used VS4 as the pricing score, which works out to roughly 8% of total conventional issuance. Most of these loans had both scores: 18% of issuance reported both FICO and VS4, while only 2% reported VS4 alone.

Thus far in November, 21% of issuance had VS4 reported and 32% of these loans used VS4 for pricing, or about 7% of total issuance.

Rocket and UWM are the main early adopters on the pricing side. In October, BofA found that Rocket and UWM together accounted for 65% of all loans with a VS4 score pulled. They also were the sources for 95% of loans that used VS4 as their pricing score in the agency MBS market.

Among other lenders that have shown they can pull VS4, just 13% of their production had a VS4 score reported and only 1% of loans actually used VS4 to set prices.

Sources indicate that “We think this disconnect largely reflects a gradual ramp-up in operational and infrastructure readiness,” BofA analysts remarked. “Pulling and reporting an additional score is relatively straightforward, while actually incorporating VS4 into loan pricing likely requires more extensive changes to lenders’ pricing systems and operational infrastructure.”.

BofA’s report also notes that loans priced with VS4 have distinctive collateral characteristics. VS4-priced loans tend to have higher average loan balances, a lower share of first-time homebuyers, and higher shares of cash-out and rate-and-term refinance loans.

Among VS4-priced loans where both scores were reported, the VS4 score was on average about 43 points higher than FICO. For FICO-priced loans with both scores present, the two models are broadly comparable, the analysts stated.

Because lenders can choose between scores when both are present, the emerging “best-of-two” selection framework is affecting the distribution of published scores. BofA found that among October loans with both scores reported, 24% had FICO scores below 700 and 21% had VS4 scores below 700, but only 17% had a pricing score below 700.

BofA also addressed investor concerns that borrowers in legacy low-FICO pools who have materially higher VS4 scores could see a one-time chance to refinance as markets and pricing grids adjust to VS4.

“We acknowledge that legacy low-FICO pools are exposed to this risk,” the analysts remarked. “However, newly issued low credit score pools may offer a way to mitigate this risk and potentially access even better convexity collateral.”.

Recent findings suggest that according to the report, low credit score pool collateral today generally consists of loans that either have both FICO and VS4 reported with both scores below 700, or are VS4-only loans. Loans with both FICO and VS4 below 700 have already been screened against the risk that a significantly higher VS4 score would give borrowers a one-time refinancing opportunity.

Additionally, a historical analysis indicates that loans with both scores below 700 exhibit better convexity than loans defined only by FICOs below 700.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Rothschild Investment LLC, the Chicago-based investment management firm, has filed its latest 13F with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), revealing its stake in the Bitwise XRP ETF.

Rothschild Investment’s filing, made on Nov. 10, indicates that the company has invested in 6,300 shares of the Bitwise XRP ETF.

Sources indicate that based on the information provided, these shares were worth $104,769 as of Sept. 30.

The investment in the Bitwise XRP ETF is listed under CUSIP 09174F107 in Rothschild Investment’s third-quarter report.

Interestingly, Rothschild Investment did not have any reported holdings of the XRP ETF in its previous quarterly filing, which indicates that the firm’s investment in the XRP ETF occurred in the third quarter of 2026.

The Bitwise XRP ETF, listed under the ticker XRP, was introduced in November 2025.

The ETF enables traditional investors to invest in the Ripple-linked cryptocurrency without needing to buy and hold XRP tokens themselves.

Although Rothschild Investment has invested in the XRP ETF, it is not a significant part of its overall portfolio.

The firm’s total portfolio value for 13F-reportable holdings is around $2.69 billion.

The firm holds 3,644 positions.

Rothschild Investment holds much larger stakes in Bitcoin and Ethereum investments.

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still claims Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

According to recent reports, circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Recent findings suggest that most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It notes: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

According to recent reports, the schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026.".

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide claims "message limits will tighten over time until no latest burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Sources indicate that circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible.".

In a recent development, funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations.".

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1.".

The main text above it notes something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:.

Industry observers note that circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

Recent findings suggest that as of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle remarked "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:.

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Sources indicate that many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:.

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

It has been revealed that for everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

Industry News: CCM leader Brady Mullen’s playbook to win reverse mortgage referrals without a hard sales pitch

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Housingwire

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that brady Mullen, divisional business development manager for CrossCountry Mortgage (CCM), spent 20 years as a financial adviser before selling his practice in 2021.
  • In seeking to close that gap, Mullen changed his career trajectory by moving into reverse mortgages, first at American Liberty Mortgage before his arrival at CCM in late 2024.
  • Recent findings suggest that in his work to grow reverse mortgage originations at one of the nation’s largest independent mortgage banks, Mullen has focused on helping loan officers build a steady stream of referral partners, including financial planners, real estate agents and attorneys.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that brady Mullen, divisional business development manager for CrossCountry Mortgage (CCM), spent 20 years as a financial adviser before selling his practice in 2021. In his experience, advisers are rarely trained on how to properly handle real estate, the biggest asset owned by most of their clients.

In seeking to close that gap, Mullen changed his career trajectory by moving into reverse mortgages, first at American Liberty Mortgage before his arrival at CCM in late 2024. He believes that reverse mortgages are the most misunderstood and underappreciated financial tools on the market.

Recent findings suggest that in his work to grow reverse mortgage originations at one of the nation’s largest independent mortgage banks, Mullen has focused on helping loan officers build a steady stream of referral partners, including financial planners, real estate agents and attorneys. That task often meets resistance as referral sources can have the same stigmas about the products as consumers.

Industry observers note that at last week’s National Reverse Mortgage Lenders Association (NRMLA) Annual Conference & Expo and San Antonio, Mullen discussed ways to create stronger referral networks. His advice in a nutshell? Take what works and let go of the rest.

It has been revealed that mullen chooses to organize his business development efforts in similar fashion to a farmer growing crops. Planting season involves prospecting and presentations. Fertilizing and nourishing involves follow-up conversations. Harvesting is what occurs when the leads arrive.

Each of the three stages includes its own subprocesses, he explained, a structure that allows a loan officer or branch manager to see where leads stall and fix the bottleneck.

In a recent development, when interacting with a potential referral source, Mullen suggests that reverse mortgage professionals remove words like “educate” and “teach” from their vocabulary. Telling another adult that “I want to educate you” sounds condescending, he stated. Instead, offer a benefit that has nothing to do with money, such as continuing education credits.

“If it’s structured as CE, you’ve set the tone to have a discussion that, by design, was created by you to go through the topics in the order that you want and to deliver them with the visuals,” Mullen mentioned.

Sources indicate that mullen told the NRMLA audience that advice on money-making activities should not be part of referral partner conversations. Other professionals know how to make money, he said, and people who have misconceptions about the product are likely to be turned off by the phrase, “Here’s how I can help you make money.” Instead, frame the discussion around providing answers. A financial adviser’s clients, for example, may want to know how they can help their parents or grandparents.

Sources indicate that “You’re not trying to sell reverse mortgages. You’re not trying to get a referral. What are you trying to get? A presentation. … That’s all you want. Don’t ask for more because you’ll spoil the opportunity,” he explained.

In a recent development, once the seeds have been planted and a referral partner has agreed to learn more, reverse mortgages professionals should create an arc with their presentations. The first step is validation, as referrals partners won’t recommend something they won’t use themselves.

Industry observers note that with Home Equity Conversion Mortgages (HECMs), emphasize the built-in protections of mortgage insurance premiums. Someone clinging to the idea that reverse mortgages are scams needs to know about their robust regulations through the Federal Housing Administration and the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau.

He also calls for simplified language. Describe the HECM product as an expanding line of credit and avoid creating confusion by explaining principal limit factors. Outline the key features that define every reverse mortgage — optional monthly payments, no balloon payments and nonrecourse provisions.

Recent findings suggest that from there, give a clear explanation of the financial benefits for borrowers. He used the example of a $300,000 loan at a 7% rate. A forward mortgage that amortizes over 15 years costs roughly $2,700 a month, while a 30-year loan costs about $2,000 a month. Interest-only options may only trim a few hundred dollars per month.

But reverse mortgages do not require a payment and can be more efficient in terms of opportunity costs. For instance, a 75-year-old couple can take $50,000 out of a retirement account or they can borrow it, but their net worth is still the same. Borrowing offers the potential added benefits of tax savings and asset control.

“Your balance sheet doesn’t care whether it’s paying an opportunity cost or interest. It treats them indifferently. It’s going to reflect both of those equally,” Mullen said. “If we’re not looking at the other side of the balance sheet, we’re missing half the picture, and that’s a lot of picture for an expert to miss.”.

Industry observers note that for the right type of referral relationship, Mullen believes that longer educational videos, rather than shorter sound bites, are more helpful. He said his most popular YouTube video on reverse mortgages is 43 minutes long. When assigned as homework before a meeting, this type of content allows the referral partner to fully absorb the concepts and share them with clients, who can potentially screen themselves out without further time and energy spent by the LO.

“Would you rather have a distribution list of 1,000 and very little engagement, or a distribution list of 80 and have a lot of engagement? The second is by far more effective,” Mullen stated.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Federal Aviation Administration today grounded all domestic flights in the U.S.
  • The rare order was issued by the Air Traffic Control System Command Center, or ATCSCC.
  • In a recent development, the ATCSCC sent today’s ground stop order to all 22 regional air traffic control centers in the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 20:36 EST / NOVEMBER 13 2026.

The Federal Aviation Administration today grounded all domestic flights in the U.S.

The rare order was issued by the Air Traffic Control System Command Center, or ATCSCC. It’s an FAA facility in Northern Virginia that is responsible for monitoring air traffic and mitigating potential risks. When ATCSCC identifies concerns such as airport congestion, it provides local officials with guidance on how to address them.

In a recent development, the ATCSCC sent today’s ground stop order to all 22 regional air traffic control centers in the U.S. The memo explained that the move was “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”.

It has been revealed that U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy elaborated in a post on X that the FAA “issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication concern impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.”.

The post didn’t provide any details about the communication issue. According to CBS News, the problem affects a “private communications network” that connects components of the U.S. air traffic control system. The outlet cited sources as saying that an enhancement caused the network to reboot, which in turn led it to crash.

According to recent reports, on Tuesday, the FAA announced that it was expanding its use of an artificial intelligence system called SMART. The software analyzes weather patterns, flight paths and related data points to generate air traffic scheduling recommendations. The FAA indicates that the software is designed to reduce delays and fuel consumption.

The agency last issued a national ground stop in January 2023. It was a response to an concern in the FAA’s NOTAM system, which it uses to notify pilots about hazards such as closed runways. The shutdown lasted about two hours and grounded 9,500 flights.

The current shutdown is already much longer, having started at 3:54 p.m. EST. More than 13,000 flights have reportedly been delayed or canceled. Eurocontrol, an organization that helps European Union member states coordinate air traffic, suspended flights to the U.S. at the request of the FAA.

In a recent development, FAA officials stated that inbound international flights will be “handled on a case by case basis.” American Airlines, meanwhile, stated that flights already airborne will proceed to their destinations. The airline reportedly expects the disruption to last all day.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Not only is Alex Vidal the latest president of REMAX, but the tech giant has clarified that his appointment to this position also encompasses REMAX Canada, making him the leader of REMAX’s Canadian operation.

Vidal was named president of REMAX in September, after The Real Brokerage completed its acquisition of REMAX, forming the Real REMAX Group.

In an emailed statement, a REMAX spokesperson told HousingWire that the president of REMAX has always overseen the company’s Canadian operation.

It has been revealed that as Vidal moves into the Canadian leadership position, Don Kottick, who has served as the president of REMAX Canada since April 2025, has unveiled aims to leave the firm on Dec. 15. This information was conveyed to REMAX brokers and franchisees via an internal memo reviewed and confirmed by HousingWire.

Recent findings suggest that “This move helps ensure every REMAX region around the world receives as much of the same focus, momentum and opportunities as possible,” the internal memo stated. “The next few months will be pivotal as we roll out upcoming technology and invest in further strengthening the REMAX brand in Canada and around the world.”.

Prior to joining REMAX, Kottick was the president and CEO of Sotheby’s International Realty Canada.

It has been revealed that before joining REMAX, Vidal served as the president of ERA Real Estate, helping lead the brand through Compass International Holdings’s acquisition of its parent organization Anywhere Real Estate. Compass and ERA are currently suing Vidal, claiming that he violated non-compete agreements through his move to REMAX. In the legal complaint filed in mid-October, Compass claims that the non-compete agreement prevents Vidal from serving as president or providing service to any competing business for a period of one year from his departure from ERA.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Villa, a San Francisco-based manufactured homebuilder, has appointed homebuilding and real estate veteran David Messenger as CEO, the company declared on Monday.
  • It has been revealed that founded in 2019, Villa says it has delivered more than 425 homes using an offsite construction model that spans accessory dwelling units (ADUs), multifamily projects and new neighborhoods.
  • Sources indicate that messenger brings decades of financial and operating experience in homebuilding and multifamily real estate, having spent more than 10 years as chief financial officer of Century Communities.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Villa, a San Francisco-based manufactured homebuilder, has appointed homebuilding and real estate veteran David Messenger as CEO, the company declared on Monday.

It has been revealed that founded in 2019, Villa says it has delivered more than 425 homes using an offsite construction model that spans accessory dwelling units (ADUs), multifamily projects and new neighborhoods. The tech giant manages feasibility, design, permitting, site preparation and installation, and partners with a network of factories for production, according to the announcement.

Sources indicate that messenger brings decades of financial and operating experience in homebuilding and multifamily real estate, having spent more than 10 years as chief financial officer of Century Communities. During his tenure, Century expanded from about 150 to 1,800 employees across 18 states, grew to $4.5 billion in annual revenue and more than 10,000 annual closings, completed seven acquisitions and raised more than $3 billion in debt and equity capital, the firm mentioned.

He also led Century’s initial public offering and helped launch its mortgage, title and insurance subsidiaries, giving him direct experience with the vertically integrated models many large homebuilders use to manage costs and capture more of the housing value chain. Earlier in his career, Messenger spent roughly a decade at UDR, a publicly traded multifamily real estate investment trust, where he advanced through senior finance roles to become CFO.

Recent findings suggest that messenger’s appointment comes as Villa looks to expand beyond individual ADUs and small projects into larger communities in partnership with land developers and homebuilders. The company is already working on latest neighborhoods including the 25-home Acacia Village in Santa Rosa, California, Alpine Village in Westminster, Colorado, and homes in Altadena, California, for families rebuilding after the Eaton Fire, according to the release.

Investors say his background in scaling a public homebuilder and in capital markets was a key factor in the decision.

“Villa has demonstrated its capabilities across ADUs, multifamily properties and new neighborhoods, and Dave is the right leader to build on Villa’s success and advance its growth strategy,” said Aaron Marsh, partner and CFO at Unless, an investor in Villa and member of Villa’s board of directors. “He brings deep housing experience, a track record of scaling businesses nationally and a clear understanding of what land and development partners need to move projects forward.”.

Messenger noted he sees an opportunity to apply processes from large-scale homebuilding to Villa’s offsite platform.

Sources indicate that “This team has done what much of our industry has only talked about: delivering quality homes through offsite construction across individual properties, multifamily communities and new neighborhoods,” Messenger mentioned in the announcement. “I see great potential to build on that foundation by bringing a large-scale homebuilder’s operating discipline to Villa, with an emphasis on predictable execution and profitable growth.”.

According to recent reports, villa’s model aims to give homeowners, multifamily operators and developers a single partner from concept through completion. The company handles site feasibility, site and home design, permitting and on-site work and uses factory partners to build homes offsite, aiming for more predictable timelines and costs than traditional stick-built construction, according to the release.

“Dave has an exceptional track record spanning homebuilding, multifamily real estate, capital markets and land development,” stated Heather Miksch, chief operating officer at Villa. “As we build on Villa’s momentum and pursue development opportunities, his experience will be invaluable in helping us grow our business while continuing to serve both homeowners and development partners.”.

The XRP holdings of former Ripple CTO David Schwartz have plummeted by a massive 23M XRP. David Schwartz, former chief technology officer of Ripple, has disclosed that he has sold the overwhelming majority of his XRP holdings over time.

It is not clear when he made the bulk of his sales or how much he made from them.

Schwartz's latest update comes after a few different revelations about his crypto sales tactics.

As reported by U.Today, the former Ripple CTO recently admitted to selling around 2.5M XRP in 2025 alone.

He has admitted that he hasn't been buying XRP for a long time now.

At the same time, Schwartz does still hold a significant amount of Ripple stock, but that also leaves him exposed to more financial risk than he'd ideally prefer.

The revelation comes at a time when there is mounting frustration among the XRP community over the cryptocurrency's lackluster price performance.

While CZ is addressing immediate market concerns, Vitalik Buterin is looking much further ahead.

The Ethereum co-founder has dramatically changed his assessment of leanPCS, a proposed cryptographic technique designed to make Ethereum more resistant to quantum computing attacks.
