According to recent reports, over the past few weeks I've gone from thinking leanPCS is total bull to being a total bull. So let me explain some of these buzzwords in more detail.At the core, 8288 is about hyper-scaling data and execution for any computation that needs to get performed on a piece of data….

The statement highlights growing confidence in an approach that could help Ethereum introduce quantum-resistant cryptography without dramatically increasing transaction costs and blockchain storage requirements.

The proposal, outlined in EIP-8288, focuses on combining individual digital signatures and cryptographic proofs into a shared mathematical proof. This is good for Ethereum because quantum-resistant signatures can be considerably larger than the cryptographic signatures Ethereum right now uses.

A standard Ethereum signature occupies approximately 65 bytes. Some proposed quantum-resistant alternatives could require between 1,000 and 6,000 bytes. Storing those larger signatures individually could consume substantial block space, potentially increasing network costs.

Sources indicate that leanPCS attempts to solve that problem by allowing computers to aggregate multiple signatures and verification checks before submitting a compact proof to Ethereum. Rather than permanently storing every bulky signature individually, the network could verify a shared proof covering multiple transactions.

Buterin favors this approach because it could provide a practical route toward quantum resistance without requiring Ethereum to commit immediately to a much larger architectural redesign.

In a recent development, ethereum’s quantum preparation is already underway, with the Ethereum Foundation targeting 2029 for core post-quantum infrastructure milestones. The potential threat remains years away, but Ethereum developers increasingly recognize that replacing cryptographic foundations requires considerable preparation.

CZ and Buterin are confronting different problems, but both developments highlight the pressures facing the crypto industry. Binance needs to maintain market confidence while investors question exchange activity, security, and institutional capital flows.

Ethereum needs to strengthen its cryptographic foundations before quantum computing potentially threatens the security assumptions underlying today’s blockchain infrastructure.

CZ’s comments offer reassurance during an immediate market downturn, while Buterin’s endorsement could accelerate an important technical discussion within Ethereum.

UPDATED 14:37 EST / NOVEMBER 14 2026.

CASE STUDY by Paul Gillin.

Sources indicate that AT&T Corp. is moving beyond using artificial intelligence to improve employee productivity, increasingly applying autonomous agents to redesign how its business operates. Nearly 500 agentic workflows are already in production, and the telecom giant aims to triple that number next year.

Recent findings suggest that AT&T now processes about 45 billion AI tokens daily across the manufacturer, according to Luke Corbin (pictured, below), assistant vice president of digital transformation and AI at AT&T Business. Its agentic AI platform handles more than 1 million transactions monthly. Many of those workflows now operate autonomously, handling tasks ranging from customer provisioning to sales prospecting.

Industry observers note that speaking at an Amazon Web Services Inc. event in Boston earlier this month, Corbin stated the firm’s approach emphasizes rethinking entire processes rather than simply automating individual tasks. AT&T has moved quickly from experimenting with generative AI to systematically identifying business processes that can be redesigned around agentic capabilities.

Industry observers note that at the heart of the transformation is Business Agent Foundry, a group established in early 2025 to work with individual business units. Rather than soliciting isolated automation ideas from employees, the foundry maps business processes using industry frameworks and identifies opportunities to eliminate unnecessary steps, organizational handoffs and legacy application dependencies, Corbin stated.

According to recent reports, one early initiative involved automating interactions with AT&T’s mainframe computers. Changes to customer fiber installation orders previously required employees to retrieve tickets from queues, manually update records and return them to the workflow.

Agentic automation eliminated portions of that manual process, reducing delays and accelerating service delivery.

“It was kind of cool having some of the most advanced technology talking to some of the oldest that we have,” Corbin said.

In another example, AT&T halved the time required to provision dedicated internet connections in buildings where fiber infrastructure was already installed.

AT&T’s architecture breaks from conventional approaches that build large numbers of independent, specialized agents. Instead, the manufacturer maintains a relatively small set of agents that execute business workflows using centrally managed business logic.

“We store the business logic in context or in memory,” Corbin said.

Retrieval agents identify applicable knowledge, while planning agents determine the actions, tools and data needed to complete a task.

It has been revealed that governance is central to the process. Individual employees can independently create personal productivity agents, but workflows affecting customers must pass through the foundry and undergo security, privacy and compliance reviews.

“We’ve democratized agents to the point where people can use them for personal productivity, but not to where you would drive business workflows that could touch your customers or materially have an impact on your business,” Corbin said.

Every production workflow initially includes human oversight. Only after accuracy reaches the mid- to high 90% range within a permissible risk profile can agents operate autonomously. Continuous monitoring evaluates performance and detects drift.

Success metrics include labor savings, revenue generation, operating costs and customer satisfaction. Corbin remarked production AI investments are achieving fivefold returns within a year.

Sources indicate that A 151-year-old company that has been using computers since they were invented “is built on a lot of legacy processes and applications,” Corbin said. “The cost of maintaining those applications, training employees to use them and ongoing maintenance is very high. When you can offset some of that with simpler generative workflows, you’ve got a business case that’s built for itself.”.

Industry observers note that sales prospecting is one beneficiary. Agents identify promising customers by validating their locations and checking fiber availability before representatives invest time pursuing sales opportunities.

Scaling up those capabilities requires more than AI models. AT&T has had to consolidate fragmented data and provide reliable connectivity across data centers, cloud infrastructure and mobile workers.

“We’ve been through a lot of mergers and acquisitions,” Corbin said. “You can imagine what our data infrastructure looks like.”.

It has been revealed that encouraging employees to come forward with ideas for using agents has helped limit resistance from those who worry AI could replace them. So has the opportunity to replace inefficient processes.

“There are a tremendous number of people in the organization who have knowledge and passion about the business process that they used to use but that they didn’t like,” he said.

Corbin stated AT&T is now shifting its focus from improving existing processes toward using agents to launch services, enter markets and support newly introduced sales channels.

Ultimately, Corbin stated responsibility for AI-driven business transformation should be distributed throughout the organization, rather than concentrated in a specialized team like Business Agent Foundry.

In a recent development, “I feel privileged to have the team that I do, but in the long run, my team shouldn’t exist,” he mentioned. “What we do should be completely distributed.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Activist investor Land & Buildings Investment Management is pressing single-family rental giant Invitation Homes to accelerate home sales, sharply increase capital returns and scale back growth plans, arguing the company’s stock trades at a steep discount to the value of its houses.

In an open letter to shareholders released Monday, the Stamford, Connecticut-based hedge fund remarked it believes Invitation Homes is “among the most undervalued companies in the REIT sector” and criticized the board and management for what it called “complacency” and “half measures” in addressing the gap.

Sources indicate that land & Buildings, which owns an undisclosed stake in Invitation Homes, is led by Jonathan Litt, a longtime activist in the real estate investment trust sector. Invitation Homes (NYSE: INVH) is the nation’s largest owner of single-family rental homes, with more than 80,000 properties concentrated in Sun Belt and other high-growth markets.

In a recent development, land & Buildings said the public market values Invitation Homes’ properties at roughly $270,000 per home, compared with an average sale price of about $460,000 on homes the manufacturer has sold since December 2025. That implies a discount of about 40%, according to the letter, which was disseminated via GlobeNewswire.

In a recent development, the firm mentioned it separately valued more than 90% of the company’s wholly owned portfolio, “address by address,” and arrived at an estimated average value of approximately $425,000 per home. That analysis underpins its net asset value estimate of about $45 per share, which Land & Buildings said is more than 65% above Invitation Homes’ current trading price even after assuming 6% selling costs on every home.

Industry observers note that “REITs with sound fundamentals and no distressed assets do not trade at such a discount indefinitely. Something has to give,” the firm said in the letter.

In a recent development, land & Buildings also highlighted what it described as sustained underperformance. Over the trailing one-, three- and five-year periods, Invitation Homes has lagged the S&P 500, the broader REIT index, its closest peer American Homes 4 Rent and the proxy peer group the board uses for benchmarking executive compensation, the letter noted.

Over the past three years, Invitation Homes ranks second to last in that compensation peer group, trailing the group average by more than 35 percentage points, according to Land & Buildings. Shareholders who held the stock for five years have lost more than 20% of their investment, including dividends, the letter remarked, even as U.S. home prices have continued to climb.

In a recent development, the firm noted that Invitation Homes’ shares now trade at an implied capitalization rate of about 7%, roughly 60 basis points wider than American Homes 4 Rent, and at a lower multiple of adjusted funds from operations. The stock trades only modestly above its $20 IPO price from early 2017 while national home prices are up nearly 80% over that period, according to the letter.

Recent findings suggest that land & Buildings blamed Invitation Homes’ strategy for much of the gap. The company was a net buyer of homes in every year from 2022 through 2025 despite “a poor cost of capital,” and earnings have “repeatedly fallen short of expectations,” the firm stated.

Recent findings suggest that the letter also pointed to legal and regulatory costs. Land & Buildings stated Invitation Homes has paid more than $79 million to resolve four legal matters related to resident treatment and business practices, including a $48 million settlement with the Federal Trade Commission in 2024. At the same time, the board approved more than $25 million in special retention awards in March 2026 for the CEO and three other executives, according to the firm.

“This troubling misalignment and lack of accountability is deeply concerning,” Land & Buildings said.

The activist laid out a three-part initiative it claims could unlock value and narrow the discount to net asset value:.

Land & Buildings estimated that a multi-year, programmatic asset sale and capital return program could deliver “substantial annual accretion” to both earnings and NAV per share, supported by what it pegged as nearly $40 billion of gross asset value.

The letter criticized what Land & Buildings characterized as incremental steps by Invitation Homes, including recent home sales and share repurchases, arguing those moves have not been sized or communicated in a way that would change how investors value the manufacturer.

“Half measures appear to be this Board’s modus operandi: do just enough to relieve pressure while preserving the status quo,” the firm wrote.

Land & Buildings also objected to the board’s Nov. 11 appointment of Colin Connolly, CEO of office REIT Cousins Properties, as a new director. The firm noted the board had previously told it that refreshment was not needed and argued that adding another sitting REIT chief executive provided “duplicative skill sets” rather than shareholder alignment and capital allocation expertise.

The activist said independent research firm Green Street wrote less than a year ago that Invitation Homes should “shrink its portfolio, return capital to shareholders, and redirect the bulk of its energy internally on operations until its valuation improves.” Land & Buildings said it had urged management to outline a clear, multi-year capital return plan at REIT conferences in September but came away with “little more than lip service.”.

Invitation Homes did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the letter or the firm’s proposals. The company has previously defended its strategy of balancing internal growth, acquisitions and select dispositions as it manages a large, geographically diverse portfolio in a tight housing market.

Recent findings suggest that the campaign underscores how corporate decisions at large institutional single-family landlords can influence for-sale and rental supply in already constrained markets. Land & Buildings’ proposal would require Invitation Homes to sell thousands of homes a year to owner-occupiers or directly to existing tenants at retail pricing.

It has been revealed that for homebuilders and real estate agents, a large program of individual home sales by Invitation Homes could add incremental existing-home inventory in high-demand metros where resale listings remain scarce. The suggested 6% down-payment rebate for tenants could create a latest pipeline of first-time buyers but might also draw scrutiny from policymakers and tenant advocates who have criticized investor ownership of single-family homes.

It has been revealed that for other single-family rental REITs and institutional owners, the dispute highlights growing pressure from investors to prioritize buybacks and capital returns over portfolio growth when shares trade at discounts to estimated property values. If Invitation Homes embraced or was forced into a multi-year shrink-to-grow strategy, it could reset expectations for capital allocation across the sector.

Land & Buildings said it prefers to work “constructively” with Invitation Homes but “will not hesitate to take whatever steps we believe are necessary to maximize value,” a signal that a proxy fight or board challenge is on the table heading into the 2027 proxy season.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

AKT stakers are close to approving Akash's move from Cosmos to Solana, with Mintscan projecting a pass at 97.2% yes as voting enters its final hours.

It has been revealed that but a yes on Proposal 346 opens a door rather than completing a move. Before a single AKT reaches Solana, two independent audits and at least two more on-chain votes still have to happen.

Sources indicate that the summary going around is simple: Akash is leaving Cosmos for Solana. The proposal itself is narrower than that, and the details matter for anyone holding AKT.

Proposal 346 on akashnet-2, titled "Migrate the Akash Protocol to Solana," closes at 15:02 UTC on November 2. A yes vote approves the migration initiative and authorises AKT to launch as an SPL token through a one-way portal that stays open for two years. It does not set a cutover date, it does not move a single lease, and on its own it does not open the portal.

Industry observers note that the technical spec for that portal was published the day after voting opened. It highlights how many further steps lie between this vote and a working SPL AKT.

The proposal text in Akash's AEP repository states a yes vote does two things:.

It also says plainly what it doesn't do: "it does not set a cutover date and does not move the marketplace." Live leases, staking and governance on akashnet-2 continue as normal. The marketplace moves only after audits and rehearsals pass and "a separate cutover proposal passes on this chain.".

A no vote would stop the whole plan. In the proposal's words: "Nothing moves; the token does not launch and the program returns to option analysis.".

At 08:43 UTC on November 2, about six hours before voting closed, Mintscan's page for Proposal 346 showed an expected result of "Will PASS":.

Sources indicate that turnout stood at 68.80% of bonded stake, against a quorum of 33.40%. The same figures can be read from Akash's own chain API, through the proposal object and its tally endpoint.

Mintscan's 97.2% is yes as a share of all votes cast. Akash's pass threshold leaves abstentions out, and on that basis yes stands at about 98.7%, far above the 50% needed. The veto share is negligible.

The tally has barely changed since early morning. A read of the chain at 07:29 UTC indicated almost exactly the same totals, with only a handful of AKT added to the yes side. With turnout and margin that large, the outcome is not in doubt. The more useful question is what happens after it passes.

Sources indicate that the portal's design is in AEP-95, "One-Way AKT Sink to Solana,", a draft published on October 27 by core developers Artur Troian and Joseph Chalabi. It describes a "deliberately one-way" bridge with no return path. The authors say this removes "the largest class of bridge attacks.".

Recent findings suggest that why supply doesn't change: every SPL AKT is backed by AKT locked on Akash, and nothing is minted independently on Solana. The token is a legacy SPL mint with six decimals and no freeze authority.

The spec's own risk table names the biggest trust point. The upgrade authority over the Solana programs could "mint without limit." That power is meant to sit with a time-locked multisig appointed by Akash governance, with monitors set to alert on every admin action.

At launch, SPL AKT has no protocol role. It will support "transfers and DEX liquidity only, with no staking or governance rights." Inflation stays on Akash. To seed trading, Overclock Labs, Akash's core developer, will send 1 million AKT through the bridge to a Solana treasury vault. That deposit follows the same rules as everyone else's.

Proposal 346 requires "two independent audits of the token and portal code before launch," with reports published within 30 days. AEP-95's launch sequence indicates what that requirement means on-chain.

So Proposal 346 is the first of at least five on-chain decisions. The "2 to 3 weeks" launch estimate depends on the audits finishing and the upgrade and parameter votes passing on schedule.

For now, nothing. The proposal's disclosures set out what changes later:.

Discussion of the proposal continues in GitHub Discussion #1123.

The proposal lists four items as "still open, to be settled and published before the cutover proposal":.

It has been revealed that the second item matters most to holders. The portal closes two years after launch, and the proposal doesn't yet say what happens to AKT that hasn't crossed by then. The final tally will confirm whether the blueprint goes ahead, but that answer, and the decisions in the votes that follow, will matter more to most holders than today's margin.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 13, 2026 at 7:24 amNovember 13, 2026 at 4:23 pm.

Sources indicate that updated at 4 p.m. PT Nov. 13 with additional Microsoft statements.

If emails sent by Outlook customers on Thursday are just now landing in your inbox, no, you haven’t gone back to the days of the Pony Express. Microsoft is still digging out from a nearly daylong outage that cut off email for businesses, schools and governments around the world.

As of early Friday, the company reported that email queues were “significantly reduced and approaching normal levels,” though some customers could still have trouble getting in or see delayed messages.

It has been revealed that in a post on X Friday morning, Microsoft said it was “deeply sorry” for the disruption to customers and partners. The manufacturer said the outage was a technical glitch, not related to a cyberattack or AI agents.

The problem was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade and surfaced after a more recent network change, the tech giant noted, adding that it has addressed the underlying issue and is still restoring service to remaining customers and regions.

According to recent reports, we are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners. We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously. We are seeing broad recovery and stability across our services.This was a technical issue….

In an update on its status page at 5 a.m. Pacific, Microsoft stated it was seeing “broader improvements now observed in North America and sustained improvements across much of Europe,” along with early signs of recovery in Asia Pacific.

The problems started Thursday morning with Exchange Online, the Microsoft service that runs Outlook email for businesses, and spread to other Microsoft 365 services that depend on it, including Teams calendars, Copilot and SharePoint.

It has been revealed that microsoft said servers were failing automated health checks and dropping out of service, which overloaded the ones that were left. The tech giant paused all deployments while it worked on a fix, and some of its repairs Thursday evening were “not taking as expected.” Microsoft said it restored service gradually, checking stability at each stage, which took longer but helped ensure a stable restoration.

Earlier, The Verge’s Tom Warren reported on X that his sources linked the outage to configuration changes in Azure Virtual Network, Microsoft’s cloud networking service.

Australia’s Home Affairs Minister, Tony Burke, told reporters in Sydney that Microsoft believes it is dealing with something similar in some ways to the 2024 CrowdStrike outage, “where there is an update that has gone awry,” the Associated Press reported.

“We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us,” mentioned Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, in a statement provided to GeekWire. He said Microsoft’s teams are reviewing what happened and how to prevent similar problems.

In a post on X Friday afternoon, Lamanna remarked the investigation points to “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter,” which made recovery harder than normal. A thundering herd happens when large numbers of clients try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He said Microsoft will publish a post-mortem “shortly” with a step-by-step timeline and the repairs it aims to make to avoid similar outages.

The outage reached well beyond email. Government offices in Japan, Singapore and the Philippines reported disruptions, according to the AP. Workhorse Group delayed its quarterly earnings call, and OpenAI and Anthropic both reported problems connecting with Microsoft 365 tools.

Recent findings suggest that credit rating agency Morningstar DBRS estimated insured losses of $300 million to $500 million, well below estimates for CrowdStrike, which ranged from $400 million to $1.5 billion. Some cyber insurance policies cover only malicious attacks, the firm noted, though it mentioned the toll could grow if the outage drags on for several days.

Industry observers note that the disruption hit close to Microsoft’s home. Ansel Herz, a spokesperson for the Seattle mayor’s office, told the Seattle Times that the outage didn’t bring city government to a halt but knocked out the systems that move documents and messages around City Hall.

The newspaper quoted Herz calling the outage “a huge pain.” In a post on X, he chided the paper for not using his whole quote, which we presume was “a huge pain in the ass.”.

According to recent reports, we’ve followed up with him to confirm this important detail. Here’s hoping he gets the email.

Industry observers note that enhancement, 10 a.m.: Herz did receive GeekWire’s message and responded, confirming the quote and saying that, to his knowledge, nothing public-facing was affected at the city. Email appears to be back and working properly as of Friday morning, he stated.

Suiball, a hardware wallet built natively for Sui, unveiled its closure on November 11, after the Sui Foundation decided that backing a hardware wallet project is too risky after the recent attacks across the industry.

It has been revealed that surprisingly, the first batch of wallets have already been developed, manufactured and ready to be sent out to the first owners. Anthropic states that Fable 5.2, released on November 9, designed three working devices from one-paragraph prompts.

It has been revealed that those devices went through the whole cycle with its partner Diode, including schematics, circuit boards and firmware. Luckily, there's no proven link between the Fable 5.2 release and Suiball's closure, as the project hasn't mentioned AI at all.

Most of the hardware wallets pre-orders were on-chain, so people will simply receive their USDC back.

Around 80% of all orders were placed this way, and refunds will reach the wallets holding the soulbound pre-order NFTs within a week. Customers do not need to take any action.

Owners who purchased their wallets with credit or debit cards will also receive their funds back. But in order to get refunded successfully, Sui urges buyers to contact them by email first. After the refund is completed, all personal data of purchasers will be deleted.

This is an improvement in the field of institutional adoption, even though it comes at a time when it might be unwarranted. The market is experiencing serious issues and constant outflows from both retail and institutional investors.

Surprisingly, the bank can provide both warm and cold storage options available directly through DB's infrastructure. According to the landing page, the platform will provide key storage via Hardware Security Modules. Access goes through Autobahn, the bank's own multi-channel gateway.

Sources indicate that compliance will also be handled by Deutsche Bank. Initially, the service will focus on core functions: custody of digital assets and transfers, with further capabilities planned.

This is an attempt to promote the adoption of EU-issued stablecoins as part of a strategy aimed at moving away from USDT dominance. EURAU is issued by AllUnity, a joint venture that includes DWS, the asset manager majority-owned by Deutsche Bank.

It has been revealed that self-custody or banks: that is the real question here. Industry experts such as Bloomberg's ETF analyst Eric Balchunas suggest that self-custody has been a worse option and that a custodian with funds protection and insurance is a better option for regular investors. Even Binance founder CZ admitted after the Ledger incident that self-custody comes with extra responsibilities.

Back in August, a Coldcard exploit drained 1,816 BTC from more than 5,000 cold-storage addresses, according to Fortune.

According to recent reports, however, it puts some pressure on those who might receive their funds from grey sources. Unfortunately for them, a bank custodian creates another barrier, as every deposit has to go through the bank's compliance checks.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that A newly introduced Security Ledger, also part of the launch, is designed to record the evidence behind each test.
  • In a recent development, detectify customers report that roughly 80% of the findings from their AI-driven static application security testing tools are noise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 03:00 EST / NOVEMBER 16 2026.

Swedish application security manufacturer Detectify AB today introduced Agentic Tooling, a set of tools aimed at letting an organization’s own artificial intelligence agents test whether suspected vulnerabilities can be exploited in running applications.

Recent findings suggest that A newly introduced Security Ledger, also part of the launch, is designed to record the evidence behind each test. Detectify is pitching the release at DevSecOps teams that are unsure whether they can trust what their AI agents report.

In a recent development, detectify customers report that roughly 80% of the findings from their AI-driven static application security testing tools are noise. Under pressure to deliver an answer, an agent can also produce a convincing report about a test it never ran, the company warned.

Industry observers note that even before AI agents enter the picture, many security teams are falling behind. Nine in 10 open critical and high-severity vulnerabilities had stayed exposed for more than 90 days, according to Detectify’s H2 2026 Cyber Hygiene Index. In a study by researchers at Fudan University and Tencent Holdings Ltd., 76% of the static-analysis alerts examined were found to be false positives. Each one took developers 10 to 20 minutes to review.

According to recent reports, through Agentic Tooling, agents can tap the testing engines Detectify has built over more than a decade. Included are payload assessments sourced from its ethical hacker community, attack surface data from its Surface Monitoring product and Alfred, an AI system the organization released in March 2025 to automate tests for known vulnerabilities.

It has been revealed that running in a customer’s own environment, the tools connect to agents through either the Model Context Protocol or a command-line interface. They operate only on the data a customer provides and are said to work with whichever agent the customer already uses.

Industry observers note that at the center of the design is loop engineering, an emerging practice of running AI agents in automated, repeating workflows rather than prompting them by hand. Kicking off each loop is a trigger such as a continuous integration run. Whether it comes from a code scan, a bug bounty report, a red team or Detectify’s own attack surface data, each finding is turned into a ticket.

In a recent development, once an agent picks up a ticket, it reads the relevant code before testing the live application from the outside, as an attacker would. Run continuously, the loop becomes what Detectify calls a verification factory.

The requests sent, the payloads used and the results returned are all logged in the Security Ledger each time an agent uses Detectify’s tools. Written by Detectify rather than the agent, the append-only ledger lets teams separate findings backed by actual tests from unsupported AI conclusions. Any ticket that could cause harm, such as a denial-of-service test, is marked unsafe for a person to decide on.

Recent findings suggest that “Ask an agent to write your code, then ask the same agent whether it’s secure. If it notes yes, you don’t actually know,” said co-founder and Chief Executive Rickard Carlsson. There are plenty of examples of agents fabricating proof to please the person asking, according to Carlsson, who described Detectify’s aim as “building proof that an agent can’t fabricate.”.

Available on request starting today, Agentic Tooling builds on the Detectify MCP Server that the firm unveiled in May to give AI agents access to its security findings. Investors include Insight Partners, which took a majority stake in October 2024, along with Balderton Capital (UK) LLP, Inventure, First Fellow Partners Oy and SquareOne App Ltd.

As the broad crypto market continues to face a prolonged downturn, it appears that South Korea's largest cryptocurrency exchange, Upbit, has seized the opportunity to stack up Shiba Inu at lower prices.

Latest data from blockchain intelligence firm Arkham shows that Upbit has recorded a sharp increase in its Shiba Inu holdings as the exchange appears to have continued accumulating the asset.

Despite the market’s persistent downturn, Upbit has expanded its Shiba Inu holdings to hit 64.16 trillion Shiba Inu (SHIB) tokens as of November 11, 2026.

At Shiba Inu’s current price, the exchange’s total Shiba Inu holdings are now worth about $284 million, according to data from Arkham Intelligence, positioning the firm as one of Shiba Inu’s largest holders.

Further details showcased on the platform show that the tokens are held in wallets labeled as belonging to Upbit, suggesting continued accumulation.

Recent reports show that an August 2026 audit also confirmed that its SHIB reserves exceeded user liabilities, further indicating its strong exposure to the leading meme token.

Apart from Upbit, the data further shows that other large companies also hold large amounts of SHIB, but Upbit remains the largest SHIB holding entity among them.

Recent findings suggest that robinhood's largest cold wallet holds about 39.27 trillion SHIB, worth about $174.37 million at SHIB’s current price. This represents about 3.93% of the asset’s supply.

Although Upbit stands as SHIB’s largest holding entity, the data show that the SHIB burn address remains the largest holder, as it contains about 410.44 trillion SHIB, representing about 41.04% of SHIB’s total supply.

  • The new service seeks to move past the first wave of AI agents in security, which Exaforce states were built to offload a single task such as alert triage, risk assessment or penetration testing.
  • Sources indicate that exaforce argues that as AI absorbs more of the routine work, security staff are now responsible for outcomes that cannot be handed off one task at a time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 07:00 EST / NOVEMBER 16 2026.

In a recent development, agentic security operations startup Exaforce Inc. today unveiled the launch of ExaU, a service that lets any security staff member spin up a personal team of artificial intelligence agents.

The new service seeks to move past the first wave of AI agents in security, which Exaforce states were built to offload a single task such as alert triage, risk assessment or penetration testing.

Sources indicate that exaforce argues that as AI absorbs more of the routine work, security staff are now responsible for outcomes that cannot be handed off one task at a time. Added to the mix is that staff are also facing a backlog of tasks, such as checks they mean to run, questions they initiative to chase down and briefings owed to senior management.

Leading the list of ExaU features is the ability to create an agent by describing the job in plain language, down to the way a practitioner wants it done. Templates are also available. Each agent is designed to retain decisions, exceptions and past instructions.

To use, a security staff member begins by telling an agent what they are responsible for. The agent then works out what needs doing next and when. The response includes discoveries, questions and recommendations.

In a recent development, the newly introduced service also supports sharing agents across a security organization. A chief information security officer’s briefing agent can gather status from the agents used by every team. Exaforce’s own example has a finding setting off a threat hunt, an activity audit and outreach to an employee at the same time. A single assessment then pulls the results of all three together.

Everything runs inside Exaforce on the customer’s own data. With connections to identity providers, cloud services and security telemetry already part of the platform, there are no tokens to mint for ExaU agents. The organization’s real-time security knowledge graph is claimed to give each agent an understanding of how systems relate from its first task.

Investigations are carried out by the agents on their own. Under the controls built into ExaU, any action affecting employees, systems or communications requires approval first. Recorded in the Exaforce audit log, every step an agent takes can be reviewed later.

It has been revealed that exabots, the agents Exaforce manages itself, already handle threat detection, alert triage and investigation for every customer on the platform. ExaU is pitched as a complement to that standing workforce. Available now as part of the Exaforce platform, the release follows the September launch of Exaforce AI Security, a kill switch for AI agents that go rogue.

Sources indicate that harbourVest Partners, Peak XV Partners, Mayfield Fund, Khosla Ventures and Seligman Ventures were among the investors in Exaforce’s $125 million Series B round in May. Including that round, total funding since the organization’s 2023 founding comes to $200 million.

Industry News: 10 ways to lower blood pressure without medication, from Mayo Clinic's full list

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3595 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mayo Clinic lists 10 lifestyle changes for lowering blood pressure without medication.
  • According to recent reports, many people who learn their blood pressure is high hope to bring it down by changing how they eat, move, drink and sleep, rather than by adding a pill to every morning.
  • New habits belong in the treatment at every stage of high blood pressure, yet only some people can use them in place of a pill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mayo Clinic lists 10 lifestyle changes for lowering blood pressure without medication. See which ones come with measured drops and which do not.

According to recent reports, many people who learn their blood pressure is high hope to bring it down by changing how they eat, move, drink and sleep, rather than by adding a pill to every morning. Before weighing that hope, a person needs to know what a pill does. Patients on a standard first-line blood pressure drug typically see the top number fall by 7 to 10 mm Hg, according to the NIH Collaboratory. That is the drop a habit has to approach to stand in for medication. Someone who gains a few points from one change in daily life has therefore achieved a meaningful share of what a drug delivers. A person keeps those points only as long as they keep the habit, though. The useful question is what someone can keep doing for years, not what they can try for a month.

New habits belong in the treatment at every stage of high blood pressure, yet only some people can use them in place of a pill. The American Heart Association recommends in its 2025 guideline that all adults whose average reading is 140/90 or higher take medication along with lifestyle changes. At that level, the guideline treats the habits as a partner to the pill rather than a replacement for it. The route without medication fits people whose pressure is creeping up, not people whose average has already reached 140/90. Even for that group, the habits are tied together. What a person eats, how much they move and what they weigh each affect the others, so the benefits of several changes often overlap rather than simply add up.

Industry observers note that mayo Clinic gathered the changes in daily routine that people can use to lower high blood pressure without medication, such as sleeping more, eating less salt and losing inches around the waist. Some of those changes come with a measured drop in pressure, while others offer a direction without a number. A reader's real task is deciding which changes deserve the most effort. The last piece is knowing whether any of it is working. A person learns from the readings on a home cuff, not from good intentions, whether skipping the pill remains the right choice.

It has been revealed that if a person who is overweight can change only one habit, losing weight should be it. "Weight loss in people who are overweight is the strongest lifestyle factor that can lower blood pressure," Mayo Clinic's staff wrote. People can track the payoff on a bathroom scale, with readings dropping about 1 mm Hg for every kilogram lost, or about 2.2 pounds. The benefit is tied to each unit of weight. A person who keeps losing keeps lowering the reading, and over a larger loss that can add up to a meaningful part of what a first pill accomplishes.

Many people look at a daunting goal weight and never start, but the benefit begins long before they reach it. The drop per kilogram counts from the first kilograms off, and losing about 3% to 5% of body weight lowers blood pressure in adults with overweight and obesity, according to NHLBI. The useful question for a reader is whether they can lose the first few percent, not how far they are from an ideal weight.

Sources indicate that the scale doesn't show where weight sits on the body or how much of it is muscle, and a tape measure fills that gap. Mayo Clinic treats a waist over 40 inches for men and over 35 inches for women as a sign of risk, and NHLBI sets its healthy limits just under those same marks. A person whose weight looks acceptable but whose waist is past that line still has reason to work on this habit.

According to recent reports, keeping a lower reading means keeping the lower weight, and that can take far more work than losing it. People may need more than 300 minutes of activity a week to lose or keep off substantial weight, according to NHLBI. That much activity is a standing commitment that a person has to blueprint the whole week around.

For an overweight person, the scale and the tape measure together show how much of this habit's payoff is still within reach.

Of all the daily changes on this list, changing what's on the plate carries the largest promised drop. Mayo Clinic reports that people who follow eating intends such as DASH can bring their top reading down by as much as 11 mm Hg. DASH is not general wellness advice. Its name stands for Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension, and it was designed to treat this exact problem. The Mediterranean diet is also named as a fit, which means the habit is a pattern of eating rather than one fixed menu. The words that matter are "as much as," and the real question is what someone eating at home actually gets.

Sources indicate that when people simply received healthier food at home, their drop was much smaller. Researchers in the GoFresh trial delivered DASH-style groceries to participants' homes, and systolic pressure fell 3.4 mm Hg, according to results from Stephen P. Juraschek, an associate professor of medicine at Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center who also directs the HCA Hypertension Center, reported by NIH Collaboratory. The two results don't contradict each other. One is the most the diet can do when everything goes right, and the other is what happened when people ate the food in their own kitchens. Anyone planning around food should count on a few points, not the full headline drop. The diet works, but it rarely does the whole job alone.

Sources indicate that people who change what they eat get several benefits at once, and those benefits overlap with other habits. Participants who received the groceries also had lower urine sodium, lower diastolic pressure and lower LDL cholesterol, according to NIH Collaboratory. Some of what a person would gain from cutting salt or managing cholesterol may already come from the plate, and those gains shouldn't be counted twice. The benefits also largely faded once the deliveries ended. Eating this way pays off only while it continues, so healthy eating depends as much on steady access to the right food as on willpower.

The plate can do real work on blood pressure, but only as a standing grocery habit, never as a short reset.

Regular exercise helps at two stages of high blood pressure. People can use it to bring down pressure that is already high, and to keep rising readings from turning into hypertension. Mayo Clinic puts the drop from aerobic activity at roughly 5 to 8 mm Hg and claims it prevents elevated readings from becoming hypertension. That second benefit matters most to someone whose numbers are creeping up. For that person, staying active can hold off the diagnosis itself rather than only trim a reading after it arrives.

It has been revealed that people who already have hypertension can lower their pressure across a full day with more than one kind of workout. A review led by Vinícius Mallmann Schneider of Universidade Federal do Rio Grande do Sul, Brazil, found that aerobic training lowered 24-hour systolic pressure by 4.73 mm Hg in adults with hypertension, according to Renal and Urology News. In the same review, combined aerobic and resistance training lowered it by 6.18 mm Hg. Both routines produced a real drop. A person can pick the routine they are more likely to stick with, whether that is walking or cycling alone or cardio mixed with weights.

Mayo Clinic frames the weekly goal as a block of time, such as 150 minutes of moderate activity, and people can fill that time in more than one way. Schneider and his colleagues remarked steady aerobic training, interval training and combined training all belong among the "primary evidence-based interventions" for adults with hypertension, as Renal and Urology News reported. A person who dreads steady jogging can still meet the same standard with intervals or a routine that mixes cardio and weights.

The choice that matters most is less which activity a person picks than whether they do enough of it, week after week.

Sodium is one of the few habits with a measured payoff, and people earn that payoff by cutting hard, not by easing off. Mayo Clinic indicates that people who bring their daily sodium down to 1,500 mg may see their blood pressure fall about 5 to 6 mm Hg. That target is much stricter than the general daily limit of 2,300 mg or less. The measured drop is tied to the lower figure, so staying under the familiar cap does not earn it. A reader who wants those points should treat the everyday limit as a starting line rather than the goal.

It has been revealed that the target is hard to reach because Mayo Clinic notes most sodium goes into food at the processing stage, before anyone at home picks up a salt shaker. Ordinary staples add to the total as well. The CDC counts bread as a major source of sodium because people eat it so often. A food doesn't have to be very salty to matter, and a modest amount eaten every day adds up without anyone noticing. For someone aiming at 1,500 mg, the effort therefore centers on which processed foods go into the grocery cart. Leaving the shaker alone helps, but it does nothing about the sodium already in the food.

Sources indicate that even a person who reaches the target can't count on the full drop. "Sodium's effect on blood pressure varies among groups of people," Mayo Clinic's staff wrote. The 5- to 6-point figure is a possible result for a person who cuts back, not a promise.

Cutting sodium is worth the effort, but no one should rely on it alone.

Drinking affects blood pressure in two ways at once. Mayo Clinic says that heavy drinkers push their own pressure higher and can blunt the drugs prescribed to bring it down. Cutting back matters most for readers whose readings have already reached the range where pills join the habits, because drinking less protects the treatment as well as the reading. People trying to stay off medication and people already taking it get the same advice, for different reasons.

The target is a limit of one drink a day or fewer. One drink of wine is 5 ounces, a single modest glass that leaves little room. That limit is advice for overall health, and no measured fall in blood pressure comes attached to it. A reader who drinks less can expect to stop adding to their blood pressure. They should not expect a set number of points to come off.

Recent findings suggest that drinking also harms the heart in ways that blood pressure readings don't capture. Alcohol misuse is linked to atrial fibrillation, a condition of the heart's rhythm, according to a 2022 report from NIAAA. In one study, patients who abstained from alcohol developed atrial fibrillation less often than patients in a control group. That study looked at heart rhythm rather than blood pressure, so it can't show how much giving up alcohol lowers a reading. Its result points to a second benefit, not a bigger first one.

A cuff measures pressure, not heart rhythm, so a better reading shows only part of what a reader gains from drinking less.

Industry observers note that quitting cigarettes is one of the surest ways to protect blood pressure, even though no one has put a number of points on it. Mayo Clinic warns that nicotine products push blood pressure up and that staying away from them helps the heart. People who smoked had a 51% higher risk of hypertension than people who used no nicotine at all, according to a 2026 study in the American Journal of Physiology – Heart and Circulatory Physiology reported by Science Media Centre. That result is a link between smoking and high blood pressure, not proof of how much of the extra risk came from cigarettes. Mayo gives no figure for how far pressure falls after a smoker quits, so a smoker can't weigh quitting against what a first pill would do. The value of quitting is that it removes a known strain on the heart rather than promising a set drop on the cuff.

In a recent development, A smoker who switches to a vape faces a less certain risk. Participants who used vapes and no cigarettes had a hypertension risk only about 5% above that of nonusers, according to Science Media Centre. That gap is too small to count as a clear link between vaping and high blood pressure. Mayo's warning covers nicotine in every form, but the study can't settle whether vaping raises pressure on its own. Nicola Lindson, an associate professor at the University of Oxford, indicates the research can't pin the health effects on nicotine, nor can it separate what vaping does from what smoking does. Vaping has not been shown to harm blood pressure the way smoking does, but it has not been cleared either. For now it is unproven, not safe.

Recent findings suggest that researchers who study vaping end up giving the same advice as the doctors. "Overall, these results are consistent with the wider evidence that vaping is less harmful than smoking, but not vaping or smoking is the safest option," Jamie Brown, director of the Tobacco and Alcohol Research Group at University College London, said, as reported by Science Media Centre. Mayo Clinic calls avoiding tobacco and nicotine one of the best things a person can do for the heart. For a smoker, the choice is clear. For someone who only vapes, the reason to quit is caution rather than a proven cost to blood pressure.

Because quitting promises no set number of points, the way to learn what it has done for one person is to watch the readings over time.

Recent findings suggest that people protect their blood pressure with sleep only when rest is a steady routine, and the risk comes from a pattern of short nights rather than from one late night. Seven hours is the line to watch, and falling short of it night after night for weeks affects blood pressure, according to Mayo Clinic. Many people treat a short night as a one-off they can make up for on the weekend, but the concern is a schedule that has quietly become normal. The question for a reader is whether an ordinary week falls below that line. Like the other habits, rest helps only for as long as a person keeps it up.

Enough sleep is a floor to protect, not a way to take points off a reading. Short sleep affects blood pressure, but the advice includes no estimate of how much more sleep lowers it. A reader therefore can't count sleep toward the drop a first blood pressure pill would bring. The sensible approach is to guard those seven hours as a base for other changes rather than as a substitute for them.

For some people, short nights have a medical cause that an earlier bedtime won't fix. Sleep apnea is a cause of high blood pressure, so for someone with apnea, the poor sleep is part of the pressure problem itself. Being overweight is one cause of apnea, which means extra weight and broken sleep can be parts of the same problem. Weight is not the only cause, though, so a slim person whose sleep is disturbed shouldn't rule apnea out. Insomnia is another condition that disturbs sleep. A person who sleeps badly night after night, even with time set aside for rest, has good reason to ask a doctor for a diagnosis.

According to recent reports, managing stress is a habit with a clear direction and no measured payoff for blood pressure. Mayo Clinic counts long-term stress as a possible factor in high blood pressure and offers no estimate of the drop a person might get from calming down. The CDC lists managing stress among its prevention habits, though it sets no target and states no effect. Both health authorities tell people to ease their stress, and their advice rests on a suspected link rather than a measured result. A reader who compares each habit with the few points a pill delivers can't make that comparison for stress at all.

Industry observers note that the case for stress relief is weaker than the case for habits whose effects are stated outright. The CDC states plainly that smoking raises blood pressure, while Mayo Clinic makes no equally firm claim for stress. The real question is whether people who lower their stress also lower their blood pressure. "But more research is needed to tell if lowering stress can help bring down blood pressure," Mayo Clinic's staff wrote. Stress relief passes the test of being worth doing, but it hasn't yet passed the test of producing a lower reading.

The practical choice is to keep a stress-relief routine and leave it out of any tally of points expected from the other habits. A person who counts on calmer weeks to deliver part of a pill's drop is counting on a result that no one has measured. Habits with a stated effect, such as quitting smoking, deserve the first claim on a person's effort.

This habit may do a person good even if it never shows up as a lower reading.

Recent findings suggest that home tracking is the one habit on this list that tells a person whether the others are working. Each change in eating, exercise, drinking or sleep promises a few points off the top number, but none of them shows whether those points arrived. Mayo Clinic says that people who track their pressure at home can confirm whether lifestyle changes work and can see patterns over time. A person who checks regularly can judge the effort by the direction of many readings across weeks rather than by one good or bad morning. Tracking is therefore a way to measure everything else a person has changed, not one more thing to change.

Industry observers note that for someone whose pressure is creeping up, going without pills is a trial with an end date. The American Heart Association recommends that lower-risk adults with an average of 130/80 or higher spend three to six months on lifestyle changes first, and that they start medication if their average is still at 130/80 or above after that trial. The average a person records at home during those months becomes the evidence a doctor uses to decide on the pill. Someone who changes habits but never measures has no way to know whether skipping medication is still a safe choice or has become the wrong one.

The equipment is the easy part of this habit, and it is also the least complete part. Anyone who wants a home monitor can get one, and no prescription is required. The American Heart Association pairs home monitoring with frequent contact with a multidisciplinary team of health professionals and with standardized ways of taking readings. The readings help only when they reach a clinician who can study the trend and say whether the trial has succeeded.

A person can watch the trend at home, but the decision about the pill gets made at the checkup.

People who work on their cholesterol and blood sugar won't see the effort on a blood pressure cuff, but they are guarding against the same heart disease that high blood pressure threatens. Mayo Clinic says that high levels of either one make heart disease more likely, even though neither pushes blood pressure up directly. Much of the work is already under way for anyone following the earlier advice. "Some of the same healthy habits that help lower blood pressure also help manage cholesterol and blood sugar," Mayo Clinic's staff remarked. Eating healthy, exercising more and not smoking are among the habits that serve both goals. A person who keeps up those habits gets more from them than their blood pressure points alone suggest, because that person is also managing risks a reading never shows.

Industry observers note that more adults are hearing from a health care provider that their cholesterol is high. A team of CDC researchers that includes Kerui Xu, the study's corresponding author, reports that among adults who have ever been screened, the share told their cholesterol was high was 33.2% in 2023, up from 29.2% in 2019. For a growing number of people, a checkup ends with a second number to manage alongside blood pressure, and they can use the same daily habits against both.

It has been revealed that nobody can learn their cholesterol or blood sugar from a home cuff, so a healthy reading is no all-clear. Young adults show how much depends on getting the blood test. Among 18- to 44-year-olds, the share told their cholesterol was high reached 20.5% in 2023, up from 16.0% in 2019, yet the screening rate for that age group was only 77.4% in 2023, according to CDC. A young adult who has skipped the test has had no chance to learn from a provider whether their cholesterol is high.

The habits that lower the number on the cuff can work on these other numbers too, but only a blood test indicates whether they have.

Uncommon Thinkers: Alexis Harroun aims for space with a new engine — and stays grounded

📅 13 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1427 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Geekwire

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 13, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:19 am.
  • Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec.
  • Recent findings suggest that A few weeks after learning that her tiny startup had won a NASA prize to fly its engine in space, Alexis Harroun was camping in Yellowstone, sitting around a fire and looking up at the stars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 13, 2026 at 7:46 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:19 am.

Editor’s note: This series profiles five Seattle-area “Uncommon Thinkers,” who will be recognized Dec. 10 at the GeekWire Gala in partnership with Greater Seattle Partners.

Recent findings suggest that A few weeks after learning that her tiny startup had won a NASA prize to fly its engine in space, Alexis Harroun was camping in Yellowstone, sitting around a fire and looking up at the stars. Satellites kept drifting past overhead — and the news finally sank in.

Sources indicate that “I’m like, oh, we’re going to be sending something up and we’re going to be able to see it,” she noted. “That was very humbling in a lot of ways and very exciting.”.

It has been revealed that harroun is co-founder and CEO of Juno Propulsion, a Tukwila, Wash.-based startup building a new kind of rocket engine. Instead of burning fuel in a steady flame, Juno’s engines use detonation, a supersonic combustion wave that releases more energy from the same amount of propellant.

“It’s essentially like a higher MPG rocket engine,” Harroun said.

Sources indicate that the technology has been studied for decades but has never flown in orbit. Juno aims to change that next year, when its engine is set to fly aboard a Momentus satellite in a mission called Project Iris.

That’s a significant goal for a manufacturer that, when the July 2025 NASA call came, was just Harroun, co-founder and CTO Ari Martinez and a summer intern working out of a one-room office.

If Iris succeeds, Juno’s engines could let satellites run on non-toxic fuel and maneuver far more freely in orbit, something both commercial and defense customers increasingly want. For Harroun, who earned her Ph.D. studying these engines, it would be the payoff of years of work.

In a recent development, harroun sees the technology as a long-overdue leap. The basic physics behind today’s rocket engines dates to the 1930s and has been refined about as far as it can go, she stated, calling it a constraint that’s “been a glass ceiling for too long, in my opinion.”.

Sources indicate that harroun grew up south of Seattle in Federal Way. She didn’t come from an aerospace family or spend her childhood dreaming about space. Her dad was a physician and her mom a flight attendant and flight instructor.

What she did pick up at home was an entrepreneurial streak. Her dad ran his own practice for about 20 years, and her mom is now a real estate agent. Harroun remarked watching them make “something out of completely nothing” has shaped her own path, especially in building Juno.

She calls herself a “late bloomer” who fell for engineering as she was finishing high school and heading to the University of Washington. Sci-fi became an inspiration along the way, and it’s now one of her favorite genres.

She spent all four years at UW working with professor Carl Knowlen, who leads the Aeronautics & Astronautics Department’s Detonation Engines Lab, and she joined the student rocketry team, eventually leading its propulsion group.

Industry observers note that knowlen “sees the potential in everyone,” Harroun stated, and the two built a strong relationship that’s still going. Juno’s $1.2 million National Science Foundation grant, awarded this summer, is a partnership with his research group.

Knowlen was also the faculty adviser for the student rocketry team, where he spent “many hot, and sometimes rainy, days” with Harroun and her teammates, test-firing motors and launching high-powered rockets.

In a recent development, “She always was level-headed and led by example,” Knowlen said. “No one worked harder than her to see these tests and rolls out go off as planned.”.

He called her “an exceptional student, natural leader, creative thinker, and very independent,” and mentioned it’s been a great satisfaction to see the engineer she has become.

It has been revealed that during college, Harroun interned at NASA, Boeing and Blue Origin. That first stint at Blue Origin, in 2016, set her next move.

“I realized that everyone who had the job that I wanted had gone to Purdue,” she noted.

In a recent development, she spent the next six years at Purdue University in West Lafayette, Ind., earning a master’s degree and a Ph.D. Her doctoral research was on the technology Juno is now building. She also met Martinez there. The two shared an office for years.

Harroun never planned to stay in academia.

Sources indicate that “That just didn’t feel like my calling,” she noted. “I wanted to use that very unique experience to get the technical chops to do the type of engineering that I wanted to do.”.

Her doctoral advisor, Purdue professor Stephen Heister, still advises her and the manufacturer.

It has been revealed that “He was one of the people who really pushed me to think about starting this tech giant,” Harroun said. “I think he saw the potential that I had as a founder, both from a technical and a leadership perspective.”.

Heister recalled their first technical discussion, when Harroun arrived as a fresh master’s student. He went deep on nozzle flows, her thesis topic, and the complications of building a nozzle for a detonation engine.

Industry observers note that “At the end of my diatribe, she sat quietly and remarked, ‘You’ve given me a lot to think about,’” Heister said. “I can’t think of any other 22-year-old student with such a response but I knew she was indeed a special talent.”.

He described Harroun as having “the unique ability to think deeply and at length,” and stated it’s “terribly gratifying” to watch her commercialize the technology she worked on as a grad student.

Sources indicate that after finishing her Ph.D. in 2023, Harroun came back to the Seattle region and started Juno. She knew the territory: her UW lab work and the rocketry team had put her in touch with local industry, and Juno now works with some of the same companies she did as a student.

Recent findings suggest that interning at Blue Origin was the first time she could say “there’s literally a rocket company in our backyard,” Harroun mentioned. Its presence helped build a regional talent pool, which she described as “a contingent of rocket scientists that just live here.”.

Starting a organization comes with many unknowns, and coming home crossed one off the list.

In a recent development, “I knew how to go start doing stuff immediately,” she noted. “So it made that calculus really easy.”.

Harroun’s ambitions reach well beyond one demo flight.

“Our mission is to be the rocket engine provider for the U.S.,” she remarked. “Think of a Rocketdyne.”.

Recent findings suggest that that manufacturer built engines for the Saturn V and the space shuttle, and it’s now part of L3Harris. Juno wants to play a similar role with a latest technology. It’s starting with in-space propulsion for satellites and plans to expand into engines for upper stages, orbital transfer vehicles and, eventually, the boosters that lift rockets off the pad.

According to recent reports, the first step is Project Iris. NASA paid Juno about $500,000 through its TechLeap program to build the payload, and it’s also covering the Momentus spacecraft and the flight. There’s no paying customer yet, but the mission is designed to mimic the maneuvers a real satellite would make.

Japan’s space agency has flown rotating detonation engines on suborbital research rockets, but going to orbit is “a whole ‘nother game,” Harroun mentioned. “Going to space is hard. I can attest to that.”.

According to recent reports, building a manufacturer has taught Harroun things her Ph.D. didn’t. Handling toxic propellants is so complicated, she learned, that operators can spend more fueling a satellite than on “the propulsion system itself, which is kind of crazy.”.

The bigger draw is mobility. For decades, satellites have mostly stayed in the orbit a rocket left them in, she remarked, and “that’s not really acceptable anymore in today’s world.”.

To get there, Juno has raised a $1.4 million pre-seed round led by SOSV, on top of its NASA and NSF awards.

As for going to space herself, Harroun admits it would be hard to say no if she got the opportunity.

But the avid hiker and backpacker is partial to terra firma. Her best-case future is one where Earth is the place humanity gets to enjoy and space is what makes that possible.

“I don’t know that I would be the traveler,” Harroun stated, “but I’d definitely like to be the enabler.”.

In a recent post on social media, Dogecoin engineer Michi Lumin noted that a GitHub billing issue affecting Dogecoin Core has been addressed, although uncertainty remains on how the expenses will be handled in the coming months.

Lumin disclosed that Dogecoin Core's GitHub account ran into billing issues, which she resolved by personally paying the arrears and then switching the billing to herself.

In a recent development, this situation follows major Dogecoin Core developer Patrick Lodder's absence on the 'core' front, with Lumin describing him as missing in action (MIA). However, Lumin clarified that this reflected her own personal experience and speculated that others might have remained in contact with him.

"So @dogecoin , Pat Lodder has gone MIA for months on the Core front (at least to ME. If others have talked to him, great!), and the Core GitHub has run into some billing issues. I've paid the arrears personally and switched billing to myself," Lumin wrote.

@Doge_France @dogecoin as far as i know it was fees for CI workers or actions that they bill/meter. I've been reachable but that's a whole other kettle of bees around here. Either way, it's paid right now, so we'll see how next month goes and i'll address it then if i need to.

The upgrade from Lumin prompted a response from Dogecoin community member 'Doge France', who offered to contribute financially if assistance was needed, saying that keeping the Core GitHub infrastructure operational should be a priority.

Responding to the offer, Lumin explained that the outstanding charges appeared to be related to GitHub Actions or continuous integration (CI) workers, whose usage is billed according to consumption.

Although the immediate payment has been completed, Lumin stopped short of confirming a long-term funding arrangement for the Core GitHub. The developer said the next billing cycle would provide a clearer picture, which will be addressed if necessary.

In a recent development, "As far as i know, it was fees for CI workers or actions that they bill/meter. I've been reachable but that's a whole other kettle of bees around here. Either way, it's paid right now, so we'll see how next month goes and i'll address it then if i need to," Lumin wrote.

The Dogecoin Foundation, a non-profit organization for which Lumin serves as principal engineer, supports open-source development, advocacy, and community work for Dogecoin and relies primarily on community contributions for its funding.

In the past month, Dogecoin revealed a consolidation across its ecosystem with the launch of Dogecoin Labs, which unites Dogecoin’s product teams, technology and applications.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data shows the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

Recent findings suggest that at the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot reveals its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham states those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

In a recent development, if Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

Sources indicate that the FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It shows how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own users. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Sources indicate that binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

Sources indicate that while the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now demonstrates:.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:.

According to recent reports, what it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." It has been revealed that what customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.
