Latest Update: 20 International Space Station facts and figures, according to NASA

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5370 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • From a crew of seven to 16 sunrises a day, 20 figures show what it takes to keep the International Space Station running.
  • Recent findings suggest that the International Space Station is usually pictured as a machine of record-breaking size, but every room, robotic arm and docking port aboard exists so that people can live and work in orbit.
  • In a recent development, A station built while people lived in it grew room by room, and those rooms came from different builders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

From a crew of seven to 16 sunrises a day, 20 figures show what it takes to keep the International Space Station running.

Recent findings suggest that the International Space Station is usually pictured as a machine of record-breaking size, but every room, robotic arm and docking port aboard exists so that people can live and work in orbit. Crews moved in long before the builders were done, and construction wasn't completed until 2011, according to NASA. For years, the station was a home and a construction site at the same time, and the people living aboard shared it with the work of building it. It has never been a finished object to admire from a distance. It has been a working outpost that its own residents help assemble and maintain. Once the station is seen as a lived-in workplace, each of its impressive figures raises a question about upkeep and human effort, not just about scale.

In a recent development, A station built while people lived in it grew room by room, and those rooms came from different builders. Its laboratories were built by the United States, Russia, Japan and Europe, according to NASA. No single country owns the rooms where the crew does its work. A home assembled this way cannot sustain itself, and it depends on its partners to keep sending people, parts and supplies. Its headline figures describe the station on the days when everything runs as planned. When crews, supplies or schedules fall short, those figures change, and the strain behind them is as much a part of the station's story as its size.

NASA gathered a collection of notable facts about the International Space Station, ranging from the five-agency partnership that runs it to Peggy Whitson's time-in-space record, the Canadarm2 robotic arm and solar arrays measured against an Airbus A380. Taken together, these facts show what it takes to keep people living off the planet without a break, and how much of that work falls to the crews themselves. They also show where the effort is still strained or incomplete. In several places, the station's routines manage a problem rather than solve it. Each figure ahead reveals something about the people and partners who keep the station working.

It has been revealed that running the International Space Station is a joint job, not one country's operation with guests aboard. NASA, Russia's Roscosmos, the European Space Agency, Japan's JAXA and the Canadian Space Agency operate the station together, according to NASA. Those five agencies speak for a much larger group, with 15 countries standing behind the partnership. A handful of agencies runs the station on behalf of many more nations, and the crews that fly show how that arrangement works in practice.

It has been revealed that the partnership highlights most clearly in who flies together. Crew-12 and Crew-13 each paired two NASA astronauts with one Roscosmos cosmonaut, according to USA Today. The fourth seat went to the European Space Agency on Crew-12 and to the Canadian Space Agency on Crew-13. For the people aboard, the partnership means working beside colleagues from several agencies, not a ceremonial roster.

More nations have sent people to the station than belong to its partnership. Visitors have come from 26 countries, according to USA Today. That count reaches well past the 15 member countries, which means people from nations with no part in running the station have lived aboard. More than 290 people have made the trip, and the station has become a destination for hundreds of travelers, not a private posting for each agency's own astronauts.

Five agencies keep the station running, and much of its reach comes from what that arrangement has opened to others.

Industry observers note that most records stay fixed once someone sets them, but the station's record for human presence has no end date yet. People have lived aboard without a break since November 2000, according to NASA. "25 years ago, Expedition 1 became the first crew to call the International Space Station home, beginning a period of continuous human presence in space that still continues to this day," NASA acting administrator Sean Duffy mentioned. The first crew moved into a home, and nobody has left it empty since. Each day that someone stays aboard adds to the total. A record that is still open can also still end.

No single crew has held this record. Continuous occupation has always meant a long series of different people, never the same crew staying put. Every departure had to be covered by someone already aboard or just arriving, and each of those handovers was a moment when the station could have been left empty. Across a quarter century of crew changes, that moment has never come. The record belongs less to any one astronaut than to the unbroken run of launches, crews and schedules that kept the station staffed through every change.

Each new crew extends a record that no one has yet closed, and keeping it open falls to whoever flies next.

The station's crew size looks like a fixed specification, the same kind of number as its length or its wingspan, but it is a staffing level that people have to keep meeting. NASA lists seven people as the station's normal crew. In early 2026, though, only three remained aboard, one American and two Russians, after a medical evacuation in January, according to PBS NewsHour. The evacuation followed a serious health problem with one astronaut, not a scheduled crew swap. A crew size that a single medical emergency can reduce this sharply depends on the health of the people aboard, and it is a target that has to be met again and again.

According to recent reports, A short crew meant the station did much less of its work, not the same work at a slower pace. While only three people remained, NASA paused spacewalks, PBS NewsHour reports, and it trimmed the research aboard as well. Outside work stopped entirely, and the labs that give the station much of its purpose produced less science. Seven is therefore a measure of what the station can do. With fewer people, the station stayed occupied, but much of its work had to wait.

Industry observers note that the crew had no way to fill the empty seats from inside the station, and only a upcoming launch could close the gap. A replacement crew arrived on Feb. 14, 2026, and brought the station back to its standard seven, according to PBS NewsHour. Refilling the crew took more than one country, because the new arrivals came from the United States, France and Russia.

The crew of seven holds only as long as people keep arriving, and the winter of 2026 revealed how promptly life aboard can fall below the station's standard figures when they don't.

Industry observers note that aboard the International Space Station, sunlight can't tell the crew what time it is. Astronauts see the sun rise and set 16 times in every 24 hours, according to NASA, and a full lap of Earth takes only about 90 minutes. A morning and a night can come and go while an astronaut works through a single task. A crew living with that much light and dark has to keep its day by a schedule instead of by the sun. It is one more part of station life that the people aboard have to manage for themselves.

It has been revealed that not every one of those laps gives people on the ground a view, but the station circles often enough to give them real chances. "But a lot of those times are during the day time, or it passes just on the horizon, but because it's doing it so often there's actually a number of times the space station passes overhead," astrophysicist Brad Tucker told ABC News in 2018. In 2018, how often a watcher could see the station depended on where the watcher lived, ranging from one a month to several a week. Catching a pass from the ground has always depended on place and timing as well as on how often the station goes around.

It has been revealed that the station's orbit is predictable, so a sighting doesn't have to depend on luck. Stargazers could check Spot the Station forecasts for passes up to 10 days ahead, according to a 2018 report by ABC News. That is enough notice to strategy a clear evening around a pass overhead.

The crew can't escape the station's 16 dawns, while people on the ground can pick which passes to watch, with a forecast to guide them.

Industry observers note that no American has spent more time in space than Peggy Whitson, who has logged 665 days off the planet, according to NASA. She holds that record in an astronaut corps that did not open selection to women until 1976, TIME reports, and the American endurance record now belongs to a member of a group that NASA once left out. Her total is more than a count of days. It shows how long one person can keep living and working in orbit, and it shows how recently NASA began choosing women to do that work.

Recent findings suggest that women entered the corps slowly after NASA opened selection to them. The 1978 class of 35 astronauts included only six women, according to TIME, and Sally Ride flew in 1983 as the first American woman to reach space. Women made up a small minority of the people NASA chose at the time, and Ride's flight marked the start of their place in American spaceflight. Women remain a minority of the corps, but a much larger one, with 19 of NASA's 46 astronauts. Once NASA opened the corps, a woman did more than take part in long-duration spaceflight. She set the American standard for it.

The American who has spent the most time in orbit comes from a group that NASA's astronaut corps once excluded entirely.

In a recent development, calling the International Space Station a six-bedroom house suggests a place with room to spread out, where every crew member has a bedroom and a guest could take the spare. The rooms behind that comparison are already claimed. The crew gets six spaces for sleeping, along with two bathrooms, according to NASA. Its residents outnumber those sleeping spaces, and NASA reports that the station supports a crew of seven, plus visitors. Those visitors come aboard a house with no empty bedroom set aside for them, and everyone uses the same two bathrooms. The six-bedroom comparison describes a household that runs close to capacity, not a roomy one. In a home this tightly shared, each room has to stay in working order every day for the crew to rest and keep clean. That makes the house as much a daily routine as a set of measurements.

According to recent reports, among the station's other rooms is a gym. An ordinary six-bedroom house might use its extra space for a den or a guest room. Aboard the station, part of the space a house would leave for comfort goes to exercise and to keeping the crew in shape. That choice matches the rest of life aboard, where the home stays livable only because the people inside it maintain themselves and the station.

The six-bedroom label counts the rooms, but the routine of the seven people who share them is what keeps those rooms livable.

The station's gym is a medical necessity, not a perk, because astronauts who live in orbit lose bone and muscle. NASA lists a gym among the station's facilities. If nothing effective is done to protect them, astronauts' bones thin by 1-2% a month, according to NASA. A loss at that monthly pace becomes serious for anyone who stays aboard for many months. For those crew members, time in the gym is closer to medical treatment than to recreation.

The workouts slow the damage, but they do not stop it. Exercise on the space shuttle and the station has not eliminated bone loss, NASA reports, and it has not eliminated muscle deconditioning either. Astronauts who keep to the routine still lose some bone and some muscle conditioning while they live aboard. Crews use the gym to manage a problem that no one has yet solved, and keeping the human body healthy in orbit remains unfinished work.

The machine at the center of that routine can't leave the station. Astronauts aboard use the Advanced Resistive Exercise Device, known as ARED, but the machine does not fit in exploration spacecraft, according to NASA. Crews bound for destinations beyond the station can't simply pack the equipment that station crews depend on. They will need another way to protect their bones and muscles on trips that keep them farther from Earth.

The station's gym reveals what it takes to keep people healthy in orbit, and how much work remains before crews can leave the station behind.

Recent findings suggest that the people who live on the International Space Station are also its builders, and some of that building can only be done outside the hull. NASA credits both astronauts and cosmonauts with spacewalks for construction and maintenance, so the outside work falls to residents from more than one partner rather than to visiting specialists. One planned walk was assigned to Mike Fincke and Zena Cardman, two U.S. astronauts already serving on the station's crew, according to CNBC. Construction on the station is also current work, with crews installing upcoming IROSA solar arrays. In practice, the crew renovates its own occupied home while wearing pressure suits.

According to recent reports, not all outside work is urgent, and building work can sometimes be set aside. In January 2026, NASA postponed a U.S. spacewalk in which Fincke and Cardman were to spend 6.5 hours outside, according to CNBC. That is most of a working day for two people, and calling it off moved the installation of a latest solar array to a later date. Still, the delay cost the station nothing it needs to keep running. The solar array upgrade is not necessary for station operations, which makes the new array an improvement the station can do without for now. Outside work comes in two kinds: work that keeps the station running and work that expands it. This walk belonged to the second kind, and NASA could put it off without harm to the station's daily operations.

Industry observers note that the building waits on the health of the builders. The walk was set aside when a medical situation led NASA to bring Crew-11 home ahead of schedule, and the crew had been due back around March, according to CNBC.

Crews add to the station only as fast as they are fit to step outside and build it.

The station's solar wings are wider than the largest passenger jet that airports are built to handle. From tip to tip, the arrays span 356 feet (109 meters), well beyond the 262-foot wingspan of an Airbus A380, according to NASA. The A380 makes a demanding yardstick because its designers built it to the largest size that airports allow. Its designers kept its wings within the maximum gate width that airport authorities permit, with a margin of under six inches at each wingtip, according to Smithsonian Air & Space. The station's arrays are far wider than any plane that the gate limit permits. On the ground, a structure that wide could not use a gate even at airports that serve the biggest jets in the world.

It has been revealed that the wingspan has a practical purpose, because the arrays are the surface the station uses to collect sunlight. Crews rely on them for between 75 and 90 kilowatts of electricity, the power that keeps the station running. That supply is still being expanded. Latest roll-out arrays, known as IROSA, are being installed on a station that remains occupied and at work, so the power system keeps growing while people live aboard. The arrays are a record-setting measurement, and they are also one more part of the station that people must keep building to keep it powered.

Even the station's widest feature remains unfinished work for the crews who depend on its electricity.

Industry observers note that the pictures of Earth that people on the ground know best come from the crew members living aboard the station, not from a separate camera program. NASA counts more than 3.5 million images of the planet that crews have shot from the station over the two decades it has been occupied. The photographers include both astronauts and cosmonauts, so the collection is the work of crew members from more than one space program. The size of the archive indicates as much about how long people have lived on the station as it does about photography. Every picture in it required someone at the window with a camera.

The photos often show the human side of Earth and its natural side in the same frame. USA TODAY reports that NASA astronaut Anil Menon took a picture in September of an aurora glowing above the lit-up cities of central Asia, with the station's own solar panels in view. The people behind the camera are working crew members, and they can capture settlements and natural events alike as they pass overhead.

It has been revealed that crews keep adding to the collection with each rotation. Crew-13 lifted off on a SpaceX Falcon 9 and Dragon in early October, according to USA TODAY, and its members joined the people who can photograph the planet from orbit. The total of more than 3.5 million is a minimum, and each arriving crew pushes it higher.

The photo archive is one of the plainest signs that the station is a place where people live, and crews can add to its record of Earth only as long as the partners keep sending them up.

Recent findings suggest that the station reached orbit as a long series of deliveries, each carrying one more piece of a home. Building it took 42 separate assembly flights, according to NASA, and each launch had to succeed before the next module could join the ones already circling Earth. Assembly was a chain of risky trips rather than a single event, and the station's shape depended on every link holding. Most of that chain ran through one country. The U.S. space shuttle flew nearly all of those missions, 37 in total, and Russia's Proton and Soyuz rockets carried the rest. The station has several partners, but getting its pieces to orbit depended heavily on a single American vehicle. A home shared by many agencies came together almost entirely along one narrow route into space.

The station has kept growing since its original assembly flights ended. A module called Prichal joined it on Nov. 26, 2021, long after the shuttle flights that carried most of its pieces. Companies now supply some of the hardware as well, and the station carries the BEAM module and an airlock called Bishop from NanoRacks. Space agencies no longer supply every new room. Some of the building also happens in orbit. The crew is installing new IROSA solar arrays, so the people who live on the station also work as its construction crew, fitting hardware into place years after they first moved in.

The assembly flights put the station in orbit, and the people living aboard have kept building it ever since.

In a recent development, the International Space Station is nearly as long as a football field. Its length from end to end is 356 feet (109 meters), just one yard short of a field, according to NASA. A familiar playing field makes the size easy to picture, and it suggests a long building that a crew could walk through from one end to the other. That picture doesn't match the station's layout. The 356-foot figure covers the station's entire outline, including large parts outside the area where people can breathe and work.

The rooms where the crew lives and works cover far less than a football field. The pressurized modules, which hold the crew's living quarters and labs, are 218 feet (67 meters) long, well short of the station's full length. Much of the remaining length belongs to the truss, an exterior frame that nobody lives in. The truss is 310 feet (94 meters) long, which makes it longer than the entire line of pressurized rooms. Most of the station's reach is therefore open framework on the outside, not enclosed space for people. The football-field comparison mostly describes the structure around the crew rather than the crew's home.

Most of the station's best-known measurement is outside its walls, and the people who keep it running live and work along a shorter, enclosed line inside.

The station's wiring is long because its power supply is spread out. The electrical wiring aboard runs 8 miles, according to NASA, and that length follows from where the electricity starts. The station collected its power with eight separate solar arrays, according to a 2018 report by CNBC. Current from each array had to be routed through the structure to the rooms where the crew works. A station that runs on sunlight cannot keep all of its power sources in one corner. Its wiring has to reach every array on the frame and bring that electricity together.

The station's sunlight is also collected in very small pieces over a large area. Its solar panels cover an acre, and those panels held 262,400 individual solar cells, according to a 2018 report by CNBC. The current from any single cell is small, and it is useful only after it is gathered with the output of thousands of others. The broad panels that make the station look so large are the same reason it needs miles of cable behind them.

Recent findings suggest that most people who picture the station think of its solar arrays, and few give any thought to the cable that carries their output. For the crew, that cable is what turns sunlight into lights, air systems and working laboratories. Behind the station's headline dimensions is a less visible network, and without it the people aboard would have no electricity to live and work by.

The station's crews do their outside work with a limb built to the scale of the station rather than of a person. NASA lists Canadarm2 at 55 feet long, with seven joints. That length covers far more of the exterior than any spacewalker could reach. With that many joints, operators can bend the arm around the station's structure instead of swinging it in a single straight line. Crews use it for jobs that a person in a pressure suit could not manage alone, from moving modules into place to setting up experiments and carrying spacewalkers to their work sites. Its duties cover both building the station and moving the people who work outside it.

The arm's construction work did not end when assembly did, because the station is still being refitted. CBC reports that crews unloaded the newly introduced IROSA solar arrays from their SpaceX Dragon with Canadarm2. On the spacewalk to install the arrays, NASA astronaut Anil Menon is the one who rides on the arm. For that job the arm serves as his transport as well as a crane, and the station's current upgrade depends on it. "There would be no way to accomplish this spacewalk without the help of Canadian robotics," said Mathieu Caron, director of the Canadian Space Agency's astronaut office.

According to recent reports, canada's part in this work does not stop at the hardware. The country runs its own Robotics Mission Control Centre in Longueuil, Que., according to CBC. Caron sees the spacewalk as a sign that the other partners recognize Canada's work in the partnership. Canada is a smaller partner, but this spacewalk could not happen without its arm and the people who operate it, and that work is the basis of Canada's stake in the station.

Sources indicate that crews can keep as many as eight visiting spacecraft docked at the same time, according to NASA. People and cargo can arrive on several ships together. They do not have to come through a single line in which each ship must leave before the next one arrives. With that many docking spots, the crew does not have to send an earlier vehicle away before a new one can attach. Cargo deliveries, crew visits and departures can all overlap. The station is built for steady traffic from the ground, and its crew can initiative around several vehicles at once rather than one at a time.

That overlap matters most when one crew replaces another. The station normally holds seven people, and during a handover it holds more, because the arriving and departing astronauts share it for a while. The extra docking spots make that arrangement possible. The vehicle that carried the new crew up and the one that will carry the old crew home can both stay attached at the same time. The incoming crew can settle in and learn the station's routines while the people who know them best are still aboard to help.

With room for eight ships at once, a latest delivery or a new crew can come aboard while earlier visitors are still attached.

Sources indicate that the International Space Station is in orbit, yet people can reach it within a single workday. Astronauts can travel from the launch pad to the station in as little as four hours, according to NASA. Measured by travel time rather than altitude, the crew lives much closer to the ground than a home in orbit suggests. That is the quickest possible trip, though, and a crew should not expect every flight to be that short.

Industry observers note that A four-hour arrival depends on the launch, the rendezvous and the docking all going right in sequence. The people flying and guiding the spacecraft have to complete each stage in order, with nothing forcing a delay or a second attempt. A trip that fast is what they can achieve when every step goes right on the same day. It gives no promise that planners can deliver the next crew or the next cargo load as quickly. Planners and crews can match that pace only when conditions allow, and on other days the journey may take longer.

For the people living aboard, the station is only as near as the next spacecraft that can reach them. On the best day, the ground is only a few hours away, but a crew cannot count on every launch day going that well.

The station's crew lives on supplies flown up from Earth, and NASA lists four types of cargo spacecraft that make those deliveries. With that range of vehicles, the people aboard do not have to depend on any single design to bring what they need. Part of the work belongs to private industry. Northrop Grumman $NOC flies the Cygnus, and SpaceX flies the Dragon. As a result, the U.S. share of resupply is in the hands of companies rather than a government agency, and it has more than one provider.

According to recent reports, the station's partners also share the job of keeping it stocked. The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency operates the HTV, and the fourth vehicle is the Russian Progress. Two companies and two national programs keep cargo moving to the station. The crew's everyday needs depend on all of them continuing to fly, and no single country guarantees those needs by itself.

Recent findings suggest that equipment aboard has made crews less reliant on those flights for one supply. The station's Water Recovery System cuts the crew's dependence on water delivered from Earth by 65 percent. That gain covers water alone. Food, equipment and every other supply still have to come up on a cargo spacecraft, so the crew still counts on each scheduled flight.

The station has reduced its reliance on the ground without ending it, and its crews manage that dependence one delivery at a time.

According to recent reports, the work done in the station's labs is the clearest result of everything it takes to keep people living aboard. Researchers have used the station for nearly 3,000 separate investigations, according to NASA. That record indicates a working laboratory that researchers have used over and over across its years in orbit, not a showpiece. None of that research could happen without people aboard to tend it and without the power, supplies and equipment that support them. The station's size, its solar arrays, its docking ports and its regular cargo flights all matter for that reason. Together they keep the research possible.

Industry observers note that the people who use the station's labs come from far more places than the partners who run it. Researchers from more than 108 countries have taken part in its investigations, a larger group than the countries that operate the station. That leaves an uneven arrangement. A small set of partners carries the daily work of keeping the station staffed, supplied and in repair. Scientists from much of the world share in the research that work makes possible, and many of them come from nations outside the partnership. If the crews, the partners or the supply runs ever falter, the cost would not stay with the agencies that run the station. Researchers in countries with no hand in its upkeep would lose their place in its labs as well.

It has been revealed that the International Space Station can seem far removed from ordinary life. It is a sealed home in orbit, where a small crew works out of reach of everyone on the ground. Its route, though, passes over most of humanity. About 90 percent of Earth's population lives under the station's path, according to NASA. The ground below that path is not limited to open ocean or polar ice. It includes the regions where people build cities, farm land and raise families, so most readers live somewhere the crew travels over.

The crews who keep the station running are therefore not working at the edge of the human world. They live and work above the same towns and cities as the people on the ground. The people beneath them make up most of the planet's population. The crew is far from home in altitude, but not in geography. Their route takes them over the places where most of humanity lives.

Readers can connect the station to their own lives through this figure more directly than through any measurement of its size or speed. Those figures describe the station from a distance. The population figure places the reader under the station itself, in the large share of humanity that lives below the crew's path.

Researchers use the outside of the International Space Station as laboratory space, in addition to the rooms where the crew lives and works. Most people picture the station as a set of sealed modules, with the hull serving as the barrier between the crew and the vacuum around them. That hull has a second purpose. NASA reports that the station can carry more than 20 experiments on its outer structure at the same time. The station's research area therefore reaches well beyond the labs its partners built inside. Its scientific work does not stop at the hatch. Researchers attach experiments to the same structure that was designed to keep a crew of astronauts safe.

It has been revealed that the equipment on the outside is working scientific hardware. One of those experiments is the Alpha Magnetic Spectrometer-02, a scientific instrument fixed to the station's exterior. Its presence indicates that researchers use the outer surfaces for active research, not as spare storage. Researchers who place an instrument outside also leave the crew's crowded indoor space free for other work. The station is a place to work in orbit as much as a place to live there, and its outside is part of that working space.

The station's walls were built to protect the crew, and their outer side is lab space too.

Bitcoin found its bottom? Bitcoin is fighting to hold $65,000 after a brutal weekend selloff pushed BTC USD below $62,000. The rebound offers bulls some relief, but the market is showing signs of a much deeper liquidity problem.

The world’s largest crypto has lost 13% since the 8th of November, with Ethereum and XRP also hitting multi-month lows. Billions in leveraged positions have disappeared as traders rush to reduce exposure.

According to recent reports, yet the selloff has created an interesting setup. Extreme fear, forced liquidations, and heavily discounted prices could signal that much of the speculative excess has finally been removed.

The problem is that capital continues leaving the crypto market. Stablecoin supply has contracted for five consecutive weeks, while US spot Bitcoin ETFs have recorded seven consecutive sessions of outflows.

Bitcoin now faces a defining question: has the market finally found its bottom, or is another crash waiting around the corner?

Recent findings suggest that the latest liquidation wave has given the Bitcoin bottom argument some credibility. When leveraged traders are forced out, selling pressure can eventually exhaust itself, leaving the market with fewer speculative positions vulnerable to another cascade. What comes down must go up, and vice versa.

Industry observers note that the weekend recovery also reveals that buyers are willing to defend the $62,000 region. BTC rebounded to $64,000 – $65,000 after briefly touching $62,006 this morning.

It has been revealed that market sentiment has also deteriorated sharply. Extreme fear is returning as investors abandon riskier positions and traders become increasingly defensive. This is often where market reversals begin. Sellers who wanted to exit have already sold, while longer-term investors start looking for attractive entry points.

Sources indicate that galaxy Research has also presented a bullish argument. In an October 26 report, the firm said it believed Bitcoin’s bottom was already in, pointing to diminished selling pressure, reduced speculative positioning, and stronger long-term fundamentals.

Sources indicate that however, a convincing recovery needs more than a short-lived bounce. Bitcoin must attract fresh spot demand and reclaim important resistance levels before bulls can claim victory.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026.

The biggest obstacle to a Bitcoin bottom is the lack of fresh money entering the market. Stablecoin supply has contracted for five consecutive weeks. Glassnode puts the 30-day decline at $17.1 billion, marking the fastest contraction since June 2022.

Stablecoins provide much of the dollar liquidity used to purchase cryptocurrencies, so when investors redeem stablecoins for traditional dollars, the market loses potential buying power.

It has been revealed that bitcoin ETFs are sending another warning. US spot Bitcoin ETFs have lost $2.35 billion over two weeks, extending a difficult period for institutional demand. Corporate buying has weakened too. Public companies collectively sold 11,647 BTC worth approximately $869 million. Strategy remained a buyer, adding 1,037 BTC, but the wider corporate treasury trend has turned negative.

Macroeconomic conditions are making the situation worse. Hotter-than-expected US inflation and employment figures have pushed interest-rate expectations higher. Futures markets now fully price a 25-basis-point Federal Reserve rate hike in December.

BREAKING: October PPI Inflation rises to 6.5%, its highest level since November 2022.Core PPI Inflation was 5.0%, in-line with expectations of 5.0%.CPI, PPI, and PCE inflation continue to push higher in the US.All signs point toward a December rate hike.

Higher rates strengthen the dollar and make non-yielding assets like Bitcoin less attractive. Meanwhile, the dollar index has climbed to 102.9, adding another headwind for crypto markets.

According to recent reports, coinbase Institutional also warned that Bitcoin could struggle to recover without renewed crypto-native demand. Its analysis places $62,000 among the crucial support levels, with $58,000–$59,000 emerging as another potential downside target.

The technical picture remains fragile. Bitcoin needs to reclaim the $66,000–$68,000 region before bulls can establish a convincing recovery. A sustained move above $73,000–$75,000 would provide a much stronger reversal signal.

Bitcoin has already experienced a substantial correction, but the rebound hasn’t settled the argument. The bullish case rests on exhausted sellers, reduced speculative exposure, extreme fear, and buyers defending the $62,000 region. The bearish case rests on shrinking stablecoin supply, ETF withdrawals, weaker corporate accumulation, and rising borrowing costs.

For now, liquidity remains the deciding factor. A genuine Bitcoin bottom needs more than liquidation-driven relief rallies. It needs fresh capital entering the market, institutional demand returning, and spot buyers absorbing available supply.

Industry observers note that if stablecoin supply stabilizes and ETF flows turn positive, Bitcoin could build a foundation for its next recovery. But if capital continues leaving the ecosystem, the $62,000 floor could give way to another painful correction.

Bitcoin may be approaching its bottom, but the market hasn’t yet shown that buyers are ready to take control.

Palo Alto Networks report finds organizations struggle to track and secure AI agents in the cloud

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1178 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced report out today from cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks Inc.
  • According to recent reports, now in its sixth year, the State of Cloud Security Report 2026 is based on a survey of 2,800 security executives and practitioners in 10 countries.
  • The use of AI agents was found to be close to universal, with 99% of respondents saying they use agents for autonomous or semiautonomous actions in their development pipelines.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 08:00 EST / NOVEMBER 16 2026.

A newly introduced report out today from cybersecurity company Palo Alto Networks Inc. finds that artificial intelligence agents have quickly become a fixture in software development, but many organizations can’t properly track or secure what those agents are doing in the cloud.

According to recent reports, now in its sixth year, the State of Cloud Security Report 2026 is based on a survey of 2,800 security executives and practitioners in 10 countries. Along with how AI is being used to build and deploy software, the report looks at how swiftly organizations are able to respond when something goes wrong.

The use of AI agents was found to be close to universal, with 99% of respondents saying they use agents for autonomous or semiautonomous actions in their development pipelines. Some 73% said the agents are allowed to modify code, pipeline configurations or production environments, and agents are even doing security testing at 44% of organizations.

Sources indicate that the amount of change is going up as a result. Some 82% said AI-driven development has increased the volume of infrastructure updates reaching their cloud, yet organizations on average enforce fewer than three of the eight predeployment security checks measured in the survey. AI is also being used to generate infrastructure-as-code templates at 42% of organizations, but only 34% scan that code before production.

In a recent development, not surprisingly, problems are getting through. Respondents remarked that on average, 19% of high and critical application security problems reached production over a 90-day period. It takes an average of 18.4 days to get a fix for a security concern found in code into production.

Industry observers note that when respondents were asked what was stopping them from fixing issues before deployment, the most common answer was business pressure to release promptly at 39%. Unclear risk acceptance policies came second at 30%.

Accountability is also an issue when it comes to agents. Two in five organizations remarked they are unable to reconstruct what an AI agent did, a share that rises to 46% in financial services, while 53% said agent activity is logged under a developer’s identity or personal access token. That means when something goes wrong, investigators first have to figure out which actions were taken by a person and which were taken by an agent before they can work out what was affected.

It has been revealed that removing access once something does go wrong is also slow. Some 60% of organizations still need manual intervention to revoke access for nonhuman identities, and it takes an average of 2.5 days to revoke or rotate compromised developer credentials, API keys or pipeline secrets.

Recent findings suggest that data governance has its own complications. Nearly all organizations, 99%, stated they had found ungoverned AI in their environment in the past year, yet only 9% are able to automatically discover and classify it. Some 40% said governed data had been copied into ungoverned AI tools, and 39% had seen sensitive or regulated data used to train or fine-tune models without authorization.

Despite the gaps, confidence is high. Almost every respondent, 97%, stated they are at least somewhat confident they can secure their AI supply chain and applications, though only 36% can monitor AI behavior in production and just 30% can detect prompt injection.

In a recent development, the final section of the report looks at the threat from frontier AI models that can find and exploit software vulnerabilities on their own. Nearly all respondents, 98%, said they are concerned about it, and 65% said it poses a significant or severe threat to global critical infrastructure and financial systems over the next 12 to 18 months. Utilities were the most likely of any sector to rate the threat as significant or severe at 79%, compared with 48% in telecommunications.

According to recent reports, interestingly, though the report refers to “frontier AI-powered capabilities,” the survey questions at the back of it call them “Mythos-grade” threats, a reference to Anthropic PBC’s Claude Mythos models. Palo Alto Networks was one of the launch partners in Anthropic’s Project Glasswing, which gave defenders early access to Claude Mythos Preview in April.

The report argues that against attackers working at machine speed, an 18.4-day fix cycle leaves organizations exposed for more than 17 days after a vulnerability can be discovered. Part of the problem, according to the report, is fragmented tooling, with only 19% of organizations saying they operate with unified telemetry and workflows across code, cloud, identity and runtime. Nearly half of organizations, 47%, still do the work of correlating application vulnerabilities with runtime threats by hand, a number that’s even higher in the U.S. at 55%.

Recent findings suggest that the report ends with a series of recommendations for organizations to secure their cloud environments as AI agents take on more work. Agents should be given their own identities with a clear owner and only the permissions they need to do their job. Security teams are also advised to automate the fixing of recurring concerns, though only after rollback procedures have been put in place.

7 Grammy snubs and surprises of 2027, from Gracie Abrams to John Summit

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The 2027 Grammy snubs and surprises include shutouts for Gracie Abrams and Hilary Duff, a single folk nod for Noah Kahan and no major-category nods for Madonna.
  • In a recent development, A Grammy nominations list does two jobs at once.
  • It has been revealed that the top of the field was crowded.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The 2027 Grammy snubs and surprises include shutouts for Gracie Abrams and Hilary Duff, a single folk nod for Noah Kahan and no major-category nods for Madonna.

In a recent development, A Grammy nominations list does two jobs at once. It indicates what voters chose to reward, and it shows whom they passed over. The list for the 2027 awards, unveiled on a Monday, delivered plenty of both. Several chart-topping releases and latest records from long-established stars came away with few nominations, or none at all, in the races that draw the most attention.

It has been revealed that the top of the field was crowded. Raye led every act with 11 nominations, and Rosalía followed with nine. Kanye "Ye" West earned a best rap album nomination for Bully. Beyoncé reached 100 career Grammy nominations with "Morning Dew (Donk)," a song released July 4 on the 20th anniversary edition of B'Day. Sabrina Carpenter picked up two nominations for best pop duo/group performance. Both came from her collaborations with Taylor Swift and Madonna.

The 2027 Grammy snubs sit on the other side of that ledger. Commercial success did not guarantee a place on the ballot. One album reached No. 1 on the Billboard 200 and still went without a single nomination. A comeback record debuted in the top three and received nothing. Veteran artists, including a seven-time Grammy winner, collected nods elsewhere while missing album, record and song of the year entirely. In one case, a documentary about a former Beatle earned two nominations, while his fresh album earned one.

Other results stood out for different reasons. A former best new artist nominee landed a single nod in a folk category. A pop star placed in all three general categories, and her total still counted among the year's surprises. A dance artist answered his result with public criticism of the awards.

According to recent reports, the seven slides that follow are a selection of notable snubs and surprises from the 2027 nominations, not a complete accounting. They cover Gracie Abrams, Hilary Duff, Noah Kahan, Madonna, Taylor Swift, Paul McCartney and John Summit. Each slide names the artist, the work in question and the nominations it did or did not earn, so any entry can be read on its own.

Gracie Abrams received no 2027 Grammy nominations for Daughter From Hell, her third album. The record had reached No. 1 on the Billboard 200.

The Hollywood Reporter counted the shutout among the snubs and surprises of the 2027 nominations.

Recent findings suggest that the Recording Academy has recognized Abrams before. She was a best new artist nominee in 2024. That category honors an artist's breakthrough rather than any single release.

According to recent reports, the Daughter From Hell result also follows an earlier miss. Last year, Abrams had been expected to earn song of the year and record of the year nominations for "That's So True." Neither nomination came.

In a recent development, those two categories reward different work. Song of the year goes to the songwriters behind a composition. Record of the year covers the finished recording, including the artist's performance and its production.

It has been revealed that the Hollywood Reporter described the 2027 shutout as not her first Grammys disappointment. Across those two cycles, Abrams went without nominations for a single that had been tipped for major categories and for an album that topped the Billboard 200.

Abrams opened for Taylor Swift on select dates of the Eras Tour.

Hilary Duff's comeback album, Luck … Or Something, received no nominations when the 2027 Grammy nominations were revealed, according to The Hollywood Reporter. The record went unrecognized in every category.

It has been revealed that the shutout followed a top-three chart debut. Luck … Or Something entered the Billboard 200 at No. 3. The Billboard 200 ranks the most popular albums in the U.S. each week.

In a recent development, duff released the album in February. It came out through Atlantic Records, her new label.

A newly introduced label, a comeback release and a No. 3 debut did not add up to a place on the 2027 Grammy ballot. Duff's album was absent from the general field and from the genre categories alike.

Noah Kahan's album The Great Divide earned one 2027 Grammy nomination, for best contemporary folk album. It received no nominations for album, record or song of the year.

According to recent reports, that outcome fell short of some forecasts. The Hollywood Reporter noted that several experts had predicted top-category nominations for The Great Divide.

In a recent development, the two kinds of category work differently. Best contemporary folk album is a genre award, so The Great Divide is up against other folk releases. Album, record and song of the year sit in the general field. There, entries from every genre compete against each other.

It has been revealed that kahan has reached the general field before. He was previously nominated for best latest artist, which is also a general-field category. This year, his only recognition came in the folk field.

Kahan responded on the Monday the nominations were confirmed. "Life goes on," he tweeted.

Recent findings suggest that madonna's album Confessions II earned four nominations for the 2027 Grammys. None of them came in the three major categories: album of the year, record of the year and song of the year.

According to recent reports, confessions II is the long-awaited follow-up to Confessions, the album Madonna released in 2005. All four of the sequel's nods came in other categories.

In a recent development, madonna is a seven-time Grammy winner. That record did not carry Confessions II into any of the three major races this cycle.

Her name also appears in another artist's results. One of Sabrina Carpenter's nominations for best pop duo/group performance came from a collaboration with Madonna.

The Hollywood Reporter included Confessions II among the notable snubs and surprises of the 2027 nominations.

Industry observers note that taylor Swift earned five nominations for the 2027 Grammys. One came in each of the three general categories: album of the year, record of the year and song of the year.

That result placed Swift in every one of the top races. It still put her on The Hollywood Reporter's list of snubs and surprises from the 2027 nominations, as a surprise rather than a shutout.

It has been revealed that the Hollywood Reporter described her five nominations as perhaps understated relative to what is expected of her. That judgment belongs to the outlet. Its point concerned the size of her total, not whether she was recognized in album, record or song of the year.

Sources indicate that swift's entry differs from the shutouts elsewhere in the 2027 Grammy snubs. Her case rests on a nomination count that the outlet measured against expectations, with no gap at the top of the field.

Paul McCartney's album The Boys of Dungeon Lane did not make it into any of the major categories in the 2027 Grammy nominations. Its only nomination came in best traditional pop vocal album.

According to recent reports, the major categories are album of the year, record of the year and song of the year. The newly introduced McCartney record appeared in none of them. The Hollywood Reporter included that result in its rundown of snubs and surprises from the nominations, which were unveiled on a Monday.

According to recent reports, mcCartney still finished with three nominations overall. Only one of them belongs to The Boys of Dungeon Lane.

According to recent reports, the other two came from Man on the Run, a documentary directed by Morgan Neville. The film covers McCartney's exit from the Beatles.

That split means a film about the end of his Beatles years drew more nominations than his newly introduced album did.

The best traditional pop vocal album nod keeps The Boys of Dungeon Lane in contention for a Grammy. That chance comes in a single genre category. It does not extend to album, record or song of the year, the three general categories.

Recent findings suggest that john Summit publicly criticized the Grammys after a dance snub in the 2027 nominations, according to a headline from The Hollywood Reporter. That headline quotes him directly: "It's All a F***ing Joke.".

Recent findings suggest that the outlet ran Summit's reaction as a separate story, apart from its main roundup of the year's snubs and surprises. The headline does not name the category, track or album involved.

Summit works in the dance music world that the snub concerns. The Chicago Sun-Times describes him as a DJ raised in Naperville. His music pairs high-energy tech house rhythms with catchy sung hooks, the paper reports.

Sources indicate that summit took an indirect path into music. Born John Schuster, he worked as an accountant and DJed on the side. He later left that corporate job to pursue music full time.

One track raised his profile. Defected Records released his song "Deep End," which went viral and helped lift him to global prominence as a DJ.

Industry observers note that summit has also built an audience online. He shares footage from major festival performances alongside glimpses of his ordinary daily routine.

Bitcoin Core Breaks Silence on Three Patched Security Vulnerabilities

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (401 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: U

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Bitcoin Core developers have revealed three key security vulnerabilities, including a high-severity flaw that could potentially disrupt the mining capabilities of the Bitcoin network, preventing miners from creating upcoming blocks.
  • Recent findings suggest that as revealed in security advisories published on Nov.
  • One of the vulnerabilities, titled CVE-2025-62861, was rated as a high-severity matter due to its potential effect on Bitcoin miners.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Bitcoin Core developers have revealed three key security vulnerabilities, including a high-severity flaw that could potentially disrupt the mining capabilities of the Bitcoin network, preventing miners from creating upcoming blocks.

Recent findings suggest that as revealed in security advisories published on Nov. 10, the vulnerabilities impacted various elements of the Bitcoin Core software that powers many nodes underpinning the world's leading cryptocurrency.

One of the vulnerabilities, titled CVE-2025-62861, was rated as a high-severity matter due to its potential effect on Bitcoin miners.

The bug has the potential to create problems after a blockchain reorganization, which is when previously accepted blocks are replaced by the network with an alternative chain.

More precisely, the concern could cause an inconsistent state in the node's mempool, where all unconfirmed transactions are stored.

The vulnerability impacted Bitcoin Core software versions 28.0-28.2 and 29.0-29.1.

It was first reported on Sept. 26, 2025, by security researcher Niklas Goegge.

Beyond the mining vulnerability, Bitcoin Core developers have announced two further security problems, rated medium severity.

The first one (CVE-2025-62859) could enable malicious network participants to slow down Bitcoin block processing through an exploit that involves changes in transaction witness data.

Under some circumstances, it could make an affected node wait for up to 10 minutes before processing a block.

Moreover, such an attack could be repeated indefinitely on the node when the latter is running in specific configurations.

The vulnerability was found by Eugene Siegel in April 2025.

The second vulnerability (CVE-2025-62860) involved Bitcoin nodes that operate on the anonymous Tor network.

In fact, the Bitcoin Core developers revealed that thousands of reachable Bitcoin mainnet nodes had been granting permissions for incoming Tor connections.

Nevertheless, the glitch did not affect nodes that do not use the optional whitelist configuration.

The three vulnerabilities are not latest discoveries.

In fact, all of the complications were already fixed by the Bitcoin Core developers in October 2025.

The fixes were integrated into both Bitcoin Core 30.0, which was released on Oct. 10, and Bitcoin Core 29.2, rolled out on Oct. 14.

The high-severity mining vulnerability was also patched in Bitcoin Core 28.3.

The delay in the disclosure of the vulnerabilities was in line with the Bitcoin Core security policy, which usually calls for developers to wait at least two weeks after the end of life of the last affected software version before publishing details of medium- or high-severity vulnerabilities.

#6143. 4 ways to check a suspected romance scammer, from the FTC's advice

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1642 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Qz ↗ Open Full Page

4 ways to check a suspected romance scammer, from the FTC's advice

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1642 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The FTC says to stop contact, talk to someone you trust, search the person's job plus "scammer," and check their photo.
  • The danger in a romance scam is rarely one convincing lie.
  • It's tempting to think only the frail or naive fall for this.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The FTC says to stop contact, talk to someone you trust, search the person's job plus "scammer," and check their photo.

The danger in a romance scam is rarely one convincing lie. It is a whole relationship built so that nobody else ever gets a look at it. That isolation is deliberate. Scammers isolate their targets from loved ones, according to a 2018 paper by Prof. Monica Whitty of the WMG Cyber Security Centre at the University of Warwick in Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking. ABC News reports that scammers also tell victims to move their conversations to encrypted messaging platforms. The courtship then takes place in a private channel that no friend or relative can see. Only one check on the relationship remains, which is the target's own judgment, and the scammer has spent weeks working on exactly that.

It's tempting to think only the frail or naive fall for this. The evidence demonstrates that people of many ages get caught, and it disagrees about where the worst risk lies. Many victims are middle-aged. In a U.K. study published in 2018 in Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking, Whitty finds that 63% of romance-scam victims were between 35 and 54. Older people still lose heavily, though. In Australia, people 65 and over lost $11.7 million, more than any other age group, according to ABC News. The two findings point to different ages as the greatest risk, and neither suggests that any age is safe. Whoever the victim is, embarrassment can stop them as surely as the scammer can. Western Australia Attorney General Tony Buti told ABC News that a "shame factor" is at work. In the U.S., the National Institute on Aging tells people who suspect a scam that they have no reason for embarrassment, because anyone can be fooled. Officials in two countries treat shame as a real obstacle, and the silence it produces is what a scammer depends on. A warning sign helps only if the person who spots it feels free to act on it without humiliation.

The Federal Trade Commission laid out what to do when you suspect a upcoming love interest is a scammer, from checking whether a profile photo belongs to someone else to searching the job the person claims to hold. Each of its steps lets someone outside the relationship look in. That person might be a friend, a stranger who has heard the same story, or the real owner of the face in the photo. All of the steps serve one firm rule from the FTC: nobody should send cash or presents to an online partner they have never met face to face. Each step is a way to keep to that rule before any money changes hands.

The moment you first suspect a newly introduced love interest is a scammer is the moment to stop talking to them. Most people want one more conversation, a chance to ask the hard question, hear the explanation and settle it face to face, or at least screen to screen. The Federal Trade Commission notes that cutting off the person right away should be the first move once you suspect fraud, and that you should stop communicating immediately. Someone running a scam may use threats or pressure a target to act immediately, according to the National Institute on Aging. A final conversation lets the scammer keep setting the pace, and it gives that pressure one more chance to work. Going silent without an explanation feels rude, but it is the one move that lets the target, not the scammer, decide what happens next.

The real reason to stop now is what the scammer is likely to ask for next. Romance scammers ask to be paid with gift cards, wire transfers or cryptocurrency. Money sent by transfer or gift card usually cannot be recovered, according to the National Institute on Aging. A request for either one is a request for money that will most likely be gone for good once it is sent. That leaves the two possible mistakes far from equal. Cutting off someone who turns out to be genuine costs an awkward apology later, while sending a transfer or gift card to someone who isn't usually means losing that money. Silence is only a pause, though. Once contact stops, the next job is to let someone outside the relationship look at what happened.

Telling a trusted friend or relative about a new love interest does the one thing a romance scammer works hardest to prevent. Most scam advice asks you to find the flaw in the other person. This step asks for the judgment of someone the scammer has never had a chance to work on. The Federal Trade Commission advises people to talk to someone they trust and to ask whether friends or family are worried about the new partner. ABC News reports that scammers may give the opposite order and tell their targets not to mention the relationship to friends and family. The FTC's question asks what the people who know you think of the new partner. Those people were never let into the courtship, so they can judge it from outside. A request to keep a new partner secret is therefore not a sign of closeness. It is a warning sign, and it is the moment to call someone.

A conversation with a friend costs nothing, while keeping quiet can cost a great deal. In Western Australia, 63 people lost about $3.8 million to romance scams in 2025, according to ABC News. Those are serious losses for the people who suffered them, and an awkward talk is small by comparison. The talk helps most early, while a friend can hear the story for the first time and before the relationship comes with a request for money.

A friend's worry about a new partner is exactly what the FTC asks you to listen for.

The job a upcoming love interest describes is often the excuse for why the two of you can never meet. The Federal Trade Commission lists working on an oil rig and serving in the military among the reasons scammers give for not meeting in person. That makes the job the part of the story worth checking first. Scammers tell the same story to many people at once, and one scheme involving Akpieyi and Hall reached 31 victims, according to Fox 8. Checking takes no special tools. Anyone can type the claimed job and the word "scammer" into a search engine and see whether other people have posted similar stories about oil rig workers or Army impostors. When those posts describe your story almost word for word, the person was most likely using the same story on other targets.

Over time, the cover story also becomes the reason the person needs money. The request sounds like more of the life the person has already described. "They'll start talking about the need for money in whatever project or in their life and just sort of make references to it, so it looks like it's just normally part of conversation," former FBI agent and attorney Mike Zummer told Fox 8. The best moment to search is when the job first comes up, before the person has asked for anything and before the story feels too familiar to question.

According to recent reports, an arrest can come years after a scheme begins. The scheme involving Akpieyi started around April 2020, and the FBI did not catch Akpieyi until 2023, at a Georgia bank, according to Fox 8. A search takes minutes, and it lets a target test the story long before any investigation reaches the person behind it. A person can also run this check without telling anyone, and someone who finds a match has solid reason to bring a friend or relative in.

A scammer can make up a job, a backstory and a way of talking, but the face in the profile usually belongs to a real person somewhere else. The Federal Trade Commission indicates that a reverse image search can show whether a profile picture belongs to another name or appears beside details that don't match, and it treats either result as a sign of a scam. Scammers build their profiles with stolen photographs, according to research by Whitty in Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking. A mismatched photo is therefore no fluke, because it comes from the way these profiles are made. The outside view on this step comes from the real owner of the face, who never agreed to take part in the romance at all. A gut feeling depends on how much the target already trusts the suitor, but this check does not. The picture either belongs to the person in the chat or it belongs to someone else.

Running the search takes little effort, but stopping to doubt someone who has spent weeks making you feel wanted takes much more. Victims of romance scams tend to act on impulse, which is the opposite of the pause this check needs. People in the U.K. who had been taken in by a romance scam showed a stronger tendency toward rash action than people who had never been scammed, according to Whitty's research published in 2018 in Cyberpsychology, Behavior, and Social Networking. A safety step that depends on stopping to check asks for a habit that runs against a trait many victims share. The search is worth running early, before attachment makes checking the photo feel like a betrayal. The Federal Trade Commission names Instagram and Facebook $META among the places where scammers get in touch with people, so a photo is worth checking even when the stranger writes through an ordinary social media account.

The moment a stranger's attractive photo starts a conversation is the moment to check the face, well before anyone asks for money.

#6142. Industry News: Emideltide Keeps Getting a ‘No’ for Compounding. What’s the Problem?

Industry News: Emideltide Keeps Getting a ‘No’ for Compounding. What’s the Problem?

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1044 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Menshealth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION has not been shy about its pro-peptide stance.
  • So what happened to that last peptide?
  • According to recent reports, EMIDELTIDE IS A nine-amino-acid peptide originally isolated from the blood of sleeping rabbits during electrically induced sleep in the late 1970s.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

THE TRUMP ADMINISTRATION has not been shy about its pro-peptide stance. US Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has pushed to make six popular yet unapproved peptides available for compounding to people with a prescription. A recent FDA advisory committee meeting voted in favor of adding six out of seven peptides to a list of substances that U.S. compounding pharmacies are allowed to manufacture and supply.

Six out of seven. So what happened to that last peptide? Emideltide, also dubbed DSIP, is a peptide people have turned to for better sleep. And it was the only peptide the FDA advisory board voted against moving out of the Category 2 list—a substance considered to carry significant safety risks, with compounding pharmacies prohibited from making it. Here’s why.

According to recent reports, EMIDELTIDE IS A nine-amino-acid peptide originally isolated from the blood of sleeping rabbits during electrically induced sleep in the late 1970s. Since its discovery, a synthetic peptide version has been administered via injection or a nasal spray.

Emideltide reportedly helps you fall asleep faster and extend the time spent in deep sleep. It’s also been used to avoid waking up multiple times throughout the night and anecdotal reports online have mentioned more vivid, Inception–like lucid dreaming. With better sleep, people online using emideltide have mentioned feeling less stress, more refreshed upon waking, and faster recovery after a grueling workout.

MOST RESEARCH LOOKING into the peptide’s role in sleep, however, took place in the 1980s and 1990s—with mixed findings.

For example, a 1984 case study reported on a 35-year-old guy with 10 years of narcolepsy who had reduced sleep attacks, less daytime napping, and more alertness with weekly emideltide injections administered in the morning.

Industry observers note that one clinical trial had 16 people take an emideltide injection or a placebo while measuring how long it took for them to fall asleep once they’re tucked into bed. People who had an emideltide injection said they felt more tired and actually went to sleep quicker than the placebo group. That should be great except when they repeated the experiment a second night, the placebo group knocked out quicker than the peptide group.

Another study in 1992 found the peptide helped chronic insomniacs feel less tired. However, there was such little difference in the time it took to fall asleep and stay asleep in the emideltide group versus the placebo group. The authors of the 1992 study stated any small improvements with the peptide were probably “due to an incidental change in the placebo group” and “not likely to be of major therapeutic benefit.”.

Sources indicate that BEYOND SLEEP, EMIDELTIDE has been explored in animal studies for potentially protecting against cancer and improving motor ability after stroke. Another realm of interest is how emideltide might help with curbing withdrawal after addiction.

Sources indicate that A 1984 study found emideltide injections helped reduce the severity of opioid withdrawal symptoms in 97 percent of people with addiction along with alcohol withdrawal symptoms in 87 percent of people with alcohol addiction. Although more peptide injections were needed in people with opiate addiction.

It has been revealed that in 1998, researchers gave a single injection of emideltide to seven people with opioid dependence. While they reported improvements in opioid withdrawal, the team also noted “it remains an open question whether DSIP could be an effective alternative detoxification approach.” Some of the issues were the small sample size, lack of a placebo group for proper comparison, and that each person knew they were getting an emideltide injection. The lack of randomization makes it hard to say for sure that a treatment actually worked or if people subjectively felt better because they knew they were getting treatment.

Recent findings suggest that WE KNOW EMIDELTIDE doesn’t act like a sedative that slows down the brain and body’s function. But how the peptide exactly works is still up for debate.

The peptide is often considered a sleep-regulator rather than a suppressant. We know emideltide doesn’t act like a sedative or sleeping pill that slows down the brain and body’s function. But how the peptide exactly works is still up for debate.

One possible mechanism is that the peptide increases delta-wave activity. These are your slowest brain waves at 0.5 to 4 Hz that are indicative of deep sleep. Deep sleep is linked to better memory, energy, and all that good stuff you get from a good night’s sleep. There may also be some neuroendocrine effects going on that could explain why people feel calm enough to pass out. A small study back in the ’80s injected a single dose of emideltide in 11 guys and found lower levels of ACTH, a hormone that stimulates your adrenal glands to release the stress hormone cortisol (though this mechanism has been disputed).

Industry observers note that the FDA advisory meeting relied on studies that focused on emideltide’s cross-talk with the opioid system in the brain. While the peptide doesn’t directly interact with opioid receptors, evidence points to emideltide somehow being able to trigger the release of endorphins. This may also provide painkiller properties (which is why it’s been proposed as a way to suppress alcohol and opioid withdrawal syndrome).

EMIDELTIDE WILL PROBABLY stay banned—and found only through the sketchy gray market—because there’s not enough information to know if emideltide might do more harm than good.

According to recent reports, since emideltide interacts with the opioid system, there is a possibility that it could lead to addiction. Right now, there are no animal or human studies that prove emideltide wouldn’t worsen addictive behaviors.

There’s also not enough data on whether repeated emideltide use would cause other safety challenges. While the small sleep trials did not report any serious side effects, withdrawal studies noted headaches, nausea, and vertigo. After the second injection, some had low blood pressure although the researchers also said it’s unclear whether those symptoms were because of the peptide or from withdrawal altogether.

In a recent development, jocelyn Solis-Moreira, MS is the associate health & fitness for Men's Health and has previously written for CNN, Scientific American, Popular Science, and National Geographic before joining the brand. When she's not working, she's doing circus arts or working towards the perfect pull-up.

Ripple-Backed Evernorth Plunges 40% as Insiders Move to Sell 73.7 Million Shares

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ripple-backed XRP treasury manufacturer Evernorth Holdings (XRPN) is under extreme pressure as its shares have declined by over 40% while big investors like Ripple Labs move closer to potentially selling millions of shares.
  • Earlier this week, Evernorth filed a prospectus with the U.S.
  • According to recent reports, evernorth's prospectus comes as the XRP-focused company is enduring a brutal stock market debut.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ripple-backed XRP treasury manufacturer Evernorth Holdings (XRPN) is under extreme pressure as its shares have declined by over 40% while big investors like Ripple Labs move closer to potentially selling millions of shares.

Earlier this week, Evernorth filed a prospectus with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC), indicating that the XRP-focused firm has registered a whopping 73,688,162 Class A shares for potential resale by existing shareholders.

According to recent reports, evernorth's prospectus comes as the XRP-focused company is enduring a brutal stock market debut. XRPN began trading on Nasdaq on Oct. 12.

On Nov. 10, Evernorth's stock price dropped 23.54%. XRPN ended the day at $7.96, compared to $10.41 in the previous trading session. Moreover, about 1.39 million shares were traded, which is a significant jump from about 369,000 shares on Nov. 9.

Industry observers note that so far, Evernorth's share price has declined by around 48% from its closing price on Oct. 28 ($15.26). The magnitude of the decline is even greater if we consider the high share price on its debut day ($19.39). XRPN's stock price is down by around 59% from that high.

Some of the biggest names and companies linked to the XRP ecosystem are shareholders who have registered shares for potential sale, as per the prospectus filed with the SEC.

Industry observers note that for instance, the biggest shareholder is Arrington XRP Capital Fund, which was a sponsor of the merger between Evernorth and Armada Acquisition Corp. II. It has about 33.82 million shares registered for possible resale.

In a recent development, similarly, the second-largest shareholder is Ripple Labs, which has about 18.14 million shares registered. Then there are various entities linked to SBI Holdings, a significant Japanese financial institution. They have 11.79 million shares registered, as per the prospectus filed with the SEC.

The Larsen Lam Children's Remainder Trust, which is linked to Ripple co-founder Chris Larsen, has about 7.15 million shares registered for possible sale.

Other names mentioned in the filing include Pantera Capital, GSR Markets Switzerland and Kraken parent firm Payward.

It is vital to understand that the fact that they've registered shares for sale doesn't mean that these investors have sold their holdings or necessarily plan to sell them.

For example, Ripple, the Arrington-sponsored entity and a Larsen-linked entity are all subject to six-month lock-up agreements following the completion of Evernorth's business combination on Oct. 9.

These lock-up agreements are typically set to expire on April 9, 2027, with some exceptions.

#6139. Breaking: 10 major video game leaks and hacks, from Half-Life 2 to Grand Theft Auto VI

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 12m • 📚 Deep Dive (2316 w)
