Breaking: 10 major video game leaks and hacks, from Half-Life 2 to Grand Theft Auto VI

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2316 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These video game leaks and hacks exposed source code, unreleased footage and player data, from Valve's Half-Life 2 theft to Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto VI breach.
  • A video game studio's most valuable assets rarely sit in a vault.
  • The nature of the threat has shifted over two decades.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These video game leaks and hacks exposed source code, unreleased footage and player data, from Valve's Half-Life 2 theft to Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto VI breach.

A video game studio's most valuable assets rarely sit in a vault. They live on servers as source code, proprietary engines, unfinished builds and plans for games the public has not yet seen. That concentration of unreleased work makes studios and platform operators targets for intruders. When the files escape, the damage can reach release dates, employees and players at once.

The nature of the threat has shifted over two decades. In 2003, source code for Half-Life 2 was stolen from Valve's network, and the stolen build leaked online that September. Valve's Gabe Newell publicly asked for help finding the person responsible. A man named Axel Gembe was later convicted in Germany. More recent incidents follow a different script. Extortion groups such as Ragnar Locker and Lapsus$ break into corporate networks, copy data and press companies for payment. When a tech giant refuses, the stolen files can end up online anyway.

In a recent development, the costs take several forms. Some leaks push back a launch. Half-Life 2's release slipped to November 2004. Others spoil a story before release, as happened when cutscene footage from The Last of Us Part II surfaced in April 2020. Ransomware attacks on Capcom, CD Projekt Red and Insomniac Games exposed source code, personal information or plans for future projects. The 2011 PlayStation Network breach exposed data from roughly 77 million accounts, according to Sony $SONY's own reporting at the time. Sony kept the network offline for about three weeks.

According to recent reports, in September 2022, a user called teapotuberhacker posted around 90 videos of in-development Grand Theft Auto VI footage taken from Rockstar Games. In June 2021, attackers claimed to have taken FIFA 21 source code and the Frostbite engine from Electronic Arts $EA. EA confirmed that game source code was taken and stated no player data was involved. Hardware makers are exposed too. Nvidia $NVDA, whose graphics cards are sold to PC gamers, confirmed an intrusion in 2022.

Recent findings suggest that what follows is a selection of 10 major video game leaks and hacks, not a ranking or a complete record. Each slide covers what was taken, who was responsible where that is known, and what happened next. The order does not reflect severity.

It has been revealed that half-Life 2 source code was stolen from Valve's network, and the stolen build of the game leaked online in September 2003. The game had not yet been released.

Recent findings suggest that the leaked material was an in-development version, not a finished product. Unfinished work from inside the studio reached the public before Valve chose to show it.

Valve did not handle the theft quietly. Gabe Newell publicly appealed for help in finding the person responsible.

According to recent reports, half-Life 2 reached players in November 2004. By then, the stolen build had already circulated online.

A German man, Axel Gembe, was later convicted in Germany over the theft.

Recent findings suggest that in September 2022, around 90 videos of in-development Grand Theft Auto VI footage appeared online after a hack of Rockstar Games. A user called teapotuberhacker posted the clips.

The leak was made up of dozens of separate videos rather than a single screenshot or rumor. Together they gave the public a wide look at a game still in production. None of the clips came from Rockstar's own channels.

The volume of the leak mattered. A single clip can be dismissed as a fake or an outlier. A set of around 90 is much harder to dispute, and it highlights a project from many angles at once.

Recent findings suggest that in-development footage differs from a finished trailer. It shows a project before its developers have decided how to present it. Clips captured during production can show work that is still incomplete. A leak of this kind takes the first public look at a game out of the studio's hands.

Recent findings suggest that the attacker behind the teapotuberhacker account was also linked to a breach of Uber $UBER. That link tied the Rockstar leak to an intrusion at a organization outside the games industry. It demonstrated that the studio was one target among several.

Arion Kurtaj, a member of the Lapsus$ hacking group, was later found to have carried out the Rockstar hack. That finding attached a name to what had begun as an anonymous online handle. It also tied the leak to a group whose other targets included Nvidia $NVDA, the graphics card maker.

In December 2023, a U.K. court ordered Kurtaj held indefinitely in a secure hospital. The order came about 15 months after the footage first appeared online. The court set no fixed end date for that period of detention.

Sources indicate that the case connects one studio's unreleased footage, a separate attack on Uber and a U.K. court order through a single attacker.

The Nintendo Gigaleak was a series of leaks, beginning in 2018, that put internal Nintendo source code, design documents and prototype material online. Files tied to the Pokémon and Super Mario series were among the material exposed.

In a recent development, the files did not come out in a single dump. They surfaced in batches from 2018 onward. Each batch added material that Nintendo had kept internal.

It has been revealed that the leaked files covered several eras of Nintendo hardware. Material from the Super Nintendo era appeared alongside files from the Game Boy Advance, the GameCube and the Wii. That range sets the Gigaleak apart from a leak centered on one unreleased game.

In a recent development, three kinds of material were involved. Source code is the human-readable programming behind a game. Developers write it before it is compiled into the form a console runs. Design documents record how a game was planned, from its mechanics to its levels. Prototype material captures a game in an earlier, unfinished state.

The Pokémon and Super Mario files tied the leak to two long-running Nintendo series. Material of this kind shows how games in those series looked while they were still in development. Final retail releases do not carry that record.

According to recent reports, attackers broke into Sony $SONY's PlayStation Network in April 2011, and Sony took the service offline for about three weeks. Data from roughly 77 million accounts was exposed, according to Sony's own reporting at the time.

The PlayStation Network is Sony's online service for its PlayStation consoles. It handles player accounts, online multiplayer and the console's digital store. While the network was down, those services were unavailable to its customers.

It has been revealed that this breach differs from most game industry leaks. Many high-profile cases involve a studio's unreleased work, such as source code, in-development footage or design files. The 2011 attack hit the customer side of the business instead. The exposed data belonged to the people who play the games, not to a product still in development.

Story details and cutscene footage from Naughty Dog's The Last of Us Part II leaked online in April 2020. The game was released in June 2020, about two months later.

It has been revealed that the leaked material came in two forms. One was written information about the game's plot. The other was cutscene footage. Cutscenes are the scripted sequences that carry a game's story between stretches of play.

In a recent development, the April leak was not an isolated event. It came during a broader run of leaks around the title before its release.

The result was that parts of the game's story were public before players could reach them by playing it.

According to recent reports, in December 2023, the Rhysida ransomware group published about 1.67 terabytes of data stolen from Insomniac Games. The files went online after a ransom demand went unmet.

In a recent development, the leaked material spanned three areas. It included content from Wolverine, information about Insomniac employees and looks for the studio's future projects.

According to recent reports, the Wolverine content came from a game that had not been released. Unfinished work reached the public on the attackers' timetable rather than the studio's.

The employee information meant the breach reached Insomniac's staff as well as its games. Personal records sat alongside game assets in the published data.

Sources indicate that the future project plans were a separate category. Their release put the studio's internal planning in public view.

The 1.67-terabyte figure describes data the group posted after the ransom went unpaid. It is a measure of what was published, not a volume the attackers only claimed to hold.

Attackers breached Electronic Arts $EA in June 2021 and claimed to have taken 780 GB of data. They said the haul included source code for FIFA 21 and the firm's Frostbite engine.

EA confirmed that game source code was taken. The firm mentioned no player data was involved.

Industry observers note that source code is the human-readable set of instructions behind a game. It indicates how features are built and how systems connect. A finished game, by contrast, reaches players in compiled form.

According to recent reports, frostbite is a different kind of asset from a single title. A game engine is the underlying software toolkit a studio uses to build games. It handles core tasks such as rendering graphics and simulating physics.

In a recent development, engine code can matter beyond one release. A publisher can build several games on the same engine. That makes the engine's code a shared foundation rather than part of one product.

Recent findings suggest that the 780 GB figure came from the attackers, not from EA. The company's confirmation covered the theft of game source code. It did not confirm the attackers' account of the full volume taken.

According to recent reports, EA's statement separated this incident from breaches that expose customer records. The material at issue was the company's own intellectual property, not its players' accounts.

Sources indicate that in February 2021, attackers behind a ransomware attack on CD Projekt Red claimed to have stolen source code for Cyberpunk 2077, The Witcher 3 and Gwent. The company refused to pay, and the data later appeared online.

The claim did not center on one unreleased title. It reached across three separate products in the studio's catalog at once.

It has been revealed that source code is the human-readable set of instructions programmers write before a game is compiled into the version players install. It shows how a game's systems were built. For a studio, it is the working blueprint behind a finished product.

A ransom demand gives attackers leverage. The organization pays, and the attackers offer to keep the files private. CD Projekt Red declined that bargain.

Sources indicate that the refusal did not keep the code out of view. Once the files surfaced online, the studio no longer controlled who could read them.

The Ragnar Locker ransomware group breached Capcom, the Japanese game publisher, in November 2020. Capcom said up to about 390,000 people may have been affected.

That number was not Capcom's first estimate. The company revised it upward from an earlier, lower figure. The scale of the breach that Capcom reported grew after its first disclosure.

Ragnar Locker made its own claim about the theft. The group stated it had taken about one terabyte of data from Capcom. That volume rests on the attackers' word.

The two figures come from opposite sides of the incident and measure different things. The terabyte claim describes how much data the group remarked it removed. Capcom's number counts the people whose information may have been exposed.

Neither figure answers the other's question. A data volume does not show whose records were inside it. A count of people does not show how many files left the network.

Read together, they give two separate accounts of one breach. One is the attackers' description of what they took. The other is the manufacturer's assessment of who was exposed.

In February 2022, the Lapsus$ hacking group claimed it had stolen about one terabyte of data from Nvidia $NVDA. Nvidia confirmed that an intrusion had taken place.

In a recent development, nvidia designs graphics cards, the components that render games on PCs. It is a hardware manufacturer, not a game studio. Its place among video game security incidents comes through those cards and the PC gamers who buy them.

According to recent reports, the one-terabyte total comes from Lapsus$, not from Nvidia. The firm's confirmation covered the intrusion itself. The size of the stolen data set remains the group's own claim.

According to recent reports, that split leaves two separate questions with two different answers. Whether someone got into Nvidia's systems is settled by the company's own statement. How much they took rests on the word of the people who took it.

The group also made a demand that went beyond the stolen files. Lapsus$ called on Nvidia to remove the crypto-mining limiter on its graphics cards. That demand targeted how Nvidia's products work, not only the data the group said it held.

Sources indicate that the limiter demand is where the breach reached the gaming market directly. It concerned the same graphics cards that PC gamers buy. A data theft at a chip designer turned into a demand about a feature of consumer hardware.

Lapsus$ later turned up in a games case. Arion Kurtaj, a member of the group, was found to have carried out the September 2022 hack of Rockstar Games. That breach led to the leak of in-development Grand Theft Auto VI footage.

In December 2023, a U.K. court ordered Kurtaj held indefinitely in a secure hospital. The Rockstar case tied the same group to intrusions at a chipmaker and a game publisher within the same year.

Goodbye, manual work: AI-native CRM platform Dreamteam raises $53M to automate enterprise sales

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1466 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Intelligent sales software startup Dreamteam AI Inc.
  • The funds come by way of a seed and Series A round led by Accel Partners with participation from Together Fund and Premji Invest.
  • Industry observers note that CRM platforms such as Salesforce and Hubspot have served as vital cogs in the wheel sales-focused enterprises for more than a quarter of a century.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 09:00 EST / NOVEMBER 16 2026.

Intelligent sales software startup Dreamteam AI Inc. mentioned today it has raised $53 million in early-stage funding to try to flip the narrative around customer relationship management platforms, which often seem like more of a hindrance than a help, by actually getting work done for sales teams.

The funds come by way of a seed and Series A round led by Accel Partners with participation from Together Fund and Premji Invest.

Industry observers note that CRM platforms such as Salesforce and Hubspot have served as vital cogs in the wheel sales-focused enterprises for more than a quarter of a century. But these days they often create just as much work as they save, claims Dreamteam co-founder and Chief Executive Anand Venkatraman (pictured, center, alongside co-founders Ramesh Parthasarathy and Senthil Kanthaswamy). While organizations are striving to use artificial intelligence to automate more of their business processes, CRMs are holding them back, he believes.

Recent findings suggest that the problem with legacy CRM platforms is that they’re totally reliant on manual data entry, Venkatraman explained. Because their architectures are built around structured data fields and rigid, hand-coded workflows, they create a tight bottleneck that makes it almost impossible for autonomous AI agents that feed primarily on semantic data to get anything done.

In a recent development, “When a sales prospect expresses price hesitation or mentions a competitor, a salesperson registers it immediately,” he stated. “But a legacy CRM, starving for unstructured nuance, misses it entirely, leaving AI agents without the vital context needed to reason effectively.”.

To provide this context, Dreamteam has rebuilt the CRM from the ground up around the idea of a “company brain,” or a living memory of the business that constantly updates itself by ingesting new information from meetings with clients, prospects and team members, emails and other connected tools. As with all AI-native platforms, there’s also a generous dose of automation in the shape of four AI agents, or teammates, which specialize in different tasks.

The agents include Rachel, which handles account research; Sally for meeting preparations and follow-ups; Raj, which monitors for pipeline risks; and Alex, which serves as the CRM administrator, keeping the platform ticking over without any human intervention.

In a recent development, venkatraman said he and his co-founders designed Dreamteam’s architecture specifically to address the historic shortcomings of legacy CRM platforms, which struggle to dig up the most vital business intelligence, leaving teams flying blind. “When a CEO asks why the quarter’s three biggest deals were lost, RevOps spends two weeks building a partial answer from whatever the reps happened to type,” he said. “The richest signals from meetings, emails, and calls were never captured, so the answer is always incomplete and always late.”.

It has been revealed that legacy CRMs also fail to capture institutional knowledge, which means that everything a senior sales representative knows about the clients they work with leaves when they depart the company. There’s also a heavy administrative tax, with owners forced to waste valuable time entering data to keep the platform up to date.

It has been revealed that “CRMs don’t have a shortage of features,” Venkatraman remarked. “But they have a shortage of context and trust, and they lack the ability to get actual work done.”.

Dreamteam does things differently. By capturing the unspoken context around each deal an organization does, it says, its platform can help to prevent newly introduced leads from going stale. Monitoring everything that’s stated and agreed to in meetings, via chats and emails and other tools, the platform can pick out the most notable signals, such as pricing sensitivities, objections and stakeholder dynamics.

It remembers all of the fine details of each specific deal. That way, even if the main sales rep involved suddenly leaves, it will retain all of the context so whoever takes over the account knows what needs to be done next.

It has been revealed that the platform also employs humanlike reasoning. “When a prospect says, ‘The board is pushing hard on costs,’ it knows the proposal should lead with ROI, not features,” Venkatraman explained. “The CRM was supposed to give companies a complete picture of their customers, yet the richest parts of that picture have always lived outside the CRM.”.

The startup has already witnessed significant traction with its agentic, contextual approach: It’s used by hundreds of organizations across the AI, healthcare, manufacturing, consulting and online media sectors. Dreamteam has enabled those early adopters to transform the way they handle sales.

It has been revealed that because the CRM continuously self-updates its records following daily customer interactions, it means sales people have much more time to focus on actually selling rather than data entry. Senior leaders have more visibility into deal pipelines, and can immediately find out why deals are stalling or how their customer’s sentiments are shifting.

In a recent development, scott Olechowski, chief product officer at the video streaming service Plex Inc., said he was especially taken with the tight level of integration with Dreamteam and the tech giant’s existing information technology stack. “The combination of simplicity and power hits the sweet spot for us,” he said. “The ability to integrate with the AI tools we are using across our organization is a game-changer.”.

Sources indicate that venkatraman believes Dreamteam can have an even greater impact in future by expanding its shared intelligence layer beyond sales operations. His ambition is to build a platform that spans the entire customer lifecycle, from onboarding to customer success, renewals and upselling, to ensure that organizations can squeeze the most value out of the deal context it captures.

Industry observers note that “Much of what’s learned during sales is lost or fragmented when a customer moves into implementation or customer success,” he pointed out. “But the same company brain that knows why a customer bought should also help teams onboard them, spot risks and find ways to grow the relationship.”.

Recent findings suggest that one way Dreamteam intends to pursue this vision is through what it calls “Magic Apps,” which is a capability that lets owners build custom dashboards and tailored CRM workflows using natural language prompts. “The apps live inside Dreamteam, inherit its data permissions and action-level authorizations, and stay connected to customer records, workflows and the Firm Brain, so you can customize without rebuilding the foundation,” Venkatraman stated.

In a recent development, premji Invest’s Saravanan Nattanmai has already bought into this vision, stressing the need for CRM systems to become more than just a system of record. He characterizes what Dreamteam is building as a “system of intelligence.”.

It has been revealed that “Dreamteam sets out to intuitively understand user intent, build deep contextual intelligence and execute workflows seamlessly through autonomous AI teammates,” he said. “We believe the future of enterprise software lies in AI-native systems that don’t just augment existing workflows but fundamentally reimagine how work gets done.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I’LL ADMIT IT: sweaters are my kryptonite. Long before I was a style editor, they were my secret weapon. Those moments have stuck with me, teaching me that style isn’t about what you wear but how you wear it. Sweaters became my canvas—and they still are, whether I’m braving the elements or dressing to impress.

According to recent reports, since 2020, the Men’s Health style team and I have tested more than 50 styles—crewnecks, cable knits, turtlenecks—to find the ones that actually deliver. Sweaters are also one of my go-to holiday gifts since they’re practical and available at just about every price point. Yield-Bearing eZAR Blurs the Line Between Stablecoin and Investment Product

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1368 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation.
  • Most stablecoin introduces promise a token that never moves.
  • Recent findings suggest that according to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to fresh institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

According to recent reports, eZAR opened its rand-pegged token to the public on November 2 with R303 million in circulation. Its reserve yield is the feature that puts the stablecoin label to the test.

Most stablecoin introduces promise a token that never moves. eZAR's disclosures say its holders can make money or lose it. The rand-pegged token went live to the public on November 2, and its fine print reads more like an investment product than a payments coin.

Recent findings suggest that according to launch reports, eZAR is now open to the public and to fresh institutional partners after almost a year of pilot operations. The company says R303 million worth of tokens had been issued and were in circulation as of October 30.

The project is a partnership between eZAR Ltd, asset manager Ninety One and AVBOB Financial Services, with AVBOB acting as lead institution and liquidity partner. CEO Sean Emery remarked the team put "getting it right" ahead of "getting it big" during the pilot. The message now is that eZAR is ready to scale.

It has been revealed that the model also departs from the typical single-issuer coin. Neobanks, retailers, insurers and payment firms can plug the token into their own branded wallets and share in the economics. Transfers between participating wallets settle within seconds at any hour and, according to the company, cost nothing.

Sources indicate that the reserves backing eZAR are invested through a money market strategy run by Ninety One, mainly in the Ninety One Money Market Fund. Returns are distributed daily to partners after partnership fees, and each partner then decides on what terms its own customers receive a share.

Recent findings suggest that ninety One's head of digital assets, Adam Duxbury, described it as fresh rails under an old discipline. His firm has run money market strategies for 25 years, he said, and South Africa should build its own digital rand rather than import a dollar coin.

The framing is clever, since it presents the yield as a feature of "digital cash that can grow." Yet that same feature makes the classification question hard to avoid.

Recent findings suggest that the risk language is the most revealing part of the launch. eZAR describes itself as a crypto asset issued by the eZAR En Commandite Partnership. It states that the token is not legal tender, not a bank deposit and not a banking product, and that it carries no guarantee.

Recent findings suggest that the details that follow set it further apart. The R1 redemption value depends on available liquidity. Money market returns can be positive or negative, so capital is at risk. Holders also own no units in the underlying fund and have no direct claim on it.

"Capital at risk" rarely appears in stablecoin terms. A payments token is meant to hold its value and let users redeem at par, yet eZAR's own documents hedge on both counts. Back in March, a market survey from Blockhouse had already noted that eZAR doesn't qualify as a stablecoin under most regulations. The live launch now tests that observation against a real product.

It has been revealed that in the major rulebooks, the yield is the sticking point. The US GENIUS Act bars permitted payment stablecoin issuers from paying holders any form of interest or yield solely for holding, using or retaining the token. The EU's MiCA framework takes a similar line on interest. The logic is that a payment token paying a return starts to function like an unregulated deposit.

Recent findings suggest that the OCC issued its final GENIUS Act rules on October 21, and they confirmed that ban for covered issuers. The contested ground lies elsewhere, in who sits between the issuer and the holder. Earlier OCC proposals set a rebuttable presumption against yield arrangements run through affiliates and related third parties, whereas the statute itself names only issuers.

eZAR's design lands squarely in that gray zone. Returns flow to partners, and the partners decide how customers share in them. Whether that amounts to an issuer paying yield or a partner passing on profit is precisely the kind of question US regulators are now wrestling with, and it would be a difficult one to argue before the OCC.

It has been revealed that eZAR doesn't operate under the US or EU regimes, so none of those rules apply to it directly. eZAR Ltd is described as an authorised financial services provider responsible for the main technology and services behind the partnership. That technology also draws on the South African Reserve Bank's Project Khokha 2, where eZAR's parent organization, Block Markets Africa, was a technical contributor.

Sources indicate that this background signals a serious, institution-backed build rather than a speculative launch. Even so, the rand stablecoin field is getting crowded. ZARU launched earlier this year as an institutional-grade rand coin, and a pattern is emerging of different models competing for the same local payments niche.

The bigger question is whether South Africa will define stablecoins narrowly, as the US and EU do, or leave room for hybrid products like this one. Because the network is permissioned, the reported circulation figure also rests on company disclosure rather than a public ledger, which makes the regulatory and disclosure framework matter even more.

Recent findings suggest that for everyday people, the appeal is easy to see. A rand token that moves in seconds, costs nothing to send and might earn a daily return makes an attractive pitch. For partners, shared infrastructure with a revenue share offers a way into digital payments without building a coin from scratch.

In a recent development, the trade-off sits in the disclaimers. A holder who treats eZAR like a bank balance could be caught off guard by liquidity-dependent redemption, or by a money market return that dips below zero. That gap between how the product feels and how it is legally defined is where regulators tend to step in.

Industry observers note that eZAR is best understood as a hybrid: a payments token with an investment return attached. It may well succeed on those terms. Still, as more jurisdictions tighten the stablecoin definition around no-yield, par-redemption tokens, products like this will increasingly be judged on what they are rather than what they are called. How South African regulators treat eZAR in the coming months will show which way that debate is heading.

  • The Tigard, Ore., startup offers instruments and software for creating images of cells and automating analysis.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 12:51 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 4:38 pm.

Araceli Biosciences, a Portland-area biotech firm, has secured $4.5 million in funding to help commercialize technology and develop latest products that support using human cells instead of animal studies to test new drugs.

The Tigard, Ore., startup offers instruments and software for creating images of cells and automating analysis. Its technologies fall under the umbrella term “Newly introduced Approach Methodologies,” which includes human-tissue models, computer simulations and AI-based approaches that reduce or avoid experimentation on animals such as mice, rats and monkeys.

Supporters of the methods, known as NAMs, argue that they can yield better outcomes because animals are not a perfect substitute for humans and can generate irrelevant findings. That can lead to costly, time-intensive development of drugs that fail to perform in people. Advocates also promote the alternatives as more humane.

The National Institutes of Health revealed $84 million in September to build infrastructure for NAMs research at 10 sites nationwide.

“[T]he efforts signal a significant investment into human-based technologies as the future of preclinical science, aiming to make research faster, more predictive, and more directly relevant to human health,” the NIH said in a release.

According to recent reports, araceli mentioned it has raised a total of $22.7 million from investors. The upcoming round was led by William Cortelyou and included Fluke Venture Partners, according to PitchBook. The company disclosed Thursday that businessman and animal welfare advocate Jeff Swickard was also an investor.

Swickard owns 54 auto dealerships across Western states and is a commercial real estate investor with $250 million invested in Portland properties.

Shawn MacDonald, chief financial officer for Araceli, noted Swickard’s “support reflects a belief that we share, which is that better science and more humane science go hand-in-hand.”.

Araceli launched in 2023 as a spinoff from Phoseon Technology, which makes UV LED units for industrial curing and life sciences applications.

It has been revealed that the company stated that companies and institutions using Araceli technology include the Max Planck Institute and Evotec in Germany, the Wertheim UF Scripps Institute in Florida, VALID Therapeutics in Boston, and Ginkgo Bioworks, as well as large pharmaceutical companies. It has 30 employees.

WHEELING, W.Va., Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- WesBanco, Inc. (Nasdaq: WSBC), a diversified, multi-state bank holding firm, confirmed today that Matthew Coppola has been appointed Executive Vice President and Chief Credit Officer, effective November 16, 2026. In this role, Coppola will report to Nathan Jones, Senior Executive Vice President, and Chief Risk Officer, and succeeds Bob Friend, who will retire at the end of 2026 following nearly 15 years with WesBanco.

"Matthew understands that growth and strong credit discipline go hand-in-hand," remarked Nathan Jones, Chief Risk Officer, WesBanco. "His combination of credit expertise, leadership and practical understanding of commercial banking make him the right leader to build on the strong foundation Bob has established and partner with our business leaders to support continued growth. We are pleased to welcome him to WesBanco.".

"I am excited to join Nathan and the WesBanco team at an vital time for the firm," mentioned Matthew Coppola, incoming Chief Credit Officer. "WesBanco has a clear commitment to disciplined growth, and I look forward to building on that strength and partnering with our leaders and bankers to help deliver an even better experience for the customers, businesses and communities we serve.".

In the Chief Credit Officer role, Coppola will be responsible for overseeing the Credit organization including credit adjudication and decisioning, secured credit, credit resolution, and retail credit operations.

Coppola has more than 20 years of experience in commercial credit, credit risk, and lending. He joins WesBanco from UMB Bank, where he most recently served as Executive Vice President and Regional Credit Officer, with responsibility for credit adjudication and risk management across several commercial lending verticals, including capital funding, asset-based lending, franchise finance, and healthcare.

Previously, Coppola held a variety of senior credit leadership roles at Huntington National Bank, including Regional Credit Officer, Credit Policy Officer, and Credit Reporting Manager. Earlier in his career, Coppola held credit and commercial lending positions with MB Financial Bank, Bankers' Bank, Independent Bankers' Bank and Merrill Lynch Business Financial Services.

He earned bachelor's degrees in finance and economics from Michigan State University.

It has been revealed that about WesBanco, Inc.With over 150 years as a community-focused, regional financial services partner, WesBanco Inc. (Nasdaq: WSBC) and its subsidiaries build lasting prosperity through relationships and solutions that empower our customers for success in their financial journeys. Customers across our ten-state footprint choose WesBanco for the comprehensive range and personalized delivery of our retail and commercial banking solutions, as well as trust, brokerage, wealth management, and insurance services, all designed to advance their financial goals. Through the strength of our teams, we leverage large bank capabilities and local focus to help make every community we serve a better place for people and businesses to thrive. Headquartered in Wheeling, West Virginia, WesBanco has $28.5 billion in total assets, with our Trust and Investment Services holding $8.1 billion of assets under management and securities account values (including annuities) of $2.5 billion through our broker/dealer, as of September 30, 2026. Learn more at www.wesbanco.com and follow @WesBanco on Facebook, LinkedIn, and Instagram.

10 stages of a DNS lookup, from phonebook idea to resolver cache

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 18 min read (3644 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~18 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ten stages of a DNS lookup, from the phonebook idea to resolver caches, and how the 2025 AWS outage highlights where each can stall.
  • Every app login, bank transfer and video call starts with a step the user never sees, in which a computer turns a name into an address it can reach.
  • The reliance on a few operators reaches all the way to the top of the system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ten stages of a DNS lookup, from the phonebook idea to resolver caches, and how the 2025 AWS outage highlights where each can stall.

Every app login, bank transfer and video call starts with a step the user never sees, in which a computer turns a name into an address it can reach. When that step failed in October 2025, an outage in Amazon $AMZN Web Services' US-East-1 region affected DNS resolution, according to Enterprise Times. Lloyds Bank, Bank of Scotland, Vodafone, BT and HMRC, Britain's tax agency, were among the British organizations affected, ABC News reports, and consumers of Robinhood, Snapchat and Roblox $RBLX lost service at the same time. A bank, a phone manufacturer, a tax office, a trading app and a video game share almost nothing except the lookup they all rely on. "Almost everything in AWS [and the internet in general] depends on DNS," Ryan Ko, director of the University of Queensland's Cyber Research Centre, said, as reported by ABC News. The Domain Name System, the internet's address book, is a single point of failure that most people don't know exists, so when people can't reach it, they experience the failure as an outage of everything at once.

The reliance on a few operators reaches all the way to the top of the system. The root of DNS, the top layer of the address book, is run by twelve entities, according to APNIC. That leaves very few organizations in control of the layer that every fresh lookup ultimately depends on. Engineers treat that concentration as a design problem rather than bad luck. ABC News reports that Junade Ali, a U.K. software engineer and fellow at the Institution of Engineering and Technology, sees the outage as a warning against relying on one region of one cloud company and as a reason to design essential services to withstand failure. The engineers who built DNS handled its enormous load by passing requests between layers of servers and storing answers close to users. Whether a site becomes unreachable, stays unreachable after a fix or recovers for one user at a time depends on which of those layers fails.

Cloudflare set out to explain, step by step, how the domain names people type become the addresses their browsers need. It covered the cache inside a user's browser, the resolver that takes a user's request and the servers at the root of the system. Each stage of that process exists to make browsing faster or cheaper to run. Each stage is also a place where a lookup can stall, return an outdated answer or hide an outage, and the slides that follow examine every stage both ways.

People find things online by name, but the machines that serve websites can be reached only by number, so a translation has to happen before any page can load. Cloudflare describes DNS as the system for converting the names people use into the addresses browsers need. Every other step of a visit waits on that conversion. On the machine side, an address takes a form such as 192.168.1.1, a string of digits no one would want to memorize for every site they use. A phonebook works the same way: nobody memorizes it, everybody needs it, and nobody thinks about it while it works.

According to recent reports, lookups happen constantly and out of sight. Every page load, app refresh and background sync needs either a fresh translation or a stored one, and the phonebook is consulted without anyone asking for it. F-root, one part of the system's top layer, is responsible for billions of requests a day, according to Cloudflare. At that volume, looking up addresses is ordinary background traffic rather than an occasional event. A service used that often and that quietly becomes invisible to the people who rely on it, and when it stumbles, they have no way to tell what has actually failed.

Without the phonebook, every number still works but nobody can find it. In Virginia alone, Amazon $AMZN runs well over 100 data centers, according to figures from The Associated Press reported by ABC News, yet all of them together counted for little when the directory broke down during the October 2025 Amazon Web Services outage. "So even though the servers were up, many systems couldn't find their way there," Ryan Ko, director of the University of Queensland's Cyber Research Centre, said, as reported by ABC News. The outage was not a malicious attack, according to AWS statements reported by ABC News. The directory went down without any intruder involved, which means a fault inside the system can be enough to cut customers off.

To a user, a missing phonebook entry looks the same as a dead site, and a fault in one quiet translation step can look like the whole internet has gone dark.

A web address seems like something a browser simply knows, but finding the number behind it takes several machines working in sequence. Loading a webpage involves four different DNS servers, according to Cloudflare. Each of the four does a separate job: the recursor takes the question to a root server, then to a top-level domain, or TLD, server and finally to the site's authoritative nameserver. Splitting the work this way keeps lookups fast because no single machine has to know everything. The cost is that the answer depends on every one of those handoffs succeeding.

The recursor works on the user's behalf, much as a librarian takes a visitor's question and goes looking for the book so the visitor doesn't have to search the shelves. The root nameserver plays the part of the library's index. It can't supply the address, but it points the recursor toward the right section. The TLD server covers one section of names, all of which share the same final label, such as the "com" in example.com. It sends the recursor on toward the specific site. With each stop, the search narrows from every name on the internet to a single domain in just a few moves.

Only the authoritative nameserver holds the site's actual address, the way one particular dictionary sits on one rack in the library. That server returns the IP address to the recursor, which carries it back to the browser. The lookup is finished only when the answer has made that return trip, not at the moment the right server finds it. The other three servers give directions rather than answers, so none of them can stand in for the one that holds the address.

When a site's name won't turn into an address, the trouble could lie at any of these four stops.

Industry observers note that A DNS lookup begins and ends on two separate machines, and the organization that runs the first one is usually not the website a person is trying to reach. Every query starts at a recursive resolver and ends at an authoritative server, which holds the site's records, according to Cloudflare. Comcast $CMCSA, an internet provider, operates recursive resolvers, and so do public services including Google $GOOGL DNS and OpenDNS. When a page won't load, the fault may lie with one of those companies rather than with the site. They are separate businesses from the sites whose addresses they look up, so a site that seems to be down may have done nothing wrong.

The two ends carry different responsibilities, so one can fail while the other keeps working. During the AWS outage, the recursive layer went offline, according to Enterprise Times. Every lookup begins at that layer, and many queries could not start at all. "Authoritative DNS defines the truth; recursive DNS delivers it," Deepika Chauhan, a product leader at DigiCert, told Enterprise Times. A website can therefore appear dead even when its own records are correct and its own servers are healthy. People see an outage of the site, but the failure sits in the layer in front of it.

In a recent development, because the two ends fail separately, site owners and users have to build backup at each one. A site owner who spreads a domain's records across several providers protects the end that holds the correct answer. That step does nothing for a user whose resolver has stopped responding. A user who switches to a second resolver gains nothing if the site's own authoritative servers are down.

The resolver that a person's internet provider or device chose for them often decides whether the internet works for that person on a given day.

It has been revealed that when a person types the name of a site their computer hasn't visited recently, no server along the way hands back an address until the very end of the search. An uncached lookup runs through eight steps, according to Cloudflare, and each step narrows the search without finishing it. The resolver's first request goes to a root nameserver, which holds directions toward the right part of the address book but no site's address. The next stop is the server for a top-level domain such as .com, where the resolver learns which server handles the site's domain but still not the site's address. The domain's own nameserver is the last server queried and the only one in the chain that holds the address. Every stop before it supplies directions rather than an answer, so a lookup that feels instant is really a sequence that can stall at any point. The resolver returns the address to the browser at the eighth step, and until then the browser has nothing it can use.

Industry observers note that the website itself waits on that lookup, because the browser requests the page only after all eight DNS steps are done. A lookup that never finishes stops a visit before any part of the site loads. AWS pointed to a problem in this part of the process during its October 2025 outage. "Based on our investigation, the concern appears to be related to DNS resolution of the DynamoDB API endpoint in US-EAST-1," AWS noted in an enhancement on its service support website, as reported by ABC News. Other AWS services in the same region were affected as well. A fault in the lookup steps for a single endpoint was enough to cause trouble well beyond that one service.

Sources indicate that when the eight steps work, nobody notices them. When the final answer doesn't come back, the browser has no partial result to show, only an address it never received and a page it never requested.

Industry observers note that every lookup that a browser can't answer from its own memory goes to one machine before it goes anywhere else. Cloudflare identifies the DNS resolver as the point where that search begins. The browser doesn't search the internet for an address on its own. It sends the request to the resolver and waits for a reply. If the resolver is slow or unreachable, the reader is stuck before any root, top-level-domain or authoritative server has received the question. A reader's resolver may belong to the company that sells them internet service, such as Comcast $CMCSA, or to a free public option such as Google $GOOGL DNS or OpenDNS. Whichever one handles a reader's requests stands in front of every uncached lookup that person makes, on every site they try to visit.

Industry observers note that the word "recursive" names two different things in DNS, and keeping them apart reveals where the effort lands. A recursive query is the request that a reader's device sends. The recursive resolver is the machine that receives that request and carries out the search. The device asks one time and expects a finished answer in return, and all the trips to other servers happen at the resolver. This distinction changes how a stalled lookup should be read. The device's part of the job ends once it sends the question. The resolver is the part that every uncached request depends on, so a problem there stops lookups for everyone who uses it.

When the resolver already holds an answer, a reader's lookup can end there without reaching any other server.

Industry observers note that A DNS lookup is a set of questions, and the way each question is phrased decides which machine does the work. Splitting the job among three kinds of query, recursive, iterative and non-recursive, shortens the distance a lookup has to cover, according to Cloudflare. The speed comes from that division of labor rather than from any single fast server. Each kind of query hands off a different share of the job. A recursive query demands a finished answer, an iterative query lets a server point somewhere else, and a non-recursive query goes to a server that already has the record. For the phone or laptop a person is using, the arrangement is simple: the device sends one recursive query and waits for the resolver to handle every other step.

Recent findings suggest that handing off the whole job has a cost when no answer can be found. A device that asks recursively waits for one of two results, the record or an error, and it gets the error whenever the resolver cannot find the record. The resolver is the only server the device ever contacts. All the work done further along the chain reaches the person at the keyboard as that single reply.

Behind the resolver, most questions are passed along rather than answered. In an iterative query, a server that lacks the record replies with a referral to a lower-level authoritative server. Each referral moves the question one level further down, and a lookup built from referrals passes through several servers before any of them supplies the record. The fastest answers skip that chain altogether. In a non-recursive query, the server already holds the record, either because it is the authority for that domain or because it kept a copy in its cache. Some of the quickest answers therefore come from stored copies rather than from the server that owns the record.

Those stored copies, which answer without consulting anyone else, are the next part of the system.

It has been revealed that most lookups never make the full trip through the address book, because an answer that someone already fetched is kept and used again. Holding that answer close to the user means faster load times, according to Cloudflare. A person sees the page sooner when no distant server has to be consulted first. The larger payoff is on the server side. Providers that keep copies on their own servers avoid extra bandwidth use and spare the servers higher up from answering the same question again and again. Caching is part of how operators keep the address book running under heavy demand, and the system as a whole depends on answers being reused.

A stored answer can't be trusted forever. If copies never expired, a site that moved to a new address would stay unreachable for anyone still holding the old one. Every cached record carries a time-to-live, or TTL, and each cache keeps the record only for that period. Users see a change made at the source only after their copy expires and a fresh lookup takes place. That expiry is the central trade-off of caching. A longer TTL saves more trips up the chain, but it also keeps an old answer in use longer, whether the change upstream is a move, a failure or a fix.

Stored answers can also keep a repaired service out of reach for some people after the fix. A person who can't load a site that has been declared fixed may be getting a stale copy, which goes away when its TTL runs out or when someone empties the cache.

The stored copies that make lookups quick can also be part of why people regain access one by one after an outage, rather than all at once.

In a recent development, the quickest DNS lookup is one that never leaves the user's own computer. When a person returns to a site, the answer can come from the browser itself, because the browser's cache is checked before any other storage, according to Cloudflare. The National Weather Service reports that a DNS cache holds the IP addresses of recently viewed webservers. For a site someone has visited recently, the address may already be stored in the browser. On those visits, no resolver, root server or nameserver further up the chain has to be asked anything, and the page can load without waiting on outside servers.

A saved address is accurate only as long as the site stays where it was. If a website moves to a upcoming server location, a stale entry in the cache can leave that site unreachable, according to the National Weather Service. Every DNS cache, the browser's included, keeps an answer for its time-to-live, and the user stays cut off from the moved site until that timer runs out or the cache is cleared. The correct address exists further up the chain, but the user's machine checks the copy closest to the user first.

It has been revealed that clearing the saved copies solves the problem, but some instructions for doing so leave the browser out. The National Weather Service explains how to flush the DNS cache on old operating systems, and its instructions do not mention caches inside browsers. A user who follows those steps works on the operating system's cache, the next local layer after the browser, and gets no direction at all for the browser's own copy, which is the first one checked.

The cache closest to the user saves the most time, yet those instructions give users no help clearing it.

When a browser has no stored address for a site, the computer still has one more place to check before the question is sent to the network. The operating system keeps its own cache of DNS records. Cloudflare explains that this cache is the second and last local stop before a query is sent off the machine. The browser's cache is checked first and the operating system's cache next. Only when neither holds the record is the question handed to the stub resolver. A match in the operating system's cache means no outside server is consulted at all, which makes this cache the last answer a device can supply for itself. The stub resolver is the device's exit point for a lookup, not another place to find the answer.

It has been revealed that the stub resolver marks a line of control. Every check before it happens on hardware the user owns, and every check after it happens on servers someone else operates. The shortcuts that let a lookup skip large parts of the address book happen at the internet provider's resolver, after the stub resolver, and not inside the operating system. A user's computer can answer a lookup from its own cache or pass the question along, and it can do nothing more. Once the question has gone out, the speed of the answer depends on what the provider's resolver has stored. By that point both of the computer's own caches have already been checked, and the machine has no other local stop left to try.

For a typical user, the operating system's cache is the last point where the answer still depends on their own computer.

A resolver doesn't climb the whole chain for every lookup. It starts at the highest point its memory can't already answer. When the resolver run by an internet provider already holds records for a domain's nameservers or its top-level domain, it can skip the root and TLD servers, according to Cloudflare. Those are the most distant stops in the chain. In the best case, a resolver holds a site's nameserver records but not its address, so it asks those authoritative nameservers directly and the lookup shrinks to its final exchange. Much of the speed a user feels when a page loads comes from what the resolver already remembers, not from how quickly the servers it asks can respond.

Skipping the root also keeps the top layer of the address book from being flooded, but that protection has limits. Resolvers contact the root servers only when they hold nothing pointing to a TLD, yet requests to the root rose 40% over 2023 and 2024, according to APNIC. Caching has not capped the load at the top of the system. About half of all requests to the root come back saying no such name exists, and ordinary stored records help only with lookups for real names. Geoff Huston, an author at the APNIC Blog, describes the technique that lets resolvers reuse a "no such name" answer as a short-term response to the root's growth rather than a long-term one. The rising load supports his view.

Stored answers also explain why trouble at the top of the chain would not reach users all at once. A resolver that holds TLD records doesn't need the root server at all. If the servers above it stopped answering, its lookups would keep working until those entries expired. "The light of the DNS would slowly fade to black bit by bit as these cached entries time out and are removed," Huston mentioned. That gradual fade buys time, but it doesn't provide safety, because the missing layer highlights once the stored entries run out. Huston suggests that resolvers keep the entire root zone on hand. On March 14, 2025, that file measured 2.2 Mbytes, according to APNIC. A resolver holding it would never have to send a request to the root servers, and an outage there would become a much smaller risk.

The stored answers that shorten a lookup are the same ones that keep the address book standing, and how much they hold decides how hard a failure lands.

  • Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture has decided not to seek further NASA funding for its Orbital Reef space station project in order to tighten its focus on lunar missions.
  • For the past five years, Blue Origin has played a lead role in Orbital Reef, alongside partners including Sierra Space and Boeing.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Alan Boyle on Nov 13, 2026 at 2:35 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 2:35 pm.

Jeff Bezos’ Blue Origin space venture has decided not to seek further NASA funding for its Orbital Reef space station project in order to tighten its focus on lunar missions.

For the past five years, Blue Origin has played a lead role in Orbital Reef, alongside partners including Sierra Space and Boeing. In late 2021, Blue Origin won a $130 million contract from NASA in the first phase of the space agency’s Commercial Low Earth Orbit Destinations program, or CLD.

Industry observers note that now NASA is seeking proposals for the next phase of the program, which will fund the development of orbital outposts to replace International Space Station in the 2030s. Proposals are due on Dec. 8, with contracts expected to be awarded next spring.

Blue Origin indicated that it will not submit a bid.

According to recent reports, “Blue Origin’s mission is to build a road to space for the benefit of Earth so that millions of people can live and work in space. Establishing a sustained human presence on the moon is a critical step toward that future,” the firm mentioned in an emailed statement.

“As our role supporting NASA’s Artemis and Moon Base missions continues to grow, we’re focusing resources on capabilities that directly advance our lunar projects,” Blue Origin said. “By sharpening that focus, we can move faster on the technologies and infrastructure needed to make lunar permanence a reality.”.

Orbital Reef was once touted as a “mixed-use business park” in space — and was even slated to star in a sci-fi thriller titled “Helios.” But much like that delayed film project, the space station is now on the back burner.

It has been revealed that orbital Reef isn’t the only initiative Blue Origin has put on hold to prioritize moon missions. In January, the manufacturer suspended its suborbital Newly introduced Shepard program for at least two years for similar reasons.

Industry observers note that blue Origin is building landers for delivering cargo and crews to the lunar surface for NASA. An uncrewed Blue Moon Mark 1 lunar lander is scheduled for launch early next year, and a crew-capable Mark 2 version is scheduled for testing in low Earth orbit next year during NASA’s Artemis 3 mission.

Last week, NASA awarded Blue Origin a $94 million base contract, plus a $140 million option, to deliver a nuclear-powered rover to the lunar south pole. Blue Origin also won a spot in NASA’s broader lunar cargo delivery program. In addition, Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin subsidiary, will contribute to a lunar power-generating project known as miniCAST.

Blue Origin is pursuing several other moon development initiatives, including a program called Blue Alchemist that aims to use lunar materials to manufacture solar cells and electrical wire.

Sources indicate that several competitors are still working on commercial space stations. Voyager Technologies, Airbus and Northrop Grumman lead the Starlab consortium, which received CLD Phase 1 funding from NASA and is expected to put in a proposal for Phase 2.

Axiom Space and Vast are also developing outposts that could take the place of the ISS. Meanwhile, Marysville, Wash.-based Gravitics is building space station hardware for Axiom and an orbital carrier for the U.S. Space Force.

Google claims an AI framework turned security patches into exploits with no human in the loop

💡 Key Takeaways
  • A upcoming report out today from Google LLC’s Google Threat Intelligence Group finds that for the first time, attackers have used an artificial intelligence framework running with no human in the loop to turn security patches into exploits.
  • Called exploit_agent, the framework turned up on an exposed staging server, where it was wired into several frontier and locally hosted large language models.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 09:00 EST / NOVEMBER 16 2026.

A upcoming report out today from Google LLC’s Google Threat Intelligence Group finds that for the first time, attackers have used an artificial intelligence framework running with no human in the loop to turn security patches into exploits.

Called exploit_agent, the framework turned up on an exposed staging server, where it was wired into several frontier and locally hosted large language models. Its job, according to GTIG, is continuous comparison of popular web application code before and after each patch announcement. Once a likely flaw is identified, the exploit it drafts is executed automatically.

Data taken from victims was sitting on the same server, alongside scripts for brute-forcing, installing webshells and even removing webshells left by rival attackers. Victim telemetry suggests the operator was most interested in French websites tied to media, entertainment and education. Written in Russian, one comment in the framework’s configuration file tells whoever set it up to enter the keys “right here, not in the chat.”.

In the previous edition of the quarterly tracker two months ago, GTIG remarked it had not observed fully autonomous attack pipelines deployed against targets in the wild. That changed over the past quarter, according to the upcoming report, titled “Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold.” Because the source material for a patched flaw is finite, GTIG believes attackers may find it more efficient to point LLMs at n-day vulnerabilities than to hunt for zero-days.

How rapidly the gap between disclosure and a working exploit can close shows in the case of two flaws in print management servers from PaperCut Software Pty Ltd., chained together and exploited as zero-days in late August. Security researchers and Huntress Labs Inc. used large language models to generate working exploits within a day of disclosure.

A campaign tracked by GreyNoise Intelligence Inc. four days after disclosure is believed to have relied on LLMs to build its exploits before it hit hundreds of organizations. One foothold in that campaign reached domain administrator within minutes, GreyNoise found.

According to recent reports, elsewhere, open-source agentic penetration testing frameworks are being used to automate discrete steps of live intrusions. During one intrusion against the U.S. aerospace sector, a threat actor was observed using the multi-agent framework CAIRN.

Another actor ran a customized platform built on PentAGI between late August and early October to scan a wide range of organizations in Asia for vulnerabilities. For now, the noisy forensic trail left by unrestricted autonomous execution is said to make the frameworks easier to detect.

According to GTIG, influence operations now use models for far more than writing posts. Using cloud phone farms, a turnkey platform that one commercial contractor was building with help from the Gemini API is designed to run more than 100,000 social media accounts. To make generated photos pass as smartphone shots, prompts behind a separate platform, which targeted political sentiment across Europe and the Middle East, are said to have called for deliberate camera flaws.

According to recent reports, among government-backed actors, photos on the fake recruiter profiles that a suspected North Korean group tracked as UNC6836 used to approach cryptocurrency organizations in North America and Europe were found to carry Google’s SynthID watermarks. By way of altered .claude/settings.json files in internal code repositories, the group later rigged each launch of Anthropic PBC’s Claude Code to download its SOMBERMEME backdoor.

Sources indicate that google stated it disabled the accounts and assets tied to the Gemini misuse it found. Google DeepMind has also used the findings to strengthen its classifiers.

Renowned investor and Shark Tank personality Kevin O’Leary has shared his thoughts on the current cryptocurrency crash, stating that the crypto industry faces problems that extend far beyond Bitcoin's dropping price.

In particular, Mr. Wonderful, as O'Leary is better known, believes that one of the biggest problems the crypto industry faces is the lack of regulatory clarity in the United States. This prevents major financial firms from adopting blockchain and stablecoin technologies.

According to O'Leary, institutional crypto adoption has slowed to a crawl. Companies are unwilling to invest any capital until there is clarity around regulations.

"It's not just about Bitcoin in the crypto sell-off. The adoption of stablecoins and blockchain within institutions has slowed down. Companies are waiting for clarity on regulations," O'Leary wrote.

Industry observers note that the billionaire investor shared that his company already utilizes Circle's USDC for treasury management and international settlements. However, many other companies are afraid to follow suit since their compliance teams aren't sure about the regulatory landscape.

"We use USDC for treasury management and cross-border settlement. But many others won't do it till their compliance guys know the rules," O'Leary added.

The famous investor focused on two major U.S. bills regarding cryptocurrency: the GENIUS Act and the CLARITY Act.

"We got the GENIUS Act going. We need the CLARITY Act for the rest," Kevin O'Leary concluded.

O'Leary has long raised concerns about the crypto space and the reasons why Bitcoin is not seeing more institutional investment yet.

Recent findings suggest that for example, on Oct. 28, the billionaire investor named two main concerns affecting Bitcoin. The first was regulatory uncertainty, and the second was the rising threat of quantum computing.

Long-term investors reaffirm commitment to supporting the combined company's growth, product innovation and customer service.

Recent findings suggest that MENLO PARK, Calif. and BOSTON, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Accel-KKR and RS2 Healthcare Partners (formerly Riverside Partners), investors in Loftware, today revealed their support for Loftware's acquisition of Seagull Software, developer of BarTender, bringing together two leading providers of product identification and labeling solutions.

The combination represents an crucial next step in the combined organization's growth, significantly expanding its global reach and ability to serve customers across their lifecycle - from emerging businesses to some of the world's largest enterprises. By bringing together Loftware's enterprise-grade platform and BarTender's broad global footprint and trusted labeling technology, the combined company will offer customers and partners a more comprehensive set of product identification solutions while creating additional opportunities to accelerate innovation.

For more than 40 years, Loftware has been at the forefront of an industry that began with labeling and has evolved into the much broader and more strategic field of product identification. As customer needs have expanded - from label design and management to traceability, compliance, product intelligence and supply chain collaboration - Loftware has continued to expand its capabilities and global footprint alongside them. The combination with Seagull Software represents the next step in that evolution.

"Loftware has a long history of leading and helping shape this market as it has evolved, and we see this combination as another notable step forward," said Park Durrett, Managing Director at Accel-KKR. "Loftware and Seagull are highly complementary businesses, and together they will be able to serve a broader set of customers, across more markets and throughout their growth journey. We see a significant opportunity for the combined manufacturer to accelerate product innovation and expand capabilities in areas such as traceability and trading partner connectivity.
