9 places on Earth that look like Mars, and how to visit them

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3898 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These places that look like Mars, from Chile's Atacama Desert to Jordan's Wadi Rum, show how red-planet terrain appears on Earth and what it takes to reach each one.
  • Ground that resembles it is already studied, filmed and explored here on Earth.
  • According to recent reports, A short set of features makes a landscape read as Martian.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These places that look like Mars, from Chile's Atacama Desert to Jordan's Wadi Rum, show how red-planet terrain appears on Earth and what it takes to reach each one.

No person has ever stood on Mars. Ground that resembles it is already studied, filmed and explored here on Earth. Scientists test instruments built for Mars in deserts so dry that the soil holds very little life. Filmmakers send actors into red sandstone valleys to stand in for the Martian plains. Research groups run simulated missions in remote terrain, where crews live and work under mission rules.

According to recent reports, A short set of features makes a landscape read as Martian. Mars gets its red color from iron oxide in its dust and rock. Iron-rich ground on Earth produces a similar palette. Extreme dryness strips away plants and leaves bare rock and loose sediment. Volcanic basalt and cinder echo the planet's ancient lava fields. Impact craters, salt flats and acidic, mineral-heavy water add further points of comparison with red planet terrain.

It has been revealed that researchers call locations used this way Mars analog sites. An analog is not a perfect copy of another planet. It is a place where one or more conditions match closely enough to test equipment, train people or study how life might survive in harsh chemistry. Some of the places that look like Mars on this list serve that scientific purpose. Others share the planet's colors and textures, which is enough for a camera crew or a traveler.

Sources indicate that the nine locations below cover a wide range of Mars-like landscapes. They include a hyperarid desert in Chile, a sandstone valley in Jordan, a salt basin in California and a simulated habitat in the Utah desert. There is also a cratered island in the Canadian Arctic and a sulfur field in Ethiopia. A red river in Spain, a volcanic summit in Hawaii and a caldera in Iceland complete the set. The list is a selection, not a ranking.

In a recent development, the path to each one varies just as widely. Some sit inside parks with visitor centers, paved roads and regular tours. Others require a guide, a four-wheel-drive vehicle or careful planning around altitude, heat or security conditions. The Arctic crater is reached through research logistics rather than independent travel. Each slide explains what the place is, why it resembles Mars and what a realistic visit involves.

Industry observers note that chile's Atacama Desert is a hyperarid region in the north of the country, and researchers have used its pale, rocky ground as a stand-in for Martian terrain. It is often called the driest non-polar desert on Earth.

Industry observers note that dryness, more than color, is what puts the Atacama on this list. One long-running question about Mars is whether life could ever have taken hold in soil that sees so little water. The Atacama poses a version of that question on Earth. Teams have brought life-detection instruments into the desert to check how they perform on ground this barren.

In a recent development, that research role separates the Atacama from places that resemble Mars only in photographs. Large areas are bare rock, gravel and salt-crusted ground with little or no plant cover. A camera sees an alien surface. An engineer sees a place to learn how equipment behaves before it goes somewhere far harder to reach.

Industry observers note that geography helps explain the dryness. The Andes rise along the desert's eastern edge and block much of the moisture that would arrive from that side. To the west, Chile's coastal mountains and the cold Humboldt Current offshore limit how much rain the Pacific delivers.

In a recent development, for travelers, the most accessible Mars-like scenery sits around the small town of San Pedro de Atacama. Two nearby areas draw most of the attention. Valle de la Luna, the Valley of the Moon, is known for wind-eroded ridges and salt formations. It falls within Chile's Los Flamencos National Reserve. Valle de Marte, the Valley of Mars, lies a short distance away and offers a similarly barren landscape of rock ridges and sand.

Most visitors reach the area by flying into Calama, the main air gateway for this part of the desert. From there, a road transfer of a little more than an hour leads to San Pedro. Tours to both valleys can be booked once in town.

Industry observers note that the altitude needs planning of its own. San Pedro and the surrounding desert sit high above sea level. Travelers $TRV arriving from the coast or from lowland cities can feel the change. Headaches and shortness of breath are common early signs. Taking the first day slowly, drinking plenty of water and holding off on strenuous hikes gives the body time to acclimatize. The dry air and strong sun at elevation also make water and sun protection basic gear for any outing into the valleys.

It has been revealed that wadi Rum is a desert valley in southern Jordan. Its red-orange sand and sheer sandstone and granite cliffs have doubled as Mars in several feature films. Paved road access, a visitor center and established local tours also make it one of the easier Mars-like landscapes for travelers to reach.

The resemblance starts with color. Wadi Rum's sand and rock share the orange-red cast of the Martian surface. Broad sandy valley floors run between steep rock walls and isolated outcrops. Plant life is sparse. In wide camera shots, the ground looks bare and open.

Industry observers note that that look has made the valley a regular film location. Ridley Scott used it for scenes in The Martian (2015), in which Matt Damon plays an astronaut stranded on the red planet. Red Planet (2000), starring Val Kilmer, also filmed there. Last Days on Mars (2013) used the desert to represent Martian terrain as well.

It has been revealed that the valley's screen history predates science fiction. Lawrence of Arabia (1962) filmed in the area. The real T.E. Lawrence passed through Wadi Rum during the Arab Revolt of World War I.

Sources indicate that UNESCO inscribed the Wadi Rum Protected Area as a World Heritage site in 2011. The listing recognizes both natural and cultural value. Alongside the desert landforms, the area holds rock carvings and inscriptions. People who lived in and crossed the region left them over thousands of years.

Most visitors reach Wadi Rum through Aqaba, Jordan's port city on the Red Sea. From there, travelers continue by road to Wadi Rum Village, the usual base for trips into the desert. Entry to the protected area runs through its visitor center.

According to recent reports, inside the protected area, Bedouin-run outfits handle most of the logistics. Jeep tours carry visitors across the sand to rock formations and narrow canyons. Many travelers stay overnight in desert camps. A night in camp puts them in the valley after dark and at sunrise. Low morning light deepens the red tones of the rock.

Desert conditions shape the trip. Summer daytime heat is intense. Nights can turn cold, especially in winter. Travelers $TRV should carry water, sun protection and warm layers. They should also confirm arrangements with their camp or tour operator before arriving.

Industry observers note that death Valley National Park in eastern California pairs two Mars-like scenes: the white salt flats of Badwater Basin and the mineral-stained hills of Artist's Palette. Both show the dry, bare, oxide-colored ground associated with red planet terrain, and both can be reached by paved road.

Badwater Basin sits 282 feet (86 meters) below sea level. That makes it the lowest point in North America. Its floor is a broad crust of salt left behind as water evaporated. The crust breaks into rough ridges and polygon-shaped plates that stretch toward the mountains on either side of the valley.

That salt is part of the Mars comparison. NASA's Mars Odyssey orbiter has mapped chloride salt deposits on the Martian surface. Those deposits are read as traces of water that evaporated long ago. Badwater offers a walkable version of the same basic process, with a parking area and a short boardwalk at the edge of the flats.

Artist's Palette supplies the color. Its hillsides are streaked in reds, pinks, yellows, greens and purples. The hues come from metals that oxidized as the area's volcanic deposits weathered. Iron compounds account for the reds, pinks and yellows. Visitors reach the viewpoint along Artists Drive, a paved one-way loop road that winds through the colored hills.

The park also holds eroded badlands. These are bare slopes carved into tight gullies, with almost no plant cover to soften their shape. Zabriskie Point, a roadside overlook near Furnace Creek, looks across one stretch of them.

Furnace Creek is the park's main hub. It has the main visitor center, lodging and fuel. Badwater Basin and Artists Drive both lie south of Furnace Creek, off Badwater Road. The nearest major airport is in Las Vegas, and the park is reached from there by car.

One feature does not match Mars at all. Mars is a cold planet, while Death Valley's summer heat is severe and can be dangerous. The National Park Service runs the park and posts current conditions and closures. Visitors should check those conditions with the park before going. They should also carry plenty of water and plan hikes for the cooler months between late fall and early spring.

The Mars Desert Research Station is a simulated Mars habitat that the Mars Society has operated in the red desert outside Hanksville, Utah, since 2001. Crews live there during each simulated mission and work in surrounding terrain that resembles the Martian surface. It is a working research site, not a tourist stop.

Industry observers note that the Mars Society is a nonprofit group founded in 1998 to promote the human exploration and settlement of Mars. Its founder, aerospace engineer Robert Zubrin, is known for the Mars Direct mission plan. The Utah station puts that advocacy into practice. Crews rehearse the daily routines of life on another planet in a place that looks the part.

Sources indicate that the station's main building, known as the Hab, is a two-story cylinder. Crew members sleep, cook and work inside it. When they go outside for field work, they wear mock spacesuits and treat each trip as an extravehicular activity on Mars. That routine lets teams practice the planning, confinement and isolation a real Mars crew would face.

In a recent development, the landscape explains the choice of site. The ground around the station is layered sedimentary rock in bands of red, purple, gray and tan, with very little vegetation. Eroded hills and dry washes give the area the bare, rust-toned look familiar from images sent back by Mars rovers.

For travelers, Hanksville is the base. The small town in Wayne County sits where Utah State Route 24 meets State Route 95. It is the nearest town to the station for fuel, food and lodging. Public roads around Hanksville cross the same kind of eroded badlands that surround the station.

According to recent reports, two protected areas lie within driving distance. Goblin Valley State Park, north of Hanksville, is known for clusters of eroded sandstone hoodoos, which are nicknamed goblins. Capitol Reef National Park lies to the west along Route 24.

Visitors should not blueprint to tour the station or drop in on a crew. Missions are designed to simulate isolation, and the facility is not set up as a regular attraction. Anyone hoping to see it should check the Mars Society's own information before going.

The region is remote desert with long gaps between services. Summer heat can be severe, and dirt roads can turn impassable after rain. Extra water, a full tank and a check of road conditions before leaving Hanksville are basic preparation for exploring the area.

Devon Island, an uninhabited island in Canada's Nunavut territory, holds Haughton impact crater. Researchers use this cold, rocky basin for Mars-style field research. It is not a tourist destination, and access runs through scientific expeditions rather than travel bookings.

The island sits in the Canadian Arctic Archipelago, north of Baffin Island. It is often described as the largest uninhabited island on Earth. No permanent community lives there. There are no hotels, stores or public services.

Recent findings suggest that planetary scientists value Devon Island for its mix of cold, dryness and bare rock. The island is a polar desert. Precipitation is low, and vegetation is sparse across much of its surface. Broken rock lies exposed over wide areas. Those conditions resemble the frozen, barren ground that orbiters and rovers have photographed on Mars.

Haughton crater adds another layer to the comparison. Craters cover much of the Martian surface. Haughton gives researchers a place on Earth to study how a large impact reshapes rock and terrain. Geologists can walk its floor and rims, sample shattered rock and compare what they find with craters seen in Martian imagery.

The Haughton-Mars Project has used the site for this kind of research over many field seasons. Teams camp near the crater during the short Arctic summer. They test field methods, vehicles, communications and procedures that future crews on Mars might use. The work treats the island as a rehearsal space for exploring a remote, hostile surface with limited outside support.

The Mars Society also built a habitat on the island, the Flashline Mars Arctic Research Station, in 2000. Crews have lived in it during simulated missions. They follow routines designed to mimic daily life on another planet.

In a recent development, reaching Devon Island is a logistical operation, not a road trip. Research teams typically stage through Resolute, a small community on Cornwallis Island, and fly in on chartered aircraft. Arctic weather can hold up flights. Polar bears range across the region. Field teams strategy for wildlife safety as part of every expedition.

Industry observers note that for readers drawn to this landscape, the practical route is through the research itself. Expedition reports, mission photographs and published findings from projects on the island offer the most accessible view of its Mars-like ground. Anyone hoping to set foot there would need to join an organized scientific or institutional expedition. An independent journey is not a realistic option.

Sources indicate that the Danakil Depression in northeastern Ethiopia is a low, hot volcanic basin. Its Dallol hydrothermal field coats the ground in yellow, green and red mineral crusts that look more like another planet than a desert on Earth.

Recent findings suggest that the basin lies in Ethiopia's Afar Region, near the border with Eritrea. It is part of the Afar Triangle, where three tectonic plates are slowly pulling apart. Much of the depression sits below sea level. Thin crust, active faults and young volcanoes shape the whole landscape.

Dallol is the main reason the region draws Mars comparisons. Hot, acidic water rises through thick layers of salt laid down by ancient seawater. As that water cools and evaporates, sulfur and salts crystallize into terraces, small chimneys and crusts. Fresh deposits tend to show bright yellow and green. Older deposits turn rust brown as iron compounds oxidize.

Sources indicate that that mix of heat, salt, acidity and iron-rich minerals matters to planetary scientists. NASA's Opportunity rover found jarosite, a sulfate mineral that forms in acidic water, at Meridiani Planum on Mars. Researchers have sampled Dallol's pools to test how much heat, salt and acid living things can tolerate. Those limits help define where scientists look for signs of past life on Mars.

Industry observers note that the volcano Erta Ale rises to the south of Dallol. Its name means "smoking mountain" in the Afar language. The crater has held a lava lake for long stretches of its recorded history. The lake's level and activity change over time. Dark basalt flows surround the summit.

Recent findings suggest that the depression is also a working landscape. Workers cut blocks of salt from the flats by hand. Camel caravans then carry the salt toward markets in the highlands.

It has been revealed that visits happen on organized tours with guides. Tours typically start from Mekelle, the capital of the Tigray Region. Many itineraries cover both Dallol and Erta Ale. Heat is severe and shade is scarce. Roads into the basin are rough, and guided tours supply the vehicles and logistics the trip requires.

Recent findings suggest that northern Ethiopia has seen armed conflict in recent years, and security conditions change. Travelers $TRV should read current advisories from the U.S. State Department or the U.K. Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office before booking.

Rio Tinto is a river in Huelva province, Andalusia, that runs a deep rust red because its water carries high levels of iron and acid linked to mining. Spain's Centro de Astrobiología has studied it as a Mars analog because of its acidic water and iron minerals.

It has been revealed that the name means "red river" in Spanish. Its banks and riverbed are stained in shades of rust, ochre and orange. In some stretches, the water itself turns a dark wine red.

The color comes from chemistry. Acidic water dissolves iron from the surrounding rock and mine waste. That iron then settles out as iron-rich minerals along the channel. Over time, those deposits coat stones and sediment in layers. The result is a valley with an oxidized, red-planet look.

People have mined this area for thousands of years. Iberian and Roman workers dug here for copper and silver. Industrial extraction expanded in the 19th century under the British-backed Rio Tinto Manufacturer, founded in 1873. The mining group that still carries the river's name grew out of that venture.

In a recent development, the Mars connection rests on mineralogy. In 2004, NASA's Opportunity rover found jarosite at Meridiani Planum on Mars. Jarosite is an iron sulfate mineral that forms in acidic water. The same mineral forms along Rio Tinto. That overlap gives researchers a place on Earth to study how such minerals develop. It also helps them judge what those minerals might reveal about past water on Mars.

The river is not lifeless. Microbes and algae adapted to acidic, metal-rich water live in it. Those organisms give scientists a working model for the kinds of life that could, in principle, survive in similar conditions beyond Earth.

According to recent reports, the town of Minas de Riotinto is the usual base for visitors. Its mining museum covers the district's long mining history, from ancient workings to the industrial era. A tourist train runs on a restored stretch of the old mining railway beside the river. Passengers get a close view of the red water and stained banks along the route.

Huelva, the provincial capital, is the nearest city, and Minas de Riotinto lies inland to its northeast. Train and museum schedules vary by season. Check current times with the museum before planning a trip.

Mauna Kea, a volcano on Hawaii's Big Island, rises to 13,803 feet (4,207 meters), and its upper slopes are covered in reddish-brown volcanic cinder. That loose, rust-colored ground has made the mountain a test site for equipment built for Moon and Mars exploration.

Sources indicate that mauna Kea is a dormant shield volcano. It grew from layer upon layer of fluid lava over hundreds of thousands of years. Near the summit, later eruptions piled up cinder cones made of fragmented, oxidized rock. Those cones and the loose debris around them give the upper mountain its red-brown cast.

Mars has shield volcanoes too, built in the same basic way. The largest, Olympus Mons, is far taller than any volcano on Earth. A mountain built from lava and ash gives engineers ground made of some of the same ingredients. Equipment can be tried out on rough, loose material rather than on a flat test surface.

Sources indicate that the summit is more than a test site. Mauna Kea is sacred in Native Hawaiian tradition, and it hosts a cluster of astronomical observatories. Its height puts the summit above much of the atmosphere's moisture, which makes it a strong location for telescopes. Visitors share the area with working scientists and cultural practitioners.

In a recent development, the Massive Island's main airports are at Hilo and Kona. Most trips up the mountain start at the Maunakea Visitor Information Station, which sits at about 9,200 feet. That is roughly 4,600 feet below the summit. Travelers $TRV arriving from sea level are already at serious altitude at that stop. Pausing there before going higher gives the body time to adjust.

Altitude sickness is a real risk on this mountain. Symptoms can include headache, nausea, dizziness and shortness of breath. Climbing too fast raises the risk. People with heart or lung conditions, and anyone who is pregnant, should get medical advice before going up.

Recent findings suggest that rules govern access to the summit road above the visitor station. Much of that stretch is unpaved, and four-wheel-drive vehicles are recommended. Conditions, permitted vehicles and opening times can change. Check the current rules before driving up, or book a guided tour that handles the transport.

It has been revealed that weather near the top can turn cold even when the coast is warm. Snow falls on the summit in winter. Pack warm layers in any season.

Industry observers note that askja is a volcanic caldera in Iceland's central highlands, surrounded by dark basalt, ash and pumice. Its bare volcanic ground shows the kind of rock that covers much of Mars, even though its astronaut history belongs to the Moon.

Sources indicate that A caldera forms when a volcano's summit collapses after magma drains from the chamber beneath it. Askja sits in the Dyngjufjöll mountains, north of the Vatnajökull ice cap. The plain around it has little soil and almost no plant life. Lava fields, cinder and loose pumice stretch out in every direction.

A large eruption in 1875 reshaped the area. In the years that followed, a smaller section inside the main caldera sank and filled with water. That basin became Öskjuvatn, a deep lake. Next to it sits Víti, a smaller explosion crater that holds warm, milky blue-green water.

Sources indicate that apollo astronauts trained in the Askja area during the 1960s. That training prepared them for geology on the Moon, not on Mars. The fieldwork focused on recognizing volcanic rock types on open ground with no vegetation in the way.

The resemblance to Mars comes from rock type rather than color. Basalt is the dominant volcanic rock on Mars. The planet also has large shield volcanoes with summit calderas, including Olympus Mons. Askja's ground is dark gray and black, not rust red. It highlights what volcanic Martian terrain looks like beneath the iron-oxide dust that gives Mars its color.

Reaching Askja takes planning. The highland roads that lead there are unpaved F-roads. They are rough and usually open only in summer. Some routes cross rivers without bridges. F-roads require a 4x4 vehicle, and many visitors book a guided tour instead of driving themselves. Tours commonly depart from the Lake Mývatn area in north Iceland.

Industry observers note that check road conditions with Icelandic road authorities before setting out. Opening dates shift from year to year with snowmelt and weather. Highland weather can also change within a single day. Warm, waterproof layers are standard even in July and August.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 13, 2026 at 3:04 pmNovember 13, 2026 at 7:58 pm.

Updated with officials’ explanation of the cause and the reopening of U.S. airspace.

In a recent development, the nationwide ground stop that halted U.S. commercial air travel Friday was not caused by the Microsoft 365 outage that began a day earlier, federal officials mentioned at an evening news conference, blaming aging FAA telecom equipment that was overloaded with data.

Industry observers note that homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened the news conference by raising the Microsoft outage himself. “I want to make sure everybody understands that there is no connection between this and Microsoft,” he mentioned. “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy likewise ruled out a role for SMART, the FAA’s upcoming AI traffic-planning tool, saying it isn’t connected to the core systems controllers use to track flights.

“There was no possible way SMART would have impacted what happened today,” he remarked.

The FAA reopened U.S. airspace at 5:15 p.m. Pacific, more than four hours after the problems began, Duffy mentioned. He said flights would resume slowly, depending on whether airlines had crews available, and some may not depart until Saturday morning.

Microsoft confirmed in a statement that it had no indication the FAA ground stop was related to its service disruption.

Asked whether a cyberattack or “rogue AI” could be ruled out, Mullin mentioned there was “nothing completely certain right now,” but “it appears that this was mechanically driven.” He said he could not rule out the possibility of a cyberattack but said there was “zero evidence” of one so far.

Sources indicate that what happened: Duffy stated the FAA began seeing unstable radar and communications data at air traffic control facilities across the country at 12:36 p.m. Pacific. Aging switches and routers in the agency’s telecom network “got overloaded with data” and began producing inconsistent information, he said, adding that the FAA still relies on “1980s little copper lines.”.

Duffy noted newer equipment held up.

Sources indicate that “Our latest IP switches did not go down. It’s the old hardware that went down,” he remarked. The FAA restored service after deploying fixes to reduce the overloading on its switches, he said.

Mullin stated the overload appeared to have been triggered by new equipment the FAA was installing. As the agency put “patches into the system” and added “new equipment and new technology,” he said, it “was overwhelming the older system.” Neither official said exactly what that equipment was.

The FAA is in the middle of replacing its legacy telecom network with a modern internet-protocol network. AT&T took over the lead role on that project in August with an initial $74.3 million award, as the FAA works toward a goal of finishing by the end of 2028.

Duffy and Mullin used the briefing to press Congress for money to finish rebuilding the air traffic control system. Mullin said President Trump has declared the situation a national emergency.

The administration has asked Congress for an additional $30.1 billion for aviation infrastructure, AeroTime reported. Duffy noted at the evening news conference that he wants $50 billion.

According to recent reports, earlier in the day, Mullin had said officials were looking into a possible link to SMART, including through DHS’s Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA). The FAA said Tuesday it was expanding the system to the airspace managed by all 22 of its en route air traffic control centers.

Recent findings suggest that the agency describes SMART as a cloud-based system that pulls in about 200 data streams, including weather, flight paths and controller staffing, to recommend flight schedules and routes. FAA specialists review its recommendations, and local facilities decide whether to act on them.

It has been revealed that SMART is part of a 12-year, $875 million FAA contract with Boston-based Air Space Intelligence, which denied any connection to the concern. “The current ground stop is not based on or a result of the SMART system, any product of ASI or our integration with FAA and ATC,” the company said.

The FAA halted departures nationwide shortly before 1 p.m. Pacific. More than 3,500 planes were in the air at the time, Duffy mentioned. It’s the second nationwide ground stop since the Sept. 11 attacks, after a January 2023 failure of the FAA’s Notice to Air Missions system.

FlightAware counted nearly 7,000 flights delayed or canceled as of Friday afternoon.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 09:00 EST / NOVEMBER 16 2026.

Industry observers note that data analytics software firm Sumo Logic Inc. today released an expanded AWS Observability Solution, a monitoring package for Amazon Web Services Inc. people that can now be deployed in one click from AWS Marketplace.

Sumo Logic is pitching the update at cloud teams that would otherwise have to build their own dashboards before they can properly watch an AWS environment. Much of the company’s recent product work has gone into artificial intelligence agents that take on incident investigations.

According to recent reports, support for AWS regions in Zurich, Melbourne and Newly introduced Zealand takes the number covered by the solution to 20. Workloads running in those three regions can now be watched with the same prebuilt alerts Sumo Logic offers elsewhere on 12 core AWS services. Lambda, DynamoDB and Application Load Balancer are among them.

Zurich has been on the firm’s list since February, when Sumo Logic said its security products would come to the AWS Europe (Zurich) Region for customers bound by Switzerland’s Federal Act on Data Protection.

Anyone signing up through Quick Launch, the AWS Marketplace option behind the one-click deployment, can now do the whole thing — buying the package, setting it up and getting it deployed — without stepping outside their own AWS account. Sumo Logic claims the deployments themselves are versioned, in Terraform and CloudFormation alike, which the manufacturer expects will mean less configuration drift over time.

Root Cause Agent, which Sumo Logic put into preview for operations teams on Oct. 13, is where much of the telemetry the package collects ends up. When an alert fires, the agent goes digging through the data on its own. A company blog post from the launch says every finding it turns up can be rerun as a search in one click.

According to recent reports, the agent belongs to Dojo AI, the agentic AI platform Sumo Logic introduced for security operations teams in September 2025. Root Cause Agent carries that investigative work over into observability. Alongside it in October came new Dojo AI packages that bill all of a customer’s agent use, with Mobot, the SOC Analyst Agent and Root Cause Agent included, against one monthly credit pool.

“AI agents are only as good as the telemetry and context provided to them,” mentioned Keith Kuchler, chief product and technology officer at Sumo Logic. Kuchler added that teams on AWS shouldn’t have to keep “working around regions their tools can’t reach.”.

Back in September, Sumo Logic gave customers a way to trim telemetry before ingestion when it expanded its Data Pipelines service. The organization, taken private by Francisco Partners in 2023 for $1.7 billion, will show the AWS package at AWS re:Invent in Las Vegas Nov. 30-Dec. 4.

Through Sumo Logic’s listings in AWS Marketplace, version 3.0.0 of the solution is available now to customers that monitor AWS infrastructure.

Canton Coin Gets SEC "Digital Commodity" Label: Here's What the Two Prongs Actually Mean

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1331 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3.
  • According to recent reports, the most notable words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made.
  • On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Industry observers note that the SEC's Division of Corporation Finance called Canton Coin a digital commodity on November 3. The ruling rests on two representations, including the absence of a "central party.".

According to recent reports, the most notable words in the SEC's Canton Coin letter aren't "digital commodity." They are the ones the staff put in front of that label: the conclusion holds "in reliance on the representations" Canton's lawyers made. The SEC didn't independently prove the network has no central party. It accepted a description and attached a conclusion to it.

On November 3, the Division of Corporation Finance's Office of Chief Counsel answered Canton Network's October 30 request. The response came from Deputy Chief Counsel Jonathan A. Ingram and was addressed to the staff team of Ted Yu, Andrew Schoeffler and Mark Vilardo. The Division remarked it views Canton Coin as a "digital commodity" as the term is described in the SEC's March interpretation.

It also said it will not recommend enforcement action if Canton Coin is minted programmatically by Super Validators, Validators and application providers, as described in the request. That holds without registration under Section 5 of the Securities Act or Section 12(g) of the Exchange Act, and it applies if the issuer relies on an opinion of counsel. The facts the staff relied on are laid out in the Canton Network's incoming letter.

It has been revealed that early coverage focused on the classification label. The more useful story, though, is how the staff got there.

In a recent development, the staff pointed to two representations. The first is that Canton Coin is intrinsically linked to, and derives its value from, the programmatic operation of the Canton Network, along with supply and demand dynamics. Its value does not come from an expectation of profits from the essential managerial efforts of others.

In a recent development, that phrase echoes the Howey test, the long-standing U.S. framework for investment contracts. The prong asks a simple question: when someone holds this token, are they betting on a team's work, or on a network that runs by itself? On the facts presented, the staff's answer was the network.

It has been revealed that this is the more familiar half of the analysis, and most token projects argue some version of it. Because almost every issuer makes the same claim, the first prong carries less weight on its own, which is why the second one deserves a closer look.

The second representation is that the Canton Network has no "central party," as the March interpretation defines that term. In the SEC and CFTC's framework, a digital commodity belongs to a functional crypto system that has no central party overseeing participation or distributing rewards to people.

Sources indicate that this prong is the one to watch, because Canton Coin is minted by Super Validators, Validators and application providers. Those are named roles in a structured network, so a skeptic could fairly ask whether the Super Validator tier looks like a central party in practice. The letter's answer rests on the word "programmatically": the minting follows protocol rules rather than anyone's discretion.

Industry observers note that legal commentators reading the March interpretation have also pointed out that it doesn't fully explain how the "central party" concept relates to its separate definition of decentralization. The Canton letter doesn't settle that either. It applies the term to one set of facts and stops there.

A no-action letter is narrower than it sounds. The Division itself states the response states its position on enforcement action only and expresses no legal conclusion on the challenges presented. It also says the positions rest on the representations in the request, and that different facts or conditions might lead to different conclusions.

According to recent reports, in practice, that comes down to three points. First, the letter is staff-level guidance rather than a Commission vote. Second, it protects reliance on the specific arrangement described, not the token in every future circumstance. Third, if the representations change, the comfort can disappear.

For a company, the letter is still valuable, since a written statement that staff won't recommend enforcement is a strong signal. Even so, it shouldn't be mistaken for a permanent legal classification. It is a snapshot of staff views based on facts someone else supplied.

The framework behind the letter is the Commission's March 17 interpretation, which the CFTC joined. It sorts crypto assets into five categories: digital commodities, digital collectibles, digital tools, stablecoins and digital securities. Four of the five are generally treated as non-securities, and the securities analysis stays fact-specific for the rest.

In a recent development, the two documents do different jobs. The interpretation is a general map: it tells the market how the Commission thinks about categories and which features push an asset one way or the other. The Canton letter is an application. It takes a named token, tests it against the map's digital commodity category, and gives a case-specific enforcement answer.

That sequence matters. The interpretation states what a digital commodity looks like, and the letter says that, if the facts are as represented, Canton Coin looks like one.

According to recent reports, the practical lesson is about preparation. Canton's request framed its facts to fit the two prongs, and the staff responded in those terms. Projects hoping for similar treatment will likely follow the same template: document how value arises from network operation, and document why no single party oversees participation or distributes rewards.

According to recent reports, the harder test will come from tokens with more visible governance or a more active operating team. Those projects will have to explain why their structure doesn't amount to a central party, and the Canton letter doesn't say where that line sits.

For now, the letter works best as an early data point rather than a final answer. The classification label drew the attention, but the representations behind it are what other projects will study. How the staff handles the next request, especially one with a messier governance story, will show whether the "no central party" prong is a narrow gate or a wide one.

Industry News: 10 major Curiosity discoveries on Mars since 2012

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Curiosity rover discoveries since 2012 include an ancient lake bed, rounded stream pebbles, organic molecules and seasonal methane — 10 findings from NASA's Mars Science Laboratory mission.
  • It has been revealed that could Mars ever have supported microbial life?
  • Curiosity landed in Gale Crater in August 2012.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Curiosity rover discoveries since 2012 include an ancient lake bed, rounded stream pebbles, organic molecules and seasonal methane — 10 findings from NASA's Mars Science Laboratory mission.

It has been revealed that could Mars ever have supported microbial life? NASA built its Mars Science Laboratory mission around that single question. The mission's rover, Curiosity, was never designed to detect living organisms. Its task is narrower and more testable: judge whether the planet once offered conditions in which microbes could have survived.

Curiosity landed in Gale Crater in August 2012. The crater holds a layered mountain that NASA calls Mount Sharp, officially named Aeolis Mons. Each band of rock in that mountain preserves a slice of the environment that existed when it formed. Lower layers are older, and higher layers are younger. A rover that crosses the crater floor and climbs the mountain's lower slopes can read that record in sequence, one rock unit at a time.

Industry observers note that the first major answer came swiftly. In early 2013, the rover drilled into a mudstone that turned out to record an ancient freshwater lake. Other results added evidence of flowing streams and a lake system that lasted a long time. They also pointed to groundwater that persisted after the lakes were gone. Together they describe a planet where liquid water appeared in more than one form.

Sources indicate that the rover's chemistry lab also found organic molecules preserved in mudstone about 3 billion years old. Organic compounds are carbon-based molecules that living things use, but they also form through ordinary chemistry. Their presence shows that Martian rock can hold such material for billions of years. It does not show that life existed. A separate set of measurements tracked methane in the air above Gale Crater. The gas rises and falls with the seasons, and its source remains unexplained.

According to recent reports, curiosity also studied the thin Martian air and the radiation that reaches the planet. Measurements of argon point to an atmosphere that was once thicker and escaped to space. A radiation detector recorded conditions both on the cruise to Mars and on the surface. That data matters for planning crewed missions.

The 10 Curiosity rover discoveries below are a selection, not an official ranking. They cover water, chemistry, atmosphere and radiation. Each slide explains where the evidence came from and what it suggests about Mars' past.

Curiosity's drilling at Yellowknife Bay produced the mission's first direct evidence that ancient Mars could have supported microbial life. In March 2013, NASA announced that the Sheepbed mudstone there records a freshwater lake bed that once held mild, near-neutral water.

Recent findings suggest that the rover drilled the rock in early 2013 at a spot the team named John Klein. Yellowknife Bay lies on the floor of Gale Crater, not far from Curiosity's landing site. The rover studied the area before heading toward Mount Sharp, the mountain at the crater's center.

According to recent reports, the drill reached past the weathered outer surface of the rock. It ground material from inside the mudstone into powder. That powder went to laboratory instruments inside the rover's body. CheMin identifies minerals by passing X $TWTR-rays through powdered rock. SAM heats samples and measures the gases they release.

According to recent reports, the rock type carries its own clue. Mudstone forms from fine sediment that settles out of still or slow-moving water. On Earth, it often marks the floor of an old lake.

It has been revealed that the chemistry of the sample delivered the central result. It contained carbon, hydrogen, oxygen, nitrogen, sulfur and phosphorus. Those six elements are the main chemical ingredients of life as scientists know it on Earth. Carbon forms the backbone of organic molecules. Phosphorus is part of DNA and of ATP, the molecule cells use to carry energy. Sulfur appears in some amino acids.

It has been revealed that the type of water also matters for habitability. Near-neutral water is neither strongly acidic nor strongly alkaline. Fresh, mild water poses fewer chemical obstacles to life than highly acidic or very salty water.

In a recent development, that contrast sets Yellowknife Bay apart from earlier rover results. NASA's Opportunity rover had found evidence at Meridiani Planum of past water that was acidic and salty. Water like that is a harsher setting for microbes.

In a recent development, the Yellowknife Bay result does not show that life existed on Mars. It shows that this lake offered conditions in which microbes could have lived. Scientists call such an environment habitable, which is different from inhabited. The finding came less than a year after the rover landed.

Recent findings suggest that rounded pebbles cemented into an outcrop called Hottah show that water once flowed across Gale Crater on Mars. Curiosity's images of this conglomerate rock gave the mission physical evidence of an ancient streambed. The science team estimated that the water was roughly ankle-deep to hip-deep.

A conglomerate is a sedimentary rock made of gravel and smaller grains bound together by finer material. On Earth, this type of rock commonly forms in riverbeds. Currents carry stones along and drop them when the flow slows. Once cemented, the mix preserves a record of the stream that laid it down.

The shape of the stones holds the key information. Pebbles start out angular when they break off a larger rock. As water pushes them downstream, they knock against each other and against the channel bed. Over distance, that grinding wears away corners and edges. A rounded pebble has therefore traveled some way in moving water.

Recent findings suggest that the Hottah pebbles had that worn, rounded profile. The team read it as a sign of long transport by flowing water rather than a short drop down a slope. Stones of this size are also too heavy for Martian wind to move and shape. That leaves running water as the explanation.

In a recent development, the depth estimate turns the rock into a picture of an actual stream. A current roughly ankle-deep to hip-deep can roll and bounce gravel along its bed. That points to moving water. Pebbles dropped into a still pond would sink and stay put.

In a recent development, spacecraft in orbit had already photographed channels and fan-shaped deposits on Mars. Those features suggested past water when seen from above. Hottah supplied evidence at ground level. Curiosity could look at individual stones and see how water had shaped them.

According to recent reports, the result matters for the rover's broader task of judging past habitability. Liquid water is a basic requirement for life as scientists understand it. A stream that moved gravel over a distance shows liquid water once ran across the Martian surface. That made the floor of Gale Crater a credible place to search for other signs of a once-habitable environment.

Curiosity's air measurements show that Mars has lost a large share of the atmosphere it once had. The rover's SAM instrument found light argon-36 depleted relative to heavier argon-38, a pattern that fits a thicker early atmosphere escaping to space.

The result was published in 2013. SAM stands for Sample Analysis at Mars. It is the largest instrument on the rover and sits inside the rover's body. The suite combines a mass spectrometer, a gas chromatograph and a tunable laser spectrometer. The three instruments can analyze gas drawn straight from the Martian air, as well as vapors released when rock and soil samples are heated.

Industry observers note that argon is a useful tracer for this question. It is a noble gas. It does not bond with rocks, ice or other gases. Chemistry cannot pull it out of the air or lock it into minerals. A shift in the balance between its isotopes therefore points to physical loss rather than chemical change.

In a recent development, isotopes of the same element behave alike chemically but differ in mass. Argon-36 has two fewer neutrons than argon-38. That makes it the lighter of the two. Processes that strip gas from the top of an atmosphere remove lighter atoms more easily than heavier ones. Over long periods, that preference leaves the remaining air relatively richer in the heavy form.

That is the signature SAM recorded. The shortage of argon-36 indicates that a substantial amount of gas left the planet. Gas that had stayed in place would have kept its original isotope balance.

Sources indicate that the finding bears on the planet's early climate. Liquid water is hard to keep stable at the surface under the thin, cold atmosphere Mars has today. A thicker envelope of gas would have made a wetter climate easier to sustain.

According to recent reports, the argon data also frame the present atmosphere as a remnant of a larger one. An isotope ratio records the cumulative result of escape. On its own, it does not show how fast that escape happened.

It has been revealed that curiosity's Radiation Assessment Detector, known as RAD, recorded radiation levels during the cruise to Mars and again on the Martian surface. Its cruise results appeared in Science in May 2013.

Sources indicate that those cruise readings came from inside the Mars Science Laboratory spacecraft as it crossed interplanetary space. That placement matters for human spaceflight. Astronauts bound for Mars would also make the journey inside a spacecraft, not exposed in open space.

In a recent development, RAD is a compact particle detector. It identifies charged particles such as protons and heavier atomic nuclei. It also registers neutral radiation, including neutrons and gamma rays. Sorting particles by type and energy lets scientists estimate how much radiation human tissue would absorb.

Recent findings suggest that two main sources produce the radiation RAD tracks. Galactic cosmic rays are high-energy particles that originate outside the solar system and arrive at a fairly steady rate. Solar energetic particles come from the sun, often in bursts tied to flares and coronal mass ejections.

On Earth, a thick atmosphere and a global magnetic field absorb or deflect much of this radiation before it reaches the ground. Mars lacks that protection on the same scale. Its atmosphere is far thinner than Earth's, and the planet has no global magnetic field. Particles reach the Martian surface with less filtering. Some strike the soil and air and generate secondary radiation.

Industry observers note that after Curiosity landed in Gale Crater, RAD kept operating on the surface. Those readings describe the conditions a surface crew or long-lived equipment at the crater would encounter.

The measurements feed into planning for crewed missions. Mission designers need measured values to judge how much shielding a spacecraft requires and how long a crew can remain in deep space. The same data inform how surface habitats on Mars should be built. Direct measurements also give engineers a check on the computer models used to estimate exposure.

RAD supports Curiosity's science goals as well. Radiation reaching the surface can break down organic molecules in rock and soil over long periods. Knowing the radiation level helps scientists judge where preserved organic material is most likely to survive. It also helps them decide which drill samples are most worth analyzing.

Recent findings suggest that curiosity's analysis of the Cumberland drill sample at Yellowknife Bay revealed that wind erosion exposed the rock about 78 million years ago. That estimate carries an uncertainty of about 30 million years. The result appeared in Science in 2014.

According to recent reports, that margin places the exposure somewhere between roughly 48 million and 108 million years ago. Mars formed about 4.5 billion years ago. Measured against that span, the Cumberland surface was uncovered recently in geological terms.

Cosmic-ray exposure dating relies on a steady physical process. High-energy particles from space strike rock and split some of the atoms near its surface. These collisions produce particular isotopes that accumulate in the stone over time. The longer a rock sits close to the surface, the more of those isotopes it holds.

The particles reach only the upper few meters of rock. Material buried deeper stays largely shielded. As a result, the exposure clock effectively starts when erosion strips away the layers above.

Mars offers little protection from these particles. The planet has a thin atmosphere and no global magnetic field. On Earth, a thick atmosphere and a magnetic field deflect or absorb much of the incoming flux before it reaches the ground.

The Cumberland result identifies wind as the force doing the uncovering at Gale Crater. Liquid water does not flow across the Martian surface today. Wind-driven sand wears down exposed outcrops over long periods. It removes overlying rock and leaves deeper layers open to the sky.

Industry observers note that that process matters for the search for ancient chemistry. Radiation breaks down organic molecules over time. Rock that has sat at the surface longest has absorbed the most of that damage. A surface uncovered more recently has had less time to accumulate it.

Sources indicate that the 2014 finding suggests that erosion on Mars can expose fresh rock for study. That gives scientists a way to choose where to drill. Surfaces where wind has removed material recently may hold chemistry less altered by radiation.

The Cumberland measurement also highlighted that a rover could date a surface with instruments carried to Mars. Scientists did not need to return a sample to a laboratory on Earth to get the age.

Mineral veins in the Kimberley area of Gale Crater contain high levels of manganese, according to measurements from Curiosity's ChemCam instrument. Manganese oxides generally form in strongly oxidizing conditions. That points to more oxygen in the ancient Martian atmosphere or water than scientists had expected.

In a recent development, the result was reported around 2014. It came from a part of the rover's route where fractures in the bedrock had filled with minerals left behind by fluids. Those veins formed after the surrounding rock did. They record water that moved through the ground later in the crater's history.

ChemCam sits on the rover's mast. It fires laser pulses at a rock target several meters away and vaporizes a tiny spot on its surface. A spectrometer then reads the light from the resulting plasma to identify the elements present. This method, called laser-induced breakdown spectroscopy, lets the team survey many targets without driving up to each one or drilling.

Manganese is useful as a clue because of its chemistry. The element dissolves readily in water when little oxygen is available. It tends to settle out as solid oxide minerals when a strong oxidant strips electrons from it. Concentrated manganese in vein material suggests the fluids that carried it met conditions capable of driving that reaction.

Sources indicate that on Earth, manganese oxide deposits became common in the rock record after oxygen built up in the atmosphere. That history is one reason geologists treat these minerals as markers of oxidizing environments.

According to recent reports, the Kimberley result does not pin down where the oxidizing power came from. It could have come from oxygen in the early atmosphere or from oxidants dissolved in the water. Either source would mean early Mars was less oxygen-poor than many models had assumed.

The degree of oxidation also matters for habitability studies. It shapes which chemical reactions were possible in the water that once moved through Gale Crater's rocks.

The layered mudstones at Pahrump Hills, at the base of Mount Sharp, are deposits left by an ancient lake. A 2015 Science paper led by John Grotzinger concluded that the lake likely persisted on the scale of millions of years.

Pahrump Hills is an outcrop at the foot of Mount Sharp, the layered mountain inside Gale Crater on Mars. NASA's Curiosity rover studied it as the rover began working on the mountain's lowest slopes.

Industry observers note that mudstone is rock built from very fine particles of sediment. Grains that small settle only where water is calm. In a fast-moving current, they stay suspended and are carried away. Fine-grained mudstone therefore points to standing water, such as a lake.

Industry observers note that the layering at Pahrump Hills adds a second clue. Each layer marks a separate episode of sediment settling to the bottom of the water. A thick stack of such layers cannot form all at once. Grotzinger's team described the rocks there as lake deposits, laid down one on top of another.

According to recent reports, duration is what separates this result from other signs of water at Gale Crater. A single wet layer could record a brief flood or a pond that dried up quickly. A thick stack of lake sediments points to water that stayed in place. The team concluded that this lake was not a passing event.

That timescale bears directly on the mission's central question: whether Mars once had conditions that could support microbial life. A brief wet spell offers only a short window for stable, watery conditions. A lake lasting on the order of millions of years keeps that window open far longer. It describes standing water present over a long stretch of Martian history, not a fleeting puddle.

Recent findings suggest that the finding does not show that anything lived in the lake. It establishes that a body of standing water existed at the foot of Mount Sharp and that it endured.

Curiosity found boron in calcium sulfate mineral veins at Gale Crater, a result the rover's science team reported in September 2017. The discovery suggests that water continued to circulate underground after the crater's lakes dried up, and that this groundwater could have been habitable.

The veins appear as pale streaks that cut through the surrounding bedrock. They form when water seeps into cracks in rock that has already hardened. Minerals dissolved in that water settle out and fill the fractures. Because the veins slice across older layers, they record a later chapter in the crater's history.

Recent findings suggest that calcium sulfate is the mineral group that includes gypsum and anhydrite. On Earth, it commonly forms where water evaporates or where groundwater carries dissolved salts through rock. Boron locked inside these deposits on Mars links the element to water circulating underground, not to open water at the surface.

ChemCam, the rover's laser instrument, made the detection. It fires a laser at rock targets from several meters away and vaporizes a tiny spot. A spectrometer reads the light from that flash to identify the elements present. The technique lets the rover check thin features such as veins without drilling into them.

Industry observers note that boron draws attention because of where it tends to collect on Earth. It is often tied to evaporated lake beds, where standing water dried out and left concentrated minerals behind. Its presence in Martian veins that formed after the lake sediments hardened places that kind of water chemistry in a later, subsurface setting.

Recent findings suggest that the timing bears on habitability at the site. Lakes at the surface offer one window in which microbes might have lived. Groundwater that persisted afterward would extend that window into a later period, beneath the surface rather than on it.

Industry observers note that boron also appears in research on the origin of life. Borate minerals are one proposed way to stabilize ribose, a sugar that forms part of RNA. The Gale Crater result does not show that such chemistry took place on Mars. It does not show that life existed there either. It shows that an element relevant to that question was present in the planet's ancient groundwater.

Recent findings suggest that curiosity found organic molecules preserved in 3-billion-year-old mudstone from Gale Crater's Murray formation. A June 2018 paper in Science, with Jennifer Eigenbrode as lead author, reported the compounds, which include thiophenes, benzene and toluene.

Organic molecules are carbon-based compounds, typically built from carbon bonded to hydrogen and often to other elements. They are the chemical building blocks of every known living thing. They also form without any biology at all. Meteorites carry them, and nonbiological chemical reactions can produce them too.

Sources indicate that that dual origin matters when reading the result. The paper reports organic compounds in the rock. It does not report life. The molecules on their own do not show whether biology had any role in making them.

In a recent development, each named compound has a distinct structure. Thiophenes are ring-shaped molecules that contain sulfur. Benzene and toluene are aromatic hydrocarbons, each built around a ring of six carbon atoms. Toluene is benzene with a methyl group attached.

Mudstone is a fine-grained sedimentary rock. It forms when silt and clay particles settle out of calm water and later harden into stone. On Earth, fine-grained sediments of this kind are a common place to find preserved organic matter.

Curiosity detected the compounds with its Sample Analysis at Mars instrument suite, known as SAM. The rover drills into rock and delivers the powder to SAM, which heats it in an oven. The released gases are then separated and identified by their mass.

Industry observers note that survival over time is a central part of the result. Mars lacks a global magnetic field and has only a thin atmosphere. Radiation that reaches the surface can break apart organic molecules over long periods. The Murray formation samples show that carbon-bearing material in rock this old can still be detected.

For later missions, the finding identifies ancient Martian mudstone as rock that can hold organic material within reach of a rover's onboard laboratory.

Methane in the air above Gale Crater rises and falls with the Martian seasons. A June 2018 paper in Science, led by Chris Webster, reported that the gas peaks in late northern summer and drops to lower levels in winter.

It has been revealed that the measurements came from SAM, the Sample Analysis at Mars instrument suite inside the rover. One of its components, the Tunable Laser Spectrometer, draws in Martian air. It then measures how strongly the gas absorbs laser light at specific wavelengths. Methane absorbs light in a distinctive pattern. That pattern lets the instrument pick it out from the far more abundant gases around it.

It has been revealed that the Martian atmosphere is thin and made mostly of carbon dioxide. Methane is only a trace component. The spectrometer is tuned to the methane molecule so it can register such small amounts.

According to recent reports, A repeating seasonal cycle is a different kind of result from a one-off reading. A single detection can leave open questions about contamination or instrument error. A pattern that tracks the Martian calendar suggests that some process on Mars adds or removes the gas on a regular schedule.

According to recent reports, methane does not last indefinitely in a planetary atmosphere. Ultraviolet sunlight and other chemical reactions break the molecule apart over time. For the gas to remain detectable, something has to keep supplying it.

In a recent development, the source of the Gale Crater methane remains unexplained. It could be geological or biological. The seasonal pattern alone does not decide between those possibilities.

On Earth, most methane comes from living things, including microbes. That link is one reason the gas draws attention in the search for life on Mars. Methane can also form without any life at all. Water reacting with iron-bearing rock, a process called serpentinization, releases hydrogen that can combine with carbon to make methane. Gas formed long ago could also be trapped underground and seep out later.

In a recent development, the methane cycle extends Curiosity's work from ancient rock into the present-day air. Most of the rover's results describe conditions on Mars billions of years ago. A gas that changes with the seasons today gives scientists a current process to track alongside the planet's older geological record.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 13, 2026 at 4:32 pmNovember 16, 2026 at 10:09 am.

Recent findings suggest that gov. Bob Ferguson is proposing $10 million to fund basic infrastructure needed for the Northwest Advanced Clean Energy Park, a master-planned industrial area in Eastern Washington that will foster development of large-scale clean energy, advanced manufacturing and supply chains. The proposal will be included in his 2027–29 capital budget.

If approved by lawmakers, the funding would support sewer, water, electrical and road infrastructure at the park.

“This investment will support thousands of good-paying jobs in the trades and advanced industries, and unlock billions in private investment,” Ferguson stated in a statement.

Sources indicate that the 1,641-acre site was formerly part of the Hanford Nuclear Reservation, a sprawling federal property along the Columbia River near the Tri-Cities that is undergoing a massive environmental cleanup. Hanford was established during World War II to produce plutonium for the Manhattan Project.

Mel Clark, president and CEO of the CleanTech Alliance, an industry trade group, welcomed the news as the state struggles to get clean power plugged into the grid.

Recent findings suggest that “Washington needs more energy generation, more clean energy, and more manufacturing,” Clark told GeekWire via email. “We’re excited to see the Governor take action to change our last-place ranking in building newly introduced clean energy projects.”.

According to the governor’s office, two projects have committed to locating at the park once infrastructure construction is complete: Atlas Agro’s low-carbon fertilizer production plant and the utility-scale Ruby Flats Solar Farm.

State officials said General Matter is also considering the location for producing advanced nuclear fuel for small reactors. That siting could potentially be beneficial for another project planned for the same area: Amazon, X-energy and Energy Northwest are developing plans for the Cascade Advanced Energy Facility, a nuclear plant comprised of clustered, small reactors.

In 2024, the Norwegian company Cenate expressed interest in building a factory at the park to produce lithium-ion battery components, according to the Tri-Cities Area Journal of Business, ultimately withdrew its plans.

The Tri-Cities is also attracting fusion-energy investment. Last year, Seattle startup Avalanche Energy landed a $10 million grant from the Washington State Department of Commerce’s Green Jobs Grant Program to develop FusionWERX, a commercial-scale testing facility for fusion technologies. The project is being developed in an existing Port of Benton building in Richland.

Washington is heading into its 2027–29 biennial budget with a multibillion-dollar shortfall, but officials have not yet settled on a definitive public estimate.

According to recent reports, ferguson has acknowledged the scale of the gap but has not publicly specified an amount. The shortfall concerns the state’s operating budget, which is separate from the capital budget funding proposed for the energy park.

Editor’s note: Comment from CleanTech Alliance President and CEO Mel Clark added 11/16.

Ripple’s Bank-Style Lending on XRPL Nears Launch: What XRP Holders Actually Get

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today.
  • The LendingProtocolV1_1 amendment on the XRP Ledger (XRPL) has collected 22 of 35 votes (62.86%).
  • It has been revealed that three more validators have signed on over the past three weeks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Disclaimer: The opinions expressed by our writers are their own and do not represent the views of U.Today. The financial and market information provided on U.Today is intended for informational purposes only. U.Today is not liable for any financial losses incurred while trading cryptocurrencies. Conduct your own research by contacting financial experts before making any investment decisions. We believe that all content is accurate as of the date of publication, but certain offers mentioned may no longer be available.

The LendingProtocolV1_1 amendment on the XRP Ledger (XRPL) has collected 22 of 35 votes (62.86%).

It has been revealed that three more validators have signed on over the past three weeks. Ripple's own nodes have already voted yes, along with the University of Waterloo and UC Berkeley.

To go live, the amendment has to clear the 80% bar (29 votes) and hold it for two straight weeks.

The related SingleAssetVault amendment (XLS-65) has 23 votes (65.7%) and needs six more.

The XLS-65 and XLS-66 standards drop overcollateralization and instant liquidations and let companies take out fixed-term, uncollateralized loans directly on XRPL. The loans work similarly to traditional bank credit, with a fixed term and pre-set interest terms.

Ripple has already tested the protocol on a private XRPL network with nine nodes that matched the hardware of its mainnet nodes.

Holders deposit XRP or stablecoins such as RLUSD into Single Asset Vaults and receive shares. Interest is paid on a cash basis. Depositors receive it only after the borrower has sent the money. Withdrawals from a vault are processed on a first-come, first-served basis.

Borrowers are vetted off-chain by Loan Brokers, who record each disbursement on the ledger. According to the XRPL documentation, the protocol "relies on off-chain underwriting and risk management to assess the creditworthiness of borrowers.".

The broker's own "first-loss capital" covers losses first when a client stops paying.

Issuers can also freeze assets or claw them back. According to Ripple, all operations in a vault and in the connected lending protocol stop when an asset issuer freezes the vault.

Until now, XRP holders who wanted passive income had to use third-party bridges and wrapped tokens. After the amendment activates, holders can deposit XRP in a pool on XRPL, with its fraction-of-a-cent fees, and collect part of the interest paid by borrowers. Their income will depend on the terms set by the loan broker and on borrowers' repayments.

If a major borrower defaults and the broker's first-loss capital runs out, depositors bear the losses and their shares drop in value.

At press time, XRP is trading at $1.04.

#6111. Strength training builds muscle, bone and independence, but only when you keep at it

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3990 w)
📖 Baca
