Strength training builds muscle, bone and independence, but only when you keep at it

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3990 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that mayo Clinic claims strength training helps muscle, bone, weight and independence at any age.
  • Many people still think of lifting weights as a hobby for young people in gyms, not as upkeep the body needs in later life.
  • The benefits people claim for lifting reach from the bones to the brain, which can make it sound like a cure-all.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that mayo Clinic claims strength training helps muscle, bone, weight and independence at any age. See what each benefit asks of you.

Many people still think of lifting weights as a hobby for young people in gyms, not as upkeep the body needs in later life. That picture leaves out how ordinary muscle loss is in old age. Sarcopenia, the muscle loss that comes with aging, affects an estimated 10% to 20% of people in their senior years, according to NIH News in Health. Weakness in later life is therefore a common condition, not a rare piece of bad luck. For most adults, the useful question is how much of that loss they can slow or reverse, not whether it will happen. That places strength training next to eating well and sleeping enough, as a habit people keep for life rather than a phase they pass through.

The benefits people claim for lifting reach from the bones to the brain, which can make it sound like a cure-all. Some of those claims rest on firmer evidence than others, so the honest summary is that the benefits are real but conditional. The condition that comes up again and again is persistence. People build strength over months and years of steady work, starting from whatever level they begin at, and no single workout decides the outcome. That makes consistency, rather than talent or starting fitness, the deciding factor. For a reader, an easy first routine is only the way in. The benefits come from keeping at it and gradually asking more of the body.

Mayo Clinic set out to explain what lifting weights offers people and how to begin, and it paired the case for strength training with practical advice for getting started. The topics include possible gains for the skeleton and a possible tie between lifting and sharper thinking late in life, along with routines that call for nothing but body weight. The benefits and the instructions tell one story. "If you stick with it, you can continue to increase your strength, no matter where you started," the clinic's staff stated. A modest start lets almost anyone begin, and what a person does after that decides which benefits actually arrive. Each promise is best judged by what it asks of a person over time, not by what it offers on the first day.

According to recent reports, A mirror is the wrong place to check whether lifting weights is working. Mayo Clinic says that strength training helps people hold on to muscle as aging wears lean tissue away, and even add to it. Keeping that tissue does not, by itself, keep older people safe. Older adults who carried more lean mass were no less likely to fall, lose mobility, break a hip or die, according to NIH News in Health. Muscle size alone is a poor guide to how safe a person will be in later life. The goal worth tracking is strength and the ability to move, not added size or a fuller-looking frame. Government aging specialists describe the purpose of lifting in the same terms. Dr. Rosaly Correa-de-Araujo, an aging expert at NIH, noted, "you need to have resistance training because this is going to help build your strength.".

Recent findings suggest that building that strength takes less time than many people assume. Two sessions a week, each lasting about 20 to 30 minutes, can be enough for a person to notice stronger muscles. That schedule fits inside an ordinary working week, and the twice-weekly minimum matches Department of Health and Human Services guidelines, so the frequency reflects a national public-health baseline rather than one clinic's preference. What matters most is how hard each set is, not how long a session lasts. For most people, one set per exercise is enough, but only when they work the muscle until the effort becomes difficult. A short session done lightly does not meet that condition. A lifter should judge a session by whether the last few repetitions were a struggle, not by the minutes spent in it.

Two short, hard sessions a week, judged by what the body can do afterward, are all a beginner needs.

According to recent reports, strength training can protect the skeleton as well as the muscles, because people who put load on their bones help keep them sturdy. "By stressing your bones, strength training protects bone health and may lower the risk of osteoporosis," Mayo Clinic staff remarked, and the word "may" matters. Mayo Clinic puts no number on how much lifting lowers that risk. No exercise trial so far has been large enough to show that lifters break fewer bones, according to Current Osteoporosis Reports. The protection is plausible but not yet proven. That leaves a reader with a practical question about how hard to load the bones.

In a recent development, the stress that builds bone is heavier than the routine most people picture. Lifters who gained bone density used loads above 80% of the most they could lift once, for fewer than eight repetitions, according to Current Osteoporosis Reports. At that intensity, people gained about 2% to 3% in lower-spine density across pooled studies, a real but modest return on hard work. Even with heavy training, people kept hip density stable at best, so the benefit is weakest at the hip. A light toning routine is still worth doing, but a reader shouldn't count on it to protect bone.

Whether those gains last, or keep growing, is still an open question. One three-year follow-up to a heavy-lifting trial offers an early hint, with participants who stayed on the heavy training showing a larger lower-spine gain, according to Current Osteoporosis Reports. That single result is too uncertain to settle the matter. Nobody has yet shown how long the bone benefit holds or whether years of lifting add to it.

It has been revealed that much of exercise's protection against broken hips likely comes from staying on one's feet rather than from denser bone. When people with fragile bones break a hip, they do so in a fall more than 90% of the time, according to Current Osteoporosis Reports, and heavy lifting did the least for bone at the hip. A routine aimed at bone health should therefore pair heavy lifting with balance work. Heavy loading also has limits on who should try it alone. Researchers excluded people who had a spinal fracture in the past year from the heavy-lifting trials, so for them the approach is untested and not something to start without supervision.

For now, lifting weight that feels heavy and practicing balance make a reasonable strategy for bone health, though not yet a proven way to prevent fractures.

In a recent development, mayo Clinic indicates that people who lift weights can keep their weight in check, burn more calories and improve the mix of fat and muscle in their bodies. People who lift to manage their weight usually judge the result by the scale, but the scale can't tell them what kind of weight they lost. That gap matters because dieting alone takes muscle with it, and roughly 20% to 30% of the weight people lose by cutting calories is lean tissue, according to BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. For a dieter, then, the goal is to lose the right pounds and keep the muscle that holds up strength in later years.

Recent findings suggest that the trials put firmer evidence behind the change in body makeup than Mayo Clinic offers, because the clinic gives no amount for it. In a 2025 review by researchers including Ahmad Binmahfoz of Umm Al-Qura University and the University of Glasgow, dieters who added lifting lost more fat than dieters who only cut calories, BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine reports, and the reviewers rated that finding high certainty. The same lifters also kept more lean tissue, though the reviewers rated that result only moderate certainty. The clearest payoff is a shift in what the body is made of, more than a lower number on the scale. A dieter who checks only the scale could miss that shift and wrongly decide the lifting isn't working.

The muscle benefit may also depend on how long a person keeps lifting. In trials lasting six months or more, dieters who lifted still lost more fat, but their edge in keeping lean tissue was no longer statistically clear, according to BMJ Open Sport & Exercise Medicine. Few trials ran that long, so this is a weak signal rather than proof that the benefit fades. One possible reason is that people stopped sticking with the program, as between 25% and 49% of participants dropped out of the longer trials. The trials also enrolled only adults ages 18 to 65 who were cutting calories, so for lifters past 65, Mayo Clinic's promise about body makeup reaches beyond what these trials tested.

Lifting belongs in a weight proposal because it helps take off fat while sparing muscle, though no one has yet shown that the muscle benefit lasts beyond the first months.

Late in life, independence depends less on how much muscle a person carries than on whether that person can still stand up, walk and stay upright. Mayo Clinic says that people who strength train gain better function and balance, fall less and protect their joints, and that together these changes help them live on their own longer. Mayo Clinic says training can improve function and gives no measure of how much, so readers should treat it as a reasonable expectation rather than a guarantee. The more pressing test is whether it holds for the people closest to losing their independence.

According to recent reports, the promise about falls is weakest for the people who need it most. Mayo Clinic says strength training lowers the risk of falls, and frail older adults fall more often than people who aren't frail, according to the Journal of Frailty & Aging. Researchers estimate that 10% to 14% of people 65 and older worldwide are frail, a sizable group of older adults and their families. Mayo Clinic doesn't say how much fall risk drops. Poonam Mehta, a researcher at the University of Technology Sydney, and her colleagues noted "the available evidence does not support exercise interventions alone as an effective strategy to reduce key fall-related outcomes in older adults with physical frailty." That leaves the benefit unproven for frail people, though not disproved.

Everyday function and balance are the more believable routes to independence, though the evidence for the frailest people remains thin. Mayo Clinic says lifting may improve the ability to handle daily activities, and evidence that exercise helps frail older adults walk faster carries very low certainty, according to the Journal of Frailty & Aging. Mayo Clinic also says strength training supports balance, yet in frail older adults the researchers saw no more than a hint of improvement, and the evidence behind it is just as weak. Mehta and her colleagues still want organized exercise programs, run under supervision and mixing strength with other kinds of movement, to remain central to care for frail people trying to keep moving and living on their own. The payoff goes to people who keep up a broad, guided routine, not to people who lift for a few weeks and stop.

For an aging reader, or anyone caring for a frail parent, strength work belongs inside a supervised routine for staying mobile, and nobody should count on it alone to prevent falls.

According to recent reports, few people pick up a dumbbell expecting relief from arthritis or a low mood, yet people living with long-term illness may have a lot to gain from lifting. Mayo Clinic says strength training may ease joint pain and help with conditions such as arthritis, diabetes, heart disease, depression and anxiety. That range covers joints, blood sugar, the heart and mental health, so strength work matters to people managing a condition and not only to people chasing fitness. Each of those benefits is a possibility rather than a guarantee, and a long-running study of diabetes highlights what it can take to turn one into a real result.

Lifting steadily for many years is tied to a much lower chance of type 2 diabetes. In a study by researchers including Edward Giovannucci, MD, ScD, of Harvard T. H. Chan School of Public Health, adults who kept up a high amount of lifting across their middle years were 42% less likely to get type 2 diabetes, according to JAMA Network Open. The people in the study were followed for 19.2 years on average, so that lower risk reflects a habit kept up through middle age, not a few strong months. People whose lifting went up and down repeatedly over the years showed no lower risk. An on-again, off-again routine may not bring the protection that a steady one does, and for this benefit the habit has to last.

In a recent development, even this result shows a lower chance of getting diabetes, not a treatment for people who already have it. The researchers watched people over time rather than running a controlled trial, according to JAMA Network Open. People who lift for decades may also live in other healthy ways, and some of their lower risk could come from those habits. For arthritis, heart disease, depression and anxiety, strength training remains a promising addition to care, not a prescription.

For anyone living with one of these conditions, the first step is a conversation with a healthcare professional, not a trip to the weight rack.

It has been revealed that many people hope that working their muscles will also keep their minds sharp as they age. The promise here is real but carefully limited. "Some research suggests that regular strength training and physical activity may help support brain health and some thinking skills in older adults," Mayo Clinic staff wrote. That claim covers only older adults and only some thinking skills, so a reader under retirement age has no brain benefit here to count on. The caution does not mean the evidence is thin. Researchers have studied exercise and thinking in trials involving 4,047 older adults, according to a review published in January 2026 in the European Review of Aging and Physical Activity. The careful wording describes a benefit researchers have tested at scale, not a guess. For an older reader, sharper thinking is a credible bonus worth counting, but it is not a sure return and not the main reason to start lifting.

Industry observers note that the brain benefit does not clearly belong to weights. Mayo Clinic ties it to strength training together with physical activity in general, so no one can credit lifting alone for it. The European Review of Aging and Physical Activity reports that among older adults already starting to lose muscle, programs that combined several kinds of exercise were the most effective, rather than resistance training alone. These are the people most exposed to age-related muscle loss. When their strength is already slipping, they may help their minds most by pairing weights with other kinds of movement. For people in that group, an instruction simply to lift leaves part of the prescription out.

An older adult whose strength is starting to fade should look for a routine that mixes weights with other movement, and keep at it.

Mayo Clinic lists three safety steps for a new lifter: check with a clinician if you have health concerns, warm up, and learn proper form. It doesn't say which conditions require a clinician's clearance, so anyone unsure whether their own concern counts should ask. Booking an appointment and spending a few minutes warming up take little effort. Learning form takes real work, and it is the step beginners most often underrate.

Sources indicate that proper form has to be taught, because lifting is not a skill the body picks up on its own. "People naturally learn to walk as part of growing up. But you don't necessarily learn how to lift weights," Joseph Ciccolo, an exercise researcher at Columbia University, stated in 2020, as reported by NIH. A personal trainer can cover the basics in a few early workouts, so the teaching costs a beginner little time. Those sessions teach control, with each lift done in smooth, steady movements and no jerking. A beginner's first weeks are for learning the movement, and heavier weight can wait.

Recent findings suggest that breathing is the risk beginners are least likely to think about. Holding your breath during a lift could change blood pressure, according to NIH guidance from 2020. People who already watch their blood pressure therefore have a concrete reason to raise lifting with a clinician before they begin. The fix is free and simple: breathe out while lifting and breathe in while relaxing. Breathing, like form, is a matter of technique rather than toughness, and a trainer can teach it in the first session.

It has been revealed that A beginner who feels pain during an exercise should stop the exercise instead of pushing through it, which keeps a minor strain from becoming an injury that ends the routine. The first weight should be light enough that the muscles tire in about 12 to 15 repetitions. That weight is only a starting line, and in 2020 Wendy Kohrt, an aging expert at the University of Colorado, advised beginners to raise it a little at a time, according to NIH.

Careful beginnings aren't meant to keep anyone timid. They let a lifter keep adding weight months later, and that added weight is where the benefits of strength training come from.

It has been revealed that A first strength routine can be far smaller than most newcomers expect. Mayo Clinic says that one round of each exercise, lifted 12 to 15 times, is enough for muscles to grow, provided each muscle group gets a day off between the sessions that work it. That rest day is as much a part of the routine as the lifting is. A higher repetition count likely means a lighter weight, so the first sessions use a load a beginner can lift many times rather than the heaviest weight they can manage. The low bar is deliberate. Almost anyone can start at this dose, and the real question is what a lifter does next.

For a beginner's first weeks, a single set holds up well. People who did one set demonstrated no significant difference in any outcome from people on a higher-volume routine, according to a trial in the Brazilian Journal of Physical Therapy. That supports the single set and tells a newcomer that extra sets add little at first. The trial lasted nine weeks, so it demonstrates what one set does in a beginner's opening stretch rather than over years. Its participants were women aged 18 to 40 with knee pain, and the result may not apply to men or athletes. One set has earned its place as a starting dose, but nobody has shown it to be the best plan for the long run.

In a recent development, the most key part of this advice is the instruction to make the work harder. Lifters should raise the weight once more repetitions come easily. In the trial, researchers raised the load whenever a participant reported more than 2 additional reps, and they lowered the repetition target in each later stage of the program, according to the Brazilian Journal of Physical Therapy. For a lifter, the first of those rules gives a simple test: Finishing a set with reps to spare means it's time for a heavier weight. Fewer repetitions go with heavier loads, so 12 to 15 is the range where a lifter begins, not a range to stay in. The measure that counts is how hard the set feels that day, not whether the lifter hits a fixed number.

In a recent development, once a lifter is past the beginner stage, the case for doing more grows. The trial's authors, led by Severo-Silveira, wrote in the Brazilian Journal of Physical Therapy that "higher-volume training is likely more beneficial for strength development once a baseline fitness level is achieved.".

One set gets a beginner started, and the lifters who add weight, and in time add sets, keep gaining.

Many would-be lifters stall before their first workout because they picture a gym membership or a rack of iron at home as the price of entry. That cost mostly isn't real. Mayo Clinic notes that people can train at home or in a gym, with options ranging from body weight to machines, so no one needs costly gear. The National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases, or NIAMS, lists pushups and pullups as resistance exercise. A person's own body is therefore a legitimate form of resistance, not a stopgap until the real equipment arrives. Squats, lunges, planks, pushups and pullups all appear among Mayo Clinic's examples of body-weight work, so a beginner has several moves to try before spending any money. The first decision is when to start, not what to buy.

In a recent development, spending rises only as a person chooses more equipment, and every step up is optional. Resistance tubing is inexpensive, while weight machines at home are possible but take an investment. People who buy those machines are paying for the convenience of lifting at home, not for something the training requires. A beginner can add equipment once the habit holds.

Recent findings suggest that the benefit comes from muscles working against a load, not from the object that supplies it. NIAMS notes that resistance training puts stress on bones and can strengthen them. Body weight is one of the resistance options Mayo Clinic offers, so a person can do this work without buying anything. The choice between home and gym comes down to what a person prefers and can easily reach.

According to recent reports, the rest of a bone-friendly routine is cheap as well. NIAMS lists brisk walking, jogging, stairs, dancing and racket sports as weight-bearing exercise, and none of them calls for strength equipment. Once cost stops serving as an excuse, the only question left is whether a person keeps showing up.

Recent findings suggest that strength training asks for much less time than the image of daily gym sessions suggests. Mayo Clinic states that two sessions a week, each lasting 20 to 30 minutes, can make muscles stronger. Two workouts a week is also the minimum that general guidance sets for adults, according to TIME. The routine that can build strength is therefore also the least an adult is advised to do, which makes it a starting point rather than a level to settle at. Even on that schedule, stronger muscles are something a person "may" notice, not a guaranteed outcome. Two short sessions give a person a chance at results but no promise of them. A schedule this light is easy to keep alongside a job and a family, and whether it pays off depends on the effort a person puts into each session.

A weak start doesn't rule anyone out. Beginners who can manage only eight or fewer repetitions of a movement should start at that level and build gradually, according to TIME. Each person sets their own starting level, and the gains come from the slow climb above it rather than from the first workout. Feeling unsure in the early weeks is also no sign that something has gone wrong. "It's totally normal to feel a little lost," Will Hewitt, a certified personal trainer and director of training at Flight House Fitness in Charlestown, Mass., said. Knowing that the confusion is common can make it easier for a beginner to come back the following week.

The two short sessions that get a person started are the same ones that produce results later, once that person keeps asking more of them.

by Todd Bishop on Nov 14, 2026 at 8:30 amNovember 14, 2026 at 12:50 pm.

This week on the GeekWire Podcast, we react to the sudden downfall of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, whose resignation Nvidia revealed Thursday after reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy.

We discuss the governance gaps at the world’s most valuable chipmaker, the long but low-profile Microsoft career of interim CEO Colette Kress, and who could take over permanently, including candidates from Microsoft, Amazon and the chip industry.

The 10 Most Comfortable Bras, According to Style Editors

Sources indicate that women's Health may earn commission from the links on this page, but we only feature products we believe in. Why Trust Us?

Sources indicate that I’ve tested more bras than I can count as a style writer. And over the years, I’ve learned that comfort is a nonnegotiable—if it digs, pinches, or rides up, it doesn’t deserve a space in my drawer. The thing is, no two boobs are exactly alike (not even your own). One might sit higher, be fuller, or have a different shape than the other. So finding the right bra isn’t about hitting a standard size—it’s about understanding your body. According to Navya Mysore, MD, a primary care physician and Women’s Health advisor, the right bra boosts comfort, improves posture, and eases back pain by evenly distributing breast tissue. If your band rides up, your straps slide, or your underwire doesn’t lie flat, it’s a clear sign something’s off.

Sources indicate that and if your usual size suddenly stops working? Totally normal. Bra fitter and undergarment educator Kimmay Caldwell indicates weight changes, hormone shifts, or your monthly cycle can impact your size. To make it trickier, some brands still use outdated sizing methods (like the “plus four” rule), while others go by your exact underbust. Bottom line: your size can change and vary between clothing brands.

All of that can make bra shopping feel like a bit of a minefield, which is exactly why I tested 20 different styles across fits, fabrics, and support levels to find the ones that are actually worth your money. These ten passed the wear test and then some, proving that comfort, support, and style actually can exist in one bra.

It has been revealed that A bra should fit your body—not the other way around—and Knix totally got the memo with this one. It feels snug at first, but it softens and molds to your shape with every wear. What really impressed me was the fit because it almost feels custom, thanks to the ultra-thin foam that contours without adding volume.

Plus, the sleek fabric (a nylon-spandex blend) moves with you, feeling super smooth against the skin and breathable enough to wear for hours.

It has been revealed that if you're after definition without the discomfort, this wire-free option def delivers. The molded cups lift and separate, while subtle side padding helps prevent spillage and sideboob. The result? A natural shape, no extra bulk, and no awkward lines under tighter tops. And with 99 sizes (!!) and eight colors, the options are actually inclusive.

The only downside? It’s not the best for high movement and workouts. I find myself adjusting it when I bend or move swiftly. Still, for everyday comfort and a super flattering fit, this one’s a standout.

If you love the shape and support of a traditional bra but can't stand the feel of underwire, the Shapermint Essentials Sweetheart Wireless Contour Bra is your happy medium. It delivers a surprisingly lifted, rounded silhouette without a single wire digging into your ribs, making it my top pick for anyone who wants all-day comfort.

In a recent development, the lightly contoured foam cups provide just enough structure to prevent the dreaded uniboob, while the wide, stretchy band stays comfortably in place without pinching or rolling. The smooth, buttery fabric feels soft against the skin and disappears nicely under T-shirts and other fitted tops.

Recent findings suggest that I was especially impressed by how supportive it feels for a wireless bra. It lifts and shapes without feeling restrictive, and the wider straps help distribute weight so your shoulders don't pay the price after hours of wear. It's one of those bras you forget you're wearing—which is pretty much the highest compliment I can give.

In a recent development, push-up bras with underwires have a bad rep, and for good reason. They’re usually stiff, pokey, and downright uncomfortable. But after wearing this Maidenform bra for months (yes, months), I can confidently say it’s a major exception to the rule.

It has been revealed that from the start, this bra felt different. The underwire doesn’t dig or jab, thanks to its soft, stretchy crochet lace that moves with you. The cups are unpadded but still offer that ideal medium support and lift, enough to give shape and a gentle push-up effect, but never so much that I feel squeezed or overly sculpted. It’s supportive without being suffocating, which is rare in the world of push-ups.And let’s talk about the straps. They’re fully adjustable and convertible, so whether I’m going for a classic or criss-cross fit, I can tweak the style to match my outfit. That kind of versatility makes it feel like you’re getting two bras in one (and who doesn’t love a multitasker?).The lift it gives is subtle but effective. It’s not the dramatic “hello, cleavage” kind of push-up, but more of a natural, perky boost that works under everything from tees to low-cut dresses. No spillage, just a flattering shape that makes me feel more confident in whatever I’m wearing. Bonus points for the range of styles: It comes in smooth fabric options to wear under clingy tees, and lace versions for when you want to have a little more fun.One of my biggest bra fears? The dreaded back and side bulge. But this bra’s smoothing side panels genuinely help—there’s no weird digging or over-compression, just a smooth, flattering fit that doesn’t fight with your body. Long story short: I tested it, I lived in it, and I’m keeping it in my regular rotation.

As someone who hates wearing bras (the wires, the bulk, the digging), this is the one I wear most. Made for fuller busts (DD+), the Cosabella Evolution Curvy Bralette lifts and shapes with lightly molded cups, no wires necessary.

“It’s the only bralette I’ve found that can actually support my chest without feeling restrictive,” notes style contributor Lily Wohlner. The soft, stretchy fabric, made from a smooth microfiber that consists of 85 percent polyamide and 15 percent elastane, molds to your body, starting snug and quickly adapting for a custom-like fit. “I will say, mine have stretched a bit over the past few years, so it might be time to re-up,” she says.

Sources indicate that this bra provides exceptional support for larger busts, even without a heavy-duty wire band. Instead, it makes use of an elasticized band that provides a surprisingly large amount of support without digging into the skin. It also has extra support at the sides to prevent spillage and to keep everything looking seamless, even under thin t-shirts and tight dresses.

According to recent reports, the adjustable straps and underband stay put, and the side coverage smooths everything out—no spillage, no weird lines under shirts. It gives a natural, rounded shape that works under pretty much anything.

It has been revealed that if you tend to scoop the girls into place to make them look perkier (a good trick!), this Cuup bra does the work for you. The rounded neckline and unlined, unpadded cups naturally lift and shape, while seamlessly extending into the straps for clean lines and a flattering fit.

It has been revealed that it runs snug, but that’s what makes it so supportive—my boobs stay put and look perkier without any adjusting. The underwire is super lightweight and flexible, so there’s zero digging or poking there. I also love that the cups are unlined, because it makes the bra feel super lightweight and barely there.

The bra is made from a microfiber blend of polyamide and elastane, so it’s buttery-smooth, stretches with you while keeping its shape, and is ultra-breathable. It’s great for warm days since it feels like next to nothing on the skin and helps wick moisture away. The microfiber is also great for pairing with thin or tight tops, since it's basically undetectable under clothing—no lines in sight.

In a recent development, the straps are fully adjustable for a customizable lift, and even though the cups are thin, they still offer enough coverage to prevent any chilly-day surprises, IYKYK. Since the cups run a bit small, sizing up might be your best bet for full coverage.

Recent findings suggest that the Honeylove CrossOver Bra is ultra-comfortable, smoothing, and supportive. The nylon and spandex blend feels soft and wearable for hours without digging into your skin while providing a completely seamless silhouette from every angle. I always wear this pick under thinner tops, tight dresses, and clingy sweaters because it creates a totally streamlined look under clothes while lifting the girls and supporting the underarm area and sides.

Plus, the bonded cradle under the bust mimics the structure of an underwire, delivering firm support without any poking or pinching. The full mesh overlay adds light compression and lift, adding to the sleek look.

“The CrossOver bra feels like a sports bra on, which is especially handy for women in search of something extra-comfortable (hi),” indicates contributor Korin Miller, who wore this bra every day for nearly a month to see how well it performed. She appreciates the flexible boning at the sides of the cups to prevent sideboob and bulging.

This bra also has one of the widest size ranges on our list, which is a major win. However, it does run a little big, so if you're between sizes, consider sizing down for the best fit.

Read More: Honeylove CrossOver Bra Review.

Sources indicate that finding a lace bra that's actually comfortable—especially if you have a larger bust—can feel like a tall order, but the Bravissimo Millie Bra proves you don't have to sacrifice support for something pretty. It's my top pick for fuller busts thanks to its soft stretch lace cups, which mold to your shape for a flexible, barely-there feel instead of digging in or gaping.

Sources indicate that unlike stiff, scratchy lace bras, this one feels surprisingly comfortable from the first wear. The unpadded cups hug your breasts without adding bulk, while the stretchy lace adapts to your natural shape for a fit that feels supportive without being restrictive. The delicate floral lace also gives it an elevated, feminine look that's pretty enough to show off under a slightly unbuttoned blouse or low-cut top.

Meanwhile, the side sling creates a naturally lifted, forward shape, and if you wear a JJ or K cup, those sizes include additional lining for even more support where you need it most. The result is a flattering silhouette that feels secure without relying on heavy padding.

The only catch is that it's designed specifically for fuller busts, so sizing starts at a D cup.

The Natori Bliss Perfection Bra nails the perfect balance of comfort and structure. It feels light and flexible but keeps everything perfectly lifted and in place. No readjusting is needed halfway through the day, as is so often the case. That's thanks to the stretchy fabric, fully adjustable straps and band, and the strong yet plush underwire.

In a recent development, the smooth microfiber fabric (a nylon and spandex blend) feels buttery-soft against the skin, with just enough stretch to move as you do. Even the lace trim—sometimes a red flag for irritation—is whisper-smooth and lies flat under clothes. And while there’s an underwire, it’s so well-cushioned that it supports without poking or digging.

In a recent development, it’s the only underwire bra I don’t rip off the second I get home. It’s really the only bra I reach for when I head to the office or if I’m wearing a top that requires a little more lift and support for that flattering look. Style-wise, it looks as good as it feels. The lightly-lined cups create a natural, rounded shape that disappears under everything from fitted tees to silk blouses, and the smooth band keeps the silhouette seamless.

Our only con? It’s handwash only. I tried washing mine in a mesh laundry bag the first time it needed a clean, and while it wasn’t destroyed, it definitely pilled a bit.

Recent findings suggest that if you have a smaller bust, you don't need a ton of padding to get a flattering fit—and the Journelle Victory Plunge Bra is proof. It's my top pick for A- to C-cups thanks to its lightly structured, unlined design that hugs your natural shape while disappearing under clothes.

The contoured cups mold to your body for a smooth, comfortable fit, and because they lie completely flat, there's no bunching or gaping to contend with. Despite having zero padding, the cups still provide full nipple coverage, so you get a sleek look under even the clingiest t-shirts without adding extra bulk.

I also appreciate that the plunge neckline works under just about everything, from V-necks to lower-cut tops, while the underwire offers just enough lift to create a naturally rounded shape. The result is polished and supportive without looking overly structured.

It has been revealed that the only drawback is that it's best suited to smaller busts, as it doesn't offer the level of coverage or support many fuller busts need. But it is available up to a G cup if you’d like to try it out yourself.

Industry observers note that if you love a deep V-neckline but hate when your bra peeks out, meet your new go-to: the Harper Wilde Bliss Triangle Bralette. It’s made with a flattering plunge that stays supportive and hidden under low-cut tops and dresses. I’ve worn it under everything from wrap dresses to tanks and it disappears under all of them. The triangle shape gives a natural lift—no wires, no padding, just your boobs but sliiightly perkier.

Comfort-wise, it lives up to the name. The modal fabric is buttery-soft and stretchy in that live-in-it kind of way. The band is wide and smooth, so it stays put without digging, and the adjustable straps let you customize the fit. It’s also lightweight enough to forget you’re even wearing it.

It’s become my go-to for daily wear, and the super-soft, barely-there material is truly the next best thing to going bra-free. While it’s equally great for bed-rotting or taking Zoom calls from home, I also feel confident wearing it out and about because it doesn’t skimp on coverage and offers just enough support.

Industry observers note that even without padding, the double-layered fabric gives solid nipple coverage. It comes in inclusive sizes and neutral shades that go with everything. The few cons? It’s not super supportive for heavy movement or fuller busts, so you may need to readjust on the go. But for everyday wear, especially with low-cut outfits, it fits the bill.

The most comfortable bras usually come down to the right blend of fabrics. Here’s what each one brings to the table:.

In a recent development, comfort is about more than just size—it’s also about ensuring the wire doesn’t create pressure points or cause discomfort throughout the day. Look for bras with flexible, padded, or cushioned underwires, which offer support without digging into your skin. The underwire should sit flat against your ribcage and follow the natural curve of your breasts. If it feels like it’s poking or shifting, it’s not the right fit. If you prefer a wire-free bra, opt for styles with flexible boning, molded cups, and wide, flexible bands to provide support.

According to recent reports, the most accurate way to find your size is to get fitted in person. Once you have your size, your newly introduced bra should feel snug and secure. The band should be comfortably tight, but not dig into the skin. A good rule of thumb is that you should be able to fit two fingers between the band and your skin, but no more. The cups should also lie flat against your chest.

The Women’s Health team has been testing bras since we first wrote this story in 2023. To find the most comfortable options, our team wore each style for at least a few weeks at a time. We wore them under different circumstances, including workouts, lounging, and long days at the office. But our main criterion for each bra was comfort. I also spoke with two bra experts and personally tested 20-plus bras over several years to lock down the ones I actually wear on repeat.

I recently re-tested a bunch of options and tapped style contributor Lily Wohlner for an revision to this story to boost our list and keep it up-to-date. The final guide includes everything from bralettes and seamless bras to push-up bras—and I actually wear all of them in my day-to-day life.

Industry observers note that BONN, Germany, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- As geopolitical uncertainty, changing trade patterns, and technological development reshape global supply chains, companies are increasingly looking for long-term logistics partners that can provide resilience and combine global scale, sector expertise, and technology. This shift is creating new opportunities for DHL Supply Chain, DHL Group's contract logistics business. In the third quarter of 2026, reported revenue increased by 12.0% year-on-year, with growth across all regions: 13.1% in the Americas, 11.7% in Europe, the Middle East and Africa (EMEA), and 9.9% in Asia Pacific. Growth spans across sectors including life sciences and healthcare, new energy, technology, retail, consumer, and automotive.

It has been revealed that "Supply chain resilience has become a strategic differentiator for many companies," said Hendrik Venter, CEO, DHL Supply Chain. "Our customers have to manage greater complexity while improving resilience to supply disruptions, productivity, and flexibility. They need long-term partners that understand their industries, can scale proven technology in operations, and have the capability to provide end-to-end supply chain solutions across global markets. The growth we are seeing across regions and sectors shows that this approach is resonating with our customers.".

Industry observers note that investing in capabilities for changing customer needsDHL Supply Chain continues to invest in identified high-growth markets, long-term partnerships, and strategic sector-specific initiatives. These investments include AI and robotics, automation, and acquisitions. Recent examples range from expanding Life Sciences and Healthcare capabilities in Latin America and the United States to specialized capacity for emerging industries such as battery logistics.

Sources indicate that in Life Sciences and Healthcare, DHL Supply Chain has progressively expanded its partnership with Sanofi, from managing logistics operations at three key distribution sites since 2024 to taking over operations at the tech giant's vaccine distribution center in Val-de-Reuil in 2026. The expanded partnership illustrates how specialized logistics capabilities and an international network can support pharmaceutical companies as they transform critical supply chains. In parallel, numerous newly built multi-user pharmaceutical warehouses are being commissioned, further expanding DHL Supply Chain's global footprint of more than 250 pharmaceutical warehouses.

Recent findings suggest that in the technology sector, the rapid expansion of AI and digital infrastructure is creating new logistics requirements. Data center logistics require specialized, globally integrated end-to-end supply chain solutions, including white-glove services. DHL Supply Chain is expanding its business across this wider ecosystem, supporting operators, technology providers, and infrastructure partners in developing data center capacity.

Recent findings suggest that long-term customer commitments provide secure future growth The Total Contract Value (TCV) of new customer contracts signed in 2026 is expected to far exceed â¬8 billion, supported by a qualified pipeline of more than â¬36 billion. TCV represents the lifetime value of contracts signed during the year rather than annual revenue and provides an indication of business secured for future operations. These commitments are broadly spread across DHL Supply Chain's global regions and sectors, with the Americas expected to account for approximately 45% of 2026 TCV, EMEA 35%, and Asia Pacific 20%.

Recent findings suggest that "For our customers, choosing a logistics partner is a long-term strategic decision," stated Andries Retief, Chief Development Officer, DHL Supply Chain. "They are entrusting us with critical parts of their operations and relying on us to support their future growth. Our ability to combine global scale, deep industry expertise, operational excellence, and innovation is what differentiates DHL Supply Chain. The strength of our commercial performance reflects customers' confidence in our ability to deliver today while helping them build the supply chains they will need tomorrow.".

With operations in more than 55 countries and a contract renewal rate of approximately 90%, DHL Supply Chain is well positioned to pursue its objective of growing a minimum of two percentage points faster than every contract logistics market it operates in.

Expanding customer relationships in pharmaceuticals, specialized logistics for new energy industries, and growing demand from the data center ecosystem illustrate opportunities in sectors undergoing major transformation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 11:25 EST / NOVEMBER 16 2026.

Alecto Conveyancing Ltd., a London-based artificial intelligence-native law firm, today confirmed it raised $20 million in seed funding led by Insight Partners to make the law more accessible to the general public.

According to recent reports, firstminute Capital, Blue Lion Global, Andrena Ventures, FJ Labs, Antiportfolio Ventures, the Rigby Group and Mischon de Reya LLP also joined in the round. Angel investors participating in the round included Octopus Group Chief Executive and founder Simon Rogerson and SwiftKey founder John Reynolds.

Founded in September 2025 by CEO Will Rice (pictured), a serial entrepreneur who previously built fintech mortgage lender Gen H, Alecto’s first service targets the United Kingdom conveyancing market, the legal work required to buy and sell property. Rice drew on his experience building a mortgage company and decided to focus initially on bringing more people into ownership. With that expertise, Alecto aims to use AI to help give everyday people greater access to the law.

In a recent development, alecto argues that traditional legal services are starved, with too few qualified attorneys and too few hours a day. Billing is based on hours, not outcomes and the service model doesn’t lean toward customers; this leads to unpredictable costs and a process that leaves customers in the dark.

It has been revealed that the law firm stated it’s using AI and legal experts to explain opaque legal processes in plain language and help clients make informed decisions. The company intends to target the property conveyancing market, which represents almost $3.3 billion in the U.K. alone, and aims to become the number one leader in property legal services by 2027.

“For too long, the legal industry has expected customers to work on its terms; now, AI presents the opportunity to put the consumer in control,” Rice said. “People don’t want to buy a lawyer’s time; they want results. Alecto exists to make the law accessible to everyone, giving control back to the consumer.”.

Consumer legal services in the U.K. value growth pushed revenue over £55 billion, around $72.5 billion, in 2026, according to a report from Research and Markets. Business and commercial practices lead with 51% market value, followed by growth in the injury and conveyancing law markets.

“Property is where we prove the model. We’re building the technology and operations to rapidly break into newly introduced countries and new areas of law,” Rice added. “Ultimately, access to exceptional legal support should not depend on how much money you have or how confidently you can navigate the system.”.

3 ways to check your car for an open recall and keep the answer current

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1363 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, NHTSA's recall lookup answers for one car by VIN or plate, leaves some recalls out, and needs a recheck twice a year.
  • It has been revealed that most drivers assume that if their car had a dangerous defect, someone would tell them about it and a mechanic would fix it.
  • Industry observers note that an open recall is a repair the manufacturer still owes the car, no matter how long ago the recall was confirmed.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, NHTSA's recall lookup answers for one car by VIN or plate, leaves some recalls out, and needs a recheck twice a year. Here is how to use it.

It has been revealed that most drivers assume that if their car had a dangerous defect, someone would tell them about it and a mechanic would fix it. Safety recalls are a routine part of owning a car, and they reach a large share of the vehicles on American roads every year. Manufacturers issued recalls covering more than 29.2 million vehicles in 2025, according to NHTSA. Many recalled cars have never gotten the repair. NHTSA reports that, on a weighted average, only 65.8 percent of the cars in recalls covering vehicles alone between 2012 and 2022 were fixed. That left a large share of recalled cars on the road with the defect still in place. A car in your own driveway may have a known safety problem that nobody has fixed.

Industry observers note that an open recall is a repair the manufacturer still owes the car, no matter how long ago the recall was confirmed. A recall never expires once a vehicle is recalled, according to NHTSA. The repair is also free to the owner. A driver who buys a used car years after a recall was issued is still entitled to the fix at no cost. That right is useful only to an owner who knows about the recall, because nobody can ask a dealer for a repair they have never heard of. The owner is the one person who can make sure the car gets fixed.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration set out to show owners how to find out whether their vehicle has an unfixed safety recall. The guidance comes from the federal agency that runs the recall system, and it covers what a clean result fails to show, a free app that checks for you, and the 17-character number in the corner of the windshield. An owner can type that number into a search box and get an answer in seconds. Staying protected depends on reading the answer correctly and checking again later.

Sources indicate that A recall notice names a type of car, and an owner reading it still has no way to know whether the one in the driveway has had its repair. An owner who searches by year, make and model gets the general recalls, investigations and complaints for every car of that type. Those results can't show whether that owner's car is one of the cars still waiting for the fix. The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration claims that a search by plate number or by the vehicle identification number, or VIN, shows whether one particular car has a recall repair outstanding. That is the difference between knowing a defect exists and knowing your own car has it.

The VIN is the backup for the times a plate search goes wrong. The license plate is quicker to type, but a plate search is only as accurate as the registration records behind it. An owner who searches by plate may see a vehicle they previously owned until the DMV updates its records, and a search by VIN gets around that problem in the meantime. Owners don't have to dig through paperwork to find the VIN, because it appears in the lower left corner of the windshield. An owner who is away from the car can find the same number on the registration card and possibly on the insurance card. A complete VIN runs 17 characters, and an owner can count them before searching to make sure none were dropped.

A match on your car is a reason to book the repair, not a fact to file away. The repair is done at the manufacturer's dealership, according to NHTSA. An open recall means calling that dealer to schedule the work. An owner who finds a recall but never makes the appointment is driving a car exactly as dangerous as it was before the search.

A clean recall result covers only the recalls the lookup holds, and for long-standing recalls and less common makes that is a narrow set. The search generally leaves out safety recalls issued more than 15 years ago unless a manufacturer chooses to cover them, according to the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration. An owner whose car was recalled that long ago and never repaired may still get a clean result. Open recalls appear only for certain manufacturers. For owners of cars from other makers, a blank result marks a gap in coverage, not a sound car. The older the recall or the less common the maker, the less weight an owner can put on a clean answer.

Industry observers note that even for a car the lookup covers, an owner can't tell from a blank result why it's blank. Safety recalls that have already been repaired don't appear in the results, and a VIN search, NHTSA reports, shows only recalls still awaiting a fix. On screen, a car whose recall was fixed last year looks the same as a car that was never recalled. An owner can learn whether any repair is still owed, but not whether past work was done, which is the question that matters when a car changes hands. For questions about repair history, the agency's advice is to contact the manufacturer.

According to recent reports, the recall lookup gives owners answers about recalls and nothing else. International campaigns are missing from it, and so are non-safety campaigns. NHTSA reports that notices and bulletins submitted by manufacturers are kept in a separate search from recalls. A fault that a maker has already addressed in a bulletin can stay hidden from an owner who runs only a recall check. Owners trying to track down a recurring problem should run that other search as well.

The plate search is convenient, but its data comes from state departments of motor vehicles rather than from the carmaker. If those state records contain a clerical error, the owner may see the wrong vehicle. In that case, the owner should contact the state DMV and search by VIN until the record is corrected.

The plate is the quicker way to an answer, but the VIN is the one to trust.

A clean recall result describes your car only on the day you checked it, and a upcoming recall can be added to that same car later. "VINs are added continuously so please check regularly," the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration stated. The agency recommends checking again twice a year, which gives every owner a simple schedule for the calendar. That habit matters because a notice mailed to warn owners may never reach the person now driving the car.

Industry observers note that recall repairs get done most often while a car is young. NHTSA reports that cars up to three years old have historically had recalls completed around 87 percent of the time, and that in older campaigns, up to 30 percent of the cars still awaiting the fix get a latest owner or a new address every year. The longer a car stays on the road, the less likely it is that its current driver is the person whose name and address a mailed notice goes to. People who bought a car used, or who have moved since the last notice, are the owners most likely to miss one. For them, their own check is the warning.

Recent findings suggest that the surest way to keep up is to have recall news sent to you instead of relying on memory. The agency offers a free app, NHTSA SaferCar, that alerts owners to recalls. Few people look on their own: in a 2019 survey, only 18 percent of people had used the agency's website to check for recalls, according to NHTSA. Any owner who gets a notice or an alert should heed the agency's temporary safety instructions and call a nearby dealer to schedule the fix.

Turn on the app's alerts, put the twice-yearly check on the calendar, and answer any notice with a call to the dealer.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

by Todd Bishop on Nov 14, 2026 at 10:35 amNovember 16, 2026 at 7:28 am.

Steven Sinofsky was relieved this week to finally give up a title he never wanted.

“Somewhat happy to say I am no longer responsible for the worst Outlook outage,” the former Microsoft executive posted on X Friday, sharing a May 2000 news story about the “I Love You” worm, which overwhelmed corporate email systems when he ran the Office group.

It has been revealed that later in the day, he aired a pet peeve. After a plumber emailed to say he’d missed an appointment because of the “Outlook outage,” Sinofsky noted that this one wasn’t really the application’s fault. “This time it is the data center layer,” he wrote.

Microsoft’s explanation backs him up. The tech giant says the failure, which cut off email for people and organizations in more than 70 countries this week, was introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade in its Microsoft 365 cloud and surfaced after a more recent network change. It hasn’t given more details.

The tech giant noted late Friday it had restored service to the remaining customers and regions. The disruption lasted about 30 hours, according to Microsoft’s incident log. Microsoft offered a public apology and promised a detailed post-mortem explaining what went wrong and next steps.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, mentioned on X Friday afternoon that “cascading failures + thundering herds at our network perimeter” made recovery more difficult than normal.

Industry observers note that A “thundering herd” isn’t a stampede of frustrated IT admins descending on Redmond, as fitting as that might have been. It happens when huge numbers of devices try to reconnect at the same time, overwhelming systems as they come back online.

He noted the post-mortem would come “shortly,” with a “step-by-step timeline and our many repair items to avoid similar outages in the future.” In a reply to another user, he said Microsoft “will be very specific on what happened.” In its notice to customers, Microsoft said it would provide a preliminary post-incident report within two business days and a final report within five.

In the meantime, like prior incidents involving AWS and others, the “Outlook outage” became the latest example of how much depends on one firm’s cloud.

Microsoft reported in January that it had more than 450 million paid commercial Microsoft 365 seats, roughly one for every 18 people on Earth.

Recent findings suggest that among those affected this week were Unity Health Toronto, a hospital network that had to declare a Code Grey, the alert for a systems failure; a Colorado jail that couldn’t take online bond payments; and Pennsylvania lawmakers who went about 18 hours without email. Unity Health said patient care continued without disruption.

In Japan, securities firms and asset managers fell back on fax machines when trade-confirmation emails stopped coming through, Business Upturn reported, citing Nikkei.

In Latest York, the city’s Emergency Management office warned of delays reaching city agencies. In Singapore, the outage disrupted some government systems, including email, and in London, the UK Supreme Court wasn’t receiving email.

About the only thing that wasn’t Microsoft’s fault was Friday’s nationwide FAA ground stop. Federal officials blamed aging FAA telecom gear. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin opened an evening news conference — before even getting to the news that U.S. airspace had reopened — by saying there was “no connection between this and Microsoft,” adding, “I know a lot of people are making that jump.”.

Microsoft itself looked to preempt the speculation a few hours earlier, posting on X that it had “no indication that the FAA’s nationwide ground stop is related to any Microsoft services.”.

The Microsoft 365 outage was at least the fourth significant one this year. A January outage lasted nearly 10 hours, and in July a bug in Microsoft’s automated network maintenance system disrupted Azure and Microsoft 365 services for hours. On Aug. 31, an Exchange Online outage also hit Teams, OneDrive and SharePoint.

Instead of “I hope this email finds you well,” many people joked, it should just be “I hope this email finds you.” (Consider this our nomination for the “Overworked Twitter Joke of the Week” on The Ringer’s Press Box podcast.).

Microsoft remarked Friday afternoon that it was watching the backlog of delayed email “to ensure all process successfully before considering the issue resolved.” The University of Washington’s IT department told its users that email delayed during the outage would be delivered as mail queues continued to be processed.

Many people coped with the flood of returning email with a bit of levity.

As the mail started flowing again, CNN chief media analyst Brian Stelter remarked he was getting “a deluge of emails from PR people pitching their clients to talk about the Outlook outage.” Most were sent during the outage, he noted, “which, fittingly, prevented the pitches from reaching me.”.

The security company Malwarebytes captured the paradox in a message to its followers: “We regret to inform you that Teams and Outlook are coming back online after a global outage.”.

HOUSTON, Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Colla Health, Inc. ("Colla Health") is providing notice of a recent data security incident that may have resulted in unauthorized access to certain individuals' personal information ("PI") and/or protected health information ("PHI"). This notice provides details about the incident, steps Colla Health is taking in response, and resources to help protect against potential misuse of PI and PHI.

Colla Health is providing this notice on its own behalf and on behalf of the practices listed at the end of this notice.

Recent findings suggest that what Happened? On or around August 18, 2026, Colla Health became aware that an unauthorized party had accessed a third-party application Colla Health uses, Metabase, who announced a previously unknown vulnerability. Upon learning of the incident, we promptly secured the application and engaged a specialized third-party cybersecurity firm to conduct a comprehensive investigation to determine the nature and scope of the incident. The investigation found evidence that certain data may have been taken from the application.

Sources indicate that based on these findings, Colla Health reviewed the affected data to identify specific individuals and the types of information involved. After verifying addresses, Colla Health notified affected individuals by U.S. First Class Mail. We are providing this substitute notice to reach individuals who could not receive direct notice of the incident.

What Information Was Involved? The information involved may include full names, addresses, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, health insurance information, medical information, and other demographic information. The types of information vary by individual, and not every individual had all the listed information involved.

What Are We Doing? Data privacy and security are among Colla Health's highest priorities, and we are committed to doing everything we can to protect the privacy and security of the PI and PHI in our care. Upon discovering the incident, we moved swiftly to investigate, respond, and confirm the security of the application. Colla Health conducted a forensic investigation to determine the nature and scope of the incident and notified affected individuals via U.S. First Class Mail. Colla Health has implemented security updates, changed administrative credentials, and enhanced security measures, and we continue to take steps to mitigate future risks. We are also offering complimentary credit monitoring to affected individuals.

What You Can Do: We encourage you to remain vigilant by carefully reviewing your financial statements for unauthorized activity, monitoring your credit reports, and placing a fraud alert or credit freeze on your credit reports by contacting the three credit reporting agencies (Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion). You can obtain more information about identity theft prevention, fraud alerts, and credit freezes from the U.S. Federal Trade Commission at www.ftc.gov.

Recent findings suggest that for More Information: If you have questions or would like to confirm whether your information may have been impacted by the incident, please call our toll-free line at (888) 213-4555 Monday through Friday, between 9 a.m. and 9 p.m. Eastern Time (excluding U.S. national holidays).

Colla Health regrets any concern or inconvenience this matter may cause and remains dedicated to ensuring the privacy and security of all information in our care.

This notice is provided on behalf of the following practices: Cancer Care Specialists, Cancer Care Specialists of Illinois, Cancer Center of Middle Georgia, Columbus Oncology & Hematology, Comprehensive Hematology Oncology, Highlands Oncology, Nebraska Cancer Specialists, New Mexico Cancer Center, Pontchartrain Cancer Center, St. Louis Cancer Care, Virginia Cancer Institute, and American Oncology Partners, P.A. d/b/a Elkhart Hematology & Oncology, Fort Wayne Medical Oncology and Hematology, Genesis Cancer and Blood Institute, Hematology Oncology Center, Hematology Oncology of Indiana, and The Zangmeister Cancer Center.

Monitor Your AccountsWe recommend that you remain vigilant for incidents of fraud or identity theft by regularly reviewing your credit reports and financial accounts for any suspicious activity. Box 105281, Atlanta, GA, 30348-5281. You may also purchase a copy of your credit report for a fee by contacting one or more of the three national credit reporting agencies.

You have rights under the federal Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA). The FCRA governs the collection and use of information about you that is reported by consumer reporting agencies. You can obtain additional information about your rights under the FCRA by visiting https://www.ftc.gov/legal-library/browse/statutes/fair-credit-reporting-act.

Industry observers note that you have the right to add, temporarily lift, or remove a credit freeze, also known as a security freeze, on your credit report at no cost. A credit freeze prevents third parties, such as credit lenders or other companies, whose use is not exempt under law, from accessing your credit file without your consent. If you have a freeze, you must remove or temporarily lift it to apply for credit. Spouses can request freezes for each other as long as they pass authentication. You can also request a freeze for someone if you have a valid Power of Attorney. If you are a parent, guardian, or representative, you can request a freeze for a minor under the age of 16. To add a security freeze, you must make a separate request to each of the three national consumer reporting agencies by phone, online, or by mail by following the instructions found at their websites (see "Contact Information" below). You must include the following information when requesting a security freeze: (i) full name, with middle initial and any suffixes; (ii) Social Security number; (iii) date of birth (month, day, and year); (iv) current address and any previous addresses for the past five (5) years; (v) proof of current address (such as a copy of a government-issued identification card, a recent utility or telephone bill, or bank or insurance statement); and (vi) other personal information as required by the applicable credit reporting agency.

You have the right to add, extend, or remove a fraud alert on your credit file at no cost. A fraud alert is a statement added to your credit file that notifies potential creditors that you may be or have been a victim of identity theft. Before they extend credit, they should use reasonable procedures to verify your identity. Please note that, unlike a credit freeze, a fraud alert only notifies lenders to verify your identity before extending latest credit, but it does not block access to your credit report. Fraud alerts are free to add and are valid for one year. Victims of identity theft can obtain an extended fraud alert for seven years. You can add a fraud alert by sending your request to any one of the three national credit reporting agencies by phone, online, or by mail by following the instructions found at their websites (see "Contact Information" below). The agency you contact will then contact the other credit agencies.

According to recent reports, for more information about credit freezes, fraud alerts, and other steps you can take to protect yourself against identity theft, contact the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) at 600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, DC 20580, www.identitytheft.gov, 1-877-ID-THEFT (1-877-438-4338), TTY: 1-866-653-4261. The FTC also encourages those who discover that their information has been misused to file a complaint with it. You can obtain further information on how to file such a complaint by using the contact information listed above.

You should also report instances of known or suspected identity theft to local law enforcement and the Attorney General's office in your home state, and you have the right to file a police report and obtain a copy of your police report.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • ZetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments.
  • Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn.
  • ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

ZetaChain's Governance Proposal 2 would halt its L1 around Dec 9, mint ZETA 1:1 on Solana and burn about 55M ZETA in monthly installments. Voting closes Nov 7.

Headlines are calling it a 55 million ZETA burn. Read the proposal's own schedule, though, and nothing close to 55 million disappears on the day the chain halts. The figure is real, but it arrives in twelve installments over 2027.

ZetaChain published Governance Proposal 2 on November 4, and its announcement post lays out the mechanics. About 55 million ZETA of undistributed validator emissions will be burned monthly through 2027, following the schedule on which they would have been emitted. The roadmap in the same post puts the pace at twelve monthly burns of roughly 4.6 million ZETA each, from January to December 2027.

That detail changes how the number should be read. Most of the early flash coverage collapsed it into a single burn, which implies an immediate supply shock. The staged schedule tells a different story. These tokens were never going to circulate, because they are validator rewards for an L1 that is about to stop. Burning them on the original emission timetable keeps the published release schedule intact and introduces no newly introduced mechanism, as ZetaChain's FAQ puts it.

It has been revealed that governance Proposal 2 builds on Proposal 68, which approved the move to Solana in September with 99.4% in favor. Proposal 2 supplies the mechanics. Voting runs 72 hours and closes on November 7, and ZetaChain says nothing moves unless it passes.

Sources indicate that if it does pass, every ZETA balance is recorded at snapshot block 20,755,000, expected around December 9. The ZetaChain L1 halts at that same height and isn't restarted. Claims open the same day through the ZetaHub migration portal, and ZetaChain's new private AI app, ZetaLabs, debuts alongside it.

The proposal also pairs the migration with a fresh whitepaper, which ZetaChain calls the document of record for the token after the move.

It has been revealed that the snapshot goes well beyond a simple wallet count. It records liquid, staked, unbonding and unclaimed-reward balances. Staked ZETA is credited automatically, so nobody has to unstake, and exchange balances convert without any action from holders. Staking rewards stop at the snapshot height.

Holders who want to claim directly face a short process. They connect the wallet that held ZETA, sign a message naming a Solana wallet, and receive the full balance shortly afterward. The claim costs no fee and requires no SOL. According to the post, the portal asks only for a signature, never for a transaction or a seed phrase. A minimum of 10 ZETA at the snapshot is needed to claim.

In a recent development, two edge cases deserve attention. First, ZETA wrapped or sitting in pools and contracts can't be claimed by a key, so holders need to unwrap and exit before the snapshot. Second, assets still held as ZRC-20 tokens at the snapshot can be claimed back on their original chain through a separate bridged-assets page, with a $5 minimum per token. Both are the kind of detail that catches people out when a deadline arrives.

Recent findings suggest that on Solana, ZETA becomes a native SPL token under the same ticker, with 9 decimals and no freeze authority. The full snapshot total is minted before the portal opens, and then the mint authority is revoked, so no one can ever mint more. No third-party bridge is involved.

That sequence is the strongest holder protection in the proposal, and it is also the part that can be checked in public. The supply stays capped at 2.1 billion less whatever has been burned, and ZetaChain says it will publish the SPL mint address and the migration program address before December 9. Once those exist, anyone can compare the minted total against the snapshot and confirm that the authority was actually revoked. That confirmation deserves the most scrutiny.

Meanwhile, the portal and its program are under independent review by Hacken, and ZetaChain notes the portal opens only after the review is complete and the report is published. The ERC-20 version of ZETA on Ethereum is unaffected by the proposal. Purchaser and core contributor vesting completes on January 1, 2027, and ZetaChain says no newly released ZETA will be sold in 2027.

The biggest practical risk is inattention. Most holders don't need to do anything until December 9, but exchange customers depend on each exchange's own conversion window, and anyone holding ZETA through a contract or pool has homework to do beforehand.

It has been revealed that scams add another layer of risk. Any migration with a claim portal invites imitators, and ZetaChain tells holders to trust only its official domains and social accounts. A simple rule of thumb helps here: a site that asks for a seed phrase should be closed immediately, since the legitimate flow only needs a message signature.

On the technical side, claims are checked against the published snapshot rather than the live chain, so they continue to work after the halt. ZetaChain indicates it will announce any change to the process in advance.

The vote decides the terms, not the direction. If Proposal 2 fails, the direction approved in Proposal 68 stands and ZetaChain returns with a revised proposal. Nothing moves on these terms.

If it passes, the sequence is clear. The security report, mint address and migration program address arrive before December 9. The snapshot, halt, mint and portal opening follow on the day, and the monthly burns run through 2027. ZetaLabs then adds a Premium tier in the first quarter of 2027, with ZETA as the token for access and payment.

In a recent development, taken together, this looks more like a retirement strategy for an L1 than a dramatic supply event. The burn is gradual, the mint is capped, and the claim process is simple on paper. Execution is what will matter most: the audit report, the published addresses and the clean revocation of mint authority. Those are the items to watch between now and December 9.
