Talkdesk’s life sciences play highlights why industry depth beats AI cost-cutting

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Siliconangle

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.
  • The customer experience arena, specifically the contact center, has been the low-hanging fruit for artificial intelligence deployments, with much of the focus on cost-cutting.
  • According to recent reports, those are legitimate goals, but they lead every vendor to the same pitch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 15:36 EST / NOVEMBER 16 2026.

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala.

The customer experience arena, specifically the contact center, has been the low-hanging fruit for artificial intelligence deployments, with much of the focus on cost-cutting. The goals include fewer agents, shorter calls, higher containment and lower cost per interaction.

According to recent reports, those are legitimate goals, but they lead every vendor to the same pitch. When everyone sells the same savings, the market becomes a price war that favors the companies with the deepest pockets.

In a recent development, talkdesk Inc. is taking a different path, and today’s announcement reinforces that. This week, the manufacturer introduced Talkdesk Life Sciences Experience Cloud, a platform designed for biopharmaceutical companies’ patient services operations. The goal is not to make calls cheaper. It is to move patients from a written prescription to therapy faster and keep them there.

That outcome is one a pharma executive will pay for, and one a generic contact-center-as-a-service platform is poorly equipped to deliver. This adds to Talkdesk’s portfolio of industry clouds, including financial services, government, retail, travel and others.

The new offering connects AI agents, human specialists, systems, and workflows across the specialty care journey, which typically includes enrollment, prior authorizations and specialty pharmacy handoffs. Talkdesk cites IQVIA research showing that nearly one in three commercially insured patients cannot access a prescribed therapy within 30 days, and Boston Consulting Group data indicating that 90% of biopharma leaders view fragmented platforms as their primary bottleneck.

Sources indicate that the platform analyzes patient service conversations to pinpoint where patients get stuck, assists specialists in real time, and coordinates tasks among hubs, providers, payers, specialty pharmacies and safety teams. It supports the U.S. Food and Drug Administration’s 21 CFR Part 11 requirements for electronic records and signatures and integrates with existing customer relationship management, hub, pharmacy and safety systems.

One of the world’s five largest pharmaceutical companies has already deployed it. That customer uses AI to classify and route inbound calls and to monitor live conversations for potential reportable events, or PREs, which are adverse event signals that must be captured and sent to pharmacovigilance systems. When the system detects a PRE, it guides the frontline agent to collect the required details, preserves the source conversation and triggers approved workflows to document and route the information.

“A prescription should mark the start of healing, not the beginning of an administrative maze,” said Patty Hayward, general manager of healthcare and life sciences at Talkdesk. “We are focusing first on Therapy Access because promptly getting patients onto prescribed treatments is one of the most urgent, measurable challenges in healthcare today.”.

Hayward’s choice of the word “measurable” is the key point. Time to therapy is a metric that appears on a drug maker’s revenue line and in patient outcomes, not just on a contact center dashboard.

Recent findings suggest that talkdesk competes in a crowded market against much larger companies. NiCE Ltd. and Genesys Cloud Services Inc. have scale in the contact center, while Microsoft Corp., Salesforce Inc., and Amazon Web Services Inc. can bundle customer service capabilities into platforms that customers already own. A smaller organization cannot outspend those rivals on horizontal features, and it should not try.

What it can do is go deeper into specific industries than the giants are willing to go. Talkdesk has been building industry-specific clouds for several years, and life sciences is a logical next step from its healthcare work. Pharmacovigilance workflows, Part 11 compliance, hub services and specialty pharmacy coordination are not features a horizontal vendor casually adds to its roadmap. They require domain expertise, regulatory knowledge and integrations that take time to build, and that time becomes a competitive moat.

The industry approach also changes the sales conversation. A generic platform is evaluated on price per seat and feature checklists, usually by the information technology department and the contact center leader. An industry platform is evaluated on whether it solves a business problem the executive team already worries about.

In pharma, patient abandonment between prescription and first fill represents lost revenue and a failed treatment. That conversation happens with the head of patient services, which is a much better place for a smaller vendor to be.

The industry approach has helped channel partners sell Talkdesk. I asked Joe Rittenhouse, co-CEO of Converged Technology Professionals Inc., one of the premier communications resellers, about it.

Sources indicate that “We’re no longer leading with features or price per seat,” he mentioned. “We’re leading with the customer’s workflows, their compliance requirements and the outcomes they’re measured on. That industry approach is a key differentiator for us. It lets us skip the generic AI conversation and get straight to the problems that keep the business up at night, shortening the sales cycle and making the deployment stick.”.

The bigger story is how this fits into Talkdesk’s customer experience automation or CXA strategy, which is not a typical contact center-as-a-service sell. The idea is to coordinate AI agents, people, knowledge and enterprise systems to resolve a customer need from start to finish, rather than simply answering or routing an interaction faster. Resolving concerns across systems is a far bigger value proposition than call deflection, but it is also much harder to deliver in the abstract.

Recent findings suggest that that is where industry depth becomes critical. End-to-end automation is only possible when the platform understands what “end” means. In a retail return, the end might be a refund. In specialty pharma, the end is a patient who has completed benefits verification, obtained prior authorization, had the drug shipped and is still taking it six months later.

Each step involves different systems, organizations and regulatory obligations. A horizontal AI agent cannot orchestrate that journey without someone first mapping it. Talkdesk is effectively packaging that work into the product.

This is also why the industry approach shifts AI from a cost story to a transformation story. Using AI to reduce handle time on patient service calls might save a few dollars per interaction, and identifying that patients in each program repeatedly stall at prior authorization, then fixing that bottleneck, can change how many patients start therapy. The first is an efficiency gain. The second changes the economics of the business.

The pharmacovigilance use case makes the same point. Missing a reportable adverse event carries regulatory consequences. AI that detects those signals and routes them correctly reduces risk and improves quality, rather than reducing headcount, a value proposition that is far easier to justify to a board.

For life sciences leaders, the lesson is to stop evaluating customer engagement technology based solely on contact center metrics. Start with the patient journey, identify where patients drop off and measure vendors on their ability to shorten time to therapy and improve adherence. Insist on proof of regulatory readiness, particularly for Part 11 and adverse event handling, and validate integration with the hub, CRM and safety systems already in place.

Recent findings suggest that for buyers in other industries, the broader point still holds. AI that only cuts costs will eventually commoditize. AI that understands your business’s specific workflows, regulations and outcomes can transform it. Ask CX vendors how well they understand your industry, not just how good their models are.

Sources indicate that for Talkdesk, life sciences is a smart focus area. It will not win every horizontal deal against larger rivals, but it does not need to. By targeting industries with complex, regulated journeys tied to clear outcomes, it can make CXA tangible and give customers a reason to buy that has nothing to do with price.

Industry observers note that zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#6086. 12 things to know about daily water, from thirst to overdrinking

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3927 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Qz ↗ Open Full Page

12 things to know about daily water, from thirst to overdrinking

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3927 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that daily water needs vary by age, health and activity.
  • Recent findings suggest that most people carry a daily water target in their heads, and many suspect they fall short of it.
  • Recent findings suggest that for most healthy people, thirst is the best guide to how much to drink.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that daily water needs vary by age, health and activity. See 12 facts on intake, dehydration, overdrinking and easy habits.

Recent findings suggest that most people carry a daily water target in their heads, and many suspect they fall short of it. Many of them are right: roughly half the world's people drink less water than experts recommend, according to NIH. Missing that mark rarely leads to harm, though. StatPearls reports that dehydration is uncommon in adults who have no medical problems and can drink water freely. The official amount is therefore a rough guide, and a person who falls short of it on a given day hasn't failed a test. Who a person is and what their body is doing that day matter more than any fixed amount, whether they are working outside in summer heat or recovering from an illness.

Recent findings suggest that for most healthy people, thirst is the best guide to how much to drink. It is also least reliable in the people who most need it. In older adults the body's thirst signal is less sensitive, StatPearls reports, and some drugs for blood pressure can leave a person unable to tell that they are thirsty, according to Cleveland Clinic. For an older adult who takes blood pressure pills, waiting to feel thirsty can mean drinking too little, too late. The opposite problem, drinking far more than the body needs, is rarer but just as real. In both cases, serious trouble with hydration is concentrated among particular people whose sense of need doesn't work reliably, and it doesn't threaten everyone equally.

Mayo Clinic set out to explain how much water people need and how to stay well hydrated. Its guide covered alkaline water, older adults whose thirst fades, endurance runners who drink too much, and a splash of juice in sparkling water. The useful answer is less a cup count than a clear sense of who should drink on a routine and who should hold back. No upper intake limit has been set for water, so people prone to drinking too much are protected mainly by knowing their own risk. For everyone else, the task is to make plain water the easy choice over the sugary drinks it would replace.

The body needs water every day, and the need is large. By weight, an adult's body is about 60% water, according to Mayo Clinic. Even the official guidance gives no single glass count for everyone. The National Academy of Medicine sets a daily amount of about 13 cups for healthy men and about 9 cups for healthy women, so no one eight-glass rule applies to all adults. If people read the amount for men as glasses of plain water, they would drink well past what at least one nutrition researcher thinks they require. CBC News reports that Speros Tsindos, an author in the department of dietetics and human nutrition at La Trobe University, considers even eight daily glasses of pure water more than people seem to need. The useful question, then, is not how anyone could drink 13 glasses, but what counts toward the official amount.

Sources indicate that much of the water a body takes in never passes through a glass. "There's nothing magical about water from a glass of water as opposed to water from a food or any other beverage," Susan Barr, a nutrition professor at the University of British Columbia, told CBC News. A baked potato is 75% water, so people take in water at dinner without lifting a glass. Caffeinated coffee and tea don't dehydrate the people who drink them, either. A person who starts the day with a mug of coffee has already taken in water that a tally of water glasses would miss.

In a recent development, the plain water a person drinks on purpose is only one part of what the body takes in each day. Someone worried about falling short should look at everything they eat and drink before adding glasses to reach a number.

The best-known daily water amounts count every fluid a person takes in, not only glasses of plain water. The National Academy of Medicine sets an adequate intake of about 13 cups for healthy men and about 9 cups for healthy women, according to Mayo Clinic. NIH reports that those totals can include juices and water-rich produce. A person who eats fruit and vegetables and drinks other beverages through the day is already covering part of the amount at ordinary meals. The share that has to come from the tap is smaller than the headline number suggests.

Recent findings suggest that the advised amount depends on what a body is doing, not only on whether the person is a man or a woman. A breastfeeding woman is advised to take in 13 cups, the same as a healthy man and well above the general figure for women. Producing milk lifts her need to the level set for men. The figures for men and women serve as a baseline that changes with a person's stage of life, not as a fixed personal assignment.

It has been revealed that there is a real health reason behind the cup counts, though it is not proof. NIH reports that adults whose blood sodium measured 144.5 to 146 mEq/L faced a 21% higher risk of premature death than adults whose levels measured 137 to 142 mEq/L. A level many people would call fine still carried a cost. That makes hydration something a doctor can check with a blood test, not only something a person tallies in cups. "People whose serum sodium is 142 mEq/L or higher would benefit from evaluation of their fluid intake," said Natalia Dmitrieva, Ph.D., an NHLBI researcher and study author. A higher risk among people with higher sodium shows a link, not evidence that drinking more water would lower that risk. The cup counts are a sensible bet rather than a proven line between health and harm.

For most healthy people, that makes the number a reason to keep water within reach, not a quota to finish by bedtime.

Counting glasses misses water that people take in without drinking it. About 20% of the water a person takes in each day comes from food, according to The Nutrition Source. The CDC reports that foods with high water content contribute to fluid intake. A lunch salad of lettuce, cucumbers, bell peppers and celery adds water to the day, and so does a bowl of melon and berries after dinner. Someone who eats plenty of produce takes in more water than a glass count highlights.

In a recent development, the other drinks in a person's day also count toward the total, and coffee and tea are among them. The one limit to keep in mind is caffeine: someone who takes in more than 180 mg of it a day may urinate more. Below that level, the coffee or tea a person already drinks belongs in the daily tally. Above it, the amount of caffeine deserves closer attention than the type of drink it comes in.

The baseline amount also changes from one day to the next, even for someone who eats well. Fever, exercise, and extreme heat or cold all raise the amount of fluid a person needs. The CDC reports that people in hot climates need more water as well. Cold also appears on the list, so a person working outdoors in extreme cold needs more fluid too. Illness that drains fluid belongs on the same list. Vomiting and diarrhea pull water out of the body, so someone with a stomach bug should drink beyond their usual amount.

Sources indicate that the daily figure is a starting point that each day revises. That leaves the question of what should go in the glass, and whether some waters are worth paying more for.

It has been revealed that alkaline water is sold as an upgrade on the ordinary kind, a drink that does more for the body than keep it hydrated. It lacks proof of any extra benefit, and plain water hydrates about as well, according to The Nutrition Source. ABC News reports that Michele Promaulayko, editor in chief of Yahoo Health, finds no studies showing that the water does anything to improve a person's health. Someone who pays extra for a bottle pays for a claim, not for a result they can count on.

The sales pitch rests on changing the body's chemistry, not on hydration. People who promote alkaline water want to bring the body to a pH of 7.4, according to ABC News. The body already regulates blood to about that level on its own. Researchers have yet to prove in a controlled trial that food or drink can move a healthy person's blood away from that level. "Our bodies need water - it's absolutely essential. But … the idea that drinking alkaline water will affect the PH of your blood is absolute nonsense," said Dr. Richard Besser, ABC News' chief health and medical editor. The strongest case against alkaline water comes from how the body works, not from whether the people drinking it stay hydrated.

Ordinary tap water needs no correcting, and its pH of about 7 is close to neutral. The EPA recommends that drinking water have a pH between 6.5 and 8.5, according to ABC News. Tap water already falls inside that range, so alkaline water fills no gap. That leaves one honest argument for it, which is whether it gets a person to reach for water more often. Someone who drinks more because the alkaline kind appeals to them gains from the extra water, not from its pH.

Anyone who already drinks enough gains nothing from paying more that they couldn't get from the tap.

Waiting to feel thirsty works poorly for people whose sense of thirst has faded. Thirst grows weaker with age and illness, and some people need set drinking routines as a result, according to The Nutrition Source. For them, drinking only when thirsty can mean drinking too little and too late. Older adults also have less water in their bodies to lose before trouble starts. "What happens as you get older, the amount of total water in your body actually goes down. That means you don't have as much water to lose," Ronan Factora, a geriatric medicine specialist at Cleveland Clinic, noted. A drinking routine for an older parent is not fussiness. It makes up for a smaller supply of water and a sense of thirst that no longer gives a reliable warning.

Some medical conditions, among them stroke and dementia, can impair the sense of thirst. People living with these conditions may not feel thirsty when their bodies need water, and a routine can supply the reminder their thirst fails to give. Other people feel thirsty and still drink less on purpose, because they live with incontinence or find it hard to reach the bathroom. For them, drinking less is a choice, and a reminder to drink will do little if the trip to the bathroom is the real obstacle. Making that trip easier is part of preventing dehydration.

It has been revealed that keeping water cool can make a drinking routine easier to follow. People most often drink their water at room temperature, yet they rate cooler water as more pleasing. Keeping cool water within reach costs nothing, and it may help people whose thirst has weakened stick to a schedule.

According to recent reports, dehydration can dull the mind and mood well before anyone would call themselves parched. People who are short by only about 2% of their body's water can already feel tired, confused or moody, according to The Nutrition Source. Tiredness, fogginess and a short temper feel like an ordinary bad day, and few people connect them with what they've had to drink. These signs help only someone who knows to treat them as a reason to pour a glass.

Recent findings suggest that the early signs are also the hardest to confirm. StatPearls reports that there is no gold-standard test for dehydration. A person who feels foggy in the afternoon has no firm way to tell whether water is the cause, and judging hydration by feel stays guesswork. Uncertainty like that leaves room for alarm. No research supports the widely shared figure that 75% of Americans go through life short of water. For most people, a vague symptom is a reason to drink some water. It is not proof of a hidden, long-running deficit.

In long-term care, the early signs are a common sight rather than a rare warning. Of the residents of those facilities, 34% are dehydrated, according to StatPearls. Caregivers and visiting family should expect to watch for tiredness and confusion in the people they look after. Older adults who live at home are dehydrated less often, at 19%, but the risk remains real outside care, even though it runs highest inside it. For an older relative, the useful habit is to notice a tired or muddled day and offer water rather than wait for them to ask for it.

Sources indicate that dehydration can do its harm slowly, through ailments that build up over time rather than in a single hot afternoon. Most people think of it as a headache after too much sun, something they can fix with a glass of water within the hour. Going short of water can raise the risk of constipation, gallstones and kidney stones, according to The Nutrition Source. These are common, nagging problems that develop out of sight. They matter most for people who can't easily drink as much as their bodies need.

Industry observers note that older adults are among those people, and for some of them the obstacle is the physical act of drinking. People with Parkinson's disease can have trouble swallowing, The Conversation reports, and they may want a drink and still struggle to get it down. For someone in that position, wanting water isn't enough to keep fluids coming. A caregiver who offers drinks on a schedule can help close that gap.

Urinary tract infections bring a separate danger for older adults. In an older person, such an infection can bring on delirium, a sudden state of confusion, according to The Conversation. An abrupt change in an older relative's thinking can therefore have a physical cause that a doctor can find and treat.

For anyone caring for an older relative, newly introduced confusion is a reason to check how much they have been drinking and to ask a doctor about infection, rather than to assume a lasting decline.

It has been revealed that A person who drinks a large amount of water quickly can harm themselves, even though most people treat water as the one thing they can't overdo. Rapid, heavy drinking can overwhelm the kidneys and push sodium in the blood to a dangerous low, though this is rare, according to The Nutrition Source. The result is a condition called hyponatremia, or low blood sodium. The harm comes from what a large, fast intake does to the body's salt balance. Nothing is wrong with water itself, so the useful caution is about how fast and how much a person drinks, not about a full glass at dinner.

Recent findings suggest that hyponatremia is uncommon, but its effects can be severe. Some of its signs are easy to dismiss, such as nausea, which few people would connect to the water they drank. Others, such as seizures, mean the brain itself is affected. With effects that range from an upset stomach to seizures, drinking too much belongs among the real risks of hydration.

For most healthy people the danger is remote, because it takes more water, drunk faster, than their kidneys can clear. The risk is greater for people who are ill and whose kidneys work poorly. When the organ that removes extra water is already struggling, a patient has less protection against overdrinking than a healthy person does. For these patients, the common advice to drink more isn't automatically sound.

Like the advice to drink when thirsty, the advice to drink more fails in particular people rather than across the board.

It has been revealed that drinking too much water is a danger for a few groups of people, not for ordinary drinkers. The risk rises with kidney illness, extreme heat, endurance exercise and a smaller body, according to The Nutrition Source. Not everyone in those groups is an athlete. People who are ill and whose kidneys work poorly are also at risk, so overdrinking is a medical concern as well as a sporting one, and these patients should hold back rather than drink by routine. Marathon $MPC runners are another group at risk, and at one race a sizable share of them had low blood sodium. The Cleveland Clinic Journal of Medicine reports that 13% of the runners tested at the 2002 Boston Marathon had it, while only 0.6% reached a critical level. Most of those cases were mild, and a serious case was uncommon but real, which calls for care rather than fear.

Long miles alone do not put athletes in danger, but the extra water they drink does. Athletes lose sodium through sweat, and they get into trouble when they drink far more than that loss calls for. Organizers of one triathlon taught athletes about the risk and offered fewer drink stations, and the share of athletes treated for hyponatremia in the medical tent fell from 22% to 3%, according to the Cleveland Clinic Journal of Medicine. Triathletes face this danger mainly because of how they drink on the course, so they can keep racing and still lower their risk sharply by drinking less.

According to recent reports, women also run into trouble more often than men in long races. At the 2000 Houston Marathon, women developed hyponatremia at a higher rate than men, according to the Cleveland Clinic Journal of Medicine. That pattern matches the higher risk for women and children. A likely reason, though not a proven one, is that slower and smaller runners spend more hours near drink stations while needing less fluid, which also fits the added risk of a smaller body. Sex and size are warning signs that may partly reflect time on the course and chances to drink, not fixed fates.

For every group at risk, the protection is to drink to need rather than at every chance.

For most healthy people, the trouble is the sweet drink they reach for, not a shortage of liquid. The Nutrition Source recommends flavorful water-based drinks as a way to help people used to sweet beverages drink more water. Many Americans fit that description, and about 30% of those 2 and older take in too much added sugar, according to the CDC. That makes this advice a sugar fix more than a hydration initiative. A reader should judge it by how many sweet drinks it replaces, not by how many glasses of water it adds.

It has been revealed that A person who trades soda for water cuts a large amount of sugar from the day. There are 10 teaspoons of sugar in a 12-ounce can of regular soda, according to the CDC, and a person who drinks two fewer cans each day removes 2,100 calories from the week while eating the same meals. The gain holds only when the replacement drink's flavor doesn't come from sugar, because sweetened waters count as sugary drinks. A bottle with "water" on the label can still put a person right back where they started, so the thing to check is what sweetens it.

Flavor alone won't keep someone away from soda if the can sits closer than the water. The CDC suggests keeping a cold jug of water in the fridge and carrying a reusable bottle through the day. Both habits put water within reach first, so a person doesn't have to rely on willpower to choose it. For the healthy majority, how they stock the kitchen matters more than whether they reach a daily cup count.

Recent findings suggest that people can make flavored water at home for less than they pay for the bottled kind. Grocery stores sell flavored waters as separate products and price them as something special. Homemade water flavored with fruit, herbs or cucumber costs less than the store-bought versions, according to The Nutrition Source. That saving counts most for a drink meant for every day. A small cost paid once a day adds up over weeks and months, while a few slices of produce in a pitcher add almost nothing to a grocery bill. A person who makes flavored water in the kitchen turns it from a purchase into a routine.

Recent findings suggest that the habit helps most the people who find plain water too bland next to the sweet drinks they usually choose. Infused water is meant to help people who are used to sweet drinks drink more water, and it uses the taste of fruit, herbs or vegetables instead of sugar to do that. A hint of flavor can be enough for someone to pick up a glass of water without going back to the sweetness they are trying to give up. The flavorings can be as simple as a few rounds of cucumber or some ginger with the skin cut away. Many people already keep these at home, so they can start the habit without a special trip to the store and keep it going with whatever is in the crisper drawer that week.

All the habit requires is a pitcher of water and a few slices of whatever produce is on hand.

People who buy bottled sparkling juices want fizz and fruit flavor, and they can mix both into a glass at home while deciding for themselves how much juice goes in. The Nutrition Source recommends a homemade version that uses only 1 to 2 ounces of juice in sparkling water, in place of sparkling juices. At that amount, the juice is a flavoring, much like a squeeze of lemon, and not a serving to drink. A person holding this glass is still mostly drinking bubbly water with a hint of fruit.

In a recent development, keeping the pour small matters for more than calories, because juice is the part of the glass to be careful with. The CDC classifies fruit juice as a simple carb, so for anyone watching their blood sugar, a smaller pour means less of the kind of carbohydrate they are trying to limit. Juice packs a lot of fruit into a small volume, with about 3 oranges squeezed into one cup, and an ounce or two holds only a small part of that. Even a generous pour is no substitute for eating fruit, since juice is missing the fiber that whole fruit has.

Sources indicate that the splash is a way to drink less juice, not a reason to count juice as a healthy drink. Stirred into 12 ounces of sparkling water, an ounce or two of juice leaves a glass that is almost entirely bubbles and water. For anyone unsure what to drink, the CDC advises plain water. That makes the homemade glass a move toward plain water, not a goal of its own. The pour is the one thing to watch, because an ounce can easily become a few, and then the glass is a sparkling juice again.

The best version of this glass is the one where the splash keeps getting smaller.

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and says it tops Gemma 4 31B.
  • A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500.
  • Sources indicate that webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

In a recent development, webAI's open-weight TwIL-8B posts 98.2 on MATH-500 and says it tops Gemma 4 31B. The card's own footnotes show why the comparison deserves a re-run.

A model small enough to run from a roughly 5 GiB file on a CPU now claims a 98.2 on MATH-500. The most revealing line in its model card isn't a score, though. It's a footnote saying the competitor numbers were never re-run.

Sources indicate that webAI released TwIL-8B as an open-weight model on November 4, and its Hugging Face model card leads with ambitious numbers. The 8.8B-parameter reasoning model is post-trained from IBM's Granite 4.2 8B using full-parameter supervised fine-tuning, followed by GRPO/DAPO reinforcement learning. A final length-aware RL stage produces the "balanced" variant, which is the default.

The card reports 98.2 on MATH-500 and 88.3 on AIME 2025. It says TwIL-8B posts the highest MATH-500 and LiveCodeBench scores in its comparison group, which includes Gemma 4 31B at about 3.5 times its size. That claim is worth testing, because small models that beat larger ones are exactly what open-weight consumers want to hear.

Recent findings suggest that on MATH-500, the card lists TwIL-8B at 98.2, Qwen3.5-9B at 96.6 and Gemma 4 31B at 87.9. On AIME 2025, TwIL-8B scores 88.3 against 87.1 for Gemma 4 31B. On LiveCodeBench, TwIL-8B scores 81.6 against 80.0, though that figure carries a dagger marking it as measured on the verbose variant, not the default balanced one.

The card is also more candid than most. It states TwIL-8B is not a knowledge model. GPQA Diamond comes in at 70.2, trailing Gemma 4 31B by 14.1 points, and the model also trails on MMLU-Pro and HLE. There is no safety or preference tuning beyond what Granite carries, and the license is non-commercial. That honesty makes the claims easier to weigh.

In a recent development, here is where the headline gets complicated. TwIL-8B's scores come from webAI's own internal high-effort pass@1 runs. The card states that competitor scores are published figures and were not re-run.

Sources indicate that gemma 4 31B's 87.9 on MATH-500 comes from Red Hat's evaluation of an FP8 build, using the lighteval harness, not from Google. The card itself notes that this figure is unusually low and may reflect answer extraction. In other words, the 10.3-point gap that anchors the headline compares one team's own harness against a third party's number that the card suspects may be understated.

None of this makes TwIL-8B's result wrong. It means the margin isn't established until both models run under the same harness, prompt and sampling settings. For reference, Google's Gemma 4 model card is the source for several of the other Gemma figures in the table.

In a recent development, read the whole table and the picture is more balanced than the headline suggests. In the card's head-to-head summary, TwIL-8B beats Gemma 4 31B on 3 of 14 shared benchmarks and loses 11. It leads on MATH-500, LiveCodeBench and AIME 2025, but trails on AIME 2026 (88.3 against 89.2), HMMT Feb 2026 (68.2 against 77.2), GPQA Diamond, MMLU-Pro and IFEval.

The AIME 2025 lead is the shakiest. The card says AIME and HMMT sets have 30 to 33 problems, so one problem is worth about 3 points, and gaps of that size sit within noise. A 1.2-point margin is well under one problem, so the result is best read as a tie.

Industry observers note that against the closest same-size rival, Qwen3.5-9B, the card indicates the models roughly level on contest math, with TwIL-8B using fewer tokens: about 19.5k per AIME 2026 problem against 31.2k. That efficiency claim may turn out to be the more durable one.

The card makes replication unusually practical. The Q4_K_M balanced GGUF weighs 4.98 GiB and runs through llama.cpp, with a command given in the card. Larger Q8_0 and F16 builds exist only for the verbose variant. The model also needs a big generation budget, since a short limit truncates its reasoning and scores far worse. The card suggests settings around 32,768 fresh tokens and a 40,960-token context.

Recent findings suggest that anyone planning a check should expect three catches. First, the card says all its scores were measured on bf16 weights, not the GGUF builds, so a CPU run tests a slightly different artifact, and the card expects small deviations, most likely at Q4_K_M. Second, MATH-500 is 500 problems and each answer can run to tens of thousands of tokens, so CPU testing will be slow. Third, the decoding setup matters, since the card says none of its numbers use low-effort or thinking-off modes.

For a fair comparison, the same prompt, answer extraction and sampling must be applied to Gemma 4 31B too, ideally at full precision.

According to recent reports, the card also lists contamination caveats. Its training pools were decontaminated against AIME, HMMT Feb 2025 and 2026, MATH-500, GPQA, MMLU-Pro, HLE, IFEval, IFBench and LiveCodeBench using 13-gram matching. HMMT Nov 2025 and the HumanEval, MBPP and CRUXEval suites weren't in the decontamination set. The MATH-500 and AIME results fall inside the protected group, which counts in the model's favor.

Overall, TwIL-8B looks like a genuinely strong small model for contest math, code and instruction following, and the card is open about its weak spots. The claim to beat Gemma 4 31B is narrower than the headline suggests: a clear lead on one benchmark, a likely tie on another and a loss on most of the rest.

The useful next step is a same-harness run of both models, with the bf16 weights as a control for the GGUF build. Until independent results appear, the 98.2 is best quoted as webAI's reported figure, and the size-beating framing is better described as unproven than wrong.

With a catalog of more than 10,000 participating merchants, banks and credit unions can now turn the banking app into the place account holders plan, shop, and pay.

Industry observers note that SCOTTSDALE, Ariz., Nov. 16, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- equipifi, the bank-native Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) platform powering more than 100 in-house programs at banks and credit unions, declared today that consumers can now use BNPL to shop directly from their digital banking app. From the app, consumers can see their purchasing power from their own bank or credit union, find and discover merchants, and choose a fixed payment plan before they buy.

This launch completes the availability of BNPL along the shopping journey, powered by equipifi. The BNPL platform already enabled eligible account holders to proposal a purchase ahead of time with extra funds, and split completed debit card transactions into installments. Now with Shop, the purchase itself can originate within the banking app, allowing consumers to get funded and begin shopping through a BNPL program the institution fully owns and controls. Each bank or credit union underwrites its own prepares and sets purchasing power based on its relationship with the account holder, so spending stays manageable.

Industry observers note that the move builds on fast-growing demand for BNPL at banks and credit unions. October BNPL volume is running at double last year's pace, according to equipifi's Purchasing Power Index, which also found that returning users are spending more than last year and that more than 80 percent of BNPL sessions during Cyber Week 2025 happened on a mobile phone.

Recent findings suggest that pioneer Federal Credit Union was one of the first financial institutions to make Shop available on its in-house BNPL program. "Pioneer Federal Credit Union brought Buy Now, Pay Later to our members so they could pay over time with a partner that has their best interests at heart," mentioned Tracey Miller, COO/EVP at Pioneer Federal Credit Union. "Shop extends the program we already offer, so members can use their purchasing power from Pioneer Federal Credit Union right from their banking app, and it keeps us at their side throughout their everyday purchases.".

In a recent development, "Account holders already open their banking app to see what they have spent, and check to see if they can make a future purchase. Shop lets them act on it right there, with their own bank or credit union behind the purchase, instead of handing that moment, the data, and the value that comes with it to a competitor's app," mentioned Bryce Deeney, Founder and CEO of equipifi. "We give financial institutions the technology to turn every shopping moment into a reason to come back to their app. That means deeper engagement, stronger retention, and newly introduced revenue for the institutions we serve.".

Recent findings suggest that by connecting their budgeting and purchasing tools, account holders also gain more control over how they spend. "Consumers expect a seamless experience wherever they choose to shop," mentioned Alex Mersereau, Head of Product at equipifi. "Their purchasing power should go with them to the merchants they already love and reflect their finances in real time, straight from the institution that provides it. That gives them the visibility, control, and confidence to make every purchase decision on their own terms.".

equipifi looks to extend the experience to feature local and regional businesses in 2027, so account holders can shop close to home and make purchases that support the community their institution serves.

Sources indicate that for the more than 10,000 merchants account holders can reach today, the banking app becomes an additional source of high-intent traffic, alongside the channels they already rely on. "These shoppers have expanded their budget before they ever reach the merchant's site," Mersereau added. "They arrive already funded by their own bank or credit union, which gives merchants a stronger audience than almost any other traffic source.".

Industry observers note that the shopping experience is available today to existing equipifi financial institution partners at no additional cost to enable and comes standard for latest partners at go-live. Banks and credit unions can learn more at equipifi.com.

Sources indicate that the Depository Trust & Clearing Corporation (DTCC) will connect its tokenization service to Solana (SOL) in the second half of 2027, the tech giant noted on Nov. 12.

The integration will allow "digital twins" of Russell 1000 stocks, major ETFs and U.S. Treasuries to be issued on the Solana blockchain. In December 2025, the SEC issued a no-action letter that allowed DTC to tokenize these assets.

In a recent development, in 2025, DTCC processed $4.7 quadrillion in securities transactions. Its depository, DTC, holds and services $114 trillion in assets from more than 150 countries.

The DTCC Tokenization Service (DTS) will let large market participants convert conventional securities into tokens, move them across the Solana network and redeem them.

"DTC-tokenized assets made available on Solana – and all blockchain networks integrated with the service – will retain the same investor protections, ownership rights and regulatory safeguards that apply to traditionally held securities," said Brian Steele, president of DTCC Clearing & Securities Services.

According to DTCC CEO Frank La Salla, the integration will also free up securities for use as collateral.

DTS went live on Oct. 28, 2026. At launch, it worked with Canton Network and a private ledger. DTCC said that it adds newly introduced networks at clients' request.

"DTCC is committed to providing an open and connected platform that provides our users with access to mature distributed ledger technology networks like Solana that have established performance, security and governance features," remarked Nadine Chakar, global head of DTCC Digital Assets.

Nick Ducoff, general manager for institutional at the Solana Foundation, also commented on the news. "Institutions choose Solana because it already runs real financial activity at scale," he said.

According to Ducoff, the integration "connects one of the most trusted names in post-trade infrastructure with a network built for always-on markets.".

Industry observers note that as of Nov. 12, distributed real-world assets (RWA) in the Solana ecosystem reached $5.13 billion across more than 1.02 million holders, according to RWA.xyz. Transfers over the past 30 days totaled $16.48 billion.

The stablecoin market cap on Solana stands at $13.85 billion, with monthly turnover of $387.41 billion.

At press time, SOL is trading at $80.94.

#6078. Breaking: 10 things to know about Record, Song and Album of the Year at the Grammys

Breaking: 10 things to know about Record, Song and Album of the Year at the Grammys

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3851 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Record, Song and Album of the Year honor different work at the Grammys, and these 10 explainers cover who each award credits, who votes and how eligibility works.
  • According to recent reports, three of the Grammys' biggest trophies have names that sound almost interchangeable.
  • Sources indicate that the Recording Academy, which presents the Grammys, groups these awards with Best Upcoming Artist in what it calls the general field.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Record, Song and Album of the Year honor different work at the Grammys, and these 10 explainers cover who each award credits, who votes and how eligibility works.

According to recent reports, three of the Grammys' biggest trophies have names that sound almost interchangeable. Record of the Year, Song of the Year and Album of the Year can read like three ways of saying the same thing. They are not. Each one honors a different kind of work, and each one sends a trophy to a different group of people.

Sources indicate that the Recording Academy, which presents the Grammys, groups these awards with Best Upcoming Artist in what it calls the general field. Those four categories are the ones not tied to a single genre. A pop single, a country album and a hip-hop track can all compete in them.

The distinction comes down to what is being judged. Record of the Year looks at a finished recording — the performance and the way it was produced and engineered. Song of the Year looks at the composition underneath it, meaning the lyrics and melody. Album of the Year covers a full body of work rather than a single track.

That difference decides who walks away with a Grammy. A Record of the Year win is shared by the performing artist with the producers, recording engineers and mixers behind the track. Under current rules, the mastering engineer is credited too. A Song of the Year win goes to the songwriters, and a performer is included only if they also helped write it. An album award reaches the widest group, from the artist to the people who produced, engineered, mixed and mastered the record.

It has been revealed that the split explains how a song can be honored for its writing while a different track takes the recording prize. At the 2024 ceremony, Billie Eilish's "What Was I Made For?" won Song of the Year. Record of the Year went to Miley Cyrus for "Flowers.".

The difference between Record, Song and Album of the Year at the Grammys also carries into the rules on eligibility, voting and nominee counts that govern the general field.

It has been revealed that the 10 explainers that follow cover each general-field category and how the eligibility window and voting work. They also track how the nominee lists have grown and look at two artists whose wins show the rules in practice.

Record of the Year honors a single recording — the finished track as listeners hear it. The Grammy goes to the performing artist, the producer, the recording engineer and the mixer. Current rules also credit the mastering engineer.

Sources indicate that of the general-field awards, this one focuses most directly on sound and performance. It judges how a track was sung, played, captured and shaped in the studio. Authorship of the words and melody is judged separately, by Song of the Year.

The list of recipients mirrors how a modern record gets made. The performing artist is the voice or act listeners associate with the track. The producer oversees the recording as a whole. That role guides arrangements, performances and creative choices from the first session to the final version.

Sources indicate that the recording engineer handles the technical work of capturing the performance. That covers microphone choice and placement, signal flow and the quality of the raw tracks. Everything that follows in the process builds on those tracks.

In a recent development, the mixer takes the recorded parts and balances them into a finished whole. Mixing sets the relative volume of each voice and instrument. It also places sounds across the stereo field and adds effects such as reverb and compression.

The mastering engineer handles the last step before release. Mastering prepares the final mix for playback across formats and devices. It adjusts overall loudness, tone and consistency. The goal is a track that holds together on any playback system.

Industry observers note that crediting all of these roles means a single Record of the Year win is shared by everyone in that production chain. The category puts the names of producers and engineers next to the artist's in one of the four general-field honors.

According to recent reports, the award is tied to a specific recording, so the track is the unit being judged, not the tune behind it. A cover, live version or remix of the same song is a separate recording. Each version has its own performers and its own production credits.

Album of the Year honors a complete album rather than a single track. The trophy goes to the artist and to the producers, engineers, mixers and mastering engineers who worked on the record.

Sources indicate that one win can send trophies to many people at once. It is one of four general-field Grammys. Voters weigh the album as a single release, from its opening track to its closing one.

Sources indicate that the credit list mirrors the way an album gets made. A producer guides the recording sessions and shapes the overall sound. That can mean choosing arrangements, coaching performances and deciding which takes make the final cut.

A recording engineer captures the performances. The job covers microphone choice and placement, signal levels and the technical quality of each take.

Sources indicate that A mixer blends the separate parts — vocals, instruments and effects — into finished tracks. Mixing sets how loud each element sits, where it is placed in the stereo field and how it is shaped with equalization and effects.

A mastering engineer handles the last step before release. On an album, mastering matches loudness and tone across the tracks. It also sets the spacing between songs so the record plays as one sequence.

A full album can involve several people in each of those roles. One producer might handle a few songs while another oversees the rest. Different engineers and mixers can work on different tracks. The Recording Academy's rules for each awards cycle decide which of those contributors are named as recipients.

In a recent development, featured artists may also be credited, depending on their role on the album. A guest appearance on one track does not by itself make someone an Album of the Year recipient. The rules look at the part a featured artist played on the record.

The name on the cover belongs to the performer. The list of recipients reflects the studio work behind that name, from the first session to the final master.

Song of the Year at the Grammys honors the composition itself — the lyrics and melody — rather than any particular performance of it. The trophy goes to the songwriters. A performer is credited only when that performer also helped write the song.

That rule separates Song of the Year from Record of the Year, the award with the most similar name. A track can stand out for its vocal, its arrangement or its production. Those qualities belong to the recording. Song of the Year voters judge something narrower: the words and the tune as written.

Sources indicate that the category has been part of the Grammys since the first ceremony in 1959. Its basic purpose has stayed the same. It is the general-field award aimed at the people who write music, whether or not they ever step in front of a microphone.

In a recent development, the 2024 ceremony offers a clear case. "What Was I Made For?" won Song of the Year that February. Billie Eilish and her brother Finneas O'Connell wrote it for the 2023 film Barbie. Both are credited songwriters. That is why both received the award. Eilish's role as the singer was not the reason she was honored in this category. Her co-writing credit was.

Industry observers note that the same song also won the Academy Award for Best Original Song in March 2024. That Oscar category likewise goes to songwriters. The two wins recognized the same piece of writing.

The 2003 ceremony shows the opposite situation. Norah Jones sang "Don't Know Why," but Jesse Harris wrote it. Harris won Song of the Year for the track. Jones did not share that award because she was not a writer on the song. Her recording of it won Record of the Year that night instead.

That split means a singer can perform the winning song and still leave without this particular trophy. It also means a songwriter who never appears on stage can win one of the Grammys' four general-field awards.

It has been revealed that the category also reflects how the music business divides ownership. A composition and a recording of it are separate pieces of property. Songwriters and their publishers hold rights in the composition. Song of the Year honors that side of the work.

It has been revealed that billie Eilish's "Bad Guy" won both Record of the Year and Song of the Year at the 2020 Grammys. One track earned one trophy for the way it was recorded and a second for the way it was written.

In a recent development, the double win came at the 62nd Grammy Awards, held in Los Angeles on January 26, 2020. Each prize went to a different set of credits. The recording award covered the finished track. The songwriting award covered only the words and melody underneath it.

Eilish wrote "Bad Guy" with her brother, Finneas O'Connell, who performs as Finneas. The two siblings shared the Song of the Year trophy as its songwriters.

The Record of the Year credits reached further. Eilish received the award as the performing artist. O'Connell was credited as producer and also as an engineer and mixer, alongside mixer Rob Kinelski. John Greenham was credited as the mastering engineer. O'Connell therefore collected trophies in both categories for the same track. One was for writing it, and the other was for making the recording.

The song was made outside a commercial studio. The siblings wrote and recorded its parent album, When We All Fall Asleep, Where Do We Go?, in O'Connell's bedroom at their family home in Los Angeles. The track's sparse bass line, whispered vocal and abrupt tempo change near the end are production choices. Those elements belong to the recording. The lyrics and melody belong to the song.

"Bad Guy" had a long commercial run before the ceremony. It reached No. 1 on the Billboard Hot 100 in August 2019. That ended the 19-week run of Lil Nas X $TWTR's "Old Town Road" at the top of the chart.

In a recent development, the two wins were part of a larger result that night. Eilish also won Album of the Year and Best Fresh Artist, taking all four general-field awards at a single ceremony. Christopher Cross was the previous artist to do so, at the 1981 Grammys. Eilish was 18 years old when she matched him.

Best Latest Artist honors a performer or group rather than a single recording, song or album. It recognizes an artist whose breakthrough into public awareness came during the Grammys' eligibility period. It sits alongside Record, Album and Song of the Year in the general field.

In a recent development, that focus on the artist sets it apart from the other three top awards. Record of the Year, Album of the Year and Song of the Year each reward a specific piece of work. Their credits can stretch to producers, engineers or songwriters. Best Fresh Artist goes to the act itself, whether a solo performer or a band. A producer or songwriter who worked on a nominee's music receives no trophy in this category.

Recent findings suggest that bobby Darin won Best Newly introduced Artist at the 1960 ceremony, the first time the category was presented. The Beatles took it home in 1965, the year after their first visit to the U.S.

New does not mean a debut release. The Recording Academy writes its criteria for the category into the rulebook it challenges each cycle. Those criteria have been revised over the years. Artists are judged on when they broke through, so an act with earlier releases can still qualify. The specific thresholds can change from one cycle to the next. Anyone tracking a contender should check the rules for that year.

Sources indicate that milli Vanilli won Best Newly introduced Artist at the 1990 ceremony. The Recording Academy withdrew the award later that year. The withdrawal followed the revelation that the duo had not sung the lead vocals on their recordings.

A newcomer can also collect the other general-field trophies on the same night. Christopher Cross became the first artist to win all four general-field awards in a single night, at the 1981 ceremony.

Recent winners show the range of genres the category covers. Jazz singer Samara Joy won at the 2023 ceremony. R&B singer Victoria Monét won in 2024, and pop singer Chappell Roan won in 2025.

According to recent reports, the general field is the group of four Grammy categories open to music from every genre. Those categories are Record of the Year, Album of the Year, Song of the Year and Best Newly introduced Artist.

Genre categories, by contrast, consider only work within one style of music, such as rap, country or jazz.

Industry observers note that that split shapes how the full awards list is organized. The Recording Academy sorts its categories into fields. Most fields are built around a genre or a family of related genres. Pop, rock, R&B, rap, country, jazz, Latin, gospel and classical music each have their own set of awards.

Inside a genre field, categories compare like with like. A rap album competes against other rap albums for Best Rap Album. A country album competes against other country albums for Best Country Album. The question in those races is narrower: how a recording stands within its own tradition.

The general field removes that boundary. Nominees there are weighed against the full range of music released during the eligibility period, not against a single style. A jazz record and a rock album can end up competing for the same trophy.

According to recent reports, the two paths are not exclusive. One recording can be nominated in its genre categories and in the general field in the same year. An album might earn a nomination for Best Pop Vocal Album alongside a nomination for Album of the Year. A win in one category does not guarantee a win in the other. Each category is decided on its own.

It has been revealed that genre fields also tend to break a style into smaller pieces. Many of them separate performance, song and album awards. Some go further and split solo work from duo or group work, as pop does with Best Pop Duo/Group Performance. That structure gives musicians within each style several separate categories to compete in, compared with the four slots in the general field.

The difference is visible on Grammy night itself. Most genre awards are handed out at the Premiere Ceremony, which takes place before the main broadcast. The general-field awards are usually held for the televised show. That placement puts Record, Song and Album of the Year, along with Best New Artist, on the main telecast.

It has been revealed that A recording can compete for a Grammy only if it was released during the eligibility period. The Recording Academy sets this window for each awards cycle. The window, not the calendar year, decides which ceremony a song or album enters.

According to recent reports, the window applies across the competition, including Record, Album and Song of the Year. The Recording Academy publishes each cycle's dates alongside its rules for that year. Best New Artist uses the same period differently. That award looks at whether an artist's breakthrough came during the window, rather than at a single release.

A release that falls outside one window is not lost. It is considered in the cycle whose window it does fall into. An album that misses one cutoff can still compete the following year.

Every entry in a cycle is measured against the same window. A record released near the window's opening and one released just before it closes can compete in the same category. By the time of the ceremony, one may have been in circulation far longer than the other.

Industry observers note that the window closes before the ceremony takes place. Once it closes, the pool of eligible music for that cycle is fixed. Nominations, voting and the awards show all come after that close. The ceremony therefore honors music released earlier. The year attached to a ceremony is not necessarily the year the winning music came out.

It has been revealed that that timing explains a common source of confusion for listeners. A widely heard release can seem absent from a year's list of nominees. If it came out after that cycle's window closed, it has not been passed over. It moves to the next cycle instead.

Recent findings suggest that the exact dates can differ from one year to the next. Anyone checking whether a specific release qualifies needs the rules the Recording Academy published for that cycle, not the rules from an earlier year.

Grammy winners are chosen by voting members of the Recording Academy, the organization that presents the awards. Those members can vote in the general field and in a limited number of genre fields.

That setup makes the Grammys a peer award. The people deciding are music professionals rather than the public, critics or sales charts. Streaming totals and radio play are not part of the count. A single can top the charts for months and still lose to a smaller release if voting members prefer the other recording.

Voting membership is tied to professional work in recorded music. To qualify, a person needs credits on commercially released recordings in a creative or technical role. Members include performers, songwriters, producers and engineers. Those are the same roles credited across the four general-field categories. The Academy also has members who belong without voting rights. Membership alone does not guarantee a ballot.

It has been revealed that the process runs in two rounds. The first round starts with entries submitted for consideration. Members vote on those entries to choose the nominees in each category. In the final round, they vote again on the nominees to pick the winners. Those results are kept sealed until the awards are announced.

The cap on genre fields is meant to keep each genre decision with people who work in that style. A jazz engineer and a country songwriter can both vote for Album of the Year. Each is expected to vote in the genre categories closest to their own work. The general field stays open to every voting member. That makes it the category group with the widest pool of judges. It also means a producer can help pick Song of the Year, even though the award itself goes only to songwriters.

Individual ballots stay private. The Academy publishes nominees and winners. It does not release vote totals or margins. The public never learns how close a race was.

According to recent reports, the Grammys' general-field categories, including Record, Album and Song of the Year, have changed the length of their nominee lists over time. Each category once had five nominee slots. The Recording Academy later raised that number to eight, then to 10.

Industry observers note that the change was not limited to the three headline awards. Best Newly introduced Artist belongs to the same general field, and its shortlist went through the same expansion. That kept all four general-field shortlists the same length.

Sources indicate that A nominee slot is one place on a category's final ballot. Voting members choose the winner from that list. Its length sets how many recordings, albums, songs or upcoming acts are still in contention on Grammy night.

According to recent reports, the first expansion, from five to eight, added three places in each category. The second, from eight to 10, added two more. At 10 slots, each shortlist was twice the size of the original five.

A longer Song of the Year list is still a list of compositions. A longer Record of the Year list is still a list of recordings. The expansion changed how many entries reach the final ballot. It did not change what each category judges or who can receive the trophy.

In a recent development, the number of slots is a rule, not a fixed feature of the awards. The Recording Academy writes the rules for each awards cycle. The nominee count is one of those rules, and it has been revised more than once.

That history affects comparisons between ceremonies. Two Album of the Year races from different eras may have shortlists of different lengths. A nomination in a five-slot year meant making a list half as long as one with 10 slots. An artist's general-field nominations across a long career can come from lists of different lengths. The official nominee list for a given ceremony reveals how many slots applied that year.

Taylor Swift has won Album of the Year four times, more than any other artist in Grammy history. Her winning albums are Fearless, 1989, Folklore and Midnights, and the fourth win came at the February 2024 ceremony.

Fearless was the first. It won at the ceremony held in January 2010, when Swift was 20 years old. That made her the youngest artist to win the category up to that point. Billie Eilish later took that distinction at the 2020 ceremony. She was 18 when When We All Fall Asleep, Where Do We Go? won the award.

Fearless was released on Substantial Machine Records, a Nashville label, and was promoted as a country album. Swift co-produced it with Nathan Chapman, who had worked with her since her debut album.

According to recent reports, 1989 followed at the February 2016 ceremony. The album marked her move from country to mainstream pop. Max Martin and Shellback were among its producers. The win made Swift the first woman to take Album of the Year twice as a lead artist.

Folklore won at the ceremony held in March 2021. The Recording Academy had pushed that year's show back from its planned January date because of the COVID-19 pandemic. Swift made the album largely remotely with Aaron Dessner of the National and with Jack Antonoff. It was released with little advance notice in July 2020. The award made her the first woman to win the category three times as a lead artist.

Midnights brought the fourth trophy. Swift co-produced it with Antonoff, and it was released in October 2022. That win moved her past Frank Sinatra, Stevie Wonder and Paul Simon. Each of them had won Album of the Year three times.

The gap between her first and fourth wins is 14 years. Her four winners also span several styles. Fearless is rooted in country, and 1989 is built on mainstream pop. Folklore leans on spare indie-folk arrangements, while Midnights returns to synth-driven pop.

Three insights you might have missed from theCUBE’s coverage of GraphSummit 2026

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that AI agents need more than enterprise data to be effective; they also need the business context that data lives in.
  • Developers are already providing AI agents with business context through prompts.
  • In a recent development, “This knowledge layer, this idea of capturing your enterprise knowledge and using it as the context engine for your agents, not only gives you the consistency … it gives you the explainability,” he said during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 15:46 EST / NOVEMBER 16 2026.

Industry observers note that AI agents need more than enterprise data to be effective; they also need the business context that data lives in. Knowledge graphs could consolidate the enterprise context at the moment fed to different AI agents into a single knowledge layer.

Developers are already providing AI agents with business context through prompts. But without a central source of truth, they must repeat that work every time they build a upcoming agent, rather than drawing on a shared knowledge layer, according to Jesús Barrasa, field chief technology officer of gen AI at Neo4j Inc.

In a recent development, “This knowledge layer, this idea of capturing your enterprise knowledge and using it as the context engine for your agents, not only gives you the consistency … it gives you the explainability,” he said during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. “That’s the source of my data. These are the elements that I use to produce the answer.”.

Sources indicate that during interviews at GraphSummit, theCUBE Research’s John Furrier spoke with industry experts from Collibra BV, Blitzy Inc., Raymond James Financial Inc., and Qiagen N.V., among others. They discussed how knowledge graphs can ground AI agents in shared, traceable enterprise knowledge to improve explainability, enable safer coding at scale, support drug discovery and transform business operations. (* Disclosure below.).

Here’s the complete video interview with Jesús Barrasa:d.

Governance is a key question for enterprise AI deployments. How do you ensure AI agents behave appropriately as they become more autonomous? Judgment calls that used to be made by people now need to be made by agents in seconds, requiring a shift toward runtime governance, according to Felix Van de Maele, chief executive officer and co-founder of Collibra BV.

Industry observers note that collibra has introduced several capabilities – Live Map, Maestro, Guardian Agents and Agent Contracts – built on Neo4j’s graph database. Together, they form a control system that helps businesses make sure their AI agents use the right information and follow the rules.

“The challenge is: how do you govern at the speed of AI, which is different than the way we had to govern five years ago?” Van de Maele told theCUBE. “Maestro gives our customers the ability to build these governance steward agents that automate up to 80% of the governance work. You’re able to govern quickly and efficiently enough to keep up with the demands of upcoming AI workloads.”.

Sources indicate that other solutions, such as Agent Contracts, focus on enforcing boundaries around AI agents’ behavior. They monitor agents’ actions and block those that violate predefined rules, helping prevent unauthorized actions, according to Van de Maele.

Here’s the complete video interview with Felix Van de Maele:.

In a recent development, changing one small piece of software can unexpectedly break something somewhere else. For Blitzy Inc., which runs thousands of AI coding agents at once to help businesses make large-scale system changes, a knowledge graph can map dependencies and the risks of change within a system.

A knowledge graph gives agents the context they need to make changes safely without being overwhelmed by millions of lines of code, according to Neeraj Deshmukh, director of engineering at Blitzy. The company also uses human-approved action looks and automated testing to keep the coding process on track.

“On top of that, we have agents who are watching other agents to make sure that they abide by the spec, the plan that we had created and approved by the human in the loop,” Deshmukh told theCUBE. “That ensures that there is no drift or hallucination.”.

Here’s the complete video interview with Neeraj Deshmukh:.

According to recent reports, A knowledge graph helps Raymond James Financial Inc. put AI agents to work on data from established sources, according to Naveen Mahankali, vice president of technology at Raymond James.

We have golden sources; we have systems that we can rely on today, and we’re able to use agents to build and compare what we are building against the golden sources,” he told theCUBE. “With the knowledge graph, even when we pull the data from different sources, it sits in the Neo4j, and we run evals compared to the golden sources and make sure they’re 100% accurate before launching.”.

Sources indicate that raymond James is also exploring how AI agents can help financial advisors serve clients more efficiently. The manufacturer has already launched Raimond, its proprietary AI assistant, explained Jeff Griffith, vice president of AI engineering and data science at Raymond James, who joined Mahankali during the interview.

“We have an AI assistant … it’s gotten huge adoption, and it’s just going to get smarter,” Griffith remarked. “That’s part of the core evolution of what we’re doing in terms of engineering. We’re changing how people — how everyone — works with a desktop that gives people the best AI tools to move from doing all the menial tasks to managing agents that are doing those tasks. In terms of skills and what we are looking for, it is shifting just from people who can do tasks to people who have a drive to solve a meaningful problem.”.

Here’s the complete video interview with Jeff Griffith and Naveen Mahankali:.

Decentralized exchange Hyperliquid has bought back and burned 21,200 HYPE over the past 24 hours, spending $1.53 million on the purchase at an average price of $72.31, according to Onchain Lens.

Sources indicate that the on-chain analytics platform also reported that Hyperliquid has permanently removed a total of 50.47 million HYPE from circulation since the launch of the token. That is 5.05% of the max supply of 1 billion HYPE, and at the current price, the burned tokens are worth around $3.51 billion.

The latest buyback comes amid the decline in the price of the cryptocurrency. On Nov. 12, the price of HYPE went down by 3.45%, and at press time, the token stands at $69.52, according to TradingView. Earlier this autumn, the price of HYPE was above $90.

Hyperliquid pays for the buybacks in dollars, so the decentralized exchange is able to buy more HYPE with the same amount of money when the price of the token goes down.

It has been revealed that deFiLlama data indicates that Hyperliquid has earned $1.41 billion for HYPE holders since December 2024. Over the past 30 days, the decentralized exchange earned $68.82 million, and its earnings for the past week stand at $15.04 million.

Over the last day, the platform collected about $1.46 million in fees, slightly less than the amount it spent on the buyback. Besides, DeFiLlama data demonstrates that Hyperliquid presently earns more in fees than Ethereum, Tron and Base.

Recent findings suggest that the largest part of the burned tokens, 48.85 million HYPE, was bought back by the Assistance Fund. The fund automatically receives between 97% and 99% of the fees from perpetual and spot trading on Hyperliquid, and the rest of the fees go to the HLP liquidity pool and to the builders of individual markets.

The Assistance Fund buys HYPE on the open market and sends the tokens to the "0xfefe...fefe" address. It is a system address that does not have a private key. In December 2025, Hyperliquid validators formally recognized the tokens held at this address as burned.

In August 2026, Hyperliquid also introduced the AQAv2 upgrade. Under the upgrade, around 90% of the yield generated by the USDC reserves on the platform now goes to the Assistance Fund. Each of these transfers brings between $14 million and $16 million to the fund.

It has been revealed that besides the Assistance Fund, HYPE is also burned through network fees. Around 1.24 million HYPE has been burned through fees and slashing on HyperCore, the base layer of Hyperliquid. Another 376,060 HYPE has been burned as gas fees on HyperEVM, the smart contract layer of the network.
