📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Virginia scores 100 and Tennessee's AI sites use 9.9% of state power in a look at 10 of the 24 states TRG Datacenters ranked.

According to recent reports, on the edge of a small town, a local planning board weighs whether a developer can build a campus packed with servers. The vote will shape what nearby households pay for energy, how much pressure falls on local resources, and how many jobs the town gains. Big money rides on decisions of this kind. Research cited by GovTech projects that more than $600 billion will flow into AI infrastructure in 2026, and the spending is heading toward places few observers would have predicted. Established tech hubs make up one part of that picture.

Sources indicate that each upcoming facility hands its host community a two-sided bargain. Jobs and tax revenue arrive, and so does fresh demand on power systems, on watersheds, and on the rate structures behind every household's monthly utility bill. Loads of this size surface in utility commission filings ahead of any headlines. An upbeat press release leaves the tradeoff intact. TRG Datacenters frames the problem around location, arguing that the spot where a facility lands decides what it does to its surroundings. A state's capacity to absorb new sites depends on more than the number it hosts today. A crowded map highlights that a state arrived early, and a head start does not settle which state is best prepared.

Gadget Review examined the question through a TRG Datacenters ranking that scored 24 states on AI readiness and set the top performer at 100. The article ties readiness to clean grids, open land, and water security. Its counts cover AI data centers alone. The source does not publish the formula or weighting behind the scores, and it gives no reporting period for the counts or the consumption figures. Three states come with figures for the share of statewide electricity AI operations consume, a gap that limits any comparison of AI's burden across the full group. What follows covers the 10 highest-scoring states among the 24, in descending order.

Virginia hits a score of 100 with seven AI data centers, a count that trails Texas by six facilities. No state but Texas runs a larger AI fleet in this group of 10, and each of the remaining eight operates five or fewer. Virginia's seven sites match the combined count of Georgia, South Carolina, Mississippi, Fresh York, and Oregon. Virginia accounts for 18.4% of the 38 AI data centers across these 10 states. Texas holds close to twice Virginia's total yet scores 19.2 points lower. Facility volume cannot explain the top mark.

In a recent development, ohio, the runner-up, sits 11.8 points behind Virginia with five AI facilities. No other pair of consecutive entries on the list reveals a gap that wide. Ohio, in turn, clears Mississippi in seventh by 11.5 points. The fall from first to second outstrips the full spread across the next six states. Virginia's lead over Ohio makes up 43% of the 27.6-point distance between the first and 10th states in the selection.

Loudoun County, Virginia, goes by the nickname data center alley, and it earns the label. CNBC reports that the county holds the largest concentration of data centers anywhere in the world.

It has been revealed that the Energy Information Administration finds that the Dominion $D zone, the section of the PJM grid that includes Virginia, serves more data centers in one location than anywhere else in the world. The agency attributes most of that concentration to fiber optic connections, available land, and power infrastructure. Access to a compact fiber backbone and four undersea fiber cables helped lift Virginia into a leading position for data centers, according to a separate Energy Information Administration analysis.

Industry observers note that open land appears both in the agency's explanation and among the conditions this ranking rewards. Any state chasing Virginia's standing will need assets of that kind, since the Texas result shows that piling on facilities falls short.

In a recent development, ohio carries an 88.2 readiness score on five AI data centers, a mark no state besides Virginia exceeds. Texas hosts more than twice as many facilities yet trails by 7.4 points. The gap suggests Ohio's appeal lies in its ability to absorb newly introduced campuses, a quality its modest current footprint does not reveal.

Ohio beats New York, a coastal tech hub, by 11.6 points, 88.2 against 76.6. Indiana, the other Midwestern entry in this group, sits 15.8 points lower at 72.4. Geography alone cannot account for Ohio's position, because the Midwest produces both the second-highest and the lowest marks among these 10 states. Ohio's edge must come from conditions Indiana does not match.

Industry observers note that AEP Ohio has written a safeguard into its rules for data center customers. A campus that cancels its project or misses its contract terms owes the utility an exit fee. The provision keeps the cost of an abandoned commitment with the developer. It speaks to the rate-structure worry that follows these projects into every host community.

It has been revealed that the U.S. Department of Energy and the Department of Commerce unveiled a partnership with SoftBank and AEP Ohio to redevelop federal land, upgrade energy infrastructure, and build advanced computing capacity in southern Ohio. The plan targets land and power, two conditions the ranking ties to preparedness. AEP Ohio plays two roles in the state's story, setting terms for data center customers while joining a federal push to expand computing.

Jerome Township has imposed a moratorium on upcoming data centers, citing utility and safety concerns. The pause highlights one community drawing a line as developers and federal partners pursue projects elsewhere in Ohio. Alongside the exit fee, the moratorium reveals a state whose appeal comes with guardrails at both the utility and township levels. A high statewide rating offers no guarantee that every town will welcome the next proposal.

Tennessee's AI data centers consume 9.9% of all the electricity the state uses, the steepest share of any state with available figures. Three facilities generate that demand. Split three ways, each would claim about 3.3% of statewide consumption, a heavy burden for a single site. A load of that size leaves no room to treat any one of those campuses as a minor customer.

Tennessee's figure runs 1.8 percentage points above Indiana's, even though both states host three AI data centers. It also exceeds Mississippi's by 2 percentage points, and Mississippi operates one fewer facility. Matching facility counts in Tennessee and Indiana translate into different demands on each state's power supply. The share hinges on how much power each campus pulls and how much the state consumes overall, and a site tally captures neither.

Industry observers note that A readiness score of 83.7, third-best in this group of 10, accompanies Tennessee's hefty electricity draw. The state earned that mark with fewer AI sites than either of the two states ahead of it. Its score also beats Indiana's by 11.3 points, despite the identical facility count and Tennessee's larger slice of the grid. Texas operates 10 more AI data centers and still finishes 2.9 points behind. Heavy AI demand and strong preparedness coexist inside one state's borders. A high mark leaves open the question of whether the grid has slack to spare.

An xAI facility stands in an industrial park on the south side of Memphis, near factories and a gas-fired power plant the Tennessee Valley Authority runs. Some community members questioned whether the city's utilities could supply so much power to a customer such as xAI. Earlier ice storms and other extreme weather had pushed the Memphis grid into rolling blackouts, and those episodes fed the doubts. The Memphis debate shows residents asking, at the scale of one city, the question Tennessee's statewide load raises for the whole grid.

In a recent development, georgia earns an 81.8 readiness mark from a base of two AI data centers, the fourth-highest result in the ranking. It outscored 20 of the 24 states TRG Datacenters evaluated. South Carolina, Newly introduced York, and Oregon are the lone states in this group with fewer sites, each running one. Georgia sits in the upper half of the table on one of the leanest footprints among the 10.

In a recent development, every state above Georgia runs more AI data centers than it does, from Virginia's seven to Ohio's five and Tennessee's three. Across the first four rows, scores and site counts descend together. Georgia's two facilities fit that line, and the order holds until the next row.

Texas sits one point behind Georgia while running 13 facilities, six and a half times as many. The biggest buildout among these states could not lift Texas past a rival with a sliver of its hardware. Georgia's standing suggests the traits behind a strong score can take hold before a large wave of construction arrives.

It has been revealed that mississippi matches Georgia's two AI data centers yet finishes 5.1 points lower, at 76.7. Identical counts produced a wide gap between the two Southern states. The number of buildings explains little about where either state lands. Whatever separates the two lies beyond anything a site tally captures.

The source reports no share of statewide electricity for Georgia's AI sites. The strain its two facilities place on the state grid stays unmeasured, unlike the loads documented in Tennessee, Mississippi, and Indiana.

Recent findings suggest that georgia's 81.8 falls inside a 3.2-point band holding four states, from Tennessee's 83.7 down to South Carolina's 80.5. Georgia trails Tennessee by 1.9 points and stays 1.3 points clear of South Carolina, with Texas wedged between Georgia and South Carolina. Margins this thin mean a modest shift in any one state's conditions could reshuffle the middle of the order.

In a recent development, texas counts 13 AI data centers, the largest total among these 10 states, yet its score of 80.8 lands it in fifth place. Virginia finishes 19.2 points higher with seven facilities. Ohio, Tennessee, and Georgia each post a stronger result while operating five, three, and two sites. The four states above Texas run 17 AI data centers combined, four more than Texas by itself.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

MSCI has published the results of its November 2026 Index Review, with Strategy among the companies set to leave the MSCI USA Index.

Metaplanet, the Tokyo-listed Bitcoin treasury firm, is also scheduled for removal from the MSCI Japan Small Cap Index.

The changes will take effect after the market close on November 30, 2026.

Across the MSCI ACWI Index, 13 securities will be added and 100 deleted. The two additions to the MSCI World Index, measured by full organization market capitalization, are Moderna (USA) and Aritzia (Canada).

The latest review follows the upcoming rules proposed by MSCI in October, among which are new measures regarding crypto treasury holding companies.

MSCI evaluates whether a firm maintains substantial operating assets and applies five financial ratio tests.

A company that fails at least four criteria across consecutive annual reporting periods may face removal from the MSCI Global Investable Market Indexes.

MSCI indexes track public companies based on market cap and investment risks. Global mutual funds and ETFs use these benchmarks to build their portfolios.

Dropping out of such index could influence investment flows as well as stock prices.

Strategy continues to accumulate BTC despite the crypto market staying in red zone.

Between November 2 and November 8, 2026, the firm acquired another 1,036 BTC at an average price of $79,012.

In a recent development, as of November 12, Strategy holds 850,364 BTC. The firm also reported about $5.5 billion in USD reserves.

However, Bitcoin's recent decline below $75,000 pushes Strategy's holdings into an unrealized loss of $500 million.

Strategy's stock (MSTR) fell 7% on Thursday, while Bitcoin is down 3.5% at the time of writing.

Top digital assets like Bitcoin (BTC), XRP, Ethereum (ETH) and Shiba Inu (SHIB) are facing heavy selling pressure following a severe setback in the crypto market after the sudden exit of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang.

The unexpected exit of the Nvidia co-founder has created pandemonium in the financial world as shares of the artificial intelligence company have been hit by a heavy sell-off, further straining an already weak crypto market.

According to reports by Reuters, Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang resigned on Nov. 12. Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has taken over as interim chief executive.

There are controversies surrounding Huang's personal life and doubts about his future at the company he co-founded over three decades ago.

The news of Huang's exit has triggered a heavy sell-off in Nvidia stock, with shares dropping over 12% in early trading, wiping out an estimated $500 billion in market value.

The sell-off has also affected crypto-related trading markets.

As recently revealed by blockchain analytics platform Lookonchain, a trader known as 0x7368 had his leveraged long position in Nvidia stock fully liquidated.

According to Lookonchain, the trader had 9,959 units of Nvidia (NVDA), worth about $1.54 million, liquidated after news of Jensen Huang's resignation hit the market.

Meanwhile, the crypto market itself is reeling from heavy losses as some top altcoins are faring worse than Bitcoin.

The recent crypto market data shows that Bitcoin (BTC) is currently trading around $71,323, shedding about 3% in the last 24 hours.

Over the last seven days, the largest cryptocurrency by market cap has lost even more, shedding about 10.2%.

However, XRP has seen a more pronounced sell-off.

The Ripple-linked cryptocurrency at the moment trades at about $1.02 after losing 3.3% in the last 24 hours.

#6069. From entry to trophy: 10 steps in the Grammy voting process

From entry to trophy: 10 steps in the Grammy voting process

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 19 min read (3751 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~19 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • How Grammy voting works, step by step: the entry process, screening committees, nomination voting and final ballot that decide which recordings win the Recording Academy's awards.
  • Sources indicate that A Grammy is not decided in a single vote.
  • Understanding how Grammy voting works starts with that sequence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How Grammy voting works, step by step: the entry process, screening committees, nomination voting and final ballot that decide which recordings win the Recording Academy's awards.

Sources indicate that A Grammy is not decided in a single vote. Each award is the end of a sequence of stages run by the Recording Academy, the organization behind the Grammys, and carried out by its voting members. By the time a winner's name is read aloud, a recording has already passed through several checkpoints that happen out of public view.

Understanding how Grammy voting works starts with that sequence. A recording first has to be eligible. That means it must have come out within the release window the Academy sets for each awards year. It then has to be entered for consideration in a specific category. Screening committees review those entries to confirm that each one meets the rules and sits in the right place. Only after that do voting members weigh in.

Voting happens in rounds. In the nomination stage, members cast ballots on the entries that cleared screening, and those results determine the nominees. A final ballot follows, and members vote again to choose winners from those nominees. The ballots are counted confidentially, and the results stay sealed until the awards are confirmed.

It has been revealed that the details inside each stage have not stayed fixed. The Academy revises its rules from time to time. Past changes have affected how many nominees a category holds, how committees operate and which categories members may vote in. The process described here is one the Academy continues to adjust.

Those mechanics shape the public conversation around the awards. Arguments over snubs and category placement often turn on a specific stage. One question might be whether an album was placed in a particular genre field. Another might be how a list of nominees was formed. Knowing where each decision happens makes those debates easier to follow.

Recent findings suggest that the Grammys also differ from fan-voted awards. The people choosing nominees and winners are music professionals who belong to the Academy, not the listening public. Their ballots reflect the judgment of peers within the recording industry rather than the preferences of an audience.

According to recent reports, the 10 slides that follow walk through the process in order. They start with the Academy's role, who is eligible to vote and the release window. They then cover submission, screening, both voting rounds, the general field review committees and how winners are tabulated and revealed.

The Recording Academy organizes the Grammy Awards. Its voting members — not network executives, sponsors or the public — choose the winners, under rules the Academy writes and enforces.

According to recent reports, the organization's original name was the National Academy of Recording Arts and Sciences, often shortened to NARAS. Its founders came from the record business. They wanted an honor for achievement in recorded music, comparable to the Oscars in film.

In a recent development, the award takes its name from the gramophone. The trophy is a gilded gramophone statuette. It refers to the early record players that brought recorded sound into homes.

It has been revealed that the Academy is a nonprofit membership organization. Its members work in music as singers, instrumentalists, songwriters, producers and recording engineers. The Academy decides who qualifies for membership. Those standards shape who sits behind every ballot. The Academy is based in Santa Monica, California, and has regional chapters in cities across the U.S.

Sources indicate that the Grammys also have a sibling award. The Latin Grammy Awards are run by the Latin Recording Academy, a separate body. Its members vote on Latin music through their own process.

For the main Grammys, the Academy's core job is the rulebook. It decides which categories exist and which recordings qualify. It also defines what happens at each voting stage.

It has been revealed that those decisions rest with the Academy rather than the television broadcaster. When a category is added, merged or retired, the Academy makes the call. The same applies to changes in eligibility and voting procedures.

The Academy publishes its rules ahead of each awards cycle. That document is the reference point for entrants, screeners and voters alike.

According to recent reports, grammy winners are chosen by voting members of the Recording Academy, who are working creative professionals in recorded music. Fans and the listening public do not vote.

The voting membership is built around the people who make recordings. That group includes performers, singers, songwriters, composers, producers and recording engineers. It also includes contributors whose crafts have their own Grammy categories, such as arrangers, album package designers and the writers of album notes.

Membership is not automatic. An applicant has to show creative or technical credits on commercially released recordings. The Academy reviews that record of work before it grants voting status. Recommendations from current members also form part of the application. The requirement limits voting to people with direct experience making music. Members are organized through regional chapters in cities across the U.S.

Recent findings suggest that each vote belongs to an individual. A label, management firm or music publisher cannot cast a ballot on behalf of its roster. Someone employed by one of those businesses votes only after qualifying as a voting member in their own right. The Academy's voting guidelines also tell members to fill out their own ballots rather than let anyone else do it.

The Academy also offers a separate, non-voting membership for industry professionals. These are people whose work supports music-making without the creative credits voting requires. They can take part in Academy programs and events. They do not help choose nominees or winners.

In a recent development, voting members pay dues to keep their status. The Academy also expects them to stay active in the recording field. It periodically reviews whether members still qualify to vote. It has revised its membership requirements over the years.

A Grammy therefore reflects the judgment of fellow recording professionals. It is not calculated from sales, streaming totals, radio play or chart positions. The Academy instructs voters to judge entries on artistic and technical merit rather than commercial performance or popularity.

Each Grammy awards year covers a defined window of release dates, and the Recording Academy sets that window. A recording can compete only if it was released inside it. The calendar decides what can be entered before any member casts a vote.

Sources indicate that the eligibility period is the first filter in the process. An album released just after the cutoff is not rejected. It waits and becomes eligible for the following year's awards instead.

Sources indicate that the window has not followed the standard January-to-December calendar year. A recording released late in one calendar year can end up competing at a ceremony held well into the next year. Its rivals may include music released many months earlier.

According to recent reports, the date that counts is the commercial release. A recording generally has to reach the public through normal distribution, such as sales or streaming. Music shared privately, played only at live indicates or circulated as an unreleased demo does not establish eligibility on its own.

As a general rule, a recording is entered in only one awards year. It cannot come back in a later cycle just because it found a bigger audience after the cutoff. As a result, one release does not collect nominations at several ceremonies.

Timing also determines which competitors a project faces. Two albums released a few weeks apart can land in different awards years if the cutoff falls between them. Each one is then measured against a different pool of entries.

According to recent reports, the release window is separate from the question of category. Eligibility by date states only that a recording may be entered this year. Where it is entered, and whether that placement holds, is handled later in the process.

The Recording Academy publishes the exact window for each awards year in its official rules, and it has revised those rules over time. Checking whether a specific album qualifies means reading the rules for that year. The dates from a previous cycle may not match.

In a recent development, A recording reaches the Grammys only after someone enters it. Recording Academy members and registered media companies, such as record labels, submit eligible recordings to the Academy. They also name the specific categories where each one should compete.

That entry step comes before any member casts a vote. A release that is never submitted does not appear on a ballot, however widely it sold or streamed. The Academy does not scan the market for contenders on its own. The awards depend on entrants putting work forward.

In a recent development, entries are filed through the Academy's online submission system. The entrant supplies details about the recording, including the title, the performing artist, release information and the people credited on it. Those credits matter later. They help determine who receives an award if the recording wins.

The Academy publishes a rulebook for each awards year that spells out entry requirements. Entrants are expected to follow the version in force for the year they are filing. Rules that applied in one cycle may not apply in the next.

The main decision an entrant makes at this stage is the category. Grammy categories are grouped into fields. Most fields cover a genre, such as pop, rock, rap, country, jazz or classical. Others cover crafts such as production, engineering, packaging and music video. A separate general field holds the broad categories open across genres. These include Album of the Year, Record of the Year, Song of the Year and Best Latest Artist.

An entrant typically places a recording in the genre field that fits its style. It may also be entered in the general field. Academy rules limit how many categories a single recording may enter, and the Academy has revised those limits over time.

Correct placement shapes who judges the work. A jazz record entered in a pop category would face a different pool of voters than its makers intended. The category an entrant picks is a request, not a final placement.

Grammy screening committees review every entry before voting begins. Their job is to confirm that each recording is eligible and sits in the right category. They do not rate quality, and they do not decide who gets nominated.

Sources indicate that the committees are made up of Recording Academy members with expertise in the genres they review. A panel focused on one field listens to the entries submitted there and compares each one with that category's definition. The question in front of them is classification, not merit.

Eligibility comes first. A screener checks whether a recording meets the Academy's rules for the awards year, including when it was released and how it was distributed. An entry that fails those checks does not advance to the ballot.

In a recent development, placement is the second test. A label or member may enter an album in one genre, while the committee concludes it belongs in another. In that case, screeners can move the entry to the category that fits it better. They can also remove it from a category where it does not belong.

A placement decision determines the competition an entry faces. A recording moved out of one genre goes up against a different set of entries. It also goes before a different group of first-round voters.

Sources indicate that the outcome of screening shapes the first-round ballot. Members see only the entries that the committees have cleared and placed. A recording that never reached a ballot in its preferred category could not be nominated there.

Genre placement has drawn public disputes. Artists and labels have objected when committees reclassified their work. Those disputes often center on music that blends styles and does not fit a single category cleanly.

Industry observers note that the Academy revises its committee procedures and category definitions over time. As a result, the specific rules screeners apply can differ from one awards year to the next.

First-round voting is where Recording Academy voting members choose nominees from the pool of entries that cleared screening. Members do not vote in every category. They vote in the general field plus a limited number of other fields set by Academy rules.

The general field holds the awards that cut across all genres. Album of the Year, Record of the Year, Song of the Year and Best Newly introduced Artist sit there. Every voting member may cast first-round votes in those categories.

In a recent development, beyond the general field, members choose among the genre and craft fields. Those cover areas such as pop, rap, country, jazz and classical. The Academy caps how many of those fields a single member may vote in. It has revised that cap over the years, along with the rules on which categories count toward it.

The limit is meant to tie each vote to knowledge of the music. The Academy asks members to vote only in categories where they have expertise. A session musician who works mostly in jazz, for example, is expected to concentrate on jazz rather than spread votes across unfamiliar genres.

Recent findings suggest that members are also told to judge entries on artistic and technical merit. Sales, chart positions and streaming totals are not supposed to drive a ballot. A recording that sold modestly can still earn a nomination if voters in its field rate the work highly.

The first-round ballot lists only entries cleared by the screening committees. Each entry appears in the category where screeners placed it. A recording therefore competes only against other entries in that category, not against every submission across the awards.

According to recent reports, individual ballots stay private at this stage. The Academy does not publish how any member voted in the nomination round.

It has been revealed that this round turns a large pool of entries into a short list for each category. It does not pick winners. Those are decided later, on a separate final ballot.

Industry observers note that grammy nominees are the entries that receive the most votes from Recording Academy voting members in the first round. In most categories, the top vote-getters become the official nominees. Only those nominees move on to the final ballot.

A few specialized craft categories follow a different path. In those categories, Academy committees with relevant expertise select the nominees rather than the full first-round vote.

Sources indicate that the first round works as a filter, not as the contest for the trophy itself. An entry does not need to win its category at this stage. It needs to finish among the leaders in member votes for that category.

The Academy sets the cutoff. The cutoff is not a fixed formula that stays the same every year. The number of nominee slots in each category is a rule the Academy has revised over time. Each revision changes how many first-round finishers advance to the final ballot.

The cutoff applies separately in each category. When a recording is entered in more than one category, its votes are counted separately in each one. The same recording can earn a nomination in one category and miss the list in another.

Screening is already finished at this point. Each entry on the first-round ballot was checked for eligibility and placed in a category before members voted. The vote count decides which entries advance. Category placement was settled at the earlier screening stage.

The Academy does not publish first-round vote totals. The public sees which entries became nominees but not how close any other entry came.

In a recent development, most nominations attach to a recording or work in its category. Academy rules decide which credited contributors, such as artists, producers or songwriters, are named alongside it. Those credit rules vary by category.

In a recent development, eligibility is tied to the release window for a single awards year. An entry that misses the nominee list generally cannot be entered again in a later year.

The outcome of this step is the list of Grammy nominations. The Academy makes that list public before final-round voting begins. From then on, members choose among a small field of nominees rather than the full pool of entries.

It has been revealed that nomination review committees were small panels of Recording Academy members that once helped pick the Grammy nominees in the general field. Under that system, first-round vote totals did not set the shortlist on their own. The panels reviewed the leading entries and chose which ones advanced to the final ballot.

The general field is the group of awards open to recordings from every genre. It includes album of the year, record of the year, song of the year and best latest artist. Entries in those categories come from across the industry rather than from a single style of music.

Members still voted first under the committee system. Their ballots produced a ranking of entries in each general field category. A committee then examined a longer list of top vote-getters rather than treating that ranking as final. Its members chose the nominees from that list. Strong first-round support therefore did not guarantee a nomination.

Recent findings suggest that the Academy kept the names of committee members confidential. Neither the public nor the artists under review knew who sat on a given panel. The committees' role also extended beyond the general field. Panels operated in a number of genre categories as well.

That extra layer drew public criticism. Artists and commentators questioned why a small, anonymous group could override the result of a wider vote. Complaints centered on transparency. Outsiders could not see who made the choices or how a committee reached them.

According to recent reports, the Academy later changed how committees operate. It removed nomination review committees from most categories, including the general field. Under that change, nominees in those categories come from the votes of eligible members rather than from a panel's selection.

Committees did not disappear entirely. The Academy kept them for certain specialized craft categories, such as best recording package and best album notes. Those awards assess work like packaging design and liner notes rather than the music itself.

The shift moved more weight onto the nomination ballot itself. In the general field, the members' own votes decide which recordings reach the final round.

It has been revealed that the final ballot is the stage where Recording Academy voting members choose the Grammy winners. Members pick from the nominees that emerged from the nomination rounds, and in each category the nominee with the most votes wins.

Sources indicate that by this point the field is fixed. No new recordings can join the race, and entries that missed the nomination cut are out of contention. Every recording or artist on the ballot has already cleared screening and earned a nomination.

In a recent development, the final round asks members a narrower question than the first round did. During nominations, voters sorted through a large pool of entries. On the final ballot, they compare a short list of finalists within each category and select one.

It has been revealed that which categories a member can vote in follows Academy rules. The general field, which includes Album of the Year and Record of the Year, is open to voting members across genres. Those awards are not tied to any single style of music.

Sources indicate that genre categories work differently. The Academy limits how many genre fields each member may vote in on the final ballot. The Academy frames that limit as a way to keep genre voting tied to members' areas of expertise. The Academy has revised these limits over the years. The allowance for any member depends on the rules in force for that awards year.

Commercial performance does not enter the count. Sales figures, streaming totals and chart positions play no part in the final tally. The outcome in each category depends only on how voting members mark their ballots.

Each category on the ballot is a separate race. A recording can be nominated in several categories and win in some, all or none of them. That structure explains why one album can lead the nominations and still leave the ceremony with fewer awards than another.

Once members submit their final ballots, the votes move on to the counting stage.

Industry observers note that after final-round voting closes, the Recording Academy's ballots are counted confidentially. Each category's winner stays sealed until it is revealed at the Premiere Ceremony or the main televised Grammy ceremony.

The count is the last stage of a long sequence. By this point, recordings have been entered, screened, voted into nomination and placed on the final ballot. Tabulation turns those final-round ballots into a single result for each category.

According to recent reports, in each category, the winner is the nominee who receives the most votes from eligible voting members. The Academy does not publish vote totals or margins. Fans and artists learn who won, but not how close the race was.

Keeping results private preserves the reveal. Nominees attend without knowing the outcome in advance. Presenters open sealed envelopes on stage and read the winner's name aloud.

Most Grammy categories are not handed out during the main television broadcast. They are presented earlier the same day at the Premiere Ceremony, which the Academy streams online. A smaller group of high-profile awards, including the general field categories, is held for the main telecast.

This two-part format means every category receives a formal on-stage announcement. Only a fraction of the awards appear on the network broadcast.

A nominee does not need to be in the room to win. Results for absent winners are announced the same way. The Academy records the award whether or not anyone walks to the stage to accept it.

Recent findings suggest that each winner receives the Grammy statuette, a gilded gramophone. The trophy's shape reflects the award's name. The word Grammy comes from the gramophone, an early machine for playing recorded sound.

It has been revealed that after the ceremonies, the Academy publishes the complete list of winners on its official website, Grammy.com. That list becomes the permanent record for the awards year. When the next eligibility period opens, the cycle starts again with a upcoming round of entries from members and registered media companies.

Base Switches Off Flashblocks as Denim Goes Live: The Migration Risks Behind 200ms Blocks

📅 06 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1236 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nulltx

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second.
  • For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises.
  • Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Base's Denim upgrade replaced Flashblocks with five canonical blocks per second. What that means for sequencers, RPC providers and smart contract developers is where the real story sits.

For about sixteen months, Base's fastest blocks were only promises. Since November 5, they are the ledger itself.

Denim went live on Base mainnet on November 5, after activating on Sepolia on October 21.

Recent findings suggest that according to the upgrade page, the chain now produces five complete canonical blocks every second instead of one every two seconds. Flashblocks, the preconfirmation layer that ran alongside the two-second blocks since July 2025, is retired.

Most coverage stopped at the speed figure. The sharper question is what separates a canonical block from a preconfirmation, because that gap decides what breaks and what improves for anyone building on the chain.

It has been revealed that those updates were the sequencer's early word on what the next block would contain. They were previews of pending state, and nothing in them had its own hash, state root or receipts until the two-second block was sealed. Developers therefore had to keep an early execution result mentally separate from a settled transaction.

It has been revealed that denim turns the 200ms unit into the real thing. Under Base's 200ms Native Blocks specification, every block carries its own number, hash, state root, receipts and forkchoice updates, and moves through the unsafe, safe and finalized stages like any other block.

The sequencer's job gets heavier and stricter. Instead of streaming fragments of a larger block, it has to build and execute a full block for every 200ms slot. The header keeps its timestamp in whole seconds, so Denim adds a metadata transaction, the BaseTime deposit, placed second in every block. It supplies the sub-second portion: 0, 200, 400, 600 or 800 milliseconds.

Timing rules are tight. Slots can't be skipped, and each block's full timestamp must land exactly 200ms after its parent's. That timestamp comes from a schedule tied to the Denim activation and the block number, not from the sequencer's clock, so wall-clock time only determines when a build begins. Once execution finishes, the client rejects any block that breaks the 200ms progression.

According to recent reports, this removes a layer of ambiguity. A preconfirmation was only as strong as the sequencer's word, while a canonical block can be validated, replayed and challenged by any node running the same derivation rules.

In a recent development, app developers face the biggest practical shift. Flashblocks streams ended at activation, so anything built on newFlashblocks, pendingLogs or the pending block tag has to move to canonical subscriptions like newHeads and logs. The migration guide lists the API changes required.

The seconds-based timestamp field stays as it was for compatibility. Block, header, transaction, log and receipt responses now include optional millisecond fields, timestampMs and blockTimestampMs, derived from authenticated BaseTime data. They are left out when that data has been pruned or is unavailable. One tooling detail deserves attention: the spec warns that the plain Alloy AnyRpcHeader type drops unknown fields, so anyone who needs millisecond timestamps must use a different type.

In a recent development, node providers will see heavier traffic too. Dwellir's analysis notes that any service doing work on every block now does it ten times as often. Five fetches a second replace one every two seconds. Denim improves latency without adding capacity, so infrastructure bills are likely to climb.

Finality hasn't gone away either. Faster production doesn't erase the confirmation policy an application picks, and each 200ms block still passes through the same unsafe, safe and finalized stages. Bridges and exchanges that wait for a specific stage before crediting funds may need to rethink how many blocks they wait for, since a block count no longer equals the same stretch of time.

This is the area that deserves the most urgent attention. Base's spec warns that block.number now advances ten times faster in real time, while block.timestamp still ticks in whole seconds. A contract that treats a block count as a duration will see that duration collapse to a tenth of what its authors intended.

The affected patterns are common ones. Timelocks and cooldowns measured in blocks expire in a tenth of the time. Vesting and emission schedules run ten times faster. Per-block rate limits reset five times a second instead of once every two seconds, which lifts the effective per-second limit tenfold. Governance voting windows set in blocks shrink the same way. Uniswap V3-style TWAP oracles stay accurate, but a fixed observation cardinality now covers less wall-clock history, so long lookbacks can revert sooner.

In a recent development, contracts built on block.timestamp are unaffected. Where a block count can be adjusted through governance, teams proposal to divide it by ten. Where it is hardcoded into an immutable contract, the spec notes it can't be retuned after activation, which leaves migration as the only fix. Denim also tightens transfer rules for Base's B20 token standard, and transfers to a token's own address now revert.

According to recent reports, the coming weeks will show how much of this stays theoretical. Three things are worth tracking: whether any immutable contract with block-count logic misbehaves, how providers cope with the jump in per-block requests, and whether apps built around Flashblocks have fully moved over.

Denim looks like a cleaner design than the layer it replaced. A preview mechanism gives way to a block anyone can verify, and developers pay for it with a real migration. Speed grabbed the headlines, but the lasting change is that Base's sub-second confirmations now stand on the same footing as the chain's ordinary blocks.

#6067. Who was James Bond based on? 10 spies tied to Ian Fleming's wartime world

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 20m • 📚 Deep Dive (3949 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Qz ↗ Open Full Page

Who was James Bond based on? 10 spies tied to Ian Fleming's wartime world

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 20 min read (3949 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Qz

⏱️ ~20 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • These 10 real spies linked to James Bond by memoirs, biographers or popular tradition range from a Yugoslav double agent to the gadget maker named as Q.
  • Sources indicate that james Bond came out of a war, not out of a single man.
  • Sources indicate that fleming served in the Naval Intelligence Division (NID) of the British Admiralty.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

These 10 real spies linked to James Bond by memoirs, biographers or popular tradition range from a Yugoslav double agent to the gadget maker named as Q.

Sources indicate that james Bond came out of a war, not out of a single man. Before Ian Fleming wrote fiction, he spent World War II inside British naval intelligence. That job put him close to the agents, operations and planners of a secret war.

Sources indicate that fleming served in the Naval Intelligence Division (NID) of the British Admiralty. He worked as personal assistant to its director, John Godfrey, and held the rank of commander in the Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve. The post gave him a view of how intelligence was gathered, protected and used. His first Bond novel, Casino Royale, appeared in 1953.

According to recent reports, fleming never named one model for 007. Bond is a fictional composite. The question of who he was based on has no single answer. What exists is a long list of candidates. Some names come from memoirs written by the spies themselves. Others come from biographers who have made a case in print. A few rest on long-standing popular claims.

Industry observers note that those sources carry different weight. A double agent's own account of crossing paths with Fleming is not the same as a documented encounter. A biographer's argument is not the same as a statement from Fleming. A superior Fleming served directly also has a different kind of claim from someone whose reputation simply matched the character.

The 10 figures below are a selection of real spies who inspired James Bond, according to the memoirists, biographers and traditions that make each link. They are not a ranking or a complete list. They include an agent born in the Russian Empire whose legend predates World War II, plus a Yugoslav double agent. An MI6 station chief in Paris and a Scottish diplomat who served in the SAS also appear. So do a Warsaw-born SOE agent, an American-born operative codenamed Cynthia and a Canadian spymaster in New York. The last three are an MI5 spymaster, a maker of concealed gadgets and the naval intelligence chief Fleming served.

It has been revealed that each slide sets out what the person did and who connects them to Bond. Where a link is unproven or contested, the slide says so. The aim is to separate documented careers from the legends that grew up around the character.

Sidney Reilly was a British agent born in the Russian Empire. His "Ace of Spies" reputation is often linked to James Bond. That connection rests on legend, not on any confirmed statement by Ian Fleming.

Industry observers note that reilly's best-known operation took place in Moscow in 1918. He took part in the so-called Lockhart plot, a scheme by Allied agents and diplomats against the fresh Bolshevik government. The plot took its name from Robert Bruce Lockhart, Britain's envoy to the Bolsheviks at the time. The plotters tried to win over the Latvian riflemen who guarded the Kremlin.

According to recent reports, the scheme fell apart in late summer 1918. On Aug. 30 of that year, Lenin was shot and wounded in Moscow. The Cheka, the Bolshevik secret police, then debuted the crackdown known as the Red Terror. Lockhart was arrested and later exchanged for the Soviet diplomat Maxim Litvinov. Reilly escaped Russia. A Soviet tribunal later sentenced him to death in absentia.

Reilly did not stay away for good. Soviet authorities say he was shot in 1925 after being lured back into the USSR. The lure is associated with Operation Trust, a deception run by the OGPU, the Cheka's successor agency. Trust posed as an anti-Bolshevik underground network. It drew émigrés and foreign intelligence contacts across the border. Reilly crossed from Finland in 1925 and never came back.

According to recent reports, his fame grew after his disappearance. In 1967, Robin Bruce Lockhart, the son of the 1918 envoy, published a book titled Ace of Spies. In 1983, the British television series Reilly, Ace of Spies, starring Sam Neill, brought the nickname to a wider audience. Both works presented him as a daring operative working against a hostile regime.

Many accounts of Reilly's early life and career contradict one another. The portion that can be stated with confidence is narrower. It covers the 1918 plot, his escape from Russia and his disappearance in 1925.

Reilly's name appears often among possible models for Bond. The comparison rests on his record as a British agent who worked against the Soviet state. Bond's chief enemy in the early novels was SMERSH, a Soviet counterintelligence organization. The resemblance is one of reputation rather than documented influence.

Dusko Popov was a Yugoslav lawyer who worked as a double agent for the British during World War II, under the MI5 codename Tricycle. His own memoir places Ian Fleming at a casino in Estoril, Portugal, watching Popov gamble.

Sources indicate that german military intelligence, the Abwehr, recruited Popov as an agent. He reported the approach to the British and agreed to work for them. MI5 then ran him as part of the Double Cross System. That operation turned German agents into channels for false information.

According to recent reports, A body known as the Twenty Committee oversaw the system. Its chairman, J.C. Masterman, later described the program in The Double-Cross System in the War of 1939 to 1945, published in 1972. Popov's reports to his German handlers were shaped by his British controllers.

In a recent development, in 1941 the Germans sent Popov to the U.S. He carried a questionnaire listing the information his handlers wanted him to gather. Some of its questions concerned Pearl Harbor, the U.S. naval base in Hawaii.

Part of that questionnaire was hidden in microdots. These were photographs shrunk to roughly the size of a printed period. Popov passed the material to the FBI. Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on Dec. 7, 1941, months after his arrival.

Popov's memoir, Spy/Counterspy, appeared in 1974. Estoril sits on the coast west of Lisbon. Portugal was neutral during the war, and the Lisbon area drew agents from both sides.

In a recent development, no independent record confirms Popov's account of Fleming at the casino. The story comes from Popov alone. He published it decades after the war, by which time Bond was already a film franchise.

Sources indicate that casino Royale, Fleming's first Bond novel, builds its central set piece around a high-stakes game of baccarat. Popov's Estoril story also unfolds at a casino table. The link between Popov and Bond rests on that parallel and on Popov's own word.

His wartime record stands apart from the casino story. Popov's work for MI5 belongs to the documented history of the Double Cross System, whether or not Fleming ever saw him play.

Sources indicate that wilfred "Biffy" Dunderdale ran the MI6 station in Paris in the years before World War II and into its early stages. A long-standing claim links him to James Bond, but no document demonstrates that Ian Fleming used him as a model.

Industry observers note that his best-documented role involves the Enigma cipher machine. Germany's armed forces used Enigma to encrypt military messages. Reading that traffic became a central goal for Allied codebreakers.

Poland got there first. Mathematicians at the Polish cipher bureau, including Marian Rejewski, began reading Enigma messages in the early 1930s. Their work also let them build replica machines.

In July 1939, weeks before Germany invaded Poland, the Polish cipher bureau shared that work with its allies. The meeting took place at Pyry, in a forest south of Warsaw. Alastair Denniston and Dilly Knox attended for Britain, and Gustave Bertrand led the French side. The Poles agreed to supply each ally with a replica Enigma machine. Dunderdale is credited with helping get the British machine to London.

Recent findings suggest that that delivery mattered for what followed. British codebreakers at Bletchley Park built on the Polish breakthrough throughout the war. Their decrypts, given the code name Ultra, went to Allied commanders and political leaders.

Sources indicate that dunderdale's post placed him where this exchange came together. The Paris station worked closely with French military intelligence. The French had their own long-running cooperation with the Polish codebreakers.

Sources indicate that the German occupation of Paris in June 1940 ended that arrangement in its prewar form. British intelligence could no longer run a station in the French capital.

The Bond connection draws on a different side of his record. Dunderdale had a reputation for polished dress and a stylish manner. That image, rather than any statement by Fleming, is what the claim rests on.

The link remains tradition rather than documented fact. Fleming described Bond as a compound of the secret agents and commando types he met during the war. Dunderdale is one of several intelligence officers whose names have been attached to that description over the years.

Fitzroy Maclean was a Scottish diplomat who became a soldier, served with the SAS in North Africa and led a British mission to Tito's partisans in Yugoslavia. He is often named as an inspiration for James Bond, but no statement from Ian Fleming confirming that link has been verified.

Maclean was born in 1911 and joined the Foreign Office as a young man. A posting to the British embassy in Moscow in the late 1930s placed him in the Soviet capital during Stalin's purges. He attended the 1938 show trial of Nikolai Bukharin. He also made long journeys into Soviet Central Asia, including regions closed to foreigners.

Industry observers note that when war came, the Foreign Office would not release him for military service. Maclean found a way around the rule by standing for Parliament. He won the seat of Lancaster as a Conservative in 1941. Leaving the diplomatic service freed him to enlist, and he joined the Cameron Highlanders as a private.

Industry observers note that in North Africa he joined the early SAS under David Stirling. He took part in a 1942 raid on the port of Benghazi, deep behind enemy lines. He was later sent to Persia, where he seized General Fazlollah Zahedi, a senior officer suspected of working with the Germans.

In 1943, Winston Churchill sent Maclean to Yugoslavia to work with Josip Broz Tito's partisans. He parachuted in as head of the British liaison mission, holding the rank of brigadier. His reports fed into Britain's decision to back Tito rather than the rival Chetnik movement of Draža Mihailović.

Maclean told the story of these years in his memoir Eastern Approaches, published in 1949. The book moves in three parts from the Soviet Union to the desert war and then to Yugoslavia.

According to recent reports, people who make the Bond comparison point to that mix of diplomatic polish, travel through closed territory and raids behind the lines. The idea has circulated for decades as a popular claim rather than a documented one.

Recent findings suggest that after the war Maclean stayed in the House of Commons. He held Lancaster until 1959, then represented Bute and Northern Ayrshire until 1974. He died in 1996.

According to recent reports, christine Granville, born Krystyna Skarbek in Warsaw in 1908, worked for Britain's Special Operations Executive in World War II. She is often suggested as a model for Vesper Lynd in Ian Fleming's Casino Royale, but that link has never been proven.

It has been revealed that the Special Operations Executive, usually shortened to SOE, was a British wartime organization formed in 1940. Its job was sabotage and support for resistance movements in occupied Europe. It ran separately from MI6, Britain's foreign intelligence service. Its agents worked behind enemy lines under false identities.

It has been revealed that skarbek served the British under the name Christine Granville, which is the name most English-language accounts use for her. Early in the war she worked as a courier into occupied Poland. Her routes included crossings of the Tatra Mountains on skis.

In a recent development, in 1944 she parachuted into southern France. The drop put her inside German-occupied territory, alongside SOE networks already working there.

Her best-known act came in August 1944 in Digne, in what is now the Alpes-de-Haute-Provence department. The Gestapo was holding three captured men there. Two were Francis Cammaerts, who led an SOE network in southeastern France, and Xan Fielding, a British officer who had earlier served with SOE in Crete.

Granville helped free all three. She negotiated with an official connected to their captors and offered a large bribe. She also warned that Allied forces landing in Provence would hold him responsible for the prisoners' fate.

In a recent development, britain later awarded her the George Medal and appointed her an OBE. France gave her the Croix de Guerre.

Granville survived the war. In June 1952 she was stabbed to death in a London hotel. Her killer, Dennis Muldowney, had become fixated on her. He was hanged later that year.

In the novel, Vesper Lynd is assigned to help Bond in his mission to beat Le Chiffre, an agent working for the Soviets, at the baccarat table. Bond falls for her. She is later revealed to have been working for the Soviets herself, and she takes her own life.

No documented statement from Fleming confirms that Granville inspired Vesper. The link remains a popular suggestion rather than an established fact.

Sources indicate that betty Pack, born Amy Elizabeth Thorpe in Minneapolis, worked for British Security Coordination in the U.S. under the codename Cynthia. In 1941 she helped British intelligence obtain naval cipher material from the Vichy French embassy in Washington, D.C.

Pack was born in 1910. She was American by birth but entered the world of British diplomacy through marriage. Her husband, Arthur Pack, was a British diplomat. His postings took her abroad in the 1930s, including to Spain and Poland. They gave her access to embassy circles in several capitals.

Industry observers note that british Security Coordination, known as BSC, was a British intelligence organization based in New York during World War II. It ran operations across the U.S. while the country was still neutral. Pack's work in Washington fell under that organization.

The Vichy French embassy was a wartime target. The Vichy government collaborated with Germany after the French defeat in 1940. Its diplomats in Washington held material used for French naval communications. Naval cipher material could give British codebreakers a way into those communications.

Pack's route into the embassy ran through Charles Brousse, a press attaché there. She built a close relationship with him. The cipher material was then copied by British intelligence. Pack and Brousse married after the war.

Sources indicate that her methods explain why her name comes up in discussions of Bond. Her approach to gathering information is often compared to the seduction that runs through Ian Fleming's novels. Bond regularly wins over women connected to his targets. Pack's career is sometimes cited as a real-world version of that pattern, with a woman as the agent.

That comparison rests on resemblance, not documented influence. No verified link between Pack and Fleming has been established. Fleming did not name her as a source for his fiction. There is no confirmed record of the two working together. She appears in discussions of Bond's origins because her story fits the pattern of his missions. Fleming never remarked he drew on it.

Industry observers note that william Stephenson, a Canadian from Winnipeg, headed British Security Coordination in Newly introduced York from 1940. He is often named among the real-life sources for James Bond. That link rests partly on Stephenson's own claims, and it remains contested.

According to recent reports, british Security Coordination, usually shortened to BSC, was Britain's main intelligence organization in the U.S. during World War II. It worked to protect British interests in a country that had not yet entered the war. Stephenson ran it from offices in Rockefeller Center in Manhattan. Its work covered intelligence, security and propaganda across the Americas.

According to recent reports, stephenson came to the post from outside the usual civil service path. He flew as a fighter pilot in World War I. Between the wars he built a business career in Britain. That background gave him contacts in industry and government on both sides of the Atlantic.

His connection to the Bond story runs through Ian Fleming's 1941 visit to the U.S. On that trip Fleming met William Donovan, a Upcoming York lawyer who later led the Office of Strategic Services. The OSS was the American wartime intelligence agency and a forerunner of the CIA. Fleming wrote a memo for Donovan on how an intelligence service might be organized. Stephenson was a close British ally of Donovan in this period.

The popular image of Stephenson owes much to A Man Called Intrepid, a 1976 book by the journalist William Stevenson. The two men's similar names often cause confusion. The book cast Stephenson as a master of wartime intrigue. It also made "Intrepid" the name popularly attached to him. Many of the book's claims have since been challenged.

Part of the Bond story comes from Stephenson's own accounts of his career. Not all of those accounts have held up. His place among Bond's inspirations is a claim, not a settled fact.

The documented record is narrower. Fleming's 1941 trip came while BSC was operating in a still-neutral U.S. Stephenson was knighted for his wartime service. He died in Bermuda in 1989.

Maxwell Knight ran MI5's agent-running section and placed informants inside Britain's Fascist and Communist groups. Biographer Henry Hemming argues that Knight was a model for M, Bond's boss in Ian Fleming's novels.

Hemming makes that case in his 2017 biography, M: Maxwell Knight, MI5's Greatest Spymaster. Knight was born in 1900 and died in 1968. His section was known inside MI5 as B5(b).

B5(b) recruited people with no intelligence background and placed them inside political organizations. Many stayed in place for years. They reported on members, meetings and outside contacts.

According to recent reports, olga Gray was one of his best-known agents. On Knight's instructions, she joined the Communist Party of Great Britain and gained the trust of its officials. Her reporting helped expose a ring passing secrets from the Woolwich Arsenal. Percy Glading, a Communist Party organizer, was convicted in 1938 as part of that case.

Industry observers note that knight's section also watched the far right. Joan Miller, another of his agents, got inside the Right Club. That pro-Nazi group was founded by the Scottish Unionist MP Archibald Ramsay. Her work fed into the 1940 case against Tyler Kent and Anna Wolkoff. Kent was an American cipher clerk at the U.S. embassy in London. He had copied embassy documents, including correspondence between Winston Churchill and Franklin Roosevelt. Both he and Wolkoff were convicted.

Sources indicate that hemming's case for the M link draws partly on a name. Within MI5, Knight went by the initial M, according to Hemming. The argument also rests on his role as a quiet chief who directed agents from a distance.

Knight had a second public life. He broadcast on natural history for the BBC. He also wrote books about animals and published two crime novels in the 1930s. Those novels were Crime Cargo, published in 1934, and Gunmen's Holiday, published in 1935.

The Knight link to M remains Hemming's interpretation. No verified statement from Fleming confirms that he based M on Knight.

Charles Fraser-Smith made concealed escape and evasion gadgets for the British Ministry of Supply during World War II, including compasses hidden inside ordinary objects. He is commonly named as a real-world model for Q, the equipment specialist in the James Bond stories.

Industry observers note that escape and evasion equipment had a narrow purpose. It was meant to help people stranded behind enemy lines avoid capture or get out of captivity. A compass was a core item in that kit. It let someone on the run hold a direction across unfamiliar country without asking anyone for help.

Recent findings suggest that concealment was central to the work. A compass discovered during a search would simply be taken away. Fraser-Smith's job was to hide such tools inside items that a soldier, airman or agent might plausibly be carrying anyway.

Industry observers note that he described his wartime work in a memoir, The Secret War of Charles Fraser-Smith, published in 1981. The book appeared decades after the war ended. By then, Bond had been a film franchise for nearly two decades.

In a recent development, the link to Q rests on resemblance rather than on any documented statement. Fleming is not on record confirming that Fraser-Smith was the model for the character. The comparison comes from the overlap between a man who built concealed devices and a fictional officer who supplies Bond with them.

Fleming's own novels handle the role differently from the films. In Dr. No, published in 1958, M calls in the Armourer, Major Boothroyd, to replace Bond's Beretta with a Walther PPK. Fleming took that name from Geoffrey Boothroyd, a firearms enthusiast who had written to him criticizing Bond's choice of pistol.

The gadget-heavy Q that most audiences know came largely from the screen. Desmond Llewelyn played the character in films from From Russia with Love in 1963 to The World Is Not Enough in 1999. That version, with its trick briefcases and modified cars, is the one usually set beside Fraser-Smith's wartime inventions.

John Godfrey served as Director of Naval Intelligence at the British Admiralty from 1939 to 1942, with Ian Fleming as his personal assistant. He is often cited as a model for M, the head of the Secret Service in the Bond novels. His claim rests on Fleming's direct service under him.

Godfrey was a career Royal Navy officer. Fleming came to the Admiralty from the City of London, where he had worked in finance. Godfrey recruited him in 1939. The assistant's post gave Fleming a wide view of the division's work, from deception planning to special operations.

Sources indicate that one early product of that partnership was the Trout memo. It was a 1939 paper on deceiving the enemy that went out under Godfrey's name. It is widely attributed to Fleming. The memo compared deception to fly fishing and listed dozens of ideas for misleading German forces. One idea, planting false papers on a corpse, foreshadowed the 1943 deception known as Operation Mincemeat.

Industry observers note that in 1941 Fleming worked on Operation Goldeneye. It was a contingency proposal to keep British intelligence and sabotage work going in Spain. It would have been used if Germany invaded the Iberian Peninsula or Spain joined the Axis. The invasion never came, and the plan was not put into action. Fleming later gave the same name to his house in Jamaica, where he wrote the Bond novels.

Fleming also helped form 30 Assault Unit. It was a commando force whose job was to seize enemy documents, codes and equipment before they could be destroyed. Its teams moved with or ahead of advancing Allied troops. Fleming oversaw the unit largely from London rather than serving in the field.

Godfrey left the intelligence post in 1942 and was succeeded by Edmund Rushbrooke. Godfrey went on to command the Royal Indian Navy. Fleming stayed at the Naval Intelligence Division through the rest of the war.

In a recent development, the Godfrey link does not rest on a memoir or on one biographer's argument, as some other claimed models do. It rests on the years Fleming spent answering to him. Bond's M remains a fictional character, and Godfrey is one of several real figures tied to the role.

Yoshitaka Kitao, head of Japanese financial group SBI Holdings, answered "YES" when asked point-blank whether he still trusts XRP.

Recent findings suggest that the question came from an X user. The user wrote that the past few weeks had been "truly exhausting" for XRP holders, and said that token holders feel that Ripple has left them behind.

Industry observers note that kitao answered in English. Most of his recent posts on X are in Japanese, and the rest of them are reposts of other accounts.

Kitao previously worked as an executive at Nomura Securities and later served as CFO of SoftBank. In 1999, he founded SoftBank Investment, which later became SBI Holdings. Today, SBI includes banks, brokerage, and insurance businesses, as well as crypto services.

In a recent development, the partnership began in 2016. SBI joined Ripple's Series B round and released a joint venture with Ripple, SBI Ripple Asia. SBI owns about 60% of the venture, and Ripple owns the remaining 40%.

The same year, SBI Ripple Asia set up a consortium of Japanese banks to test Ripple's technology for payments, and the consortium later grew to more than 60 banks.

Sources indicate that in 2018, SBI launched the interbank app MoneyTap. The same year, SBI's crypto exchange, now called SBI VC Trade, started operations with XRP trading. In 2019, Kitao joined Ripple's board of directors.

From 2020, SBI began handing the token out to shareholders as bonuses, and the payment service SBI Remit released remittances using it with on-demand liquidity (ODL), including in the major Japan-Philippines corridor.

SBI kept working with Ripple during the SEC lawsuit against the company, which lasted from December 2020 until 2025.

It has been revealed that back on February 15, 2026, in rare long-form tweets in English, Kitao denied rumors that SBI holds $10 billion worth of XRP: "Not $10 billion in XRP, but around 9% of Ripple Labs. So our hidden asset could be much bigger." By his account, the combined valuation of Ripple Labs and its ecosystem is "enormous," and SBI owns more than 9% of all of it.

Kitao also talked about XRP at SBI's quarterly briefing on November 2, 2026. He stated that investors buy Bitcoin mostly to hold it, and that the value of XRP depends on its use in payments and business ecosystems.

According to recent reports, in August 2025, SBI VC Trade and Ripple agreed to bring the RLUSD stablecoin to Japan. In October 2025, SBI also invested $200 million in Evernorth, a company that holds XRP in its treasury. By now, SBI VC Trade has more than two million accounts.

At press time, XRP is trading at $1.02.

Your competitors may not have hired another employee. They may have built one.

Sources indicate that entrepreneurs are creating custom AI agents to help with marketing, video editing, reporting and scriptwriting while they focus on running their businesses. If you’re still figuring out what an AI agent even does, that can feel intimidating. The good news: It’s not too late to learn. In this video, I break down where to start, what separates an agent from another chatbot and why your first assignment matters more than you might think.

The shift is already underway. In a 2026 G2 survey of 1,019 B2B decision-makers, 66% said their organizations had AI agents running in limited or scaled production. That’s a survey of business software decision-makers, not a measure of every small business. But it’s a sign that agents are moving beyond experiments and into real workflows.

The question for entrepreneurs is where they fit into yours.

It has been revealed that think about everything that happens between an idea and a result. A marketing campaign needs research, a script, content, editing, distribution and a review of what worked. A report needs information gathered and checked before you can make a decision. Each task might seem manageable on its own, but together they can consume the time you wanted to spend growing the business.

AI agents could help take on parts of that work. But giving an agent a job doesn’t automatically mean it will do the right job, understand your standards or know when to ask for your input. That’s where the opportunity and the risk meet.

Industry observers note that if you’ve seen my earlier video on ChatGPT’s dots and seven ways entrepreneurs can use them, you’ve already seen how accessible these tools are becoming. The next question is how to turn that access into useful support for your business.

Recent findings suggest that in this video, I share an example from my own work and explore how to identify a worthwhile first job for an agent, without trying to automate your entire business at once. You’ll also see why moving too promptly can create a latest bottleneck instead of removing one.

You don’t have to master every AI tool today. But as your competitors learn to build teams that can help them move faster, the work you choose to hand off first could make all the difference.

The free AI Success Kit, available to download for a limited time, comes with a free chapter from my new book, The Wolf is at The Door – How to Survive and Thrive in an AI-Driven World.
